Glidex

Introduction

Glidex is a control plane for KVM virtual machines. It runs VMs on Cloud Hypervisor (the default), QEMU or Pylon, a Cloud Hypervisor fork for elastic VMs, and you drive it from a web UI, the gxctl CLI, or its REST and RPC APIs. It runs on a single Linux host, or on many hosts joined into one cluster.

Features

  • Three hypervisors, one feature set. Cloud Hypervisor, QEMU and Pylon all boot distribution cloud images through UEFI firmware, or a kernel directly, take networks, disks and PCI (VFIO) devices, and support pause, resume and graceful shutdown.
  • Elastic CPU. A VM can have a range of vCPUs and a CPU weight. On Pylon the host parks idle vCPUs in microseconds; on Cloud Hypervisor and QEMU you change a running VM’s vCPUs within the range.
  • Images and disks. Pull checksum-verified cloud images (Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, AlmaLinux) from a built-in catalog, or any image from an HTTPS URL. Each VM gets a thin root disk linked to its image, grown together with its root partition.
  • Datastores. Keep disks on each node’s own disk, on a shared filesystem (NFS, CephFS), in LVM-thin pools, or in a hyperstor cluster, and move them between datastores.
  • GPUs and host resources. Pass through GPUs and other PCI devices, by address or from device pools shared out to projects, with NUMA placement, dedicated CPUs and hugepages.
  • Guest logins. Store a username with a password and/or SSH keys once, and pick it when you create a VM. Glidex puts it into a cloud-init seed it generates for the VM.
  • Networking. NAT networks with DHCP, isolated networks, and bridged networks on the host’s own LAN, built on Open vSwitch. Uplinks can use the kernel, AF_XDP or DPDK; VM ports are tap or vhost-user.
  • Console. Each VM’s serial console in the browser or in gxctl, shared by any number of clients and logged to disk.
  • Projects and access control. Projects with members and quotas, roles and teams, tenants and directories, API tokens, login with local accounts (PAM), single sign-on (OIDC, Google, JumpCloud) or passkeys, invitations, Cedar policies, and an audit log.
  • Workload identity. Software in a VM gets short-lived identity tokens, and can act as a service account, from the VM’s metadata endpoint, with no secret stored in the guest.
  • Usage. Metered CPU, memory, disk and network use, per project, VM, disk or network, by hour, day or billing month.
  • Clustering. Many hosts act as one. Servers keep the cluster’s state in a replicated store; agents only run VMs. Nodes join with a one-time token over mutual TLS, a scheduler places VMs and explains its choice, and nodes can be drained, removed and rejoined. Every node serves the web UI.
  • Cluster networks. With OVN, networks span every node, NAT traffic leaves through shared gateway nodes, and projects can have their own routers.

How these docs are organized

  • Quick start: install Glidex on one host and boot your first VM.
  • Concepts: the objects Glidex manages and the words these docs use for them.
  • User guide: everyday work with VMs, images, disks, credentials, networks, projects, the console and usage.
  • Operator guide: installing, configuring, securing and running hosts and clusters.
  • Developer guide: the architecture, design decisions, algorithms and performance figures, for contributors.
  • gxctl reference: the CLI’s commands.
  • API reference: the REST and RPC APIs.

If you use VMs on a Glidex host someone else runs, start with Logging in. If you are setting up a host, start with the Quick start.

Quick start

This page takes one Linux host from nothing to a running VM: install Glidex, log in, create a NAT network, pull a cloud image, add a login for the guest, then create, start, use and stop a VM. Each step shows gxctl and, where it helps, the web UI.

For more choices at any step, see the User guide and the Operator guide.

Requirements

  • Linux on x86_64 or aarch64, with KVM enabled (/dev/kvm exists).
  • A package manager the installer knows: apt-get, dnf/yum or pacman.
  • An account with sudo rights. The installer asks for your sudo password, and nothing else unless the host is on a Tailscale tailnet (see step 3).
  • git, and a Rust toolchain to run the installer from source (for example from rustup.rs). The installer then installs or updates everything else, including Rust itself.
  • Internet access, to download packages, the hypervisors and images.

Check KVM first:

ls -l /dev/kvm

If it’s missing, enable virtualization in the firmware settings and load the module (sudo modprobe kvm_intel or sudo modprobe kvm_amd).

1. Install

git clone https://github.com/CMKL-APEX/glidex.git && cd glidex
cargo run -p glidex-install

The installer installs what is missing and updates what is outdated: system packages, Cloud Hypervisor and its UEFI firmware, QEMU with OVMF, Open vSwitch for VM networking, and the Glidex binaries and web UI. It sets up these systemd services:

  • glidex-control-plane: the API, running as the glidex system user.
  • glidex-ui: the web UI, running as glidex-ui.
  • glidex-authd: checks local account passwords (PAM) for the web UI.

It also sets up helper services the control plane uses: glidex-netd (host networking), glidex-stord (LVM-thin volumes) and glidex-metad (the metadata endpoint VMs reach).

When it finishes, it prints a summary like this:

glidex runs as systemd services (control plane as 'glidex', web UI as 'glidex-ui'):
     web UI:  https://host.example.org:5173
     API:     /run/glidex-cp/api.sock (members of glidex-users), https://host.example.org:8841 (tokens)
     web UI certificate SHA-256: 3A:7F:…:C2
     API certificate SHA-256: 91:0B:…:5E

Keep the two certificate fingerprints: you check them in step 3. The installer doesn’t open any firewall ports; if you’ll use the web UI from another machine, allow TCP 5173 (and 8841 for the API) yourself.

Re-run cargo run -p glidex-install at any time to update. See Installation for its options.

2. Log out and back in

The installer adds you to two groups:

  • glidex-users: lets you use gxctl on this host and log in to the web UI with your account’s password.
  • glidex-admin: makes you an administrator of this Glidex host, and owner of its default project.

Group changes apply to new logins only, so log out and back in (or reconnect your SSH session). Then check:

id -nG            # lists glidex-users and glidex-admin
gxctl whoami

On the host, gxctl talks to the control plane over its Unix socket (/run/glidex-cp/api.sock) and identifies you by your Unix account: there is no separate login.

gxctl with no arguments starts an interactive shell (gxctl>, with Tab completion and help). With arguments it runs one command and exits. This page uses the one-command form; inside the shell, type the same words without gxctl.

3. Open the web UI

Print its address:

gxctl ui

Open https://<host>:5173 in a browser. Unless an administrator configured a certificate, the UI uses a self-signed one, so the browser warns you. Before you accept the warning, open the certificate details in the browser and compare its SHA-256 fingerprint with the web UI certificate SHA-256 line the installer printed. Accept only if they match.

If you no longer have the installer’s output, print the fingerprint on the host:

sudo openssl x509 -in /var/lib/glidex-ui/tls/ui.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256

On a host on a Tailscale tailnet with HTTPS certificates, the installer asks once whether the web UI should serve the node’s Tailscale certificate (--tailscale-cert turns it on without asking). With it on, open the https://<node>.<tailnet>.ts.net:5173 address the installer printed: browsers trust that certificate, so there is no warning and no fingerprint to compare. Other names and addresses keep the self-signed certificate. See Tailscale certificates.

Sign in with your Unix username and password. The header shows the pages you can use (VMs, Images, Disks, Credentials, Networking, Projects and, as an administrator, more) and a Project selector; leave it on default.

To replace the self-signed certificates, see TLS.

4. Create a NAT network

Glidex creates no network by itself. Create a NAT network: VMs on it get an address by DHCP and reach the outside through the host. Name it default and the VM forms preselect it.

gxctl network-add default

network-add makes a NAT network unless you pass --isolated or --bridged <bridge>. Its subnet is the first free /24 in 10.88.0.0/16 unless you pass --subnet <cidr>. Only your default project (here, default) may use it until you grant it to others.

In the web UI: Networking → Add Network, enter the name default, keep Mode at NAT (DHCP + masquerade), and click Create.

More in Networks and Host networking.

5. Pull a cloud image

List the catalog, then pull an image. gxctl follows the download until the image is verified and ready.

gxctl image catalog
gxctl image pull ubuntu-26.04

The catalog also lists UEFI firmware. The control plane imports the firmware the installer set up (cloudhv-edk2 for Cloud Hypervisor, ovmf for QEMU) at its first start, so you don’t need to pull it. gxctl image list shows both.

In the web UI: Images → Cloud image catalog, then Pull on the image you want.

More in Images and disks.

6. Add a guest credential

A credential is a username with a password, SSH public keys, or both. Glidex sets it up in the guest when the VM first boots. Without one, you can’t log in to the VM.

gxctl credential-add

It asks for a username (default: yours), a password (twice; leave it empty for SSH-key-only login), and SSH public key files (default: your ~/.ssh/*.pub). Give it a password if you want to log in on the console in step 8.

In the web UI: Credentials → Add Credential, fill in Username, a password and/or SSH public keys (optional), and click Add.

More in Guest credentials.

7. Create and start a VM

gxctl create asks its questions one by one; press Enter to take the default shown in brackets. For an Ubuntu VM on Cloud Hypervisor:

$ gxctl create
VM name: my-vm
GPUs (count[:pool][:nvlink], e.g. 4:a100; sizes the VM from the pool; optional):
vCPU count [1]: 2
Memory (MiB) [512]: 2048
Hypervisor [cloudhypervisor/qemu/pylon] (default: cloudhypervisor):
Configure elastic CPU scaling (min/max vCPUs, weight)? [y/N] [n]:
UEFI firmware [...] [cloudhv-edk2]:
Boot disk from [image/disk/path] [image]:
Image (ubuntu-26.04) [ubuntu-26.04]:
Root disk size in GiB [10]: 20
Data disks (optional, comma-separated disk names):
cloud-init seed image (optional, default: auto-generated):
Login credential (...) [alice]:
Networks (comma-separated; available: default; 'none' for no NIC) [default]:
VFIO PCI devices (comma-separated, e.g. /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0):
Device pools (comma-separated pool[:count], e.g. a100:2; optional):
VM created successfully!

An empty answer for the root disk size gives 10 GiB, or the image’s own size if that is larger.

The VM is created stopped. Start it; start waits until it runs:

gxctl start my-vm
gxctl list

In the web UI: VMs → + Create VM. Fill in VM Name, set vCPU Count and Memory (MiB), keep Boot Mode at UEFI firmware (distro cloud image) and Boot Disk at New disk from an image, pick the Image, set Root disk (GiB), pick your Login Credential, and check the default network under Networks. Check Start it now to skip the separate start, then click Create VM. Without Start it now, click Start on the VM’s card.

More in Virtual machines.

8. Open the console

gxctl connect my-vm

You’re on the VM’s serial console. The first boot takes a little while for cloud-init to apply the credential; then log in with its username and password. Press Ctrl+] to detach; the VM keeps running. gxctl log my-vm prints what the console showed so far.

In the web UI: Open Console on the VM’s card or its detail page.

Once the guest has an address on the NAT network (gxctl get my-vm shows it), you can also SSH to it from the host with the keys in your credential.

More in The console.

9. Stop the VM

gxctl stop my-vm --graceful

--graceful presses the guest’s power button and waits up to 60 seconds (--graceful <secs> to change that) for it to shut down, then stops it. Without --graceful, stop ends the VM at once, like pulling the plug.

In the web UI: Shut down for the graceful stop, Force off for the immediate one.

To remove the VM and the root disk made for it (it asks first; add --keep-disk to keep the disk):

gxctl delete my-vm

  • Read Concepts for how projects, images, disks, networks and VMs fit together.
  • Use Glidex from another machine: Logging in.

  • Add more hosts: Clusters.

Concepts

This page explains the objects Glidex manages and the words the rest of these docs use for them. Each entry links to the page with the details.

Control plane

The control plane (glidex-control-plane) is the service that holds the state of everything (VMs, disks, images, networks, projects, users) and acts on it: it starts hypervisors, creates disks and asks the host’s network helper to set up networks. It serves:

  • the REST API and the RPC API (gRPC, gRPC-Web and Connect) on HTTPS port 8841, and on a local Unix socket for gxctl on the host;
  • the console of every VM.

The web UI (glidex-ui, HTTPS port 5173) and gxctl are clients of that API: anything you do in one you can do in the other. See the API reference and the gxctl reference.

The control plane doesn’t sit between a VM and its hypervisor: with the installer’s systemd units, each VM runs in its own unit, so VMs keep running when the control plane restarts or is upgraded.

Nodes, servers and agents

A node is a host that runs VMs. A standalone host is a single node.

Several hosts can form a cluster. Each node has a role:

  • A server keeps a copy of the cluster’s state in a replicated (Raft) store and answers the API. Run one, or three or more for a quorum that survives the loss of a server.
  • An agent only runs VMs. It has no API of its own; opening its web UI takes you to a server’s, at that agent’s Host page.

Each node has a Host page in the web UI (/hosts/<node>): its capacity, topology, networking, VMs, disks, roles and operations, reachable from any server. Servers publish their web UI’s address (cluster.ui_url, or the one glidex-ui reports), and agents send browsers there. See Host pages.

Nodes join with a one-time join token and talk to each other over mutual TLS. A scheduler picks the node for each new VM, and explains its choice. A node can be drained (no new VMs are placed on it), removed, and rejoined. See Clusters.

A VM stays on the node it was placed on. An administrator can place a stopped VM, or a lost one whose node was forgotten, again on another node, when its disks can go there (see Placing a stopped or lost VM again).

Tenants and projects

A project is where VMs, disks, guest credentials and project networks live. Each of these belongs to exactly one project. A project has members with roles, and optional quotas: limits on VMs, running VMs, vCPUs, memory, disk, networks and routers.

Every install starts with a project named default. In gxctl, --project <p> picks a project for one command and project use <p> sets your default; in the web UI, the Project selector in the header does both. See Projects.

A tenant is the organization that owns projects. A standalone host has an operator tenant admin, which runs the host, and a tenant default, which holds the default project. Most single-site installs don’t need more than that.

The directory is where users, teams, login connectors and tenants are kept; a control plane hosts one, shared by every server of a cluster. The web UI’s Directory page shows it.

Virtual machines

A VM has a name, a project, a hypervisor, vCPUs and memory, a boot disk, zero or more data disks, network interfaces (one per network it attaches to), optional PCI devices, and an optional guest credential.

Glidex separates what you ask for from what it last saw:

  • The desired state (the spec) is what you want: the VM’s configuration, and whether it should be running, paused or stopped. Start, stop, pause and edits change only this, and return at once.

  • The state (the status) is what the control plane last observed:

    StateMeaning
    createdNever started.
    startingThe hypervisor is being launched.
    runningThe guest is running.
    pausedThe guest is paused.
    stoppingA stop is in progress.
    stoppedNot running.
    failedIt couldn’t be started, or it crashed.
    unknownThe control plane can’t tell whether its hypervisor is still running.

A controller keeps working until the state matches the desired state. While it does, the web UI shows both (for example, Stopped → Running) and gxctl start waits for it. Some changes only apply at the next start; the VM then says a restart is required.

Two settings say what happens when the VM stops on its own:

  • Restart policy (If It Crashes in the web UI): restart it with backoff (the default) or leave it stopped.
  • On host boot (After a Host Reboot): start it again if it was running, or leave it stopped.

Stopping is either graceful (press the guest’s power button, wait, then stop) or immediate. Each VM keeps a short list of events: starts, exits, restarts. See Virtual machines.

A VM boots in one of two ways, fixed when it is created:

  • Firmware boot (the default): UEFI firmware runs the boot loader on the root disk, which picks the kernel.
  • Direct kernel boot: the hypervisor loads a kernel, an optional initramfs (the small root filesystem a kernel starts from before it mounts the real one) and a command line that Glidex hands it. With following the guest’s kernel (kernel_from_disk), Glidex takes the kernel the guest installed out of its disk before a start, so it boots next time.

See Kernel boot.

Hypervisors

Each VM runs on one hypervisor:

  • Cloud Hypervisor (cloudhypervisor in gxctl, HYPERVISOR_CLOUD_HYPERVISOR in the API), the default.
  • QEMU (qemu in gxctl, HYPERVISOR_QEMU in the API).
  • Pylon (pylon in gxctl, HYPERVISOR_PYLON in the API), a Cloud Hypervisor fork for elastic VMs, on hosts installed with --with-pylon.

All three support the same features in Glidex: UEFI boot of cloud images, direct kernel boot, networks, disks, PCI passthrough (VFIO), pause and resume, and graceful shutdown. You pick the hypervisor when you create the VM. Pylon boots through the same firmware as Cloud Hypervisor.

A VM can be elastic: it has a minimum and a maximum number of vCPUs, and a CPU weight. On Pylon the guest has all its maximum vCPUs and the host parks the idle ones in microseconds; on Cloud Hypervisor and QEMU you change the count of a running VM within the range. See Elastic CPU.

Images and firmware images

An image is a read-only file disks are made from. Images belong to the host (or cluster), not to a project: everyone can use them, and administrators with the image role pull and delete them.

  • A cloud image is a bootable distribution disk image (qcow2 or raw). Pull one from the built-in catalog by key (for example ubuntu-26.04, debian-13, fedora-cloud) or from an HTTPS URL. Catalog images are checked against their published SHA-256; an image from a URL without a checksum is kept but marked unverified.

  • A firmware image is the UEFI firmware a VM boots through, built for one hypervisor: cloudhv-edk2 (CLOUDHV.fd) for Cloud Hypervisor, ovmf for QEMU. A new VM uses the newest firmware image for its hypervisor unless you choose another.

  • A kernel image is a kernel, an optional initramfs and a default command line, for direct kernel boot. Pulling a catalog image also makes one from it by kernel extraction: Glidex reads the image’s /boot inside a small VM, never on the host. A kernel taken from a VM’s own disk is a VM-owned kernel image, deleted once no VM uses it.

An image is downloading, verifying, extracting (a kernel image), ready, failed or missing (its file is gone). See Images and disks and Kernel boot.

Disks

A disk is a virtual disk in a project. It is attached to at most one VM at a time, as its boot (root) disk or as a data disk. A disk is:

  • blank, of a size you choose, or
  • made from an image: either linked (thin: a qcow2 overlay on the image, so it takes space only for what the VM writes) or a full copy.

When you create a VM from an image, Glidex makes a linked root disk for it, grows it to the size you ask for, and extends the guest’s root partition to fill it. That disk belongs to the VM and is deleted with it unless you keep it. Disks can be resized; a resize of a disk that is in use is held until it can be applied.

Datastores

A datastore is where disks live; every disk is on one. See Datastores.

  • local, built in: each node’s own disk directory. The default for new disks until an administrator picks another.
  • A node-local datastore is a directory each node has its own of. A disk on it, as on local, is bound to one node, and so is its VM.
  • A shared datastore is one filesystem every node mounts (NFS, CephFS). Its disks are bound to no node: their VM can be placed on any node that reaches it. A marker file in its directory proves to each node that it sees the right filesystem; the disk’s worker is the node that works on its file; a volume lock keeps two nodes from using one disk at once.
  • An LVM-thin datastore (driver lvm) keeps disks as raw thin volumes carved from a thin pool in a volume group on each node; it is node-local. A root helper, glidex-stord, manages the volumes, and only in the volume groups an administrator allows. Each node keeps an image volume, a read-only copy of an image, that linked disks there are thin snapshots of. A full thin pool stalls the guests. See LVM-thin.
  • A hyperstor datastore (driver hyperstor) keeps disks as volumes of a hyperstor cluster’s pool, replicated across its nodes. Like a shared datastore, its disks are bound to no node. See Hyperstor.

A disk no running VM uses can move to another datastore. A linked disk is then rebased on the image’s copy there, or flattened into a standalone copy.

Host resources

Glidex knows each host’s host topology: its NUMA nodes, cores, hugepages and PCIe tree. See Host resources.

  • A NUMA policy keeps a VM’s memory, vCPUs and devices on one NUMA node (a socket, or part of one): preferred, or strict. The aligned policy instead splits the VM over exactly its devices’ NUMA nodes, one guest NUMA node each.
  • Dedicated CPUs give each vCPU a host CPU no other VM uses.
  • Hugepages back guest memory with large pages (2M or 1G), counted per node; a VM’s page_kib says what it got.
  • A device pool is a named set of like devices (GPUs, NICs) a VM asks for by count. A tenant pool is a tenant’s share of one, split among its projects. A pool’s per-device sizing (per_device) is the vCPUs and memory a VM gets with each device.
  • A GPU request (gpus) asks for N GPUs from a pool: the VM gets the aligned NUMA policy and, unless it sizes itself, the pool’s per-device sizing. See GPU requests.
  • Boot devices are the devices the installer’s --vfio-devices and --sriov bind to vfio-pci, or give VFs, at every boot (glidex-vfio-boot.service). See Keep it across reboots.
  • A device is ready when it can be passed through as it is, and cordoned when an administrator keeps it from new VMs.

Guest credentials

A guest credential is a login for inside VMs: a username with a password, SSH public keys, or both. Credentials belong to a project. Glidex stores only a hash of the password.

When you create a VM with a credential, Glidex generates a cloud-init seed that creates that user in the guest. It is applied on the VM’s first boot only: later changes to the credential don’t reach VMs that already booted. You can also give your own cloud-init seed instead. See Guest credentials.

Networks

A network connects VM interfaces. Its mode is one of:

  • NAT: a private subnet with DHCP; VMs reach the outside through the host (masquerade).
  • Isolated: VMs on it reach each other and nothing else.
  • Bridged: VMs sit on an existing network of the host (in a cluster, a provider network on a physical network).

A host network is created by an administrator and offered to the projects allowed to use it. A project network belongs to a project, and its owner can share it with other projects.

On a standalone host, networks are Open vSwitch bridges on that host. In a cluster with OVN enabled, a cluster network spans every node. A VM’s interface is a tap device (the default) or a vhost-user port (with OVS-DPDK).

A network is pending, ready or degraded, or reports that the host’s network helper is unavailable. See Networks and Host networking.

Console

Every VM has one serial console. Any number of clients (browser tabs, gxctl connect) can share it at once, and everything it prints is logged to disk, so you can read what happened before you connected. See The console.

Users, teams and roles

A user is a person known to Glidex. Users log in through a login connector: local accounts (PAM), or single sign-on through an OIDC provider, Google or JumpCloud. On the host itself, gxctl identifies you by your Unix account. A user can have several sign-in methods (a local password and a Google account, say), each giving the same roles. A passkey is one more: a WebAuthn credential (the device’s fingerprint, face or PIN, or a security key) that signs in to the web UI and counts as multi-factor. Passkeys belong to the passkeys’ domain (auth.passkeys.rp_id) and work on every web UI name under it. See Passkeys. A team is a group of users; teams can mirror Unix or identity-provider groups.

A connector can also be provisioned: the identity provider (IdP) creates, changes and removes its users and groups in Glidex over SCIM, and only those users can log in through it. Such users and teams are managed by the connector: their names, and whether a user is enabled, are changed at the IdP, not in Glidex.

A Google Workspace connector can pull instead (directory sync): Glidex reads the members of the Google groups you name, as a Google service account whose key you give it, every 15 minutes, and the users it brings in are managed the same way. A safety stop holds a run that would disable too many users until an administrator confirms it. See Directory sync from Google Workspace.

An invitation is a one-time link that lets one email address into a tenant, with a role, through one connector, even when that connector doesn’t create users by itself; or, with no connector, by making a passkey. It expires, after 7 days by default. An administrator can also pre-add a user by email, with no link: the first sign-in through the named connector with that verified address takes the account.

A role binding gives a user, team or token a role on a resource. Project roles, each including the one before it:

RoleCan
viewerSee the project, its VMs, disks and usage.
operatorAlso start, stop, pause and change VMs, and use their consoles.
editorAlso create and delete VMs and disks, attach disks and networks, and manage guest credentials.
ownerAlso manage members and service-account tokens, read the project’s audit log, and manage and share project networks and routers.

Host roles cover the host or cluster itself: auditor (read-only, including the audit log), image-admin (images), net-admin (host networks and PCI devices), and system-admin (everything). In a cluster, auditor and net-admin can also be given on one host only. Tenant roles (tenant-admin, tenant-auditor) cover one tenant and its projects. See Access control.

Tokens

An API token lets a script or another machine call the API. A token has a name and always expires: after a default lifetime, or after the number of days you choose, up to a limit the site sets.

  • A personal token acts as you. It can be narrowed to some of your roles.
  • A service-account token belongs to a project and has only the roles it is given.

The secret is shown once, when you create the token. Create tokens with gxctl token create or on the web UI’s Tokens page; revoke them the same way. See Logging in.

Software in a VM can act as a service account without a stored token (workload identity): the VM’s metadata endpoint, 169.254.169.254, hands it short-lived identity tokens and, when the VM is given a service account, Glidex tokens. See Workload identity.

A workload federation lets CI jobs and other workloads (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Kubernetes) use the API without a stored token. A tenant trusts their issuer and maps tokens whose claims match a rule to one of its service accounts; a job exchanges its platform’s token for a short-lived Glidex token acting as that service account. See Workload federation.

Policies and the audit log

Every request is authorized by Cedar policies: built-in ones that implement the roles above, plus optional site policies an administrator adds to allow or forbid more. Some sensitive operations also need a recent login. Changes, and refused requests, are recorded in the audit log: who did what, to what, and with what result. See Access control.

Usage

Glidex meters what each VM, disk and network uses (CPU, memory, disk I/O and network traffic) and reports it per project, VM, disk, NIC or network, by hour, day or billing month. See Usage.

User guide

This guide is for people who run VMs on a Glidex host or cluster that someone else installed: logging in, working inside a project, and creating, connecting to and removing VMs and what they use.

If you are setting Glidex up, start with the Quick start and the Operator guide. The Concepts page explains the words used here: projects, images, disks, credentials, networks.

Three ways in

Everything in this guide can be done in at least one of these:

  • Web UI, at https://<host>:5173 by default. Sign in with your account; the header has a project selector, a page per resource (VMs, Images, Disks, Credentials, Networking, Projects, Tokens, Usage, and Audit for project owners), an indicator of work in progress, and your name, which opens your account menu. Pages follow changes as they happen, without reloading.

  • gxctl, the command-line client. Run gxctl for an interactive shell (gxctl> prompt, Tab completion, help lists every command), or gxctl <command> to run one command and exit:

    gxctl list                  # one command, then exit
gxctl                       # the shell

    On the host itself it uses the local socket and needs no login; from another machine it logs in once and keeps a token.

  • The API, REST over HTTPS on port 8841 by default, plus an RPC API, authenticated with a bearer token. The web UI and gxctl use it too, so anything they do can be scripted. See the REST API and RPC API references.

Each page shows the web UI path and the gxctl commands, with a short API example where it helps. The full command list is in the gxctl reference.

Pages

  • Logging in: the web UI, invitations, your sign-in methods and passkeys, several accounts in one browser, gxctl on the host and from another machine, login profiles, API tokens, whoami.
  • Projects: what a project holds, members and roles, teams, quotas, choosing the project you work in.
  • Images and disks: the image catalog, pulling images and firmware, creating, attaching, resizing and deleting disks.
  • Guest credentials: the login cloud-init creates in a VM, passwords and SSH keys, custom cloud-init seeds.
  • Virtual machines: create, start, stop, resize, delete.
  • Networks: attaching VMs to networks, project networks and sharing.
  • The console: the serial console in the browser and in gxctl.
  • Usage: resource usage, bandwidth and metering reports.

What you can do depends on your role

Glidex checks every request against your roles. Within a project you are a viewer, operator, editor or owner (see Roles); a few things, such as pulling images or changing host networking, need a host-wide role that administrators hold. The web UI hides or disables what you can’t do; gxctl and the API answer not allowed: <action>, naming what was refused. If you need more access, ask a project owner or an administrator.

Logging in

How you prove who you are depends on where you connect from:

FromHow
The web UIYour account’s password (PAM), single sign-on (OIDC, Google, JumpCloud) or a passkey, whichever the site enables
gxctl on a Glidex hostNothing: the local socket knows your Unix account
gxctl on another machinegxctl auth login once; it saves a token in a login profile
Scripts and the APIAn API token, sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>

Which login methods exist, and who may log in, is set by the operator (see Authentication).

The web UI

Open https://<host>:5173 (gxctl ui prints the address it knows). The sign-in page shows what the site enables:

  • Username and Password, then Sign in: a local account of the host, or of the site’s PAM setup. By default the account must be in the glidex-users group.
  • Sign in with <provider> (or Sign in with SSO): your organisation’s single sign-on, one button per provider the site offers, such as its Google Workspace or JumpCloud.
  • Sign in with a passkey: a passkey you added earlier (see Passkeys). There is no user name to type.

If the page says No login method is enabled on this host, ask an administrator, or use gxctl on the host.

Some single sign-on providers create your Glidex account for you ahead of time (provisioning): the identity provider pushes it over SCIM, or Glidex reads it from your organisation’s Google Workspace (a directory sync). Through such a provider:

  • only people it provisioned can sign in; anyone else is refused (login_not_allowed), even with an invitation. With a directory sync, that is the members of the Google groups your operator chose;
  • your first sign-in is matched to the account it made, by your provider’s id or, over SCIM, your verified email address;
  • your name and email come from the provider, and if the provider deactivates you, you can’t sign in until it reactivates you. With a directory sync, being suspended in Google or taken out of the groups counts as deactivated. An administrator may also disable you in Glidex; then only an administrator can enable you again.

A directory sync reads Google every 15 minutes unless the operator chose otherwise, so after you are added to a group (or come back), it can take that long before you can sign in.

In a cluster, open a server’s web UI. Opening an agent’s sends you to a server’s, at that agent’s Host page; sign in there. Any server will do, also behind a load balancer: your session, account changes and passkeys work through whichever server answers. A password (PAM) sign-in is the exception: it is an account of the server that checked it. If signing in with your password on another server gives you a user with no projects, ask an administrator to link that server’s account to your user.

The first time, your browser may warn that the certificate is not trusted: the host made its own. Compare the SHA-256 fingerprint the browser shows with the one your operator gives you before you accept it (see TLS). If the host is on a Tailscale tailnet and your operator turned on its Tailscale certificate, open the UI at its https://<node>.<tailnet>.ts.net:5173 address instead: the browser trusts that one, with no warning (see Tailscale certificates).

A browser session ends after 30 minutes without activity and after 12 hours at most, unless the operator changed these. Log out, in the header, ends it now. Some actions (changing policies, host networking or the cluster) need a recent login: the UI then asks you to sign in again (Confirm it’s you) and retries the action. Confirm with a passkey answers it too.

The header also shows who you are and the project you are working in; see Projects.

Invitations

An administrator may let you in with an invitation: a link of the form https://<host>:5173/invite/<id>#<secret>. Open it in your browser. The page says which tenant and role it is for, and which address and provider to sign in with; Sign in with <provider> takes you there. Sign in with that address: another account doesn’t take the invitation.

  • A link works once, for one person, and expires (after 7 days unless the administrator chose otherwise).
  • Keep it to yourself until you have used it: it works like a password.
  • If the page says the invitation was already used, revoked or has expired, ask for a new one.

An invitation can make you a passkey instead, for a directory with no single sign-on yet. The page then shows your email and Create a passkey and sign in: confirm in your browser’s or device’s prompt, and you are signed in. You sign in with that passkey from then on, and can add your organization’s sign-in later under Your account (see Passkeys).

Added before you sign in

An administrator may also add you by email before you have ever signed in, with no link. Sign in through the provider they name, with that address: your first sign-in takes the account, with the tenant and role they gave it. The provider must say your address is verified. Until you sign in, administrators see you as not signed in yet.

Your account

Click your name in the header and choose Account settings for Your account. Its Sign-in methods card lists the ways you can sign in as yourself, for example a local password and a Google account; each gives the same roles.

  • Under Add a way to sign in, pick one of the site’s single sign-on providers and sign in there; it is added to you. This needs a recent login. A provider that provisions its users, by SCIM or a directory sync, can’t be added: its sign-ins belong to the accounts it manages.
  • Remove takes one away. You can’t remove your last one.

Signing in a second way without adding it first makes a second, separate user. If a sign-in already belongs to another user, an administrator must remove it from that user before you can add it.

Passkeys

A passkey lets you sign in with your device’s fingerprint, face or PIN, or a security key, instead of a password. When the site has passkeys on, Your account has a Passkeys card; it says so if your browser can’t make passkeys.

To add one:

  1. Sign in another way, and open Your account.
  2. Under Passkeys, type a Name (such as work laptop) and click Add a passkey. If your login isn’t recent, the UI asks you to sign in again first.
  3. Confirm in your browser’s or device’s prompt.

The card lists your passkeys with when each was made and last used, and synced for one your device keeps in sync across your devices. It also appears as Passkey under Sign-in methods. Rename changes its name; Remove deletes it. You can have up to 10.

To sign in, click Sign in with a passkey on the login page and pick the passkey in your browser’s prompt. Closing the prompt just cancels.

  • Keep another sign-in method, or a second passkey. You can’t remove the one that would leave a single passkey as your only way in.
  • If the card says passkeys made here work under this page’s name only, a passkey you add works only at that address of the web UI. Open the UI at the same address to use it.
  • If you lose a device, sign in another way and remove its passkey. If you have no way left to sign in, ask an administrator.
  • gxctl doesn’t use passkeys; use a password, single sign-on or a token there.

Your organization’s sign-in

A host can serve the sign-in of several organizations, each its own directory with its own people. Type your work email under Signing in with your organization? on the sign-in page: it takes you to your organization’s page, which offers only its ways to sign in. Your administrator can also give you that page’s address, https://<host>:5173/login/<directory>.

A cluster can also admit a tenant of another organization, whose people sign in at their own organization’s Glidex. Its sign-in page then has a Sign in with <tenant> button for each such organization (with at <host> under it). It takes you to your organization’s sign-in and brings you back signed in to the cluster. Signing out there signs you out of the cluster too, within a minute. Logging out of the cluster signs you out of the cluster only: you stay signed in at your organization.

Several accounts in one browser

If you have accounts in several directories (say, at your university and at a research partner), your browser can stay signed in to all of them and switch between them. Click your name in the header:

  • Switch to lists your other accounts. Click one to use it; the page starts over as that account, in every open tab.
  • Add another account keeps the one you’re using and opens the sign-in page. Sign in to another directory; both are then in the list.
  • Sign out of all accounts signs out every one and empties the list.

Log out signs out only the account you’re using. Its directory stays in the list, marked signed out, and so does one whose session ended: click it to sign in there again. Under Account settings, Your accounts in this browser lists them all; Remove signs one out and takes it off the list. The sign-in page lists them too, so you can switch back without signing in again.

You can hold up to 5 accounts, one per directory: signing in to a directory you already have replaces that account. The list is kept only in your browser: nobody else sees it, and the host keeps no record of which accounts you hold together. Each account keeps its own session limits, and switching is not a new sign-in, so an action that needs a recent login may still ask you to sign in again. On a computer you share, use Sign out of all accounts when you’re done.

gxctl on a Glidex host

On a host that runs the control plane, gxctl talks to its Unix socket (/run/glidex-cp/api.sock) and the control plane identifies you by your Unix account. There is no login and no token:

gxctl whoami

You need to be in the glidex-users group (log out and back in after being added). Members of glidex-admin are administrators.

--socket <path> (or GLIDEX_SOCKET) picks another socket. On a cluster agent node there is no local API: log in to a server node from there as from any other machine (gxctl auth login --url https://<server>:8841 …, which runs on the agent itself).

gxctl from another machine

gxctl auth login connects to a control plane over HTTPS, checks its certificate, gets you a token and saves the lot as a named login profile in ~/.config/glidex/config.json (mode 0600). Later commands use the current profile without asking again.

Pick a profile name and a way to prove who you are:

# Your account's password (asked for, never on the command line)
gxctl auth login --url https://host.example.org:8841 --profile lab --pam-user alice

# Single sign-on: open the link it prints and enter the code
gxctl auth login --url https://host.example.org:8841 --profile lab --oidc

# An API token you already have (typed hidden, or piped)
gxctl auth login --url https://host.example.org:8841 --profile ci --token < token.txt

# Your directory: approve the login in the web UI, however you sign in there
gxctl auth login --url https://host.example.org:8841 --profile lab --directory

With --directory, gxctl prints a link to the web UI’s Device login page and a code. Open it, sign in the way you usually do (password, single sign-on, a passkey), check that the code matches, and approve. gxctl then holds no long-lived token: it keeps a refresh token for your directory and asks it for a short-lived access token for this cluster (one hour by default) whenever the one it holds is about to expire. The refresh token lasts while you keep using it (30 days unused at most; 30 to 90 days in all, as the operator’s sign-in providers allow), and ends when you or an administrator end your sessions, when your account is disabled, or at gxctl auth logout.

  • --connector <id> picks one of several sign-in providers. A Google provider works with --oidc only if the operator set it up for device logins; otherwise it answers device_flow_unsupported.
  • --name <name> names the token it creates (default gxctl@<profile>), so you can tell your machines apart in gxctl token list.
  • --directory [id] logs in at one of the host’s directories (local, the default, until a host serves several).
  • --days N asks for a shorter or longer --pam-user token, within the site’s limit (30 days unless the operator changed it). An --oidc login gets a token valid for one day.
  • For a cluster, repeat --url with several server nodes; gxctl tries them in turn.
  • Without --profile, --url refreshes the profile that already points at that host; for a new host add --save to name the profile after it: a host name’s first label (host.example.org gives host), or a whole IP address with dashes (192.0.2.10 gives 192-0-2-10).

The first profile you create becomes the current one; --use makes a later one current. Run the same auth login --profile lab again when its token expires.

Certificates and fingerprint pinning

gxctl verifies the control plane’s certificate. A certificate from a CA your machine trusts just works. A self-signed one (the default) is not trusted, and auth login shows its fingerprint:

the certificate of host.example.org is not trusted by this system:
  SHA-256 AB:CD:…   (the control plane prints this line at startup)
  reported by the server as its own: it matches what we are being handed (…)
Trust this exact certificate for profile 'lab'? [y/N]:

Compare the fingerprint with the one your operator gave you through another channel, then answer y. The profile pins that certificate: from then on gxctl accepts exactly it for this profile, and refuses to connect if it changes. If the line says the two do not match, stop and ask the operator: something between you and the host is presenting its own certificate.

Without a terminal (CI), there is no prompt; give the fingerprint up front:

gxctl auth login --url https://host.example.org:8841 --profile ci \
  --pin sha256/<fingerprint> --token < token.txt

When the operator legitimately replaces the certificate (for example after rotating a cluster’s CA), confirm the new fingerprint with them and re-pin:

gxctl auth login --profile lab --pin sha256/<new fingerprint> --rebind

--rebind is also what lets a profile log in to a machine that now answers for a different cluster than the one it first saw; without it gxctl refuses.

gxctl auth trust list shows a profile’s pins and extra CAs.

Instead of a profile, a one-off --url connection trusts a self-signed certificate through GLIDEX_CA_CERT, the path of a PEM copy of the host’s certificate that your operator provides.

A cluster of another organization

If your tenant uses a cluster run by another organization, log in to it with your own directory’s account: first make a profile for your directory’s host (as above, --directory), then one for the cluster, reaching your directory through that first profile:

gxctl auth login --profile acme --url https://id.acme.example:8841 --directory local
gxctl auth login --profile north --url https://north.example.org:8841 --directory local --via acme

The second login asks you to approve it at your directory, like the first. The north profile then holds a login of its own at your directory, and gets access tokens for the north cluster only; its refreshes and auth logout --revoke go to your directory through acme’s connection and certificate.

Managing profiles

gxctl auth status             # the profile in use: target, cluster, trust, token
gxctl auth profiles --all     # every profile; * marks the current one
gxctl auth use lab            # make 'lab' current
gxctl --profile ci list       # use another profile for one command
gxctl auth logout             # forget this profile's token (target and pins stay)
gxctl auth logout --revoke    # revoke it on the server first, then forget it
gxctl auth profiles remove lab

auth profiles remove <name> deletes a profile from the file. It refuses one that still holds a token, since the token stays valid on the server: run gxctl auth logout --profile <name> --revoke first, or add --forget-token to drop it unrevoked (revoke it later from Tokens or gxctl token revoke). Removing the current profile leaves none current; pick another with gxctl --profile <other> auth use <other>.

GLIDEX_PROFILE does what --profile does. --url on a command overrides the target for that run but keeps the profile’s trust; the profile’s token is only sent if the URL points at one of the profile’s own hosts.

Once the profile file holds any profile, gxctl uses profiles instead of the local socket. To reach the local socket on a host where you also keep profiles, run it with the file switched off:

GLIDEX_CONFIG= gxctl whoami

GLIDEX_CONFIG=<path> reads profiles from another file.

Older single-token login

gxctl --url https://host.example.org:8841 login --oidc (or login --token) still works when you have no profiles: it saves one token in ~/.config/glidex/token and gxctl --url … sends it. logout [--revoke] removes it. Profiles are the better choice: they remember the target and pin its certificate.

GLIDEX_TOKEN, when set, is sent instead of any saved token.

API tokens

An API token lets a script, CI job or another tool act through the API. There are two kinds:

  • Personal: acts as you, and can never do more than you can. Give it roles to narrow it further (only viewer in project lab, say); without roles it can do everything you can.
  • Service account: belongs to a project, not a person, so it keeps working when people leave. It can only do what its roles in that project allow; without roles it can do nothing. Creating one needs the project’s owner role.

Tokens expire: after 90 days unless you ask otherwise, at most 365 (the operator sets both). The secret is shown once, when you create the token; Glidex keeps only a hash of it.

Web UI

Tokens in the header (shown when you are signed in with an account, not with a token):

  1. + Create Token.
  2. Enter a Name and Expires in (days). For a service account, choose Kind: Service account of <project> (offered if you own the selected project).
  3. + Add role for each role, and pick its project, or leave none.
  4. Create Token, then Copy the token and store it in a secret manager or a file only you can read. It is not shown again.

The table lists your tokens with their roles, expiry and when they were last used; Revoke ends one immediately.

gxctl

gxctl token create laptop --days 30                                 # personal, all your rights
gxctl token create readonly --role viewer@lab                       # personal, narrowed
gxctl token create ci --service-account --project lab --role editor # service account
gxctl token list
gxctl token revoke <token-id>

--role ROLE[@PROJECT] repeats; roles are viewer, operator, editor, owner (see Roles). A service account’s roles apply in its own project; without --project it goes into the project selected with --project or your default project.

A token works only on the cluster where you make it. If your tenant also uses clusters of other organizations, --cluster <cluster-id> (repeat it) lets the token work on those as well, and --all-clusters on every cluster your tenant uses (gxctl tenant clusters <tenant> lists them). Those clusters receive the token’s hash with their next update from your directory, within a minute; revoking it reaches them the same way. Ask for as few as you need: a cluster that can check a token could also replay it to the others it lists.

Using a token

export GLIDEX_TOKEN=<token>
gxctl --url https://host.example.org:8841 whoami

curl --cacert host.crt -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" \
  https://host.example.org:8841/auth/whoami

Or store it in a profile: gxctl auth login --profile ci --token. The REST calls are GET /tokens, POST /tokens and DELETE /tokens/{id} (REST API).

If a token leaks, revoke it at once and create a new one.

Who am I?

gxctl whoami (or gxctl auth whoami) shows how the control plane sees you:

  User:     alice (<user-id>)
  Method:   token via https://host.example.org:8841
  Token:    gxctl@lab (<token-id>)
  Teams:    -
  Host roles: -
  Default project: lab (<project-id>)
  Project roles:
    lab                  role.editor    via user:<user-id>

Method is peer on the local socket and token whenever a token is sent (as gxctl does from a profile); a web UI session is pam, oidc or passkey. The user id is what others need to add you to a project. Over the API: GET /auth/whoami.

Projects

A project is where your work lives. Every VM, disk, guest credential and project network belongs to exactly one project; who may do what is granted per project; quotas cap what a project may use.

Images are different: they are a library shared by every project (see Images and disks).

Every installation has a project named default, created at install. It can’t be deleted. The members of the glidex-admin group at the control plane’s first start are made its owners.

Seeing your projects

Web UI: Projects in the header lists the projects you are a member of, with each one’s use against its quotas. Click a project for its page: quotas, members, networks.

gxctl:

gxctl project list
gxctl project show lab

If you are in no project yet, the list is empty: ask a project owner or an administrator to add you.

Choosing a project

Most commands work in one project at a time: lists show its VMs and disks, and new resources are created in it.

Web UI: the Project selector in the header. Every page then shows that project’s resources. On a project’s page, Select this project does the same. Your choice is also saved as your default project.

gxctl: a project is chosen, in this order, by

  1. --project <name|id> (or -p, or GLIDEX_PROJECT) on the command:

    gxctl --project lab list

  2. a "project" key in the login profile in use;

  3. your default project, kept by the control plane and shared with the web UI:

    gxctl project use lab     # set it
gxctl project use -       # clear it

  4. if none is set and you belong to exactly one project, that project.

gxctl whoami shows your default project and the one this session uses. Over the API, pass ?project=<name|id> or a "project" field.

Roles

Each member of a project has one of four roles. Each role includes everything of the roles above it.

RoleCan
viewerSee the project, its VMs, disks and usage
operatorAlso start, stop, pause and change VMs, and open their consoles
editorAlso create and delete VMs and disks, attach disks and networks to VMs, and see and manage guest credentials
ownerAlso manage members and service-account tokens, read the project’s audit log, and create and share project networks

Viewers and operators don’t see guest credentials.

Host-wide roles (for example image-admin for pulling images, or net-admin for host networking) and how administrators assign them are described in Access control.

Members

A member is a user or a team bound to a role in the project. Owners manage members.

Web UI: the project’s page, Members card. The table lists each binding; Remove deletes one. To add one, choose a Role, a Principal type (User or Team) and the user or team, then Add role. If you can’t list users, type the user’s id (they can find it with gxctl whoami).

gxctl:

gxctl binding list lab
gxctl binding add lab editor user:<user-id>
gxctl binding add lab viewer team:<team-id>
gxctl binding remove lab <binding-id>

Roles can be written short (editor) or in full (role.editor). A principal is user:<id>, team:<id> or token:<id>. binding list shows each binding’s id.

Over the API: GET/POST /projects/{id}/bindings and DELETE /projects/{id}/bindings/{binding-id}.

Teams

A team is a named group of users; binding a team to a project gives every member of it that role. Administrators create teams and manage their members (the Directory page’s Users & roles tab in the web UI, gxctl team …):

gxctl team list
gxctl team create ops
gxctl team add-member ops <user-id>
gxctl team remove-member ops <user-id>

Teams can also come from outside Glidex:

  • on the local socket, each of your Unix groups counts as a team named unix:<group>, so team:unix:lab-users grants a role to that group’s members when they use gxctl on the host;
  • the operator can map groups from the site’s PAM or single sign-on setup to teams;
  • an identity provider that provisions users over SCIM can push its groups as teams, and a directory sync from Google Workspace makes teams of the Google groups it reads. Such a team shows from <connector>: its name and the members the IdP put in it change at the IdP (in Google, for a directory sync), not in Glidex (Glidex refuses with 409 managed_by_connector). Administrators can still add members by hand.

gxctl whoami lists the teams you are in.

Quotas

A project’s quotas cap what it may hold. Each is a number or unlimited:

QuotaCounts
vmsVMs
running_vmsVMs running at once
vcpusvCPUs of all VMs
memory_mibMemory of all VMs, in MiB
disk_gibDisk space, in GiB
networksProject networks (2 by default)
routersProject routers (1 by default)
external_ipsOutside addresses of routers (1 by default)
devices.<pool>Devices VMs ask for from a device pool, per pool (for example devices.a100)

A request that would go over a quota is refused with the limit, what is in use and what was asked for. Administrators may go over a quota; that is recorded in the audit log. New projects get the site’s default quotas: unless the operator changed them, only the last three are limited.

Web UI: the Projects list and the project’s Quotas and usage card show use against each limit, with Devices: <pool> for each pool that has a limit or is in use. Edit quotas (shown if you may change them) takes a number per quota, and one per device pool the project may use; an empty field is unlimited.

gxctl:

gxctl project quota lab                       # show use/limit
gxctl project quota lab vms=10 memory_mib=none
gxctl project quota lab devices.a100=2

none (or unlimited) removes a limit; keys you don’t name keep their value. gxctl sets the first six quotas in the table and devices.<pool>; routers and external_ips are set in the web UI or the API.

A pool’s devices count when a VM asks for them, whether it runs or not, like vcpus. Over the limit, the request is refused with quota_exceeded and resource devices.<pool>.

Changing quotas is an administrator’s task, as is creating and deleting projects.

Device pools

GPUs and other host devices are handed out from device pools that an administrator grants to projects or tenants. To see the pools your project may use and how many devices of each are free:

gxctl pci pools --project lab

Anyone with a role in the project may look. The list includes the project’s tenant pools: shares of a cluster pool that the tenant’s administrator gave to some of its projects, each with a maximum (from, max and used in the API’s GET /pci-pools?project=lab). The web UI’s create form offers the same pools: GPU pools under GPUs (optional), the others under Device Pools (optional). How a VM asks for devices is in Devices from a pool.

Creating and deleting projects

If you may create projects, Projects shows + Create Project: give a Name (1-32 lowercase letters, digits and dashes), an optional Description and, optionally, an Owner. Or:

gxctl project create lab --description "Lab VMs"

gxctl project create adds no owner; add one with binding add.

To delete a project it must not own any VMs, disks or credentials: Delete project on its page, or gxctl project delete lab (it asks for confirmation). Its service-account tokens are revoked with it.

On an installation with several tenants (organisations), each project belongs to one tenant, shown in the Tenant column. See Access control.

Images and disks

  • An image is a read-only base: a distro cloud image that VMs’ disks are made from, or the UEFI firmware VMs boot through. Images are a library shared by every project.
  • A disk is a writable volume in a project: a VM’s root disk or an extra data disk. A disk can start blank or as a copy of an image.

Pulling and deleting images needs the host-wide image-admin role; everyone can see and use the library. Creating, resizing and deleting disks needs the editor role in the disk’s project.

The catalog

Glidex has a built-in catalog of distro cloud images. Each entry points at the vendor’s current build, and every download is checked against the checksum the vendor publishes next to it.

KeyImage
ubuntu-26.04Ubuntu 26.04 LTS
ubuntu-24.04Ubuntu 24.04 LTS
ubuntu-22.04Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
debian-13Debian 13
debian-12Debian 12
fedora-cloudFedora Cloud Base, latest release
alma-9AlmaLinux 9

Each is available for x86_64 and aarch64; Glidex fetches the one for the host.

Web UI: Images, Cloud image catalog. Downloaded entries say so.

gxctl:

gxctl image catalog

Pulling an image

Web UI: Images, then Pull on a catalog entry. The image appears under Cloud images and shows its download progress, then Ready.

gxctl:

gxctl image pull ubuntu-24.04

It follows the download until the image is ready; Ctrl-C stops watching, not the download. --name <name> names the image (default: the catalog key, or the file name for a URL); names are 1-64 characters of letters, digits, ., _ and -.

From a URL

Any qcow2 or raw image reachable over HTTPS can be pulled too:

gxctl image pull https://images.example.org/my-image.qcow2 --name my-image --sha256 <sha256>

Web UI: Images, Download from URL: Type Cloud image (qcow2 or raw), the Image URL (https), the sha256 and an optional Name.

Give the sha256 whenever you can: without it the image is stored but listed as unverified. URLs must be https:// and, unless the operator allows it, on a public address.

Listing, retrying and deleting

gxctl image list
gxctl image retry my-image     # download a failed image again
gxctl image rm my-image

image list shows each image’s state (downloading 40%, verifying, ready, failed: <reason>, missing), size and source. In the web UI the image tables have Retry for a failed download, Cancel for one in progress and Delete.

An image can’t be deleted while a disk is being made from it or a linked disk still uses it as its base (see Clone modes).

In a cluster, a server downloads and checks the image, and nodes copy it from there when they need it. When pulling in the web UI you can pick Copy to nodes to have copies ready sooner; the Images page shows each node’s copy and can copy an image to another node or let a copy go.

Linked disks on a shared datastore use a copy of the image kept in that datastore. The Images page lists these copies apart from the node copies (in 1 shared datastore); they go when the image is deleted.

Firmware images

VMs that boot a cloud image start through UEFI firmware built for their hypervisor. Firmware is managed like the other images:

KeyFirmwareHypervisor
cloudhv-edk2Cloud Hypervisor’s EDK2 build (pinned)Cloud Hypervisor, Pylon
ovmfOVMF from the host’s packageQEMU
ovmf-debianOVMF from a pinned Debian packageQEMU

The control plane imports cloudhv-edk2 (from the installer’s copy) and the host’s OVMF by itself, once, at its first start. If they are missing, add them:

Web UI: Images, Firmware catalog: Pull (or Import for the host’s OVMF). Firmware you have appears under Firmware.

gxctl:

gxctl image pull --firmware cloudhv-edk2
gxctl image pull --firmware ovmf

gxctl image catalog lists the firmware catalog after the cloud images, with a hint when a host package is missing.

Other firmware builds can be pulled by URL: in Download from URL choose UEFI firmware (.fd) and For hypervisor; or

gxctl image pull https://fw.example.org/OVMF_CODE.fd --firmware-for qemu \
  --sha256 <sha256> --vars-url https://fw.example.org/OVMF_VARS.fd --vars-sha256 <sha256>

--vars-url is the variable store that goes with a split OVMF build; each VM gets its own copy of it.

A new VM uses the newest firmware image for its hypervisor unless you pick another when creating it (see Virtual machines).

Kernel images

A VM can also boot a kernel directly, without firmware: a kernel image is a kernel, an optional initramfs and the kernel command line VMs get by default.

From a cloud image. Pulling a catalog image also takes the kernel out of it: a second image, <image>-kernel, appears and becomes ready a few seconds after the image (state extracting meanwhile). It is the kernel the image’s own bootloader would boot, with its initramfs and command line (root=…, then console=ttyS0). To skip it, pull with "with_kernel": false; to take the kernel of any other disk image, including one pulled from a URL:

curl … -X POST /images -d '{"kernel_from": "my-image"}'

or Extract kernel on the image under Images, or gxctl image extract-kernel my-image. gxctl image pull <key> --no-kernel skips it.

glidex reads the image inside a small, network-less VM it builds from pinned Debian packages the first time (a 35 MB download), never on the host. Hosts that can’t download it can turn this off with GLIDEX_KERNEL_EXTRACTION=off.

From a URL:

curl … -X POST /images -d '{
  "url": "https://example.org/vmlinuz-6.8.0-147-generic", "sha256": "<sha256>",
  "kind": "IMAGE_KIND_KERNEL",
  "initrd_url": "https://example.org/initrd.img-6.8.0-147-generic", "initrd_sha256": "<sha256>",
  "cmdline": "root=LABEL=cloudimg-rootfs ro console=ttyS0"
}'

or, for an administrator, from files on the host ("kernel_path", "initrd_path", "cmdline"). Kernel images appear under Images, Kernels, with their release; gxctl image list shows them as kernel <release>. Like firmware, a kernel image can’t be deleted while a VM boots it or keeps it to go back to (409 conflict, naming the VMs).

Use the kernel the cloud image was built with: the guest loads the kernel’s modules from its own disk. Extraction does that for you; for a URL, Ubuntu publishes each build’s kernel and initramfs next to the image, in unpacked/.

Extraction runs on a host of the image’s architecture (x86_64, or aarch64 with Cloud Hypervisor); in a cluster, a server of another architecture hands it to a ready node of the image’s architecture. An aarch64 kernel gets console=ttyAMA0 instead of console=ttyS0; a failed extraction fails only the kernel image (Retry, or gxctl image retry). See Kernel boot to boot VMs from kernel images and to follow the guest’s kernel.

Disks

Creating a disk

Creating a VM from an image already makes its root disk (see Virtual machines). Create disks yourself for data, or to keep a root disk independent of any one VM.

Web UI: Disks, Create Disk:

  • Name: 1-64 characters of letters, digits, ., _ and -. Disk names are unique.
  • Contents: Blank disk, or an image.
  • Size (GiB): required for a blank disk. From an image it defaults to the image’s size or 10 GiB, whichever is larger, and can’t be smaller than the image.
  • Format: qcow2 (default) or raw. On a block datastore (LVM-thin or hyperstor) the form shows raw (block volume) instead: such disks are always raw.
  • Clone (from an image): Linked or Full copy. A raw disk on any other datastore can only be a full copy.
  • Datastore: where the disk lives, shown once the operator has registered more than local (Datastores). The default is preselected and marked (default).

gxctl:

gxctl disk create data1 --size-gib 50                    # blank qcow2
gxctl disk create web-root --image ubuntu-24.04 --size-gib 20
gxctl disk create web-root2 --image ubuntu-24.04 --full --raw
gxctl disk create data2 --size-gib 50 --datastore nfs1   # on a datastore other than the default

When a disk is made from an image and given more space than the image has, Glidex extends its root partition to fill it (the guest grows the filesystem when it boots). --no-extend leaves the partition as it is.

If the image is still downloading, the disk waits for it. On a shared datastore, a linked disk also waits while the image is copied into the datastore.

A datastore whose operator turned overcommit off refuses a disk that doesn’t fit in its free space (507 insufficient_storage).

Clone modes

  • Linked (default for qcow2): a thin overlay on the image. Fast and small, but the image must stay as long as the disk exists.
  • Full: an independent copy. Needed for raw disks, except on a block datastore, where a linked disk is a raw thin snapshot (LVM-thin) or clone (hyperstor) of the image.

Listing and inspecting disks

gxctl disk list
gxctl disk show web-root      # size, format, partitions, free space at the end

disk list shows the disks of the selected project (see Choosing a project), with their size, format, origin, status and the VM each is attached to. In the web UI, click a disk’s name for its details and partitions.

Attaching a disk to a VM

A disk is attached to one VM at a time.

  • As the root disk when you create a VM: in the web UI choose Boot Disk, Existing disk; in gxctl create answer disk at Boot disk from.

  • As a data disk: gxctl create asks for Data disks (disk names, comma-separated). For an existing VM, pick a free disk of the project under Disks on the VM’s page and click Attach, or:

    gxctl> attach-disk my-vm data1
gxctl> detach-disk my-vm data1

    Over the API, POST /vms/<vm-id>/disks with {"disk": "data1"} attaches it and DELETE /vms/<vm-id>/disks/<disk> detaches it (see Data disks).

    On a running VM either change takes effect the next time the VM starts. Detach next to the disk on the VM’s page detaches it too; the disk and its data stay. A disk detached from a running VM stays attached to it until the VM stops (or is deleted), and can be deleted from then on.

Growing and shrinking

Web UI: Disks, Resize, enter the New size (GiB). When growing a disk made from an image, Extend the root partition into the new space is ticked.

gxctl:

gxctl disk resize web-root 40               # grow, and extend the root partition
gxctl disk resize data1 100 --no-extend     # grow, leave the partitions alone
gxctl disk resize data1 30                  # shrink
  • Growing counts against the project’s disk_gib quota.
  • Shrinking only gives back unpartitioned space at the end of the disk; Glidex never shrinks filesystems. A size that would cut into a partition is refused with the smallest size allowed.
  • A resize of a disk a running VM uses is recorded and applied once the VM stops.
  • A disk on a block datastore (LVM-thin or hyperstor) can only grow; shrinking it is refused (400 invalid_disk).

To grow the root partition into space that is already there (say, after a resize with --no-extend):

gxctl disk extend-root web-root             # from the host, once no running VM uses the disk
gxctl disk extend-root web-root --on-boot   # by the guest, at its next boot

In the web UI it is Extend root on the disk’s row. --on-boot relies on the cloud-init seed Glidex generates; a VM with a custom seed has to grow the partition itself (see Guest credentials).

Deleting a disk

Web UI: Disks, Delete (disabled while the disk is attached).

gxctl:

gxctl disk rm data1

It asks for confirmation; the disk’s data is gone afterwards. A disk attached to a VM can’t be deleted: detach it or delete the VM first. A disk that is still being made (a create that is copying, or retrying after a failure) can be deleted: the delete is taken, and the disk goes once the running attempt ends. A disk busy with a resize, move or root-partition extension refuses it (409 conflict, disk … is busy (…)). A root disk that was created along with a VM is deleted with the VM, unless you delete the VM with --keep-disk (in the web UI, Keep disk in the delete dialog); a kept disk is then like any other and can be deleted. The VM’s page lists its disks and marks that one deleted with the VM.

Where a disk lives

A disk lives on a datastore. On the built-in local, or another datastore each node has its own of, it lives on one node: the node of the first VM that uses it, and its VMs run there. On a shared datastore (one filesystem every node mounts), it is tied to no node, and its VM can run on any node that reaches the datastore; disk access then goes over the network. A hyperstor datastore is shared in the same way. The Disks page has a Datastore column once there is more than local; gxctl disk show names it too (local, or the datastore’s id). The Datastores page, and gxctl datastore list, show every datastore, the default, and its free space of its total (the most any node reports; — while no node reports it).

In a cluster, the Disks page’s Node column shows a disk’s node, shared · <node> for a disk on a shared datastore (the node currently working on it), or unbound for a node-local disk no VM has used yet.

Over the API, node (a node’s name or id) binds a new disk on a node-local datastore to that node when it is created; an unknown node is refused with 400 invalid_config, and a disk on a shared datastore can’t be bound to a node (400 invalid_disk).

A VM’s root disk made along with the VM goes to the default datastore. To put it on another, create the disk first with --datastore (or the Datastore field) and create the VM from that disk.

Disks on an LVM-thin datastore

An LVM-thin datastore keeps each disk as a raw volume in a volume group on one node (see LVM-thin). Like other node-local disks, it lives on one node and its VMs run there. What differs:

  • Always raw. Leave the format out (gxctl disk create does) and the disk is raw; asking for qcow2 is refused (400 invalid_disk, disks on a block datastore (lvm, hyperstor) are raw volumes; leave format out). In the web UI, the form shows Format as raw on such a datastore, and offers both Linked and Full copy.
  • Linked or full. A linked disk (the default with gxctl) is a thin snapshot of the image on that node: quick to make, and small until the guest writes. A full disk is an independent copy. Either way the image stays as long as a linked disk uses it.
  • Grow, never shrink. gxctl disk resize to a larger size works as usual, root partition included; a smaller size is refused.
  • Moves make full, raw copies. Moving a disk onto an LVM-thin datastore, or off one, always copies it whole: Flatten makes no difference. On the volume group it becomes raw; moved off to a directory it stays raw.
gxctl disk create db-root --image ubuntu-24.04 --size-gib 40 --datastore thin1   # linked, raw
gxctl disk create db-data --size-gib 200 --datastore thin1
gxctl disk move data1 --datastore thin1

Disks on a hyperstor datastore

A hyperstor datastore keeps each disk as a volume of a hyperstor cluster’s pool, replicated across that cluster’s nodes (see Hyperstor). Like a disk on a shared filesystem, it is tied to no node: its VM runs on any node that reaches the datastore. What differs from a disk file:

  • Always raw, as on LVM-thin: leave the format out; qcow2 is refused (400 invalid_disk).
  • Linked or full. A linked disk is a hyperstor clone of the image’s volume in that datastore, made at once. The image is written into that volume the first time a linked disk needs it.
  • Grow, never shrink, root partition included.
  • No moves yet onto or off the datastore.
  • A full pool refuses new disks with 507 insufficient_storage, whether or not overcommit is on. Disks already there keep working.
gxctl disk create app-root --image ubuntu-24.04 --size-gib 40 --datastore hs1   # linked, raw

Moving a disk

A disk can move to another datastore while no running VM uses it (stop the VM first, or detach the disk). Its data is copied and checked, then the old file is removed; if the move fails, the disk stays where it was.

Web UI: Disks, Move on the disk’s row (shown when there is more than one datastore): pick the datastore. For a linked disk, Flatten makes it a full copy instead of an overlay on the image there.

gxctl:

gxctl disk move data1 --datastore nfs1
gxctl disk move web-root --datastore fast --flatten

It waits up to five minutes and prints the disk, or that it is still moving; follow it with gxctl disk show. A linked disk moved to a shared datastore waits for the image to be copied there first.

While a disk moves, the Disks page shows it · moving, with Resize and Move disabled. Resizing it is refused (409 conflict), adding it to a VM’s data disks is refused (400 invalid_config), and a VM using it waits to start (condition DisksReady False, reason DiskNotReady) until the move is done.

Moving needs the editor role in the disk’s project, and the right to use the destination datastore. It is refused:

  • for a disk that is being deleted, already moving, not ready, or used by a running VM (409 conflict);
  • for the datastore the disk is already on, or one that the node with the disk, or its VM’s node, doesn’t reach (400 invalid_disk);
  • for an unknown datastore (404 not_found);
  • when the destination has overcommit off and lacks the space (507 insufficient_storage).

Onto or off an LVM-thin datastore, a disk is always copied whole; see Disks on an LVM-thin datastore. Disks can’t move onto or off a hyperstor datastore yet: the move fails (disk … can’t be moved onto a hyperstor datastore yet) and the disk stays where it was.

Moving a disk from one node’s own storage to another node’s isn’t possible directly: move it to a shared datastore, then from there. A disk on a shared datastore lets its VM move between nodes (see Placement on a cluster).

Over the API

api() { curl --cacert host.crt -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' "$@"; }
api -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/images -d '{"catalog": "ubuntu-24.04"}'
api -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/disks -d '{"name": "data1", "project": "lab", "size_gib": 50}'
api -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/disks -d '{"name": "data2", "project": "lab", "size_gib": 50, "datastore": "nfs1"}'
api -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/disks/data1/resize -d '{"size_gib": 100}'
api -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/disks/data1/move -d '{"datastore": "nfs1", "wait_secs": 300}'
api -X DELETE https://host.example.org:8841/disks/data1

See the REST API for every field.

Guest credentials

Distro cloud images ship with no usable login: they wait for cloud-init to create one on first boot. Glidex stores the logins you want as credentials and hands the one a VM names to cloud-init.

A credential is a Linux username with a password, SSH public keys, or both. Credentials belong to a project and are used by that project’s VMs; seeing and managing them needs the editor role.

How a credential reaches the guest

When a VM boots a cloud image through UEFI firmware, Glidex writes a small cloud-init seed volume for it (NoCloud, labelled CIDATA) and attaches it. From the VM’s credential, cloud-init creates the user in the guest:

  • with passwordless sudo and /bin/bash;
  • with the credential’s password, and SSH password logins on, if it has one; the password locked otherwise;
  • with the credential’s SSH keys as authorized_keys.

The seed also sets the guest’s hostname from the VM’s name, turns on DHCP on each of its network interfaces, and grows the root filesystem to fill its partition.

cloud-init applies the user on the VM’s first boot only. Changing or deleting a credential later does not change VMs that already booted; change the login inside those guests instead.

VMs without a credential

A VM created without a credential still gets a seed, with the guest user cloud, no SSH keys and a locked password: nobody can log in, on the network or on the console. Glidex never adds keys or passwords of its own. Pick a credential when you create the VM (see Virtual machines).

Adding a credential

Web UI: Credentials, Add Credential:

  • Username: lowercase letters, digits, _ and -, starting with a letter or _, at most 32 characters.
  • Password and Confirm (optional): 8 to 256 characters.
  • SSH public keys (optional): one OpenSSH public key per line (ssh-ed25519 AAAA… alice@laptop).
