A password, a key, or both is required. If you have a local account on the host, the form fills in your username and the public keys in your ~/.ssh/*.pub.

SSH keys from your organisation’s directory

If you sign in through your organisation’s Google Workspace, your operator may have Glidex read your SSH public keys from your Google account (see SSH keys from Google). Then Add Credential fills those keys in, and says Filled in from your directory account; choose the username yourself.

  • Your keys are kept in Google: ask whoever manages your Google account to add or change them. Glidex picks up a change at its next read, every 15 minutes unless the operator chose otherwise.
  • Only public keys are used; anything else in that field is ignored.
  • A local account on the host comes first: if you have one, the form offers the keys in its ~/.ssh/*.pub instead, even if there are none.
  • The keys are copied into the credential when you save it, like keys you paste. Changing them in Google later doesn’t change the credential, nor VMs that already booted with it: replace the credential’s keys with Edit, and change authorized_keys inside those guests yourself.
  • gxctl credential-add doesn’t use them: it offers the .pub files of the machine you run it on.

gxctl:

$ gxctl credential-add
Username [alice]:
Leave the password empty for SSH-key-only login.
Password:
Confirm password:
SSH public key files (comma-separated; 'none' for no keys) [~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub]:
Credential created: alice (password: set, SSH keys: 1)

It offers your login name and your own ~/.ssh/*.pub files as defaults. Give .pub files, never private keys: gxctl refuses a file that holds a private key.

The credential goes into the selected project (see Choosing a project); use gxctl --project lab credential-add for another.

These usernames are refused because distro images already have them: root, ubuntu, daemon, bin, sys, sync, games, man, lp, mail, news, uucp, proxy, www-data, backup, list, irc, nobody, systemd-network, systemd-resolve, messagebus, sshd and syslog.

Listing, changing and deleting credentials

Web UI: Credentials lists each username, whether it has a password, its number of SSH keys and when it changed. Edit sets a new password (leave it empty to keep the current one) or replaces the keys; Delete removes it.

gxctl:

gxctl credentials                 # list
gxctl credential-passwd alice     # set a new password (asked twice, hidden)
gxctl credential-keys alice       # replace the SSH keys; empty removes them all
gxctl credential-rm alice

A credential must keep a password or at least one key, and can’t be deleted while a VM uses it.

Passwords are hashed (SHA-512-crypt) as soon as they arrive. Glidex never stores, logs or returns the password itself, and the API never returns the hash; the lists only say whether a password is set.

Using a credential

When you create a VM that boots a cloud image:

  • Web UI: choose it under Login Credential. If the project has a credential with your username, it is preselected.
  • gxctl create: answer the Login credential prompt; the default is the credential named like you, if there is one, and none creates the VM without a login.
  • API: "credential": "alice" in POST /vms.

A credential only works with the seed Glidex generates: a VM that brings its own seed (cloud_init_path), or boots host kernel files with a root filesystem file path, can’t use one. A kernel image or a managed boot disk gets the seed as with firmware.

Your own cloud-init seed

To provision a guest your own way (other users, packages, files), give the VM a cloud-init seed image you made, instead of the generated one: gxctl create asks for a cloud-init seed image, and the API takes "cloud_init_path": "/srv/seeds/web.img". The control plane then attaches that file as it is.

  • It is a path on the host, opened by the control plane: it needs the host-wide grant.host-paths permission (ask an administrator), and the file must be readable by the service (under the systemd units, not in your home directory or /tmp).
  • The VM can’t use a credential, and Glidex doesn’t add networking, hostname or root-partition growth: put what you need in the seed.

A seed is what cloud-init’s NoCloud datasource reads: a small FAT or ISO volume labelled CIDATA (or cidata) holding user-data and meta-data (and optionally network-config). Make one with cloud-localds from the cloud-image-utils package, or with mkfs.vfat -C -n cidata seed.img 2048 and mcopy -i seed.img user-data meta-data :: (from dosfstools and mtools).

Over the API

api() { curl --cacert host.crt -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' "$@"; }
api -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/credentials \
  -d '{"project": "lab", "username": "alice", "ssh_authorized_keys": ["ssh-ed25519 AAAA… alice@laptop"]}'
api 'https://host.example.org:8841/credentials?project=lab'
api -X DELETE 'https://host.example.org:8841/credentials/alice?project=lab'

See the REST API for updating a credential.

Virtual machines

A VM belongs to one project. You create it stopped (or ask for it to start at once), then start, pause, stop and delete it. Each of these changes the VM’s desired state; the control plane then works until the VM gets there. See Concepts for the model.

In the web UI, the VMs page lists the VMs of the selected project. Click a VM for its details, actions, usage and events.

In gxctl, commands take a VM’s name or id. Names are unique within a project; use --project <p> (or project use <p>) when the same name exists in two projects you can see.

gxctl> list                       # the VMs: id, name, project, state, node, vCPUs, memory, hypervisor
gxctl> get my-vm                  # one VM: state, last exit, NICs and their addresses

Before you start

A VM that boots a cloud image needs:

  • an image (or an existing disk made from one), and a firmware image for the hypervisor. See Images and disks;
  • a guest credential, or the VM has no way to log in. See Guest credentials;
  • a network your project may use, or the VM has no NIC. See Networks.

You need the editor role in the project to create, change and delete VMs, and operator to start, stop and pause them and to open their consoles. See Projects.

Create a VM

Web UI

On the VMs page, click + Create VM and fill in the form. The fields come in this order:

FieldWhat it is
VM NameThe VM’s name in the project.
Hypervisor BackendCloud Hypervisor (the default), QEMU or Pylon. Fixed once created.
vCPU Count, Memory (MiB)Defaults 1 vCPU and 1024 MiB. On Pylon with Elastic CPU scaling, the vCPU count is the maximum and can’t be edited.
Elastic CPU scalingMin vCPUs, max vCPUs and weight. See Elastic CPU.
GPUs (optional)A count from each GPU pool your project may use (it sizes the VM; see GPUs), and the node’s own GPUs to tick: those ready for passthrough and held by no other VM can be ticked, the others are greyed and say why not. In a cluster, the node’s GPUs appear once a node is chosen under Placement.
Boot DiskNew disk from an image, Existing disk (an unattached disk of the project), or Disk image file path.
Image, Root disk (GiB)For a new disk from an image: a linked disk is created for this VM, its root partition extended, and deleted with the VM.
Login CredentialA credential of the project, provisioned by cloud-init on first boot; or none.
Service Account (optional)Shown when the project has service accounts: the identity software in the VM gets glidex tokens for. See Workload identity.
NetworksOne NIC per ticked network, in that order. A network named default, or else the project’s only network, is ticked for you.
Device Pools (optional)How many devices to take from each pool other than GPU pools (NICs, NVMe…) your project may use.
PlacementClusters only: Automatic, or a node. See Placement on a cluster.
Advanced optionsFolded away; its heading shows the boot mode and firmware or kernel chosen. It opens by itself when a choice in it is missing (no firmware image for the hypervisor, say). It holds the fields below.
Boot ModeUEFI firmware (distro cloud image) or Direct kernel boot.
UEFI FirmwareThe firmware image to boot through; the newest one for the hypervisor and the VM’s architecture is preselected.
VFIO PCI Devices (optional)Other host PCI devices to pass through, by path. See Devices.
If It CrashesRestart it (with backoff) or Leave it stopped.
After a Host RebootStart it again if it was running or Leave it stopped.
Start it nowStart the VM as soon as it is created.

With Direct kernel boot, the form asks for a Kernel instead of UEFI Firmware: a kernel image (the one taken from the chosen image comes first and is the only one preselected; Extract it from the image makes it if there is none. Another image’s kernel usually won’t boot this one: its initramfs waits for that image’s root disk), or, for administrators, Kernel files on the host (administrators) (kernel and initramfs paths, see Host paths). Kernel Arguments default to the kernel image’s own command line. Follow the guest’s kernel boots the kernel the guest installs (see Kernel boot). The boot disk and login credential work as with firmware.

On the VM’s page, Kernel shows the kernel image (and, when following the guest, the kernel it boots and the one before), lets you pick another one with Use from the next start, and Extract from its disk now while the VM is stopped.

gxctl

create asks for each setting in turn; press Enter to take the default in brackets.

gxctl> create
VM name: web-1
GPUs (count[:pool][:nvlink], e.g. 4:a100; sizes the VM from the pool; optional):
vCPU count [1]: 2
Memory (MiB) [512]: 2048
Hypervisor [cloudhypervisor/qemu/pylon] (default: cloudhypervisor):
Configure elastic CPU scaling (min/max vCPUs, weight)? [y/N] [n]:
UEFI firmware [cloudhv-edk2, 'kernel' for direct kernel boot, or a host path] [cloudhv-edk2]:
Boot disk from [image/disk/path] [image]:
Image (ubuntu-26.04) [ubuntu-26.04]:
Root disk size in GiB [10]: 20
Data disks (optional, comma-separated disk names):
cloud-init seed image (optional, default: auto-generated):
Login credential (one of: alice; 'none' for no login) [alice]:
Networks (comma-separated; available: default, lab; 'none' for no NIC) [default]:
VFIO PCI devices (comma-separated, e.g. /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0):
Device pools (comma-separated pool[:count], e.g. a100:2; optional):

For a direct kernel boot, answer kernel at the firmware prompt: gxctl then asks for a kernel image (the one from the boot image is the default), whether to follow the guest’s kernel, and offers the kernel’s command line as the default arguments. Later, kernel web-1 shows the VM’s kernel; kernel web-1 --set <image> and --follow on|off change it from the next start, and --extract takes the kernel on its disk.

The VM is created stopped; start it with start web-1. gxctl create doesn’t ask for a node, a restart policy or a host-boot policy: they take their defaults (use the web UI or the API to set them).

API

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/vms -d '{
    "name": "web-1", "vcpu_count": 2, "mem_size_mib": 2048,
    "image": "ubuntu-26.04", "root_disk_size_gib": 20,
    "credential": "alice", "networks": [{"network": "lab"}],
    "power": "POWER_STATE_RUNNING"
  }'

name, vcpu_count and mem_size_mib are required (with gpus, only name: see GPUs). Values from a fixed list take their full names, as in the table below (POWER_STATE_RUNNING, not running); a short name is refused with 422 (see Proto JSON). See REST API for every field.

VM settings

SettingAPI fieldNotes
NamenameUnique in the project. The generated cloud-init seed makes it the guest’s hostname.
ProjectprojectId or name; default: your default project.
vCPUsvcpu_countAt least 1. Changeable; applies at the next start, or live within an elastic VM’s range. On an elastic Pylon VM it is always max_vcpus. See Elastic CPU.
Elastic vCPUsmin_vcpus, max_vcpusmin_vcpus ≤ vcpu_count ≤ max_vcpus. Absent: both are vcpu_count (a fixed size). See Elastic CPU.
CPU weightcpu_weight1 to 10000, default 100: the VM’s share of contended host CPU.
Memorymem_size_mibIn MiB, at least 1. Changeable; applies at the next start.
HypervisorhypervisorHYPERVISOR_CLOUD_HYPERVISOR (default), HYPERVISOR_QEMU or HYPERVISOR_PYLON. Fixed.
Boot diskimage, root_disk or rootfs_pathExactly one. Fixed. See below.
Root disk sizeroot_disk_size_gibWith image only. Default: the image’s size, at least 10 GiB.
FirmwarefirmwareA firmware image (name or id). Fixed.
Kernel bootkernel, or kernel_image_path and initrd_path; kernel_argsInstead of firmware (not both). A kernel image (kernel) can be changed and applies at the next start; host paths are fixed; arguments changeable.
Follow the guest’s kernelkernel_from_diskWith kernel and image or root_disk: boot the kernel the guest installed. See Following the guest’s kernel. Changeable; applies at the next start.
Generate seedgenerate_seedOverrides whether Glidex generates the cloud-init seed; not with cloud_init_path. Fixed.
CredentialcredentialA credential of the project. Needs the generated cloud-init seed: firmware boot, or kernel boot of a kernel image or a managed root disk, without cloud_init_path.
NetworksnetworksUp to 8 NICs, in order. Changeable; applies at the next start.
Data disksdata_disksDisks of the project, attached after the boot disk. Changeable; applies at the next start.
PCI devicesvfio_devicesChangeable while the VM runs.
Restart policyrestart_policyRESTART_POLICY_ON_FAILURE (default) or RESTART_POLICY_NEVER. Changeable.
On host booton_host_bootHOST_BOOT_POLICY_RESUME (default) or HOST_BOOT_POLICY_STOP. Changeable.
Stop gracestop_grace_secsSeconds a stop waits after the power button; 0 (default) stops at once; at most 300. Changeable.
Initial powerpowerPOWER_STATE_STOPPED (default), POWER_STATE_RUNNING or POWER_STATE_PAUSED.
NodenodeClusters: pin the VM to a node (name or id). Fixed, except by placing the VM again.
HugepageshugepagesBack guest memory with hugepages. Changeable; applies at the next start.
Hugepage sizehugepage_size2M or 1G, with hugepages; the memory must be a whole number of pages. Default: the host’s default size (usually 2M). Changeable; applies at the next start.
NUMA policynuma_policyNUMA_POLICY_NONE (default), NUMA_POLICY_PREFERRED or NUMA_POLICY_STRICT: keep the VM’s memory, CPUs and PCI devices on one host NUMA node; NUMA_POLICY_ALIGNED: across exactly its devices’ NUMA nodes. See NUMA and dedicated CPUs. Changeable; applies at the next start.
GPUsgpus{"count": 4, "pool": "a100"}: that many GPUs, NUMA-aligned, the VM sized from the pool unless you size it. See GPUs. Fixed: change devices and the sizing instead.
Device poolsdevices[{"pool": "a100", "count": 1, "same_switch": false}]: devices the scheduler picks from a pool your project may use; shown as pool_devices. See Devices from a pool. Changeable; applies at the next start.
CPU policycpu_policyCPU_POLICY_SHARED (default) or CPU_POLICY_DEDICATED: each vCPU on a host CPU of its own. Changeable; applies at the next start.

Boot disk

Give exactly one of:

  • image: Glidex creates a linked root disk from the image for this VM (named <vm>-root) on the default datastore, grows it to root_disk_size_gib, and extends the guest’s root partition at first boot. The disk belongs to the VM and is deleted with it, unless you delete with --keep-disk. To put it on another datastore, create the disk first (gxctl disk create … --datastore) and give it as root_disk.
  • root_disk: an existing, unattached disk of the project (name or id). It is not deleted with the VM.
  • rootfs_path: a disk image file on the host, used as is.

The image (or the root disk’s image) and the firmware must be for the same CPU architecture.

Firmware or kernel boot

A VM with an image or root_disk boots through UEFI firmware: the newest firmware image for its hypervisor (and architecture), unless you name one with firmware. If there is none, the create fails and tells you which one to pull (cloudhv-edk2 for Cloud Hypervisor, ovmf for QEMU).

For a direct kernel boot, name a kernel image with kernel instead. The VM then needs no firmware image, gets the kernel image’s command line as its default kernel_args, and works with image, root_disk and a login credential exactly like a firmware boot: glidex generates the same cloud-init seed. A kernel image comes from a URL (POST /images with "kind": "IMAGE_KIND_KERNEL", initrd_url and cmdline), or an administrator copies one from host files (kernel_path, initrd_path). It should be the kernel the cloud image was built with: its modules are on the image’s disk.

Following the guest’s kernel. With "kernel_from_disk": true (a VM booting a kernel image from a managed disk), glidex takes the kernel out of the VM’s disk again before a start whenever the disk changed, so a kernel the guest installed (apt upgrade) boots next time. The VM shows booted_kernel and previous_kernel; if extraction fails, it boots the kernel it has and says so (KernelExtracted). To go back, set kernel (to the previous_kernel, say), which turns following off. POST /vms/<id>/extract-kernel does one extraction on demand, for a stopped VM, as a new kernel image you can then set as kernel.

An administrator can also give host paths: kernel_image_path (and a root filesystem in rootfs_path), plus initrd_path if the kernel needs an initramfs (distro kernels do). With host paths, or a kernel image without a command line, the default kernel arguments are console=ttyS0 root=/dev/vda reboot=k panic=1 on both hypervisors. The console is on the serial port, unless the last console= in the arguments names hvc… (such as hvc0), which selects the virtio console. A distro cloud image needs its own root, e.g. console=ttyS0 root=LABEL=cloudimg-rootfs ro for Ubuntu. See Kernel boot for kernel images, the command line, the console and following the guest’s kernel.

Host paths

rootfs_path, kernel_image_path, initrd_path, cloud_init_path and firmware_path name files on the host. Using them needs the system-admin role, and the files must be readable by the service user the control plane runs as. Most users should use images, disks and firmware images instead. A path under /tmp or /var/tmp is refused: VMs have a private /tmp.

Credential and cloud-init

Without cloud_init_path, Glidex generates a cloud-init seed for a VM that boots through firmware, or that boots a kernel image or from image or root_disk (kernel boot): its hostname, the root partition grow, and, if you name a credential, that user with its password and SSH keys. cloud-init applies it on the VM’s first boot. Without a credential the guest has no login. See Guest credentials.

cloud_init_path replaces the generated seed with your own (a host path, see above); a credential can’t be combined with it.

Workload identity

Software in a VM can prove which VM it is, and act as a service account, without any secret stored in the guest. It asks the metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254, which only answers from inside the VM, with the header Metadata-Flavor: Glidex:

H='Metadata-Flavor: Glidex'
curl -s -H "$H" http://169.254.169.254/v1/instance          # which VM this is
curl -s -H "$H" 'http://169.254.169.254/v1/identity?audience=sts.amazonaws.com'
curl -s -H "$H" http://169.254.169.254/v1/glidex/token      # needs a service account
  • Identity tokens are short-lived JWTs (15 minutes; ask for 10 to 60 with &ttl=<seconds>) for the audience you name, signed by your directory. Their subject is the VM’s SPIFFE ID, spiffe://<trust domain>/tenant/<t>/project/<p>/vm/<id>. Outside services that trust your directory’s issuer (AWS, Vault, Kubernetes, or glidex itself) can verify them against its published keys.
  • Glidex tokens act as the VM’s service account, for 15 minutes, with that account’s roles. Give a VM one in the create form, on its page, with gxctl service-account <vm> --set <account>, or with "service_account" in POST /vms. That needs the right to manage the account’s project’s service tokens (project owners), and needs no restart: the next token is for the new account. The endpoint hands out the same token until 80% of its life has passed, then a fresh one, so ask again whenever you need one.
  • An identity token addressed to your cluster can also be exchanged for a glidex token at POST /auth/exchange with federation=<tenant>/vm.
  • Every process in the guest can ask, as on any cloud. Requests through a proxy in the guest (Forwarded, X-Forwarded-For) are refused.

The endpoint serves VMs on single-host NAT networks, on any node of a cluster; OVN networks and isolated or bridged networks come later. A NAT network’s guests reach the host’s own API only if the network allows it (The host from a NAT network).

Networks

Each entry of networks adds one NIC, in order (at most 8):

"networks": [
  {"network": "lab"},
  {"network": "storage", "mac": "02:00:00:00:10:01", "queue_pairs": 2}
]

network is a network’s name or id that your project may use. mac is optional: by default each NIC gets a stable MAC derived from the VM’s id. queue_pairs (1 to 8) is optional. The address each NIC got shows in the VM’s details. See Networks.

Data disks

data_disks lists disks of the project (names or ids), attached in order after the boot disk. A disk is attached to one VM at a time.

To attach or detach a disk later: under Disks on the VM’s page, pick a free disk of the project and Attach, or Detach one; or

gxctl> attach-disk my-vm data-1
gxctl> detach-disk my-vm data-1

or with the API:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/vms/<id>/disks -d '{"disk": "data-1"}'
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" \
  -X DELETE https://host.example.org:8841/vms/<id>/disks/data-1

On a running VM the change applies at the next start (gxctl says so). See Images and disks.

PCI devices

vfio_devices passes host PCI devices (a GPU, a NIC) through to the guest. Give each as /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0 or the bare address 0000:41:00.0. Using one needs a grant from an administrator. See PCI passthrough.

A device is used by one VM at a time on its host, and it takes its IOMMU group with it (devices that the host can only pass through together). Asking for a device another VM on the host holds is refused with 409 conflict:

  • PCI device 0000:41:00.0 is used by VM other-vm: that VM has it, or its running instance still does.
  • PCI device 0000:41:00.1 shares IOMMU group 31 with 0000:41:00.0, used by VM other-vm: another device of the group is that VM’s. A VM that already holds a device of the group may add the others.
gxctl> pci                                          # host PCI devices
gxctl> attach-device my-vm /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0
gxctl> detach-device my-vm /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0

On a running VM, devices are hot-plugged. On a paused VM, the change waits until it runs again.

Devices from a pool

Instead of naming devices, ask for a number of them from a device pool your project may use; Glidex picks which. To see the pools and how many devices are free:

gxctl> pci pools --project lab        # pool, class, free

In the web UI’s create form, Device Pools (optional) lists them with their free counts: set how many devices to take from each, and tick Under one PCIe switch to keep several together (for GPUs that talk to each other). gxctl create asks for them as a100:2 or a100:2:switch. Over the API:

"devices": [{"pool": "a100", "count": 2, "same_switch": true}]

The picked devices are on the NUMA node of the VM’s other devices when they can be, and show as pool_devices (gxctl get <vm> and the VM’s page list each request with what it got). The VM gets them at its next start and keeps them until the request changes or the VM is deleted. Asking needs a grant for the pool:

  • no device pool a100 (400): no such pool for this project.
  • forbidden (403): the project may not use the pool.
  • quota_exceeded with resource devices.a100: the project’s quota for the pool is used up (see Quotas). tenant_quota_exceeded with tenant_pool.<name>: a tenant pool’s maximum is reached.
  • pool a100: 1 of 2 free: not enough free devices. On a cluster the VM waits for them; on a single host it is refused (409).

A pool your tenant set up for some of its projects (a tenant pool) is asked for by its own name; the VM shows the cluster pool it draws from and tenant_pool. Devices from pools are metered (device.alloc.<pool>, see Usage).

GPUs

For GPUs there’s a shorter way: ask for a count, and the pool places and sizes the VM.

{"name": "train-1", "image": "ubuntu-24.04", "credential": "alice",
 "gpus": {"count": 4, "pool": "a100"}}

gpus is filled in when the VM is created:

FieldFrom gpusWhen you give it yourself
devices{"pool": "a100", "count": 4}Refused if devices asks the same pool.
numa_policyNUMA_POLICY_ALIGNED (see NUMA and dedicated CPUs)Yours is kept.
vcpu_count, mem_size_mibThe pool’s per-device vCPUs and memory, times the countYours are kept.
hugepages, cpu_policyThe pool’s, when the operator set themYours are kept.
  • The pool: a cluster pool or a tenant pool by name. Without pool, the project’s only GPU pool is used.
  • Sizing: what each GPU brings is set by the operator. The web UI shows it next to the pool (14 vCPUs and 56 GiB each), and GET /pci-pools?project=<p> as per_device_vcpus and per_device_memory_mib. A pool without it needs vcpu_count and mem_size_mib.
  • Quotas and metering are those of the pool’s devices (devices.a100, device.alloc.a100).
  • On the VM: it keeps gpus and shows what it came to: devices and pool_devices, the policies, the sizing, and for GPUs on several NUMA nodes each node’s share (numa). gxctl get <vm> prints GPUs: 4 from a100 and a NUMA <i>: line per guest NUMA node; the VM’s page shows NUMA layout.
  • Changing it: gpus can’t be changed (PATCH refuses it). Change devices, vcpu_count and mem_size_mib instead; they apply at the next start.
  • Placement preview: POST /scheduler/preview takes gpus too, and shows each node’s split.

gxctl: create asks GPUs right after the name: 4, 4:a100. With GPUs, an empty vCPU or memory answer takes the pool’s sizing.

Web UI: the GPUs section, right after the VM’s size:

  • From a pool: the count of the first GPU pool is sent as gpus, and fills in the vCPU and memory fields from the pool until you change them by hand. A GPU pool with Under one PCIe switch ticked is an ordinary pool request instead, without the NUMA alignment or the sizing.
  • This node’s GPUs (Or pick this node’s GPUs, under the pools): each display-class device the node could pass through, with its address, vendor, ids and NUMA node. A ticked one is sent in vfio_devices. One not ready is greyed with the reason (for example not bound to vfio-pci (driver: amdgpu)): an operator prepares it on the node’s page. One another VM holds is greyed with its name (PCI device 0000:43:00.0 is used by VM gpu-a), whatever project that VM is in; a stopped VM keeps its GPUs. Listing them needs a host role on that node; without one, only pools are shown. These GPUs don’t size the VM.

Refusals (400 invalid_config):

MessageWhy
gpus: count must be at least 1A count of 0.
gpus: no device pool h100No such pool for this project.
gpus: name the pool, one of a100, t4The project may use several GPU pools.
gpus: this project may use no GPU poolNo pool given, and no GPU pool is granted to the project.
gpus: give vcpu_count and mem_size_mib, or set per_device on pool a100The pool has no per-device sizing.
gpus and devices both ask pool a100Ask the pool in one place.
gpus: NVLink needs a fabric …, and pool … has none"nvlink": true (4:a100:nvlink in gxctl). NVLink between passed-through GPUs isn’t available yet; leave nvlink out, and it is false.

A pool the project may not use is refused as with devices (403 forbidden), and so are quotas.

Lifecycle

ActionWeb UIgxctlAPI
StartStartstart <vm>POST /vms/{id}/start
Resume a paused VMResumestart <vm>POST /vms/{id}/start
PausePausepause <vm>POST /vms/{id}/pause
Graceful stopShut downstop <vm> --graceful [secs]POST /vms/{id}/stop?graceful_timeout_secs=60
Immediate stopForce offstop <vm>POST /vms/{id}/stop
DeleteDeletedelete <vm> [--keep-disk]DELETE /vms/{id}
Place a stopped or lost VM on another node (system-admin)Place on another nodeplace <vm> [--node N]POST /vms/{id}/place

gxctl waits up to 60 seconds for the VM to get there (longer for a graceful stop) and prints the state it reached; --no-wait returns at once. If the VM isn’t there yet, it says what it is waiting for. The web UI follows the VM and shows In progress until it gets there. The API returns at once (202), or, with ?wait=<secs> (at most 300), once the VM got there. See Waiting for the controller.

Starting a stopped VM counts against the project’s running-VM quota.

Stop

A graceful stop presses the guest’s power button, waits for the guest to shut down, and stops the VM hard if it is still running after the timeout:

gxctl> stop my-vm --graceful          # wait up to 60 s
gxctl> stop my-vm --graceful 120      # wait up to 120 s (at most 300)

The web UI’s Shut down waits 60 seconds. Force off stops the VM like pulling the plug, after you confirm; it also cuts short a shutdown that is still waiting for the guest.

The timeout you give is kept as the VM’s stop grace (stop_grace_secs) and used again by later stops that don’t give one, such as stop without --graceful. Pass --graceful 0 (or graceful_timeout_secs=0) for an immediate stop after a graceful one. The web UI’s Force off always sends 0.

Pause and resume

A paused VM keeps its memory but gets no CPU time. Resume in the web UI, or start in gxctl, runs it again.

Restart

There is no restart action: stop the VM, then start it. A reboot from inside the guest restarts the guest and the VM stays running.

When the VM stops on its own

  • The guest powers off (for example poweroff inside it): the desired state becomes stopped, and the VM stays stopped whatever its restart policy.
  • The hypervisor crashes: with the restart policy on failure, the VM is started again after 10 seconds, doubling with each crash in a row up to 5 minutes; after 10 minutes of running the count starts over. With never, the desired state becomes stopped.
  • It fails to launch: the VM is failed and Glidex retries with a growing delay. Its details and events say why.
  • The host reboots: with the host-boot policy resume, a VM that was running is started again; with stop, it stays stopped.

Change these policies with the API:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X PATCH https://host.example.org:8841/vms/<id> \
  -d '{"change": {"restart_policy": "RESTART_POLICY_NEVER"}, "update_mask": "restart_policy"}'

Change a VM

Change vCPUs, memory, networks, data disks, PCI devices, device pool requests, kernel arguments, the kernel image and following it (kernel, kernel_from_disk), the credential, hugepages and the policies with PATCH /vms/{id}. The body has two fields: change holds the new values, and update_mask lists the fields to change (comma-separated; without it, the fields present in change are changed). Settings outside change are refused:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X PATCH https://host.example.org:8841/vms/<id> \
  -d '{"change": {"vcpu_count": 4, "mem_size_mib": 8192}, "update_mask": "vcpu_count,mem_size_mib"}'

networks and data_disks replace the whole list. The hypervisor, the boot disk, the firmware and host paths can’t be changed.

The web UI and gxctl have no edit form for most settings. Both change the vCPUs and the elastic range (Scale CPU / Elasticity on the VM’s page, gxctl scale; see Elastic CPU), the memory (Change memory on the VM’s page, gxctl memory my-vm 8G) and data disks (Data disks), and gxctl changes PCI devices (attach-device, detach-device).

A change to vCPUs, memory, kernel arguments, the credential, hugepages, policies, device pool requests, networks or data disks of a running VM takes effect at the next start: the web UI says Configuration changes take effect at the next start, and the API sets restart_required. Stop and start the VM to apply it. A new credential doesn’t change logins in a guest that already booted (cloud-init runs once).

Pass the VM’s resource_version in an If-Match header to refuse the change (409) if someone else changed the VM since you read it.

A change to vCPUs, memory, hugepages, policies, devices or networks of a VM that already has a node is fitted again on that node: its hugepages, NUMA node, dedicated CPUs and pool devices are picked again. If it no longer fits there, the change is refused with 409 and the reason, for example node agent1: not enough 2M hugepages (1024 of 2048 MiB taken).

Delete

gxctl> delete my-vm                 # asks for confirmation
gxctl> delete my-vm --keep-disk     # keep the root disk created for it

Deleting stops the VM if it runs, releases its NICs and their addresses, and detaches its disks. A root disk created for the VM from an image is deleted with it, unless you keep it (--keep-disk, ?keep_disk=true, or Keep disk in the web UI’s delete dialog, which names the disks that go and those that stay). Other disks are only detached.

A VM whose root disk is still being made (say, by a create that keeps failing) can be deleted too: its disk starts no new attempt, and the VM goes once the running one ends, taking its own root disk with it.

States and events

The state shows where the VM is; while it is on its way to its desired state, gxctl and the web UI show both, for example stopped → running.

StateMeaning
createdNever started.
startingBeing provisioned or launched.
runningThe guest runs.
pausedThe guest is paused.
stoppingA stop is in progress.
stoppedNot running.
failedIt failed to launch, or crashed and waits to be restarted.
unknownThe control plane can’t tell, for example because the VM’s node stopped reporting.

In the API, states are VM_STATE_RUNNING and so on, and the desired state is desired_state. The VM’s conditions say what is in the way (the Ready condition), and last_exit says how the last run ended: stopped on request, stopped by the host, guest powered off, crashed (with its exit code or signal), failed to launch, host rebooted, or lost.

On a cluster, a VM that boots through a firmware image, or boots a kernel image, needs that image’s copy on its node. Until the node has fetched it, the VM waits with the condition DisksReady False (firmware <name> has not been copied to this node yet, or kernel <name> has not been copied to this node yet), and carries on by itself once the copy is there.

A VM also doesn’t start while one of its disks is being moved to another datastore (DisksReady False, reason DiskNotReady: disk … is moving to datastore …), or while another node holds the lock of a disk on a shared datastore (reason DiskBusy: disk … is in use elsewhere (… is locked)). See Volume locks.

Each VM keeps a list of events: created, spec changes, launches, exits, restarts, warnings such as a lost network port.

gxctl> events my-vm           # time, who, reason, message

In the web UI they are under Events on the VM’s page, where new ones appear as they happen. With the API, GET /vms/{id}/events.

To follow every VM, disk, image and network of your projects as they change:

gxctl> watch                  # Ctrl-C stops
gxctl> watch vms

Hugepages

hugepages: true backs the guest’s memory with hugepages, which can make memory-heavy guests faster. hugepage_size picks 2M or 1G (default: the host’s default size, usually 2M); the memory must be a whole number of pages. Set them over the API (POST /vms or PATCH /vms/{id} with update_mask hugepages,hugepage_size):

{"name": "db", "vcpu_count": 8, "mem_size_mib": 32768, "hugepages": true, "hugepage_size": "1G", "...": "..."}

The VM takes its memory from the host’s hugepages, which the administrator reserves. They are counted per node and size and never overcommitted, and a VM holds them while it exists, running or not. If there aren’t enough, the VM waits for a node (on a cluster) with a reason like not enough 1G hugepages (30720 of 32768 MiB taken), or its start fails with the counts.

A VM with a vhost-user NIC gets 2M hugepages without asking when the host has them to spare, and ordinary memory otherwise. The VM’s page_kib says what it got: 4 for ordinary memory, else the page size in KiB.

NUMA and dedicated CPUs

On a host with several NUMA nodes (sockets, or parts of one), a VM runs faster when its memory, its vCPUs and its PCI devices (a GPU, a NIC) are on the same node. Two settings ask for that:

  • numa_policy:
    • NUMA_POLICY_PREFERRED puts the VM’s memory on one NUMA node: the one with its PCI devices, else the one with the most room. When no node has room, the VM goes anywhere on the host, and its NumaAligned condition is False.
    • NUMA_POLICY_STRICT refuses a host where that isn’t possible: PCI devices on two NUMA nodes, a device whose firmware gives no NUMA node, or no node with the memory (and CPUs) left. On a cluster the VM waits for a node; on a single host the create is refused (409).
    • NUMA_POLICY_ALIGNED is for VMs whose devices are on more than one NUMA node, say 4 GPUs on a host with 2 per node; GPUs ask for it. The VM spans exactly its devices’ NUMA nodes. Its vCPUs and memory are split between them by their device counts: 4 GPUs on nodes 5 and 7 with 16 vCPUs and 128 GiB give 8 vCPUs and 64 GiB on each (an uneven split gives the remainder to the first nodes).
      • Devices picked from a pool fill as few NUMA nodes as can hold them, so 2 GPUs go to one node when one has 2 free.
      • Each node’s share must fit that node’s free memory, hugepages and (dedicated) CPUs, or the host is refused, naming the node.
      • With devices on one node only, it is like STRICT. With no devices, it is like PREFERRED.
      • Every device needs a NUMA node, even on a host with one NUMA node. If the firmware gives none, ask for NUMA_POLICY_PREFERRED yourself (it wins over what gpus sets).
      • The VM shows its split as numa (one entry per guest node: host node, vCPUs, memory, devices), and the web UI shows it as NUMA layout.
  • cpu_policy: CPU_POLICY_DEDICATED gives each vCPU a host CPU of its own, which no other VM uses. It implies NUMA_POLICY_PREFERRED. By default a dedicated VM takes whole cores: both hyperthreads of a core, so vCPUs 0 and 1 share a core and an odd count leaves a thread idle. The first core of each NUMA node stays with the host, and so do OVS-DPDK’s CPUs. Shared VMs then run only on the CPUs dedicated VMs leave free, and running ones are moved when that changes.

A VM with shared vCPUs and a NUMA policy has its memory on the node but its vCPUs anywhere on the host, so no node’s CPUs sit idle.

Set them over the API, at creation or with PATCH /vms/{id} (update_mask numa_policy,cpu_policy); the web UI and gxctl don’t have them yet, except through GPUs, which set NUMA_POLICY_ALIGNED:

{"name": "train", "vcpu_count": 16, "mem_size_mib": 65536,
 "numa_policy": "NUMA_POLICY_STRICT", "cpu_policy": "CPU_POLICY_DEDICATED",
 "devices": [{"pool": "a100", "count": 2}], "...": "..."}

The VM shows where it went: numa_node, and for dedicated vCPUs cpus (vCPU i on cpus[i]), in GET /vms/{id} and the scheduler preview. A change to its vCPUs, memory, policies, devices or networks picks again on the same host, and applies when it next starts.

When a VM can’t be placed this way, the reason says why:

ReasonMeaning
NUMA node 1: not enough memory (… of … MiB taken)That NUMA node is full.
NUMA node 0: not enough free CPUs (8 dedicated vCPUs, 6 CPUs free)Too few CPUs left for dedicated vCPUs.
its PCI devices are on NUMA nodes 0 and 1A strict VM’s devices are split.
PCI device … has no NUMA nodeA strict or aligned VM’s device has no NUMA node.
its devices are on 2 NUMA nodes, so it needs at least 2 vCPUsAn aligned VM needs a vCPU on each of its nodes.
NUMA nodes 5 and 7 would back its memory with different page sizesAn aligned VM’s nodes would back its memory with different page sizes. Give it hugepages with a hugepage_size each of its nodes has.

A PREFERRED VM that didn’t fit on one NUMA node runs anyway, with its NumaAligned condition False.

What the guest sees

A VM aligned over several NUMA nodes sees one guest NUMA node per host node, in the order of numa:

  • guest node i has its share of vCPUs (numbered in order: node 0’s first) and of memory, bound to host node numa[i].node;
  • each guest node has its own PCI root with the devices of its host node, so the guest sees which GPU is near which vCPUs and memory (numactl -H, nvidia-smi topo -m). Virtio disks and NICs stay on the main PCI root;
  • with dedicated CPUs, vCPU i runs on host CPU cpus[i], on its node. Shared vCPUs float over the host, as for one node.

The distances between guest NUMA nodes are the hypervisor’s defaults, not the host’s, and a GPU and a NIC that share a PCIe switch on the host don’t share one in the guest. Both hypervisors lay the guest out this way.

Elastic CPU

An elastic VM has a range of vCPUs instead of a fixed count:

FieldMeaning
min_vcpusThe fewest vCPUs it runs on. At least 1; 0 on Pylon, where an idle guest can park all of them.
max_vcpusThe most it can have. At most 64 on Pylon.
cpu_weight1 to 10000, default 100: its share of host CPU when VMs compete (cgroup cpu.weight; on Pylon also pylond’s priority).

A VM is elastic when min_vcpus is less than max_vcpus. Without them it has a fixed size, vcpu_count. A VM with dedicated CPUs can’t be elastic.

How the range is used depends on the hypervisor:

  • Pylon. The guest boots with all max_vcpus and keeps them. pylond, the host’s core arbiter, parks the vCPUs the guest doesn’t need and wakes them on demand, between min_vcpus and max_vcpus, in microseconds and without CPU hotplug. So an elastic Pylon VM’s vcpu_count is always its max_vcpus: Glidex sets it, and the web UI and gxctl show it so. lscpu in the guest shows max_vcpus CPUs.
  • Cloud Hypervisor and QEMU. The guest boots with vcpu_count vCPUs online and room for max_vcpus. Change vcpu_count within the range and Glidex adds or removes vCPUs while the VM runs (CPU hotplug); nothing changes the count on its own.

Make a VM elastic

In the web UI, tick Elastic CPU scaling in the create form and set Min vCPUs, Max vCPUs and Weight. On Pylon, vCPU Count follows Max vCPUs.

For a VM that exists, click Scale CPU / Elasticity under its vCPU count. Tick Elastic CPU scaling to give a fixed-size VM the range 1 to its vCPU count, then change it; untick it to give the VM a fixed size again. On Pylon the dialog shows the vCPUs the guest has.

With gxctl, create asks whether to configure elastic CPU scaling (the default is yes on Pylon), and scale changes a VM:

gxctl> scale web-1 --min 1 --max 8 --weight 200
gxctl> scale web-1 --vcpus 4

With the API, set min_vcpus, max_vcpus and cpu_weight at create or in a change. To make an elastic Pylon VM fixed again, set min_vcpus and max_vcpus to the same count as vcpu_count: a change of vcpu_count alone keeps it elastic, and its count goes back to max_vcpus.

When a change applies

ChangePylonCloud Hypervisor, QEMU
vcpu_count within the range(Always max_vcpus.)At once, on a running VM.
min_vcpus, lower max_vcpusAt once.At the next start.
Raise max_vcpusAt the next start: the guest keeps the vCPUs it booted with.At the next start.
cpu_weightAt once for pylond; the cgroup weight at the next start.At the next start; the VM isn’t marked for a restart.

A change that waits for the next start sets restart_required, and the web UI says Configuration changes take effect at the next start, except where the table says otherwise. A change that applies at once but can’t yet, because the VM is paused, sets the VcpuResizePending condition until it runs.

Quotas count vcpu_count, so an elastic Pylon VM counts its max_vcpus.

Placement on a cluster

On a cluster, the scheduler picks the node for a new VM when it is created. It considers only nodes that are active, ready and not draining, that have the hypervisor, enough vCPUs and memory left, the PCI devices, hugepages and physical networks the VM needs, and that hold its disks and node networks, or reach the datastores its disks are on. Of those, it prefers the least loaded.

Hugepages are counted on their own: a VM with hugepages needs that much left of the node’s hugepages of its size (see Hugepages). A VM with a NUMA or CPU policy needs a NUMA node with room (see NUMA and dedicated CPUs), and a VM asking for devices from a pool needs a node with enough free devices of it.

PCI devices are claimed per node: nodes with a device at the same address each take one VM with it. A node where another VM holds the device, or a device of its IOMMU group, is skipped. If every such node’s device is taken, the VM waits, and the reason names the VM holding it. A VM pinned to a node where its device is taken is refused instead. Nodes where a device is cordoned by an administrator, or where your project has no grant for it, are skipped too (PCI device … is cordoned, its PCI devices are not granted to the project on this node).

A VM stays on its node: Glidex doesn’t move it, and doesn’t restart it elsewhere if the node fails. If no node can take the VM, it is still created and waits for one; its page says Waiting for a node with each node’s reason.

A VM whose disks are on shared datastores (see Where a disk lives) can be placed on another node by an administrator (system-admin): when it is stopped, or when its node was lost and forgotten. On the VM’s page it is Place on another node (Place on a live node for a lost VM), with a node or Where there is room; with gxctl, gxctl place <vm> [--node N]; over the API, POST /vms/{id}/place with an optional node. A VM with a disk on a node’s own storage can go only to that node, and nowhere once the node is lost; a VM with a host-path root, PCI devices or a node network can’t move.

With a node, the VM is pinned there; without one, its old pin goes. Start it again afterwards. A QEMU VM’s UEFI variables stay on the old node: it starts with fresh ones from its firmware. See Placing a stopped or lost VM again for what is refused.

In the web UI’s create form, Placement shows Automatic (now: <node>) and each node with its free vCPUs and memory, or why it can’t take the VM. Pick a node to pin the VM there. With the API, set node when you create the VM. To ask the scheduler without creating anything:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/scheduler/preview \
  -d '{"vcpu_count": 2, "mem_size_mib": 2048, "hypervisor": "HYPERVISOR_QEMU"}'

The answer has the node it would pick (pick) and every node’s fit (nodes, with refused when it can’t take the VM).

The VM’s node shows in gxctl list and on its page. If the node stops reporting, the page shows the VM’s last known state; the VM may still be running there.

See Clusters for nodes and draining.

Kernel boot

A VM boots in one of two ways:

  • Firmware boot (the default): the hypervisor runs UEFI firmware, and the firmware runs the boot loader on the VM’s disk, which picks the kernel. See Virtual machines.
  • Kernel boot (direct kernel boot): the hypervisor loads a kernel, an optional initramfs and a kernel command line that Glidex hands it. There is no firmware and no boot loader.

A distro cloud image boots either way: the same root disk, the same cloud-init seed and credential, and the same console.

When to use it

Use kernel boot when you want to choose the kernel from outside the guest:

  • to set the kernel command line yourself, for example to debug a guest that doesn’t boot;
  • to boot a kernel the guest doesn’t have, or keep a VM on a known kernel build;
  • to boot a bare root filesystem with no partition table or boot loader.

Stay with firmware boot when the guest should manage its own kernel through its boot loader, as on a physical machine. With kernel boot, a kernel the guest installs (apt upgrade, say) doesn’t boot unless you turn on following the guest’s kernel.

A VM’s boot mode is fixed when it is created: you can’t switch a VM between firmware and kernel boot.

Kernel images

A kernel image is an entry in the shared image library holding a kernel, an optional initramfs and a default command line. VMs name it with kernel, as they name firmware with firmware. Like other images, kernel images are visible to everyone, and adding and deleting them needs the image-admin role. See Images and disks.

A kernel image is never replaced: a newer kernel is a new image, and each VM keeps the one it names until you change it.

From a cloud image

Pulling a catalog image also takes the kernel out of it: a second image, <image>-kernel (for example ubuntu-26.04-kernel), appears in state extracting and becomes ready a few seconds after the image. It is the kernel, initramfs and command line the image’s own boot loader would boot, with console= replaced by the serial console: console=ttyS0, or console=ttyAMA0 for an aarch64 image. So the kernel always matches the modules on the image’s disk.

  • A pull with a name names the kernel image <name>-kernel.

  • gxctl image pull <key> --no-kernel ("with_kernel": false) skips the extraction; "with_kernel": true extracts from a URL pull too (off by default for URLs). gxctl image pull waits through extracting and prints the kernel’s release and command line.

  • To take the kernel out of an image you already have, including one pulled from a URL: Extract kernel on the image under Images, gxctl image extract-kernel my-image [--name <name>], or

    curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/images -d '{"kernel_from": "my-image"}'

    The answer is 202 with the new kernel image (200 with the one already extracting from that image).

Glidex reads the image inside a small VM without network, never on the host. It builds that VM the first time it extracts, from pinned Debian packages for the image’s architecture (a one-time download of about 35 MB on x86_64, 30 MB on aarch64).

That VM runs under KVM, so an image’s kernel is extracted on a host of the image’s architecture:

ImageExtracted on
x86_64an x86_64 host with Cloud Hypervisor or QEMU
aarch64an aarch64 host with Cloud Hypervisor

In a cluster, the server you ask needn’t be that host: when it can’t extract the kernel itself, the extraction runs on another ready node of the image’s architecture with KVM. So a cluster with one aarch64 node extracts aarch64 kernels whichever server takes the pull.

An administrator can also turn extraction off on a host (for a host without internet access, say). Where no node can run it, kernel_from is refused with 400 invalid_image and the reason, for example kernels can’t be extracted here: aarch64 kernels are extracted on a aarch64 host; this one is x86_64 (in a cluster, followed by and no other ready node is aarch64 with KVM), and catalog pulls bring only the disk image.

If extraction fails, only the kernel image fails, with the reason; the disk image stays ready and firmware boot is unaffected. Retry in the web UI or gxctl image retry <name> runs it again.

From a URL

gxctl> image pull https://images.example.org/vmlinuz-6.8.0-147-generic --kernel --sha256 <sha256> \
         --initrd-url https://images.example.org/initrd.img-6.8.0-147-generic --initrd-sha256 <sha256> \
         --cmdline "root=LABEL=cloudimg-rootfs ro console=ttyS0"

or over the API:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/images -d '{
    "url": "https://images.example.org/vmlinuz-6.8.0-147-generic", "sha256": "<sha256>",
    "kind": "IMAGE_KIND_KERNEL",
    "initrd_url": "https://images.example.org/initrd.img-6.8.0-147-generic", "initrd_sha256": "<sha256>",
    "cmdline": "root=LABEL=cloudimg-rootfs ro console=ttyS0"
  }'

The URL rules are those of any image pull: https://, and listed as unverified unless every file had a sha256. Use the kernel the cloud image was built with: the guest loads the kernel’s modules from its own disk. Ubuntu publishes each build’s kernel and initramfs next to the image, in unpacked/.

From host files

An administrator who may use host paths can copy a kernel from files on the host into the library:

gxctl> image pull --kernel-path /srv/kernels/vmlinuz-custom --initrd-path /srv/kernels/initrd-custom \
         --cmdline "root=/dev/vda1 ro console=ttyS0"

or over the API:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/images -d '{
    "kernel_path": "/srv/kernels/vmlinuz-custom", "initrd_path": "/srv/kernels/initrd-custom",
    "cmdline": "root=/dev/vda1 ro console=ttyS0", "name": "custom-kernel"
  }'

VMs then boot it like any kernel image; their users need no access to host paths.

What a kernel image may hold

  • An x86_64 bzImage (64-bit), an ELF vmlinux for x86_64 or aarch64, or an arm64 Image. Anything else fails the image.
  • An aarch64 kernel as distributions ship it is unwrapped to the plain Image Cloud Hypervisor boots: Ubuntu’s vmlinuz (an EFI stub holding the kernel), the kernel’s own compressed EFI image (gzip or zstd), or a gzip file. This applies to extracted, downloaded and host-file kernels; a host file is unwrapped into the copy and never changed. The kernel image’s size and sha256 are the unwrapped file’s.
  • At most 128 MiB for the kernel and 1 GiB for the initramfs, unless an administrator changed the limits.
  • A cmdline of at most 2047 bytes, without control characters.

The kernel’s release (7.0.0-34-generic) is read from its header when the format carries one (a bzImage does).

Listing and deleting

Web UI: Images, Kernels (shown once there is one): each kernel image with its release, whether it has an initramfs, its command line, its status (Extracting…, Ready), its source and the VMs that boot it.

gxctl:

gxctl> image list            # kernel images show as "kernel <release>"
gxctl> image rm ubuntu-26.04-kernel

The source column says where a kernel came from: its URL, the host file, or extracted: <partition>:<path> (extracting until done).

A kernel image can’t be deleted while a VM boots it, or keeps it to go back to (see Kernel versions): the delete is refused with 409 conflict, naming the VMs. The image’s used_by_vms lists them.

Create a VM with kernel boot

Name a kernel image with kernel and the root disk as for firmware boot (image or root_disk):

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/vms -d '{
    "name": "web-1", "vcpu_count": 2, "mem_size_mib": 2048,
    "image": "ubuntu-26.04", "kernel": "ubuntu-26.04-kernel",
    "credential": "alice", "networks": [{"network": "lab"}]
  }'
  • The VM needs no firmware image. Giving both a kernel and a firmware (firmware or firmware_path) is refused with 400 invalid_config.
  • The kernel image must be ready and of the root image’s architecture. Using it needs read access to the image, as for firmware.
  • The VM gets the kernel image’s command line as its kernel_args, unless you give them.
  • Glidex generates the cloud-init seed as for firmware boot (the hostname, the root partition growth and the credential), so credential works the same. See Guest credentials.
  • On a cluster, the VM’s node gets its own copy of the kernel image. Until it has one, the VM waits with the condition DisksReady False (kernel <name> has not been copied to this node yet).

Web UI: Create VM, Advanced options, Boot Mode Direct kernel boot. The Kernel choice (A kernel image) replaces UEFI Firmware: pick it under Kernel Image. Only the chosen image’s own kernel is preselected; when it has none, the choice stays empty and Extract it from the image makes one. Other kernels are listed as — from <image>, and picking one shows a warning: another distribution’s initramfs usually can’t find this image’s root. Kernel Arguments show and default to the kernel image’s command line. Follow the guest’s kernel turns on following. The boot disk and login credential work as with firmware.

gxctl: in gxctl create, answer kernel at UEFI firmware, then pick the kernel image at Kernel (the default is only the boot image’s own kernel; another image’s kernel prints a warning), and answer Follow the guest’s kernel. Kernel arguments default to the kernel image’s command line.

Host paths

An administrator who may use host paths can boot files on the host directly instead of a kernel image:

FieldWhat it is
kernel_image_pathThe kernel.
initrd_pathIts initramfs, optional; distro kernels need one. Only with kernel_image_path.
rootfs_pathA root filesystem or disk image, used as is. Over the API, image and root_disk work too.

In the web UI: under Advanced options, Direct kernel boot, then Kernel Kernel files on the host (administrators), with the kernel and initramfs paths; a root filesystem file is the boot disk’s path source. In gxctl create, answer kernel at UEFI firmware, give a host path at Kernel, then the Initramfs path (optional).

Host paths can’t be changed after create. A VM with a host-path kernel and a host-path root filesystem gets no generated seed, so it can’t have a credential; one with image or root_disk gets the seed. generate_seed (true or false) overrides this at create, and can’t be combined with cloud_init_path.

The kernel command line

kernel_args is the kernel command line:

  • Default: the kernel image’s command line; with host paths, or a kernel image without one, console=ttyS0 root=/dev/vda reboot=k panic=1 (console=ttyAMA0 … on aarch64). The architecture is the kernel image’s, else that of the node the VM is pinned to, else the host’s.
  • Limits: at most 2047 bytes, no control characters (400 invalid_config).
  • The root: a cloud image’s root is on a partition, so root=/dev/vda doesn’t find it. A cloud image needs its own root, for example root=LABEL=cloudimg-rootfs ro for Ubuntu; an extracted kernel’s command line has it. A VM with a managed root disk whose arguments have no root= is created with the warning kernel_args has no root=; the kernel may not find the root disk.

Change them with PATCH /vms/{id} (kernel_args); they apply at the next start. Changing the kernel doesn’t change them.

The console

With kernel boot, the last console= in kernel_args picks the device Glidex connects the console to:

Last console=Guest deviceCloud HypervisorQEMU
hvc… (for example hvc0)the virtio consolevirtio console, no serial portvirtio console, no serial port
anything else (ttyS0, ttyAMA0), or nonethe serial portserial portserial port

Both hypervisors behave the same. Firmware boot always uses the serial port. The default arguments and extracted kernels name the serial port, console=ttyS0 (console=ttyAMA0 on aarch64, where ttyS0 would leave the console silent), so the console shows the kernel from its first line, and a panic is visible. The virtio console only starts once the kernel’s virtio driver is up: put console=hvc0 last only if you want it.

A Cloud Hypervisor VM created by an earlier version of Glidex keeps the console=hvc0 it was created with, and so the virtio console.

Following the guest’s kernel

A kernel-booted VM boots the kernel Glidex hands the hypervisor, so a kernel the guest installs doesn’t boot by itself. To boot it anyway, turn on kernel_from_disk: Follow the guest’s kernel on the VM’s Kernel panel or in the create form, gxctl kernel my-vm --follow on, or:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X PATCH https://host.example.org:8841/vms/<id> \
  -d '{"change": {"kernel_from_disk": true}, "update_mask": "kernel_from_disk"}'

It is also a field of POST /vms, and needs a kernel image (kernel) and a managed root disk (image or root_disk): 400 invalid_config otherwise. It applies at the next start.

Before each start, Glidex then takes the kernel out of the VM’s root disk again if the disk changed since the last time (its size or modification time), the same way it extracts from a cloud image. A VM that was only stopped and started pays nothing.

  • The VM shows booted_kernel, the kernel image it boots, and previous_kernel, the one before. Its kernel stays what you chose: the kernel it starts from, and its fallback.
  • A new kernel logs the event KernelUpdated (old → new release).
  • If extraction fails, the VM boots the kernel it has. Its condition KernelExtracted is False with the reason, the event KernelExtractFailed is logged, and the next start tries again. Only a VM with no kernel at all fails to start (KernelNotExtracted).
  • The VM keeps its kernel_args; the new kernel’s command line from the disk isn’t applied.
  • Extraction takes a few seconds on each start after a change, during which the disk is busy.

To go back to an earlier kernel, set kernel, for example to the previous_kernel:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X PATCH https://host.example.org:8841/vms/<id> \
  -d '{"change": {"kernel": "<previous_kernel>"}, "update_mask": "kernel"}'

Changing kernel without kernel_from_disk in the mask turns following off, so the VM stays on the kernel you set. Put both in the mask to keep following on.

Extract once

To take the guest’s kernel without following it, extract it once from a stopped VM: Extract from its disk now on the VM’s page, or

gxctl> kernel my-vm --extract

which waits until the new kernel image is ready and prints how to use it (kernel my-vm --set <kernel-image>). Over the API, POST /vms/<id>/extract-kernel answers 202 with the new kernel image, extracting; wait for it to be ready (GET /images/<image-id>), then set it as the VM’s kernel with PATCH.

  • It needs the editor role in the VM’s project.
  • The VM must be stopped (409 conflict otherwise), boot a kernel image, and have a managed root disk (400 invalid_config otherwise).
  • On a cluster, a disk on another node’s own datastore is read on that node; if that node can’t extract now, the call is refused with 409 (disk … is on …, which can’t extract … kernels now: …). A disk the server can’t reach (on a shared datastore it doesn’t mount, say) is 409 too (disk … is not reachable from this node: ask a server on a node that has it), and so is a disk being moved to another datastore.

Kernel versions

Kernels taken from a VM’s own disk are kernel images the VM owns: their owner is the VM’s id, they are named <vm>-kernel-<id prefix>, and they are never marked verified (the guest writes that disk).

  • A launch-time extraction that finds a kernel and initramfs already stored (the same files) uses that image instead of keeping a copy. A VM following an unchanged guest boots the cloud image’s own kernel image. extract-kernel always keeps its new image.
  • A VM uses a kernel image while its kernel names it, or it boots it or keeps it as previous_kernel. Such an image can’t be deleted, and on a cluster it is copied to the VM’s node.
  • A VM-owned kernel image is deleted by itself once no VM uses it (at least five minutes after it was made).

So VMs of the same image can run different kernels side by side, each kept while a VM needs it.

Change a VM’s kernel

kernel can be changed on a stopped or running VM that boots a kernel image; it applies at the next start. On the VM’s page, Kernel shows the kernel image (and, when following the guest, the one it boots and the one before); pick another and Use from the next start. With gxctl:

gxctl> kernel my-vm                              # the kernel, booted and previous
gxctl> kernel my-vm --set ubuntu-26.04-kernel
gxctl> kernel my-vm --follow on                  # or off

Over the API:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X PATCH https://host.example.org:8841/vms/<id> \
  -d '{"change": {"kernel": "ubuntu-26.04-kernel"}, "update_mask": "kernel"}'

A change of kernel, kernel_from_disk or kernel_args on a running VM sets restart_required, and the web UI says Configuration changes take effect at the next start: the VM boots the new kernel the next time you stop and start it.

The new kernel must be a ready kernel image of the same architecture. A firmware VM can’t change to a kernel (400 invalid_config), and kernel_image_path, initrd_path and generate_seed can’t be changed.

Limits

  • Kernel boot has no UEFI firmware, so no Secure Boot and no UEFI variables.
  • Kernel extraction runs only on a host of the image’s architecture (x86_64 or aarch64), and on aarch64 only with Cloud Hypervisor; in a cluster, on any ready node of it. Where there is none, add kernel images from a URL or host files.
  • With a host-path kernel, the file must exist on the VM’s node; Glidex doesn’t copy it.

API

CallWhat it does
POST /images with catalog (and with_kernel)Pull a cloud image and, by default, its kernel.
POST /images with kernel_fromExtract the kernel of a disk image.
POST /images with kind: IMAGE_KIND_KERNEL, url, initrd_url, cmdlineDownload a kernel image.
POST /images with kernel_path, initrd_pathCopy a kernel image from host files.
POST /vms with kernel, kernel_args, kernel_from_diskCreate a kernel-boot VM.
PATCH /vms/{id} with kernel, kernel_args, kernel_from_diskChange its kernel, command line or following.
POST /vms/{id}/extract-kernelExtract the kernel on a stopped VM’s disk.

A VM shows boot (BOOT_MODE_FIRMWARE or BOOT_MODE_KERNEL), kernel, kernel_from_disk, booted_kernel and previous_kernel. A kernel image has kind IMAGE_KIND_KERNEL, its kernel (release, cmdline, initrd), and for_image or owner. See REST API for every field.

Networks

A network connects VM NICs. Glidex creates no network by itself: an administrator creates host networks and offers them to projects, and a project’s owner can create networks of the project’s own. A VM gets one NIC per network it attaches to.

This page is the user’s view. Setting up the host side (Open vSwitch, bridges, uplinks, OVN) is in Host networking.

Network modes

ModeWhat VMs getAddresses
NATA private IPv4 subnet behind the host. VMs reach the outside through the host (masquerade); nothing outside can open a connection to them.DHCP from Glidex.
IsolatedVMs on the network reach each other and nothing else, not even the host.None on a single host (configure them in the guest); DHCP on a cluster network.
BridgedVMs sit on an existing LAN through one of the host’s bridges, as if plugged into it.From the LAN (its own DHCP).

NAT networks can’t reach each other, and a guest reaches the host only for DHCP, DNS and ping on its gateway. Glidex has no port forwarding: to reach a VM from outside, put it on a bridged (or, on a cluster, provider) network.

A VM’s NIC is a tap device (the default) or a vhost-user port, which needs OVS-DPDK on the host. The network decides which.

Where a network lives

On a single host, a network is an Open vSwitch bridge on that host.

On a cluster, a network is either:

  • a cluster network (on OVN), which spans every node: VMs on any node can use it, and traffic between nodes goes through tunnels. Needs OVN turned on for the cluster. A NAT cluster network reaches the outside through the cluster’s shared edge, which an administrator sets up first;
  • a node network, a bridge on one node: only VMs placed on that node can use it, and the scheduler places them there.

On a cluster with OVN on, new networks span the cluster unless you ask for a node network. The cluster’s bridged networks are provider networks: they sit on a named physical network that the nodes map, optionally on a VLAN.

Who can use a network

  • A host network has no project. An administrator (net-admin) creates it and grants it to projects, to whole tenants, or to every project.
  • A project network belongs to a project. Its owner creates it (NAT or isolated only) and can share it with other projects. It counts against the project’s network quota.

To attach a VM to a network you need the editor role in the VM’s project, and the network must be usable by that project.

gxctl> networks                     # host networks, and project networks you can see
gxctl> network show lab             # id, mode, scope, bridge, phase, grants or shares

In the web UI, the Networking page lists the networks the selected project can attach VMs to (with host rights, every network and the host’s bridges). Its Status column shows ready, or what the network is waiting for.

A network is pending, ready, degraded (part of it is missing on the host; Glidex restores it), or reports that the host’s network helper is unavailable.

Create a project network

You need the owner role in the project.

Web UI

On the project’s page, under Project networks, click Create a project network, or click Add Network on the Networking page and pick Project <name> under Network for. Then:

  • Spans (clusters with OVN on): Every node (cluster network on OVN) or This node only (a bridge here).
  • Name: lowercase letters, digits and -, at most 32 characters.
  • Mode: NAT (DHCP + masquerade) or Isolated (VM-to-VM).
  • VM port: tap or vhost-user (DPDK).
  • Subnet (optional): for NAT (and isolated cluster networks). On a single host, the default is the first free /24 in 10.88.0.0/16; on a cluster, a free range from the cluster’s pool.
  • Leaves through / Routed through: a router of the project, for a cluster network. See Project routers.

gxctl

gxctl> network create lab --project my-project                 # NAT
gxctl> network create backend --project my-project --isolated
gxctl> network create lab2 --project my-project --subnet 10.88.42.0/24 --mtu 1450

--vhost-user makes its NICs vhost-user ports.

API

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST https://host.example.org:8841/projects/my-project/networks \
  -d '{"name": "lab", "mode": "NETWORK_MODE_NAT"}'

See REST API.

Create a host network

Host networks need the net-admin role. In the web UI, click Add Network on the Networking page and pick Host network; in gxctl:

gxctl> network-add lab                       # NAT, default subnet
gxctl> network-add lab --subnet 10.88.7.0/24
gxctl> network-add backend --isolated
gxctl> network-add lan --bridged br-lan      # on an existing glidex bridge with an uplink
gxctl> network-add lab --cluster             # or --node, on a cluster

--vlan <n> puts a network on a VLAN, --vhost-user makes its NICs vhost-user ports, and --bridge <name> names the bridge of a NAT or isolated network. A bridged network needs a glidex bridge with an uplink first, and a cluster provider network a physical network the nodes map: see Host networking. Provider networks are created from the web UI (Provider (a physical network), with its Physical network and VLAN) or the API.

Then grant it. The lists replace the current grants:

gxctl> network grant lab --project my-project --project other-project
gxctl> network grant lab --tenant acme
gxctl> network grant lab --all-projects

Share a project network

A project’s owner offers a share to another project, whose owner accepts it within 7 days. Then the other project’s VMs can attach to the network.

gxctl> network share lab <other-project-id>        # offer
gxctl> network shares other-project                # offers and shares of a project
gxctl> network accept other-project lab            # accept, as the other project's owner
gxctl> network leave other-project lab             # stop using it
gxctl> network unshare lab <other-project-id>      # withdraw an offer or a share

In the web UI, the network’s row on the project page has Offer share; the other project’s page lists it under Networks shared with this project, with Accept and Leave.

Attach VMs

Pick the networks when you create the VM: the Networks checkboxes in the web UI, the Networks prompt in gxctl create, or networks in the API. One NIC per network, in order, at most 8. A network named default, if the project can use one, is preselected.

To change a VM’s networks later, PATCH its networks (the whole list); it applies at the VM’s next start. See Virtual machines.

Addresses

  • NAT (single host): the gateway is the subnet’s .1, and each NIC gets a fixed address from the rest of the subnet, by its MAC. The NIC keeps it across restarts until the VM is deleted. The gateway also answers DNS.
  • Cluster networks (NAT and isolated): Glidex reserves an address for each NIC from the network’s subnet and serves it by DHCP. A NIC can only send from its own MAC and address (on provider networks, its own MAC).
  • Bridged and provider: the LAN’s DHCP server, or static addresses in the guest.
  • Isolated (single host): no DHCP; configure addresses in the guest.

NAT networks are IPv4 only. The address of each NIC shows in the VM’s details: Network on its page in the web UI, NIC <n> in gxctl get <vm>, nics[].ipv4 in the API.

The host from a NAT network

Guests of a single-host NAT network reach the outside world, but on their own host only its DHCP, DNS, ping on the gateway and the metadata endpoint: every other service of the host is closed to them. A host network administrator can open the host’s glidex API (port 8841) to one network’s guests, for software in them that calls glidex with the tokens the metadata endpoint gives:

gxctl> network host-api lab on
gxctl> network host-api lab off

or PUT /networks/<id>/host_api with {"host_api": true}. Guests then call https://<gateway>:8841. To open it on every NAT network of a host, set "nat_host_api": true in its control-plane.json. The API still needs a valid token for everything.

Delete a network

A network can’t be deleted while any VM uses it, even a stopped one.

gxctl> network rm lab          # or network-rm lab; waits up to a minute

In the web UI, Delete on the network’s row (project page) or on the Networking page.

Project routers (clusters)

On a cluster with OVN on, a project’s NAT cluster networks leave through the cluster’s shared edge, each on its own: they can’t reach each other. A router of the project changes that for the networks attached to it:

  • they reach each other through the router;
  • with an outside address (an external router), they leave with that address instead of the edge’s. Without one (internal only), they reach each other and nothing outside;
  • an isolated network attached to a router gets a gateway (the subnet’s .1) and is routed like a NAT one. Running VMs learn it when their DHCP lease renews, or when they restart their network or reboot.

Only NAT and isolated networks that span the cluster can go on a router; node networks can’t. VMs keep their addresses when their network moves to or from a router, but connections open through the old way out are cut.

Routers are managed on the project’s page, in the Routers card (it shows only with OVN on), with the owner role:

  1. Click New router, give it a Name, and tick Reaches outside, with its own address for an external router (possible once an administrator gave the edge a pool of addresses for routers). An external router counts against the project’s external IP quota. Administrators can also choose its Address and Gateway nodes.
  2. On the router’s row, Attach network… puts existing networks on it, and + network on <router> creates a new one there. Detach puts a network back on the edge.
  3. Delete removes a router once no network is attached.

There are no gxctl commands for routers. With the API:

api=https://host.example.org:8841
auth="Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN"
curl -H "$auth" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -X POST $api/projects/my-project/routers \
  -d '{"name": "r1", "external": true}'
curl -H "$auth" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -X PUT $api/projects/my-project/networks/lab/router \
  -d '{"router": "r1"}'                  # {} puts it back on the edge
curl -H "$auth" -X DELETE $api/projects/my-project/routers/r1

The console

Every VM has one console. You can type into it from the browser or from gxctl, as many clients at once as you like, and everything it prints is logged, so you can read what happened before you connected. Opening a console or reading its log needs the operator role in the VM’s project.

What the console shows depends on the guest: a cloud image booted through UEFI firmware prints the firmware, the boot loader and the kernel there, then a login prompt; with kernel boot it starts at the kernel. Log in with the VM’s guest credential.

Which guest device the console is depends on how the VM boots, the same on Cloud Hypervisor and QEMU:

BootConsole device in the guest
UEFI firmwareThe first serial port, ttyS0.
Kernel boot, last console= in the kernel arguments is hvc…The virtio console, hvc0. The VM then has no serial port.
Kernel boot, any other last console=, or noneThe first serial port, ttyS0.

The default kernel arguments, and kernels extracted from cloud images, say console=ttyS0. A Cloud Hypervisor VM created with kernel boot by an earlier version of Glidex keeps the console=hvc0 it was created with. There is no second console: to move the console, change the VM’s kernel_args (see The console); it applies at the next start.

In the browser

On the VM’s page, click Open Console. The console opens in the page and connects at once; the Status at the top says connecting, connected, closed or error. Type into it as into a terminal: input goes straight to the guest’s console device.

When you connect, the console first replays what the VM printed so far (its current log), then follows live output. The replay leaves out the questions the guest asked its terminal earlier (such as where the cursor is), so opening the console doesn’t type stale answers like ^[[38;1R at the guest’s prompt.

If the connection drops (a network blip, or a proxy cutting it), the page reconnects by itself: the status shows reconnecting, and the log is replayed. If the console closes (the VM stopped, or the control plane restarted), or reconnecting fails five times, click Reconnect. Back to VM leaves the console; closing the page detaches without affecting the VM.

In a cluster, the console opens from any server’s web UI, whichever node the VM runs on, also behind a load balancer. If the cluster’s leader changes just as the console opens, it fails once: open it again.

Terminal

The Terminal: menu at the top picks the terminal the page draws the console with:

  • ghostty-web (the default): Ghostty’s terminal engine, run in the browser. It draws on a canvas, so screen readers can’t read the console’s text.
  • xterm.js: keeps the text in the page, so it works with screen readers.

The choice is remembered in this browser. Switching reconnects the console, with a fresh replay of the log.

Copy and paste

KeysWhat they do
Ctrl+Shift+CCopy the selection.
Ctrl+Shift+VPaste into the console.
Ctrl+CSent to the guest as ^C, as in any terminal.

On macOS, ⌘C and ⌘V copy and paste too. ghostty-web also copies a selection as soon as you make it.

Terminal size

The terminal fills the page and follows the window’s size, but the size isn’t passed to the guest: a serial console has none. Programs in the guest use their default (often 80×24) or what they find out by asking the terminal. If a full-screen program draws in only part of the window, set the size in the guest, for example stty rows 40 cols 120, or run resize if the guest has it.

With gxctl

gxctl> connect my-vm
Info: Connected to the VM console via ...
Tip: Press Ctrl+] to detach from console
