console and attach are aliases of connect. Press Ctrl+] to detach; the VM keeps running. If the console closes from the other end (the VM stopped), gxctl says Console closed.

connect works over the local socket on the host and, after gxctl auth login, from another machine over HTTPS (see Logging in). On a cluster it reaches VMs on any node.

connect refuses when the VM has no running instance: start it first.

Several clients

Any number of clients can be connected to one VM at the same time: browser tabs, gxctl sessions, or both. They all see the same output, and what any of them types goes to the same console. A client that falls far behind (several MiB of output it hasn’t read) is disconnected; it can reconnect and replay the log.

The console log

Everything the guest prints on the console is written to a log on the VM’s host, from the first firmware output on, whether or not anyone is connected. Glidex adds a line when each run of the VM starts and ends, for example:

--- glidex: instance <id> started 2026-10-17T09:12:03Z ---
...
--- glidex: instance <id> exited: clean_exit ---

The log is kept across stops and starts, and when the control plane restarts. When it reaches its size limit (16 MiB by default; an administrator can change it), it is rotated: the previous log is kept, and older output is dropped.

Read the log without connecting:

gxctl> log my-vm              # the last 1 MiB of the current log

With the API, GET /vms/{id}/console/log returns the raw bytes: the last 1 MiB by default, ?tail_bytes=<n> for less, and ?previous=true for the rotated log. The web UI has no log view of its own; opening the console replays the current log.

After the guest exits

When the guest powers off or the hypervisor exits, the exit line is logged and live output stops. Until the control plane notices the exit, a client can still connect and replay the log; then the console closes, connect says the VM is not running, and the browser console reports an error. The log stays readable with log or the API until the VM is deleted.

API

Programs reach the console in two ways:

  • The RPC glidex.vm.v1.VmService.Console, a stream both ways: the first message opens the VM’s console, later ones carry input, and the answers carry output. This is what gxctl connect uses. See RPC API.
  • A WebSocket at GET /vms/{id}/console/ws, which the web UI uses: binary messages carry the console’s bytes in both directions. Browsers first get a single-use ticket (POST /vms/{id}/console/ticket, valid for 30 seconds) and pass it as ?ticket=. See Console WebSocket.

Clients with an API token or on the local socket need no ticket. Neither way carries a terminal size.

Usage

Glidex meters what VMs, disks, images and networks use: running time, CPU, memory, disk space, disk I/O and network traffic. It keeps the figures by the hour and reports them per project, VM, disk, NIC, network or node, by hour, day or billing month. You can also see a VM’s current rates and its last day of activity.

Who sees what:

  • Anyone with a role in a project (viewer and up) sees that project’s usage, and the usage of its VMs and disks.
  • The host roles auditor and system-admin see every project, including deleted ones, and host-wide figures such as stored images.

How it is measured

The control plane samples every running VM, every disk and every network every 30 seconds (an administrator can change the interval), and adds what it saw to hourly records. An hour is closed a couple of minutes after it ends; until then its figures are provisional. Reports say how far they are complete (Complete through in the web UI, complete through in gxctl).

Usage keeps accruing while the control plane restarts: the next sample covers the gap, spread over the time it lasted.

A billing month is a calendar month in the billing time zone, UTC unless an administrator set another (a fixed, whole-hour offset).

Hourly records are kept for 90 days, then as daily totals for 5 years; the 5-minute figures behind the percentiles are kept for 100 days. Administrators can change these.

What is measured

MeterOfShown asWhat it is
vm.running, vm.pausedVMhoursTime running, and time paused.
cpu.allocVMvCPU-hoursvCPUs × time running (not paused).
cpu.usedVMcore-hoursCPU time the VM actually used, the hypervisor’s own included.
cpu.cores_peakVMcoresHighest CPU rate over one sample interval.
mem.allocVMMiB-hoursMemory size × time running or paused.
device.alloc.<pool>VMdevice-hoursDevices the VM got from a device pool × time running or paused (for example device.alloc.a100).
mem.usedVMMiB-hoursMemory the VM’s processes held × time.
mem.peakVMMiBMost memory held in the hour.
vmio.read_bytes, vmio.write_bytesVMGiBDisk I/O on the host side, after the host’s page cache.
disk.allocdiskGiB-hoursProvisioned size × time, attached or not, running or not.
disk.storeddiskGiB-hoursSpace the disk file takes on the host × time.
image.storedimageGiB-hoursSpace an image takes × time (host-wide).
disk.read_ops, disk.write_opsdiskopsOperations the guest issued.
disk.read_bytes, disk.write_bytesdiskGiBBytes the guest read and wrote.
disk.read_time_ns, disk.write_time_nsdisksTime spent in I/O, for latency (QEMU only).
net.rx_bytes, net.tx_bytesNICGiBTraffic the VM received and sent on that NIC.
net.rx_packets, net.tx_packetsNICpacketsThe same, in packets.
net.ext_rx_bytes, net.ext_tx_bytesNIC (NAT)GiBThe part of it that crossed the NAT gateway (in practice, the internet).
bridge.bytesnetworkGiBTraffic through the network, each frame counted once.
bridge.ext_rx_bytes, bridge.ext_tx_bytesnetwork (NAT)GiBThe network’s traffic through its NAT gateway.

Directions are the guest’s: rx is what the guest received.

device.alloc.<pool> counts only devices a VM got from a device pool, under the cluster pool’s name (a tenant pool’s devices count under the pool it draws from). Devices passed through by address aren’t metered. gxctl usage lists it with the other meters (--meters device.alloc.a100 for that pool alone); the web UI’s Usage page doesn’t show it yet.

A VM on Pylon, on a host where pylond runs, also has these meters, from pylond:

MeterUnitWhat it is
pylon.cores_allocatedcore-secondsHost cores pylond gave the VM × time.
pylon.core_usecµsCore time pylond allocated to the VM.
pylon.cooperative_yieldscountCores the guest gave back by itself (its vCPUs parked when idle).
pylon.forced_preemptionscountCores pylond took back from the guest.

gxctl usage lists them as raw numbers, without the unit; they are in the API’s usage rows too. The web UI’s Usage page doesn’t show them.

Some meters are derived when you read them:

  • net.bytes = received + sent; net.ext_bytes = the external part; net.internal_bytes = the rest (VM to VM, DHCP, DNS). Likewise bridge.ext_bytes and bridge.internal_bytes for a network.
  • Averages over each bucket: net.rx_kbps_avg, disk.read_iops_avg, disk.read_kBps_avg and so on; disk.read_latency_us, disk.write_latency_us where time counters exist.
  • Peaks over one sample interval: net.rx_kbps_peak, net.pps_peak, disk.iops_peak, disk.kBps_peak and so on.

The per-VM and per-network views of traffic differ on purpose: a frame from one VM to another on the same network counts for both VMs, but once for the network. A VM or a project is charged by its own NICs (net.bytes).

Only NAT networks split external from internal traffic; on bridged and isolated networks the ext meters are absent, not zero.

A row can carry flags: provisional (its hour isn’t closed yet), revised (corrected after the hour closed), interpolated (spread over a gap between samples), reset (a counter went backwards), incomplete (usage was lost, for example at a host reboot), source_proc (CPU and memory read from /proc instead of the VM’s cgroup), ext_gap (external traffic may be short) and network_total_unavailable (a provider network has per-VM figures but no network total).

Rates and percentiles

For bandwidth, disk I/O, and CPU and memory, Glidex also keeps a 5-minute average per VM, NIC, disk and network, and reports per billing month:

  • the average;
  • the peak: the busiest sample interval (30 seconds by default);
  • the 95th percentile (p95) of the 5-minute averages, over the slots the subject was running.

Billable bandwidth is the larger of in and out; billable disk I/O is read + write. CPU is reported in cores and as a share of the VM’s vCPUs, memory in MiB and as a share of its size; both include the hypervisor’s own overhead, so they can pass 100 %. Disk latency isn’t available on Cloud Hypervisor.

Once a month is over, its percentiles are stored and no longer change.

Web UI

The Usage page

Usage in the header opens it. Pick a Month, a Project (or All projects, with host rights) and Group by, then a tab:

TabShowsGroup by
UsageThe month’s totals: CPU used, vCPUs and memory allocated, disk provisioned and stored, images stored, network traffic and its internet part, host disk I/O. Grouped by network: traffic through each network.project, vm, disk, network
BandwidthAverage, 30-s peak and p95 in and out, billable p95, internet p95, in Mbps.project, vm, nic, network
Disk I/OIOPS, throughput and latency: average, peak, p95.project, vm, disk
CPU & memoryCores and memory: average, peak, p95, and their share of what is allocated.project, vm

The line above the table says how complete the figures are, or whether the month is Final or Month to date. Download CSV saves the table’s data.

A VM’s usage

The Usage section of a VM’s page shows its current rates (CPU per vCPU, memory working set, network in and out, disk reads and writes) and charts of the last 24 hours in 5-minute averages, with the 95th percentile as a dashed line. It refreshes every 30 seconds.

gxctl

gxctl> usage                                     # this billing month, by project
gxctl> usage --project my-project --by vm        # one project, by VM
gxctl> usage --from 2026-10-01T00:00Z --to 2026-10-08T00:00Z --granularity day --by vm,nic
gxctl> usage --meters cpu.used,net.bytes --by vm
gxctl> usage --by vm --csv > october.csv
FlagMeaning
--project PProjects (comma-separated); default: the selected project, or all you can see.
--from D, --to DRFC 3339 or unix seconds; default: from the start of this billing month to now.
--by K,…Group by project, vm, disk, nic, network (and node).
--granularity Ghour, day or month (the default).
--meters M,…Only these meters (derived ones included).
--tz ZTime zone for day and month buckets: UTC, +07:00, or a zone with a fixed offset such as Asia/Bangkok.
--csvCSV instead of a listing.

Monthly rates and percentiles:

gxctl> usage bandwidth                           # this month, by project
gxctl> usage bandwidth --month 2026-09 --by vm,nic
gxctl> usage disk-io --by disk
gxctl> usage compute --by vm --csv

For one VM, disk or network:

gxctl> stats my-vm                               # current rates: CPU, memory, NICs, disks
gxctl> bandwidth my-vm                           # 5-minute series, last 24 h, with p95
gxctl> bandwidth --network lab
gxctl> io my-vm
gxctl> io --disk data-1
gxctl> compute my-vm
gxctl> compute my-vm --from 2026-10-10T00:00Z --to 2026-10-12T00:00Z

API

EndpointReturns
GET /usageUsage rows; host-wide with host rights, else the projects you may read.
GET /projects/{id}/usageOne project.
GET /vms/{id}/usageOne VM and its NICs; ?include=disks adds its attached disks.
GET /disks/{id}/usageOne disk.
GET /usage/bandwidth, /usage/disk-io, /usage/computeMonthly average, peak and p95.
GET /vms/{id}/statsCurrent rates.
GET /vms/{id}/bandwidth, /vms/{id}/io, /vms/{id}/compute5-minute series.
GET /disks/{id}/io, /networks/{id}/bandwidth, /networks/{id}/statsThe same for a disk or network.

Usage queries take project, from, to (RFC 3339 or unix seconds), month (YYYY-MM), granularity (hour, day (the default) or month), group_by, meters, tz, and format=csv. A query covers at most 400 days. Monthly reports take project, month (default: this month), group_by and format=csv; series take from and to (default: the last 24 hours, at most 31 days).

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" \
  'https://host.example.org:8841/usage?project=my-project&month=2026-09&granularity=month&group_by=vm'

CSV exports are recorded in the audit log. See REST API.

Operator guide

This guide is for the people who install and run Glidex: they set up hosts, decide who may log in and what they may do, connect VMs to the network, join hosts into clusters, and keep it all running. Using VMs, disks and networks inside a project is in the User guide.

Components

On every host, the installer sets up these systemd units:

UnitRuns asWhat it does
glidex-control-plane.serviceglidexThe control plane: the REST and RPC API on port 8841 and on /run/glidex-cp/api.sock, the database, images and disks, and the controllers that keep every VM in the state asked for.
glidex-ui.serviceglidex-uiThe web UI on port 5173. Serves the UI and passes its API calls to the control plane over /run/glidex-cp/ui.sock. Holds no rights of its own. On a cluster agent, it sends browsers to a server’s web UI instead.
glidex-authd.socket, glidex-authd.servicerootChecks local passwords with PAM for web logins. Started on demand; answers only the control plane.
glidex-netd.servicerootHost networking: Open vSwitch bridges, NAT and DHCP, uplinks, VM ports, and binding NICs for DPDK and PCI passthrough. Takes changes only from the control plane.
glidex-stord.servicerootThe storage helper for LVM-thin datastores: makes, activates, grows and removes Glidex’s logical volumes, only in the volume groups listed in /etc/glidex/stord.json (none by default), and lets each VM’s unit open exactly its own volumes. Takes requests only from the control plane; keeps no state. Installed and enabled with the services, idle until a volume group is allowed.
glidex-metad.serviceglidex-metadThe metadata endpoint guests reach at 169.254.169.254 for their workload identity. Holds no key: it asks the control plane over /run/glidex-cp/metad.sock, which only this user may use. Installed with networking and the services.
glidex-vm@<id>.serviceglidexOne per running VM, in glidex-vms.slice: a small supervisor and the VM’s hypervisor (Cloud Hypervisor or QEMU), in their own sandbox. Started and stopped by the control plane, never enabled.
glidex-pylond.serviceroot (group glidex)Pylon’s core arbiter, on hosts with Pylon. Starts before the control plane.
glidex-vfio-boot.servicerootA one-shot unit that sets SR-IOV VF counts and binds devices to vfio-pci at boot, before the other services. There only with the installer’s --vfio-devices or --sriov (see Keep it across reboots).

Open vSwitch runs under its own units, and on cluster members so does OVN. The control plane needs glidex-netd only for VM networking and glidex-authd only for password logins, and glidex-stord only for LVM-thin datastores: without them VMs run without NICs, users log in another way, and disks live in directories.

VMs belong to their own units, not to the control plane: restarting or upgrading the control plane leaves them running, and it picks them up again when it comes back. After a host reboot the control plane starts the VMs that were running (see reconcile.on_host_boot in Configuration).

Check the services:

systemctl status glidex-control-plane glidex-ui glidex-authd.socket glidex-netd glidex-stord
journalctl -u glidex-control-plane -b

gxctl on the host/run/glidex-cp/api.sock (not on a cluster agent)Your Unix account (in glidex-users)

  • Authentication: the local socket, local accounts, single sign-on, login connectors, access tokens and sessions.

Installation

glidex-install installs Glidex and everything it needs on one host, and brings an existing install up to date. Run it again at any time: it only changes what is missing or outdated.

Requirements

  • Linux on x86_64 or aarch64, with KVM enabled (/dev/kvm). QEMU is installed on x86_64 only; on aarch64 VMs run on Cloud Hypervisor.
  • systemd, for the services. Without it the installer still builds and installs the binaries, and you start them by hand.
  • A package manager the installer knows: apt-get, dnf, yum or pacman.
  • sudo rights. Run the installer as your normal user; it asks for your sudo password when it first needs root.
  • git and a Rust toolchain (cargo) to build and run the installer itself. The installer keeps Rust up to date with rustup afterwards.
  • Internet access to the distribution’s package mirrors and to GitHub (Cloud Hypervisor, its firmware, Bun). Rustup, Bun, Cloud Hypervisor and its firmware are checked against a pinned SHA-256 before use. Once running, Glidex itself also connects out for image downloads, logins and, if you use them, directory sync and kernel extraction: see Outbound connections.

For LVM-thin datastores only: LVM with thin-pool support (lvm2 and the thin-provisioning tools), and a volume group with a thin pool that you make. The installer installs neither.

If /dev/kvm is missing, the installer says how to enable it (CPU virtualization in the firmware setup, then modprobe kvm_intel or kvm_amd) and carries on; no VM can start until it is there.

Install

git clone https://github.com/CMKL-APEX/glidex.git && cd glidex
cargo run -p glidex-install

The installer prints its plan, then:

  1. Installs or updates system packages: build tools, OpenSSL headers, the disk and cloud-init tools (qemu-img, sgdisk, growpart, mkdosfs, mtools), QEMU and OVMF, setcap, and OVN and conntrack for cluster networks.
  2. Installs Rust (if missing) and a pinned Bun release, then builds the Glidex binaries and the web UI. With --prebuilt it skips this step.
  3. Creates the service users and groups (see Users and groups).
  4. Installs a pinned Cloud Hypervisor release, Pylon when asked for or found, the Glidex binaries and the web UI, and the UEFI firmware.
  5. Sets up VM networking: Open vSwitch, glidex-netd and the boot devices, if any (see Host networking).
  6. Writes the systemd units and configuration files, then starts or restarts the services.
  7. Joins a cluster (with --join), registers datastores, and on a cluster member brings OVN up to the cluster’s version (see OVN on cluster members).

At the end it prints where the web UI and the API are, and the SHA-256 fingerprints of their certificates:

     web UI:  https://<host>:5173
     API:     /run/glidex-cp/api.sock (members of glidex-users), https://<host>:8841 (tokens)
     web UI certificate SHA-256: <fingerprint>
     API certificate SHA-256: <fingerprint>

Compare these with what your browser shows before you accept the certificate warning (see TLS certificates). With --tailscale-cert, the summary also gives the https://<node>.<tailnet>.ts.net:5173 address, and says whether the UI already serves the Tailscale certificate there.

The installer added you to glidex-users and glidex-admin. Log out and back in so your session has the new groups, then check:

systemctl status glidex-control-plane glidex-ui glidex-authd.socket
gxctl whoami

The installer does not change the firewall. Open what remote clients need: TCP 5173 for the web UI, 8841 for the API (remote gxctl and API clients), and 8842 between the nodes of a cluster.

Options

Choices are saved in /etc/glidex/install.conf and reused by later runs; a flag on the command line overrides the saved choice. Pass options after --:

cargo run -p glidex-install -- --no-qemu --ovs-profile dpdk
OptionEffect
--no-qemuSkip QEMU and OVMF (Cloud Hypervisor only).
--no-networkingSkip Open vSwitch, glidex-netd and the host network settings. VMs then have no NICs.
--no-servicesDon’t install the systemd units, users and groups. You run glidex-control-plane and glidex-ui yourself.
--ovs-profile kernel|dpdkOpen vSwitch datapath. kernel (default) needs nothing special, and turns off DPDK an earlier dpdk profile left on; dpdk reserves hugepages and PMD cores. See Back to the kernel profile.
--pmd-cpu-mask MASKOVS-DPDK PMD CPU mask, in hex. auto clears it.
--allow-ovs-restartAllow restarting ovs-vswitchd while it has bridges (interrupts their traffic), also to turn DPDK off under the kernel profile. Not saved.
--release-hugepagesKernel profile only: give back the hugepages an earlier dpdk profile reserved, once DPDK is off. Kept by default. Not saved.
--no-ovnSkip OVN. Cluster networks need it; by default it is installed with its services off until the host is in a cluster.
--tailscale-certServe the web UI with this node’s Tailscale certificate, trusted by browsers at https://<node>.<tailnet>.ts.net:5173. Grants glidex-ui TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID in a tailscaled drop-in and restarts tailscaled once; refused, changing nothing, when another user already holds it or there is no tailscaled. Off unless chosen: an interactive run on a node with HTTPS certificates asks once. See Tailscale certificates.
--no-tailscale-certTurn it off: removes the drop-ins the installer wrote (a grant you set by hand stays) and restarts tailscaled if it removed its grant.
--with-pylon (or --pylon)Install the Pylon hypervisor and its pylond core arbiter. You build them first from the CMKL-APEX/pylon repository, checked out next to this one (cargo build --release -p cloud-hypervisor -p pylond): the installer takes target/release/pylon (or cloud-hypervisor) and pylond from there, or from this checkout’s target/release. Without the option, they are installed when found there. Refused when asked for and not found. See Pylon.
--no-pylonSkip Pylon and pylond.
--qemu, --networking, --services, --ovnUndo an earlier --no-….
--datastore NAME=PATHRegister PATH (a directory under /srv/glidex, mounted on every node) as shared datastore NAME. Repeatable. Not saved. See Registering at install time.
--local-datastore NAME=PATHRegister PATH as a node-local datastore NAME. Repeatable. Not saved.
--datastore-defaultMake the first of these datastores the default for new disks. Not saved.
--stord-allow-vg VGLet glidex-stord make LVM-thin volumes in volume group VG: adds it to allowed_vgs in /etc/glidex/stord.json (never removes one) and restarts glidex-stord. Repeatable. Not saved; the file keeps the list. You make the volume group and its thin pool. See LVM-thin.
--vfio-devices LISTBind these to vfio-pci at every boot, before glidex and other hypervisors start: pools of control-plane.json or PCI addresses, comma-separated, each with its IOMMU group. A device already on vfio-pci is left alone. Recorded and enabled only (glidex-vfio-boot.service, /etc/glidex/vfio-devices.json, /etc/modules-load.d/glidex-vfio.conf); applied at the next boot. Not with --no-networking. See Keep it across reboots.
--sriov PF=NGive physical function PF N SR-IOV VFs at every boot, before the binding. Repeatable or comma-separated; the last count for a PF wins.
--no-vfio-devicesStop both at boot, and remove the unit and its files (what is bound now stays so until the next boot).
--nowApply --vfio-devices and --sriov now as well, not only at the next boot. Never touches a device on vfio-pci, nor the VF count of a PF with a VF on vfio-pci. Not saved.
--prebuiltInstall the binaries already in target/release (or $CARGO_TARGET_DIR/release) and the built UI in crates/glidex-ui/ui/dist (built on another host with the same OS) instead of installing Rust and Bun and building. Refused, naming what is missing, unless every binary and the UI are there. Not saved. Installing one build on several servers keeps their UI files the same, which a load balancer needs (see Behind a load balancer or tunnel).
-h, --helpShow the options.

/etc/glidex/install.conf holds qemu, networking, services, ovs_profile, pmd_cpu_mask, ovn, and, once chosen, tailscale_cert, with_pylon, vfio_devices and sriov. The options marked not saved above apply to the run they are given on only.

Without --datastore or --local-datastore, an interactive run offers each filesystem mounted directly under /srv/glidex that isn’t a datastore yet: register it as a shared datastore named after its directory (default no), and make it the default for new disks (default no). Datastores are registered only when the services are installed (not with --no-services); if that fails, the installer warns and goes on.

Options for joining or leaving a cluster (--join, --role, --token-file, --advertise, --node-name, --import, --rejoin, --node-id, --leave, --keep-resources --offline) are described in Clusters. None of them is saved.

OVN on cluster members

A member’s OVN must be at least as new as the cluster’s ovn-northd: an older ovn-controller can’t run the flows a newer northd compiles, and VMs on that node lose their traffic on cluster networks. On a cluster member with OVN on, the installer checks this after a join and on every re-run:

  1. It reads northd’s version from the cluster’s southbound database, with the node’s own certificate. Until the cluster’s OVN is on here, it says so and skips the check; re-run the installer later.
  2. If the local ovn-controller is older, on apt-get hosts it upgrades ovn-host (and ovn-common, ovn-central where installed): from the distribution when it has a new enough version, else, on Ubuntu, from the Ubuntu Cloud Archive pocket that has one. For the Cloud Archive it installs ubuntu-cloud-keyring and writes /etc/apt/sources.list.d/glidex-uca-ovn.list and /etc/apt/preferences.d/glidex-uca-ovn, pinned so that only OVN comes from there.
  3. It refuses to upgrade when the upgrade would remove another package (a vendor’s OVS, say), and on other package managers it asks you to install the right OVN version yourself. Both stop the installer with the version needed.

An agent installs ovn-host only; servers and standalone hosts also get ovn-central.

/etc/systemd/system/glidex-ui.service.d/50-tailscale-cert.conf, /etc/systemd/system/tailscaled.service.d/50-glidex-cert.confWith --tailscale-cert: the drop-ins that turn the UI’s Tailscale certificate on and let glidex-ui fetch it.
/etc/polkit-1/rules.d/50-glidex-vm.rulesLets the glidex user start and stop its own glidex-vm@ units.
/etc/glidex/control-plane.json.exampleEvery control plane setting with its default. The installer never writes control-plane.json itself.
/etc/glidex/authd.jsonglidex-authd settings, written once and then left alone.
/etc/glidex/stord.jsonThe volume groups glidex-stord may use (allowed_vgs). Written only with --stord-allow-vg; without it stord allows none. Yours to edit; kept on uninstall like your other files there.
/etc/glidex/vm-shim.jsonThe hypervisor binaries VMs may run.
/etc/glidex/policies/Site policy files (root:glidex, mode 0750), empty.
/etc/glidex/install.confThe installer’s saved choices.
/etc/pam.d/glidexThe PAM service for web logins with local passwords.
/etc/sysctl.d/90-glidex.confnet.ipv4.ip_forward=1 for NAT networks and, with --ovs-profile dpdk, vm.nr_hugepages (kept after going back to the kernel profile unless --release-hugepages). The previous values are recorded for the uninstaller.
/etc/modules-load.d/glidex.confLoads vfio-pci at boot, with --ovs-profile dpdk.
/etc/glidex/vfio-devices.json, /etc/modules-load.d/glidex-vfio.conf, /etc/systemd/system/glidex-vfio-boot.serviceWith --vfio-devices or --sriov: what to bind and set at boot, and the unit that does it.
/srv/glidex/The datastore root (root:root, mode 0755), empty: mount or create datastores under it.
/var/lib/glidex-control-plane/The glidex user’s home. Its .glidex/ holds the database, images, disks, firmware and the self-signed certificate.

The installer also puts a copy of the Cloud Hypervisor firmware in your own ~/.glidex/, for a control plane you run by hand.

Pylon

With --with-pylon, the host runs glidex-pylond.service. It listens on /run/pylon/pylond.sock (group glidex) and starts before the control plane. Pylon VMs register with it, and it parks and wakes their vCPUs (see Elastic CPU).

  • Which CPUs it manages. pylond arbitrates the host CPUs in PYLON_CORES, 2-7 by default. To change it, write PYLON_CORES=<list> (such as PYLON_CORES=4-31) to /etc/default/glidex-pylond and restart glidex-pylond.

  • CPUs it reserves. While pylond runs, the control plane reserves the first two cores of the host for it, with their hyperthreads: no VM is placed on them, and gxctl node topology shows them as reserved for pylon. See Host resources.

  • The sched_ext scheduler. On a kernel built with sched_ext (6.12 or later), pylond attaches Pylon’s scx_pylon kernel scheduler when it starts, and falls back to its own core table if that fails. This needs a pylond built from Pylon with CMKL-APEX/pylon#9; an earlier one never attaches it from this service. scx_pylon then schedules every task on the host, not only VMs, until pylond stops. Check it with cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/ops (enabled, pylon). To keep it off, start pylond with --no-scx in a drop-in (sudo systemctl edit glidex-pylond), if your pylond has that option:

    [Service]
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/pylond --socket /run/pylon/pylond.sock --cores ${PYLON_CORES} --no-scx

A host offers Pylon when /usr/local/bin/pylon is there; Pylon VMs also need pylond running to scale. Elastic VMs run on any host with Cloud Hypervisor or QEMU.

Users and groups

NameKindPurpose
glidexsystem user and groupRuns the control plane and the VM units. Only this user is in the glidex group, which opens glidex-netd’s, glidex-authd’s and glidex-stord’s sockets.
glidex-uisystem user and groupRuns the web UI. It may only use the control plane’s UI socket.
glidex-metadsystem user and groupRuns the metadata endpoint. It may only use the control plane’s metad.sock.
glidex-usersgroupPeople who may use gxctl on the local socket, /run/glidex-cp/api.sock, and log in to the web UI with their local password.
glidex-admingroupBreak-glass administrators: full rights on the local socket, whatever the policies say.

The installer adds you to glidex-users and glidex-admin, and takes you out of glidex if an earlier install put you there. Add other people with usermod:

sudo usermod -aG glidex-users alice     # gxctl on this host, web UI login
sudo usermod -aG glidex-admin bob       # break-glass administrator

Keep glidex-admin small. On the first start, every member of glidex-admin becomes a Glidex administrator (see Access control); after that, give people roles instead of adding them to this group.

Updating

Pull the new source and run the installer again:

git pull
cargo run -p glidex-install

It updates system packages that came from its own list, Rust, Bun, Cloud Hypervisor, the binaries and the UI, and restarts the services whose binary or unit changed. Running VMs keep running across a control plane restart: each runs in its own glidex-vm@<id> unit. A running VM keeps the Cloud Hypervisor binary it started with until it is restarted. Reload web UI tabs that were open before the update to get the new UI.

With the kernel profile saved, the installer also turns off DPDK it finds on in ovs-vswitchd, for example after gxctl ovs dpdk-init or a profile switch in the web UI, which don’t change the saved profile. With bridges it only says so unless you pass --allow-ovs-restart. To keep DPDK, save the profile once with --ovs-profile dpdk.

On a cluster member, a re-run also brings OVN up to the cluster’s ovn-northd (see OVN on cluster members).

If something else listens on port 8841 or 5173 (a control plane or UI you started by hand), the installer leaves the service stopped and tells you how to start it once the port is free.

Uninstall

See what would be removed, then remove it:

cargo run -p glidex-install -- uninstall --dry-run
cargo run -p glidex-install -- uninstall

The uninstaller stops every VM (each gets its power button and grace period), the services and glidex-netd; tears down Glidex host networking (uplinks give the host’s address back to its NIC, NAT, bridges and VM ports are removed); then removes the units, binaries, installer-written configuration, runtime directories, the users and the groups. It also removes the boot devices’ unit and files (devices stay on vfio-pci until the next boot). Kernel settings the installer changed go back to their previous values. With --tailscale-cert on, it also removes the installer’s tailscaled drop-in and restarts tailscaled; a TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID you set yourself stays.

By default it keeps your data and site configuration, and says so:

  • /var/lib/glidex-control-plane and ~/.glidex (VM database, credentials, images, disks, firmware);
  • your files in /etc/glidex (control-plane.json, netd.json, policies, certificates);
  • a locally edited /etc/pam.d/glidex;
  • Open vSwitch, its DPDK settings and the hugepages they need, and the cloud-hypervisor, pylon and pylond binaries.

It never touches /srv/glidex and the datastores under it, nor the volume groups of LVM-thin datastores and the volumes in them, not even with --purge-user-data: unmount and remove them yourself.

OptionEffect
-n, --dry-runShow the plan and change nothing.
-y, --yesDon’t ask for confirmation.
--remove-ovsAlso remove Open vSwitch: the openvswitch-switch / openvswitch-switch-dpdk packages (via apt-get), or the source build in /opt/glidex.
--reset-dpdkClear the DPDK settings Glidex put in Open vSwitch.
--remove-cloud-hypervisorAlso delete the cloud-hypervisor binary.
--remove-pylonAlso delete the pylon and pylond binaries.
--purge-user-dataAlso delete ~/.glidex, /var/lib/glidex-control-plane (every VM, disk, image and credential) and the site configuration in /etc/glidex. This can’t be undone.

Take a host out of its cluster before you uninstall it (see Clusters).

Configuration

The control plane reads /etc/glidex/control-plane.json at start. The file is optional: without it every setting has its default, and that is how the installer leaves a host. /etc/glidex/control-plane.json.example lists every top-level setting with its default; copy it to start:

sudo install -m 0640 -o root -g glidex \
  /etc/glidex/control-plane.json.example /etc/glidex/control-plane.json
sudoedit /etc/glidex/control-plane.json
sudo systemctl restart glidex-control-plane
  • Keep the file root:glidex, mode 0640: the control plane (user glidex) must be able to read it, nobody else needs to.
  • Changes take effect on restart. Restarting the control plane leaves running VMs running.
  • The file is checked strictly. An unknown key (a typo), a wrong type or a value out of range stops the control plane with a message naming the setting; it never falls back to defaults. Read it with journalctl -u glidex-control-plane -b.
  • Every key is optional. A section you leave out, or a key inside one, keeps its default.
  • The file holds no secrets. TLS keys, the OIDC client secret and the secrets key are given to the service as systemd credentials (see Secrets).

authz, quotas, pci, audit

KeyTypeDefaultMeaning
authz.policy_files_dirpath"/etc/glidex/policies"Directory of read-only site policy files (*.cedar). See Access control.
authz.policy_historyinteger, 1–100050Versions kept of each site policy.

Keys: vms, vcpus, memory_mib, disk_gib, running_vms, networks, routers, external_ips, and devices ({"a100": 2}: devices per pool). An omitted key is unlimited, except networks (2), routers (1) and external_ips (1); null is unlimited.
pci.allowarray[]PCI devices projects may pass through without host rights: {"bdf": "0000:01:00.0", "projects": [...], "tenants": [...], "node": "gpu-01"} (ids or names; node optional: without it, the device at that address on every node), or {"pool": "a100", ...} for a pool. See PCI passthrough.
pci.poolsarray[]Device pools VMs ask for by count: {"name": "a100", "class": "gpu", "match": {"vendor_id": "0x10de", "device_id": "0x20b0"}, "nodes": [...], "prepare": true}; prepare binds the pool’s devices to vfio-pci when glidex starts; match.vf_of (a match of PFs) takes their SR-IOV VFs; per_device: {"vcpus": 14, "memory_mib": 57344, "hugepages": true, "cpu_policy": "dedicated"} is what a VM asking gpus gets per device unless it sizes itself (vcpus and memory_mib required, hugepages and cpu_policy ("shared" or "dedicated") optional, other keys refused). See Device pools and GPU requests.
audit.retention_daysinteger90Audit log entries older than this are deleted.
trust.default_max_staleness_minutesinteger60How long a trusted directory’s sessions and tokens stay good here after its last feed, unless set for that directory (gxctl admission staleness); see Clusters.

The control plane refuses to start when the pools or grants don’t add up, with one of:

  • pci.pools: pool names must be set and unique (…);
  • pci.pools: pool <name> matches every device; give it a match;
  • pci.pools: pools <a> and <b> match the same devices;
  • pci.allow: no pool <name>: a grant names an unknown pool;
  • pci.allow: each grant names one bdf or one pool.

cluster

Read only on hosts that are, or are about to become, part of a cluster. See Clusters.

KeyTypeDefaultMeaning
cluster.listen"addr:port""0.0.0.0:8842"The node API, between nodes.
cluster.advertise"addr:port"listen, with this host’s first non-loopback addressWhere other nodes reach this one.

cluster.raft.election_ms[min, max][1000, 2000]Raft election timeout; min at least 3 heartbeats, max above min.
cluster.raft.log_keep_entriesinteger, ≥ 10010000Raft log entries kept once every server has applied them.

cluster.scheduler.memory_overcommitnumber, ≥ 1.01.0Guest memory placed per MiB of host memory.

cluster.node_reserved.memory_mibinteger2048Memory per node kept for the host.

cluster.scheduler.dedicated_whole_coresbooleantrueDedicated vCPUs take whole SMT cores (a sibling no other VM shares). false: single threads.

Set it to a load balancer’s address in front of the servers (the same on each). It is also an accepted origin (put first in auth.allowed_origins) and the default SSO callback. Unset: the address glidex-ui reports (its Tailscale name, else the first GLIDEX_UI_HOSTS name, else the host’s FQDN, with its port), else the first auth.allowed_origins entry. See The web UI’s address.

cluster.role and cluster.tunnel_ip are accepted and ignored: a node’s role and tunnel address come from gxctl cluster init or its join.

The other cluster.ovn keys (enabled, underlay_mtu, nat_supernet, edge, snat_ct_zones, dns_servers) are still accepted, but once the cluster’s OVN settings are saved (on the web UI’s Cluster page) those decide, and the file’s are ignored with a warning in the log.

glidex-stord

glidex-stord, the root helper behind LVM-thin datastores, reads /etc/glidex/stord.json at start (--config <path> for another file). Without the file it allows no volume group. A file it can’t read or parse, or an unknown key, stops it from starting (journalctl -u glidex-stord). Restart it after a change: sudo systemctl restart glidex-stord.

KeyTypeDefaultMeaning
allowed_vgsarray of strings[]The volume groups stord may act on. The installer’s --stord-allow-vg VG adds one. See Allow it in glidex-stord.
 
{ "allowed_vgs": ["vg-glidex"] }

Keep the other keys stord accepts at their defaults. Its log filter is RUST_LOG (default info).

glidex-netd

glidex-netd reads /etc/glidex/netd.json at start (--config <path> for another file). Without the file every setting has its default. A file it can’t read or parse stops it (journalctl -u glidex-netd). Restart it after a change: sudo systemctl restart glidex-netd; VMs keep running.

KeyTypeDefaultMeaning
nat_supernetCIDR"10.88.0.0/16"The range node NAT networks take their subnets from. A value that isn’t a CIDR is ignored.
groupstring"glidex"The group allowed on netd’s full socket (the control plane’s).
admin_groupstring"glidex-admin"Break-glass administrators allowed on the full socket too.
policyobjectboth groups: ["*"]Group → the operations its members may send, by name, *, or a prefix ending in * ("list_*"). root may send any. netd logs the policy in force at start (netd policy).
gateway_check_secsinteger20How long a moved host address waits for the gateway to answer through the bridge.
commit_window_secsinteger60How long an address move waits for the client’s commit before netd rolls it back.
ovs_bin_dirpathunsetWhere ovs-vsctl and the other OVS tools are, when not on PATH.

Example

A host reached as glidex.example.org, with its own certificate and single sign-on:

{
  "server_name": "lab",
  "tls": { "cert": "/etc/glidex/tls/glidex.crt" },
  "auth": {
    "allowed_origins": ["https://glidex.example.org:5173"],
    "oidc": {
      "enabled": true,
      "issuer": "https://idp.example.org",
      "client_id": "glidex",
      "required_groups": ["glidex-users"],
      "group_teams": { "lab-staff": "staff" }
    }
  },
  "quotas": { "default": { "vms": 10, "vcpus": 32, "memory_mib": 65536 } }
}

allowed_origins here lets browsers call the API on port 8841 under that name and gives OIDC its default redirect_uri; the web UI doesn’t need it. The TLS key and the OIDC client secret are not in the file: see Secrets.

Secrets

Secrets go to the control plane as systemd credentials, never in control-plane.json, on the command line or in the environment. Keep the source files root:root, mode 0600; systemd copies each into a directory only the service can read. Add them in a drop-in:

sudo systemctl edit glidex-control-plane

[Service]
LoadCredential=tls-key:/etc/glidex/tls/glidex.key
LoadCredential=oidc-client-secret:/etc/glidex/oidc-client-secret
CredentialUsed for
tls-keyThe private key of a configured certificate (when tls.key is not set).
oidc-client-secretThe client secret of auth.oidc.
secrets-kekThe key that encrypts the secrets of login connectors made through the API. Without it the control plane keeps one in secrets.kek beside its database.

Then sudo systemctl restart glidex-control-plane.

Files and directories

Under the installed services:

PathWhat
/etc/glidex/control-plane.jsonThis file.
/var/lib/glidex-control-plane/.glidex/Data directory: glidex.db (the database), secrets.kek, images/, disks/, firmware, tls/ (the self-signed certificate).
/run/glidex-cp/Run directory: api.sock, ui.sock, metad.sock, tls.crt (a copy of the API’s certificate for local clients), and one private directory per running VM.
/run/glidex/glidex-netd’s sockets.
/run/glidex-authd/auth.sockglidex-authd’s socket.
/etc/glidex/netd.jsonglidex-netd’s settings, if you write one.
/etc/glidex/stord.jsonglidex-stord’s settings: the volume groups it may use.
/run/glidex-stord/glidex-stord’s sockets: stord.sock (root:glidex, mode 0660) for the control plane.
/var/lib/glidex-ui/tls/The web UI’s self-signed certificate.
/srv/glidex/The datastore root: registered datastores are directories under it. The installer creates it (root:root, mode 0755).

The data directory is ~/.glidex of the user the control plane runs as; for the service that user is glidex, whose home is /var/lib/glidex-control-plane. The service can only write inside that home, so image and disk directories, and files you give the API by path, must be inside it or readable by glidex outside /home, /root, /run/user and /tmp.

A control plane you start by hand uses your own ~/.glidex and the run directory $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/glidex (else /tmp/glidex-<uid>).

Outbound connections

Besides what Installation needs, the control plane makes these outbound HTTPS connections:

ToWhen
Image and firmware URLs, and the catalog’s mirrorsPulling images.
Your OIDC provider, Google, JumpCloudLogins through those connectors.
oauth2.googleapis.com, admin.googleapis.comA directory sync from Google Workspace, from the cluster’s leader: allow it from every server.
snapshot.debian.orgThe first kernel extraction on a host: the pinned extractor packages for the host’s architecture (about 35 MB on x86_64, 30 MB on aarch64), kept afterwards. Not needed with GLIDEX_KERNEL_EXTRACTION=off.

GLIDEX_DISK_DIR<data dir>/disksWhere disks are kept.

Set them for the service in a drop-in (sudo systemctl edit glidex-control-plane) with Environment=NAME=value lines.

gxctl reads its own variables (GLIDEX_SOCKET, GLIDEX_TOKEN, GLIDEX_CA_CERT, GLIDEX_PROFILE, GLIDEX_PROJECT); see the gxctl reference. In gxctl’s environment GLIDEX_CONFIG names its login profile file (~/.config/glidex/config.json by default), not the control plane’s configuration.

Web UI

glidex-ui has no configuration file. The installed unit sets GLIDEX_UI_DIR and GLIDEX_API_SOCKET; change the others in a drop-in (sudo systemctl edit glidex-ui).

VariableDefaultMeaning
GLIDEX_UI_LISTEN0.0.0.0:5173,[::]:5173Comma-separated addresses to listen on.
GLIDEX_UI_HOSTSthis host’s names and addressesAllowed Host values, host[:port], comma-separated; other requests get 421. Set it when users reach the UI under another name. The ts.net names of GLIDEX_UI_TLS_TAILSCALE are allowed either way.
GLIDEX_UI_TLSautoauto (HTTPS) or off (plain HTTP, loopback addresses only).
GLIDEX_UI_TLS_CERTa self-signed certificatePEM certificate chain.
GLIDEX_UI_TLS_KEYthe ui-tls-key credentialPEM private key. Prefer the credential.
GLIDEX_UI_TLS_TAILSCALEoffon: also serve the node’s Tailscale certificate to its ts.net names (TLS).
GLIDEX_UI_CLIENT_IP_HEADERunsetA header that carries the browser’s address, such as CF-Connecting-IP, trusted only on connections from this host itself (a tunnel such as cloudflared running here). Set it when a tunnel on the host connects to the UI, or every user’s address is 127.0.0.1 in the audit log and shares one rate limit. See Behind a load balancer or tunnel.
GLIDEX_UI_TAILSCALE_SOCKET/run/tailscale/tailscaled.socktailscaled’s local API socket.
GLIDEX_UI_DIR/usr/local/share/glidex/ui (unit)The built UI.
GLIDEX_API_SOCKET/run/glidex-cp/ui.sockThe control plane’s UI socket, used when it exists.
GLIDEX_API_URLhttps://127.0.0.1:8841The control plane over TCP, when there is no socket (development).
GLIDEX_API_CA_CERTthe local control plane’s certificatePEM file to trust for GLIDEX_API_URL.
RUST_LOGinfoLog filter.

For example, to serve the UI on one address under a DNS alias:

[Service]
Environment=GLIDEX_UI_LISTEN=192.0.2.10:5173
Environment=GLIDEX_UI_HOSTS=glidex.example.org,192.0.2.10

Behind a reverse proxy or a tunnel that runs on the host (such as cloudflared), list the public name users open in GLIDEX_UI_HOSTS, with the host’s own names if people still use them: the variable replaces the default list. (On a cluster server, cluster.ui_url’s name is accepted without it.) Also set GLIDEX_UI_CLIENT_IP_HEADER, so the audit log and rate limits see each browser’s address instead of 127.0.0.1:

[Service]
Environment=GLIDEX_UI_HOSTS=glidex.example.org,host.example.org
Environment=GLIDEX_UI_CLIENT_IP_HEADER=CF-Connecting-IP

See Behind a load balancer or tunnel for what else a proxy in front of several servers needs.

TLS certificates

The control plane API (port 8841) and the web UI (port 5173) serve HTTPS on every address of the host. Each uses a self-signed certificate unless you give it your own. Local gxctl users on the Unix socket don’t use TLS at all.

Self-signed certificates

On first start, the control plane and the web UI each generate a certificate (ECDSA P-256, valid for five years) for this host’s names and addresses: its fully qualified name, its host name, localhost, the loopback addresses and the addresses of its interfaces at that moment.

ServiceCertificateKey
Control plane/var/lib/glidex-control-plane/.glidex/tls/cp.crtcp.key next to it, mode 0600
Web UI/var/lib/glidex-ui/tls/ui.crtui.key next to it, mode 0600

A certificate is kept as long as it loads and is valid for more than 30 more days, so its fingerprint stays the same for the clients that trust it. It is regenerated when it is missing, unreadable or close to expiry.

Fingerprints

Browsers warn about a self-signed certificate. Before you accept it, compare the SHA-256 fingerprint the browser shows with the one the service printed:

  • the installer prints both at the end of every run;

  • the control plane logs it at every start (SHA-256: line):

    journalctl -u glidex-control-plane -b | grep SHA-256
journalctl -u glidex-ui -b | grep fingerprint

  • or compute it from the certificate:

    openssl x509 -in /run/glidex-cp/tls.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256
sudo openssl x509 -in /var/lib/glidex-ui/tls/ui.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256

/run/glidex-cp/tls.crt is a public copy of the API’s certificate (never the key) that the control plane writes at every start and after it reloads a replaced certificate, for local clients to trust.

New names or addresses

A self-signed certificate only covers the names and addresses the host had when it was made. After you rename the host or give it a new address clients will use, generate new ones:

sudo systemctl stop glidex-ui glidex-control-plane
sudo rm /var/lib/glidex-control-plane/.glidex/tls/cp.{crt,key} \
        /var/lib/glidex-ui/tls/ui.{crt,key}
sudo systemctl start glidex-control-plane glidex-ui

The fingerprints change: tell your users, and update gxctl profiles that pinned the old one (see gxctl). Running VMs are not affected.

Your own certificate

Use a certificate from your CA for anything users reach over the network. Put the files somewhere outside /home, for example /etc/glidex/tls/; the certificate must be readable by the service’s user, the key only by root:

sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/glidex/tls
sudo install -m 0644 glidex.crt /etc/glidex/tls/glidex.crt   # chain, leaf first
sudo install -m 0600 glidex.key /etc/glidex/tls/glidex.key

The certificate must name what users type: the host’s DNS name (and its address, if they use it).

API (control plane)

In /etc/glidex/control-plane.json:

{ "tls": { "cert": "/etc/glidex/tls/glidex.crt" } }

Give the key as the tls-key credential:

sudo systemctl edit glidex-control-plane

[Service]
LoadCredential=tls-key:/etc/glidex/tls/glidex.key

sudo systemctl restart glidex-control-plane

tls.key can name the key file instead, but then it must be readable by the glidex user; the credential keeps it root-only.

Web UI

sudo systemctl edit glidex-ui

[Service]
Environment=GLIDEX_UI_TLS_CERT=/etc/glidex/tls/glidex.crt
LoadCredential=ui-tls-key:/etc/glidex/tls/glidex.key

sudo systemctl restart glidex-ui

With a configured certificate the UI also sends Strict-Transport-Security.

If users reach the UI under a name that isn’t one of the host’s own, also set GLIDEX_UI_HOSTS (see Configuration). The control plane accepts the browser’s requests through the UI for any name the UI serves.

Renewing

Both services check their certificate and key files once a minute and serve a replaced pair without a restart. Replace each file in one step (write a new file, then mv it over the old one), the key and the certificate in either order: until the two match again, the service keeps serving the previous pair and logs a warning. The control plane also refreshes its public copy, /run/glidex-cp/tls.crt.

A key given as a systemd credential (LoadCredential=) is copied when the service starts, so a renewal that changes the key needs a restart; running VMs keep running:

sudo systemctl restart glidex-control-plane glidex-ui

journalctl -u glidex-ui (or -u glidex-control-plane) shows TLS certificate reloaded with the new fingerprint.

Tailscale certificates

On a host that is on a Tailscale tailnet with HTTPS certificates enabled (admin console → DNS → HTTPS Certificates), the web UI can serve the node’s Let’s Encrypt certificate to browsers that open https://<node>.<tailnet>.ts.net:5173. There’s no browser warning and no fingerprint to compare. Every other name and address keeps the UI’s usual certificate, and the API on port 8841 is unchanged.

Before you turn it on: every Let’s Encrypt certificate is published in public Certificate Transparency logs, so <node>.<tailnet>.ts.net becomes public. Tailscale can give your tailnet a randomly generated DNS name that reveals less. The name only resolves and routes inside the tailnet; use Tailscale ACLs to limit who can reach port 5173. Don’t expose the UI with Tailscale Funnel.

The installer sets it up: --tailscale-cert (an interactive run on such a node also asks once). It checks the steps below for you, refuses rather than take the permission from another service, and prints the ts.net URL once the certificate is served. --no-tailscale-cert and uninstall undo it. To do it by hand instead:

tailscaled hands certificates only to root or to the one user named in its TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID. If that variable is already set for another service (a web server, say), these steps would take the permission away from it; stop and resolve that first:

systemctl show tailscaled -p Environment
grep TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID /etc/default/tailscaled

Grant it to glidex-ui (restarting tailscaled drops the tailnet connection for a few seconds):

sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/tailscaled.service.d
printf '[Service]\nEnvironment=TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID=glidex-ui\n' |
  sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/tailscaled.service.d/50-glidex-cert.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart tailscaled

Then turn it on in the UI:

sudo systemctl edit glidex-ui

[Service]
Environment=GLIDEX_UI_TLS_TAILSCALE=on

sudo systemctl restart glidex-ui
journalctl -u glidex-ui -f    # "Tailscale certificate" with its fingerprint and expiry

The first certificate can take a minute to be issued; until then, and whenever tailscaled can’t provide one, the ts.net name gets the UI’s usual certificate and the log says why. The UI asks tailscaled every six hours, so renewals happen in place, without a restart. Connections served the Tailscale certificate get Strict-Transport-Security with a one-day lifetime.

To turn it off, remove the line from the drop-in and restart the UI; to also revoke the permission, delete 50-glidex-cert.conf and restart tailscaled.

Plain HTTP

"tls": "off" (API) and GLIDEX_UI_TLS=off (UI) serve plain HTTP, and are refused unless every listener is a loopback address:

{ "tls": "off", "listen": ["127.0.0.1:8841", "[::1]:8841"] }

Use this only behind something on the same host that terminates TLS. On its HTTPS port the web UI answers a plain-HTTP request with a redirect to https://.

Client trust

Browsers

With a CA-issued certificate, browsers need nothing. With the self-signed one, users compare the fingerprint once and accept it.

gxctl

On the host itself, gxctl uses the Unix socket and needs no certificate. Over TCP to a loopback address it trusts the published /run/glidex-cp/tls.crt automatically.

From another machine, gxctl trusts the system’s CA store. For a self-signed certificate, either:

  • copy the host’s /run/glidex-cp/tls.crt (it is public) and point GLIDEX_CA_CERT at it:

    export GLIDEX_CA_CERT=~/glidex-lab.crt
gxctl --url https://glidex.example.org:8841 login --oidc

  • or let a login profile pin the certificate. gxctl auth login shows the fingerprint of a certificate it doesn’t trust and asks whether to trust exactly that one; compare it with the one the control plane printed. Non-interactively, pass the fingerprint you checked:

    gxctl auth login --url https://glidex.example.org:8841 --profile lab \
  --pin sha256/<fingerprint> --oidc

    A pin trusts that one certificate; dates and the host name are still checked. When the certificate changes, gxctl refuses to connect rather than ask again. Once you have confirmed the new fingerprint through another channel:

    gxctl auth login --profile lab --pin sha256/<new-fingerprint> --rebind

    gxctl auth trust list shows a profile’s pins and CA, gxctl auth trust fetch compares the fingerprint the server reports with the certificate it presents.

Prefer a CA-issued certificate, or a pin, over any option that turns verification off. See the gxctl reference for login profiles.

API clients

Give clients the certificate to trust, for example with curl:

curl --cacert glidex-lab.crt -H "Authorization: Bearer $GLIDEX_TOKEN" \
  https://glidex.example.org:8841/auth/whoami

Clusters

Nodes of a cluster talk to each other on port 8842 with mutual TLS under the cluster’s own CA, which Glidex manages. That is separate from the certificates on this page; see Clusters.

Authentication

Every request to the control plane is authenticated, on every listener. How depends on where it comes from:

ClientHow it is identified
gxctl on the host, on /run/glidex-cp/api.sockThe caller’s Unix account, from the socket. No login.
Web UIA browser session, after a login with a local password, single sign-on or a passkey.
gxctl from another machine, scripts, API clientsAn access token (Authorization: Bearer …).
CI jobs and other workloadsA short-lived token, exchanged for the workload’s own signed token through a workload federation.

What an authenticated user may then do is decided by roles and policies: see Access control.

The local socket

The control plane listens on /run/glidex-cp/api.sock. It reads the caller’s user id from the socket itself and looks up their groups on every request:

  • members of glidex-users (users_group) are let in as themselves;
  • root and members of glidex-admin (admin_group) are break-glass administrators: they may do anything, whatever the roles and site policies say;
  • everyone else is refused.

A local user gets a Glidex user the first time they use the socket. Their Unix groups count as teams named unix:<group> for requests on the socket, so a role can be given to a whole Unix group (see Access control).

Adding someone to a group takes effect on their next request:

sudo usermod -aG glidex-users alice

/run/glidex-cp/ui.sock is the web UI’s: only the glidex-ui user may use it, and it carries the browser’s session, never rights of its own.

Local accounts

People in glidex-users can log in to the web UI with their Unix user name and password. The control plane doesn’t read passwords itself: it asks glidex-authd, a small root helper that checks them with PAM.

  • glidex-authd.socket listens on /run/glidex-authd/auth.sock; systemd starts glidex-authd.service on the first login.
  • It answers only the glidex user (the control plane).
  • It uses the PAM service /etc/pam.d/glidex, which includes the system’s normal authentication and account checks (common-auth and common-account on Debian and Ubuntu, system-auth elsewhere).
  • Every failure is answered after a fixed delay, and repeated failures are rate-limited per user and overall.

The installer manages /etc/pam.d/glidex while it contains the line Managed by glidex-install. Delete that line to keep your own edits; later installs and the uninstaller then leave the file alone. PAM stacks that need network access from the helper itself (LDAP or RADIUS without sssd) or setuid helpers are not supported.

Who may log in

Two lists must both allow a user, and should match:

  • allowed_groups in /etc/glidex/authd.json (the helper’s own);
  • auth.pam.allowed_groups in /etc/glidex/control-plane.json.

Both default to ["glidex-users"]. To let a second group log in:

{ "service_user": "glidex", "allowed_groups": ["glidex-users", "lab"] }

{ "auth": { "pam": { "allowed_groups": ["glidex-users", "lab"] } } }

sudo systemctl restart glidex-authd.service glidex-control-plane

/etc/glidex/authd.json:

KeyDefaultMeaning
service_user"glidex"The only user allowed to ask.
allowed_groups["glidex-users"]A user must be in one of these groups.
failure_delay_ms1000Delay before every failure answer.
max_connections8Connections served at once.
allow_rootfalseAlso answer root. For debugging only; leave it off.

The rest of the PAM settings are in auth.pam (see Configuration): enabled turns password logins off, jit: false stops new users from being created at their first login, and group_teams maps Unix groups to Glidex teams, updated at every login.

A user’s local account and their password logins are the same Glidex user. In a cluster, local accounts are per node (alice on one node is not alice on another) unless cluster.shared_local_accounts is set.

Single sign-on (OIDC)

Glidex logs users in through any OpenID Connect provider, with the authorization code flow (PKCE) in the browser and the device authorization grant for gxctl.

  1. Register Glidex with the provider as a confidential web client:

    • redirect URI: https://<ui-host>:5173/api/auth/oidc/callback, with the name users type to reach the web UI;
    • grant types: authorization code, and device code if gxctl users should log in with it;
    • make the provider put the user’s groups in the ID token (a groups claim) if you use required_groups or group_teams.

  2. Put the client secret in a root-only file and hand it to the service as a credential:

    sudo install -m 0600 /dev/null /etc/glidex/oidc-client-secret
sudoedit /etc/glidex/oidc-client-secret       # paste the secret
sudo systemctl edit glidex-control-plane

    [Service]
LoadCredential=oidc-client-secret:/etc/glidex/oidc-client-secret

  3. Configure auth.oidc in /etc/glidex/control-plane.json:

    {
  "auth": {
    "oidc": {
      "enabled": true,
      "issuer": "https://idp.example.org",
      "client_id": "glidex",
      "redirect_uri": "https://glidex.example.org:5173/api/auth/oidc/callback",
      "required_groups": ["glidex-users"],
      "group_teams": { "lab-staff": "staff" }
    }
  }
}

  4. Restart: sudo systemctl restart glidex-control-plane. The login page now has a Sign in with Single sign-on button.

Set redirect_uri explicitly: by default it is built from the first of auth.allowed_origins, which, when that list is empty, is the host’s own name. The web UI needs no allowed_origins entry for the name users reach it by; GLIDEX_UI_HOSTS decides which names it answers. The issuer must be an https:// URL; the control plane fetches its discovery document and keys from it, so it needs outbound HTTPS to the provider.

Who gets in:

  • required_groups: only members of one of these groups (from groups_claim). Empty lets in everyone the provider authenticates for this client, so set it, or restrict the client at the provider.
  • allowed_domains: only users whose email is in one of these domains, and verified: the ID token says email_verified: true. Some providers, such as Microsoft Entra ID, never send email_verified, because the organization assigns its users’ addresses; for those, set trust_email: true and a token that doesn’t say counts as verified. A token that says email_verified: false is refused either way.
  • jit: false: only people who already have a Glidex user.

group_teams maps provider groups to Glidex teams, which must exist (gxctl team create staff); memberships are updated at every login. Users are identified by the provider’s issuer and subject, never by email or name.

From another machine:

gxctl --url https://glidex.example.org:8841 login --oidc

gxctl prints a code and a URL to open in a browser, then saves a token valid for one day.

Login connectors

Each way to log in is a login connector. auth.pam and auth.oidc above appear as the connectors file-pam and file-oidc; they can only be changed in the file. Directory administrators can add more, from the web UI (Directory page, Connectors tab, + Add Connector) or with gxctl connector:

KindFor
pamLocal accounts of the host.
oidcAny OpenID Connect provider.
googleGoogle Workspace, or personal Google accounts (see Google).
jumpcloudJumpCloud SSO (see JumpCloud).

google and jumpcloud are OIDC with the provider’s endpoints and rules built in: you give a client id and secret, not an issuer.

gxctl connector add oidc corp --issuer https://login.example.com \
  --client-id glidex --name "Example Corp" --require-group glidex-users \
  --team lab-staff=staff
gxctl connector secret set corp                 # hidden prompt
gxctl connector secret set corp --from-file /path/to/secret
gxctl connector test corp
gxctl connector list
  • Each oidc, google and jumpcloud connector gets its own Sign in with <name> button on the login page, and its own redirect URI: https://<ui-host>:5173/api/auth/c/<id>/callback. The web UI’s connector form shows it, on the address you opened the UI with.
  • Secrets are read from a hidden prompt, standard input or a file, never the command line, and are never shown again. In the web UI, each secret field has its own Set secret button. They are stored encrypted with the host’s secrets key (secrets.kek beside the database, or the secrets-kek credential); back that key up with the database.
  • --mfa admits only logins the provider reports as multi-factor (amr contains mfa, or acr is one of the --mfa-acr values).
  • --token-max-days N caps the tokens a login through the connector mints (default 30 days).
  • --jit / --no-jit, --require-group, --team GROUP=TEAM, --domain and --trust-email work as in the file settings (allowed_domains, trust_email). In the web UI’s connector form they are Allowed email domains and The IdP verifies its users’ addresses. gxctl connector update doesn’t change --domain, --trust-email, --allow-email or --mfa-acr; change them in the web UI’s connector form (Edit).
  • --allow-email E (an oidc connector’s Allowed emails): with --jit, only these verified addresses get an account. --domain still gates every login, so a connector can let in anyone at the domain who already has an account and create accounts for the listed people only. Each address must be in one of the domains.
  • --default-tenant <t> makes new users members of tenant <t>. If that is the admin tenant or another operator tenant, a connector that creates users must also have --require-group.
  • --provisioning scim and --group-mode mapped|auto let the IdP create and remove the connector’s users (oidc and jumpcloud only); see Provisioning with SCIM. --provisioning pull makes Glidex read them from Google Workspace instead (google only); see Directory sync from Google Workspace.
  • Changing a connector needs a recent login (see Sessions and re-authentication).

Run gxctl connector without arguments for every option.

Google

A google connector logs in Google accounts. In the Google Cloud console, create an OAuth client of type Web application with the connector’s redirect URI. For gxctl login --oidc, create a second client of type TVs and Limited Input devices: Google only allows device logins through that type.

# Google Workspace: accounts of these domains.
gxctl connector add google gws --client-id <web-client-id> --domain example.org \
  --device-client-id <tv-client-id> --name "Example (Google)"
gxctl connector secret set gws client_secret            # hidden prompt
gxctl connector secret set gws device_client_secret
gxctl connector test gws

In the web UI, choose Kind Google, then Google accounts: Google Workspace (by domain) or Any Google account (invited or listed people). The web client and the device client each have their own Set secret button.

  • Workspace (the default) allows the accounts of the --domain domains. It checks the Workspace the account belongs to, never the email address: anyone can open a personal Google account under any address. Set the OAuth consent screen’s user type to Internal as well, so only the Workspace’s accounts can use the client. Public mail domains (gmail.com, googlemail.com) can’t be Workspace domains.
  • Logins must come with a verified email address.
  • Google doesn’t report whether a login used a second factor. If the Workspace enforces 2-step verification, --trust-2sv makes its logins count as multi-factor. The admin tenant and operator tenants only take a Workspace connector with --trust-2sv.
  • --consumer allows personal Google accounts too, but only for people you already know: an invitation, an address in --allow-email, or a Google account already linked to a Glidex user. With --jit (create users at their first login) it must also have --allow-email; without --jit, the default for connectors made with gxctl, new people get in by invitation only. A personal account can’t join the admin tenant or an operator tenant.
  • Without a device client, gxctl auth login --oidc through the connector fails with device_flow_unsupported. connector test reports whether device logins are set up.
  • Google sends no groups at login, so --require-group doesn’t apply, and --team only does with a directory sync, which reads the groups from Google. Otherwise give people roles in Glidex.

Directory sync from Google Workspace

A Workspace google connector can pull its users from Google: the members of the Google groups you name, nested groups included, get Glidex users ahead of their first login, and nobody else logs in through it. Glidex reads the directory every 15 minutes, and on demand. It is the Google Workspace counterpart of SCIM: Google can’t push users to Glidex, so Glidex reads them instead.

Glidex reads the directory as a Google Cloud service account with domain-wide delegation, read-only:

  1. In the Google Cloud console, in a project of your organization: enable the Admin SDK API, create a service account (it needs no roles in the project), and create a JSON key for it. Keep the key file safe; it goes only into Glidex’s secret, below.

  2. In the Google Admin console, Security → Access and data control → API controls → Domain-wide delegation → Add new: the service account’s client ID (the number on its page, not its email), and exactly these two scopes:

    https://www.googleapis.com/auth/admin.directory.user.readonly
https://www.googleapis.com/auth/admin.directory.group.readonly

  3. Pick the administrator it acts as: a super administrator, or a delegated administrator who may read users and groups.

  4. Switch the connector to the pull, and set the key:

    gxctl connector update gws --no-jit --provisioning pull --group-mode auto \
  --sync-admin admin@example.org --sync-group glidex-users@example.org
gxctl connector secret set gws service_account_key --from-file <service-account-key.json>
gxctl connector test gws      # the key, the token, and each group
gxctl connector sync gws

    Give the key with --from-file: it is several lines long, and the hidden prompt reads one. In the web UI: the connector’s form, Provisioning Directory sync, Save, then Set service account key (choose the JSON file, or paste it). Either way, delete the key file afterwards: Glidex keeps the key encrypted and never shows it, not even in the form.

  5. Let the control plane reach Google: it needs outbound HTTPS to oauth2.googleapis.com and admin.googleapis.com. In a cluster, the runs happen on the leader, so every server node needs it. Unlike SCIM, nothing has to reach Glidex from outside.

The settings, as gxctl flags and in the form (Directory sync):

FlagFormMeaning
--sync-admin EMAILAdministrator to act asThe Workspace administrator of step 3.
--sync-group GROUP (repeat it)Groups1 to 50 group emails. Their members, nested groups’ members included, are who gets in.
--sync-interval MINEvery (minutes)Minutes between runs: 15 by default, at least 5.
--sync-max-disable PCTStop above (%)The safety stop: 10 by default, 1 to 100.
--ssh-keys-field SCHEMA.FIELDSSH key fieldOptional: where the users’ SSH keys are.
  • A pull needs a Workspace connector (Google Workspace (by domain), not --consumer) with --no-jit; the web UI turns JIT off for you.
  • Any of the --sync-… flags sets them all: repeat the ones you keep when you change one, or edit them in the web UI.
  • --group-mode auto makes each named group a Glidex team, named after the group. With mapped (the default), --team GROUP=TEAM puts a group’s members in an existing team, by the group’s email or name. In the form, this is Groups, A team per IdP group or Mapped to teams below. Only the named groups become teams; members of a nested group count as members of the group that holds it. A group you stop naming leaves its team behind, as a group deleted at a SCIM IdP does (see Teams).
  • --default-tenant <t> makes new users members of tenant <t>.
  • connector test checks the key is set, that the service account gets a token as the administrator, and that it can read each group.

To stop pulling, set Provisioning back to None in the web UI’s connector form, or delete the connector (below).

What a run does

A run reads the groups’ members and those users from Google first, then compares them with the connector’s users and teams, then applies the difference:

  • New members get a Glidex user, managed by the connector, and join --default-tenant. Someone already suspended in Google gets none.
  • First login. It is matched to the pulled user by Google’s account id (the subject of Google’s login), never by email address. Someone the pull didn’t bring in is refused (login_not_allowed). Invitations can’t be taken through the connector, and nobody can add it to their account as a sign-in method. --mfa and --trust-2sv still apply.
  • Changes in Google (name, primary email) reach Glidex at the next run.
  • Leaving. Someone suspended or archived in Google, deleted there, or no longer in any of the groups is disabled in Glidex: their sessions end, their personal tokens are revoked, and they leave the teams the pull put them in. The user stays managed by the connector.
  • Coming back. Once they are active and in a group again, the next run enables the user. Not if an administrator disabled it in Glidex: then only an administrator enables it again.
  • Users who logged in before the pull through the same connector are adopted: the pull takes over the user they already have, with its roles, rather than making a second one. So are users who added the connector as a sign-in method before Glidex refused that; the audit log’s oidc-link entries show who did, and removing that sign-in method before the next run keeps their account out of the pull.
  • What Google owns. A pulled user’s name, email and whether it is enabled are Google’s, and the pulled teams’ names and memberships too: see Users an IdP manages.
  • Every change a run applies is in the audit log, done by system:sync:<connector-id> (the action syncConnector); a run that changed nothing isn’t recorded.

A disabled connector isn’t pulled on schedule. Deleting the connector disables its users, unless gxctl connector remove gws --detach-users (or the choice in the web UI) keeps them, as for SCIM.

The safety stop

A run that would disable more than --sync-max-disable percent of the connector’s users changes nothing at all, and shows as blocked, listing who it would disable. Up to 5 can always be disabled. It guards against a group renamed, emptied or deleted by mistake, which would otherwise read as “everyone left”.

  • If a group was changed by mistake, fix it in Google. The next run (or Sync now) sees it and applies normally.
  • If the change is right, apply it: gxctl connector sync gws --confirm, or Review blocked sync in the web UI, which lists the users first. This reads Google again and applies what it finds then, without the stop, once. It needs a recent login (see Sessions and re-authentication).

An error from Google, or an answer Glidex can’t read, changes nothing either: the run shows as failed, with Google’s message, and the next one tries again. Glidex retries Google’s 429 and 5xx answers a few times within a run; any other error ends it.

Watching the runs

gxctl connector show gws prints the pull’s settings and the last run; the Connectors tab shows it under each pulled connector:

StateMeaning
ok (synced)Applied. How many users were created, adopted, updated, disabled and enabled.
FAILED (failed)Google’s error, or a missing or unreadable key. Nothing changed.
BLOCKED (blocked)The safety stop: who it would disable. Nothing changed.

Sync now (or gxctl connector sync gws) runs one at once and shows its result; if a run of that connector is already going, it is refused with 409 sync_running. directory-auditor sees the status; running a sync takes directory-admin.

SSH keys from Google

With --ssh-keys-field <schema>.<field>, each run also reads the users’ SSH public keys from a Workspace custom attribute:

  1. In the Google Admin console, add a custom attribute for users (a category, which is the schema, and a field in it), of type text, multi-valued.
  2. Put one OpenSSH public key per value (ssh-ed25519 AAAA… alice@laptop) on the users who need it.
  3. Set --ssh-keys-field <schema>.<field> (in the form, SSH key field), for example glidex.ssh_keys.
  • Only public keys are kept: OpenSSH keys of a known type, without repeats, at most 32 per user. Anything else, such as a private key pasted by mistake, is dropped.
  • Each run replaces the user’s keys with what Google holds.
  • The keys go into a VM only through a guest credential: when the user has no local account on the host, the web UI’s Add Credential form fills them in (see Guest credentials). Removing a key in Google doesn’t remove it from credentials or VMs that already have it.
  • Whoever can edit the attribute in Google decides which keys a user is offered: keep it to administrators.

JumpCloud

A jumpcloud connector logs in JumpCloud users. In JumpCloud, add an SSO application with OIDC:

  • Redirect URIs: the connector’s redirect URI, https://<ui-host>:5173/api/auth/c/<id>/callback.
  • Login URL (where JumpCloud’s user portal sends people): https://<ui-host>:5173/api/auth/c/<id>/start.
  • Client Authentication Type: Client Secret Basic. Glidex sends its client secret that way, the OpenID Connect default; with Client Secret Post JumpCloud refuses the login (invalid_client).
  • Include group attribute, if logins should carry the user’s groups, and the user groups allowed to use the application.
gxctl connector add jumpcloud jc --client-id <client-id> --groups-claim memberOf \
  --require-group glidex-users --team lab-staff=staff
gxctl connector secret set jc
  • --groups-claim is the name set under Include group attribute (memberOf by default); --require-group and --team read it.
  • --allow-email limits which addresses get a new account with --jit.
  • JumpCloud’s addresses are set by your organization’s administrators, so an address the login doesn’t mark as unverified counts as verified (for --allow-email and invitations).

In the web UI, choose Kind JumpCloud; the form shows the redirect URI and the Login URL to enter in JumpCloud.

Provisioning with SCIM

A JumpCloud or OIDC connector can be provisioned: the IdP creates, updates and removes its users and groups in glidex over SCIM 2.0, ahead of their logins. Then only people the IdP provisions can log in, and deactivating someone in the IdP takes their access away at once.

  1. Switch the connector to SCIM. It stops creating users at login:

    gxctl connector update jc --no-jit --provisioning scim --group-mode auto

    --group-mode auto makes a glidex team per IdP group. The default, mapped, fills existing teams named by --team GROUP=TEAM. In the web UI, these are Provisioning and Groups in the connector’s form.

  2. Make a token for the IdP. It is shown once:

    gxctl connector scim-token create jc --name jumpcloud

    Or use the connector’s SCIM button on the Connectors tab, which also shows the endpoint URL. A token lasts 180 days by default (--days, at most 365). A connector can have five at once, so make the next one before the old one expires, then revoke the old one:

    gxctl connector scim-token list jc              # ids, names, expiry; never the tokens
gxctl connector scim-token revoke jc <token-id>

    The token is a password for the connector’s users: whoever holds it can create users and put them in teams. Paste it straight into the IdP, keep any copy in a secret manager, never in shell history, scripts or tickets, and revoke a token that may have been exposed. Making and revoking tokens needs a recent login; a connector that isn’t --provisioning scim refuses them (409 not_provisioned). Expired tokens stay listed for 30 days.

  3. Make the endpoint reachable from the IdP (see below).

  4. In JumpCloud, open the application’s Identity Management, choose SCIM 2.0, and enter:

    • Base URL: the endpoint, for example https://<name>.<tailnet>.ts.net/api/scim/v2/c/jc;
