NoMarkerShared: no marker, so probably not mounted on this nodeMount it
NotEmptyShared: files but no marker; not claimed, since they aren’t Glidex’sRegister an empty directory
ForeignMarkerShared: another datastore’s or another cluster’s directoryUse another export or directory

An LVM-thin datastore has reasons of its own; see Node status.

gxctl datastore list          # each datastore, how many nodes reach it, free space
gxctl datastore show nfs1     # each node's path, free space, or why it can't

gxctl datastore list shows how many nodes reach each datastore (NODES OK, such as 2/3) and the most free space on one of them. On the Datastores page that is Nodes reaching it (2 of 3, in amber when some don’t); click a datastore’s name for each node’s path, status and free space.

The VMs of a disk on a registered datastore are placed only on nodes that reach it; other nodes are refused with datastore … is not reachable here (see the VM form’s Placement).

Mount warnings

A node that reaches a shared datastore on NFS also looks at the mount’s options, and records a warning for:

  • soft or softerr: mounted soft: an NFS server outage fails the guests’ disk writes; mount it hard;
  • node-local locks, nolock or local_lock= other than none: NFS locks are local to this node (…): disk locks don’t keep other nodes off a disk. The volume locks then no longer keep two nodes’ hypervisors off one disk.

The datastore stays reachable. gxctl datastore show prints the warnings under the node; on the Datastores page the node shows reachable, with warnings, with the warnings listed. Remount with the right options; the warning goes at the node’s next check.

Disks on a shared datastore

Workers

A disk on a shared datastore isn’t bound to a node. One node at a time, its worker, does the work on its file (making, resizing, deleting it): the node of its VM once the VM is placed, otherwise a ready node that reaches the datastore, chosen again when nodes come and go. The Disks page’s Node column shows it as shared · node2.

Volume locks

Glidex locks every disk on a shared datastore while a VM runs it or the worker works on it, with a lock file in the datastore’s .locks/ directory. A VM whose disk is locked by another node doesn’t start (reason DiskBusy: disk … is in use elsewhere (… is locked)), and a disk operation waits until the lock is free. This keeps two nodes from writing one disk, for example if a node that seemed gone still runs the VM.

The locks are POSIX record locks on the shared filesystem. Use a filesystem that enforces them between nodes (NFSv4 does, with locking on; see Mount warnings).

The default for new disks

New disks go to local unless they name a datastore, or another one is the default. A VM’s root disk made along with the VM goes there too. Keeping local (fastest, but its disks tie VMs to their node) or choosing shared storage (VMs can move, at network-storage speed) is your call.

gxctl datastore set nfs1 --default        # takes it from any other
gxctl datastore set nfs1 --no-default     # back to local

In the web UI it is Make default on the datastore’s row (on local’s row to go back). Disks that already exist stay where they are.

Overcommit and capacity

Disk files and LVM-thin volumes are thin, so by default (overcommit on) a datastore accepts disks bigger than its free space, as local always has. With overcommit off, a new disk, or a disk moved in, that doesn’t fit in the free space of the best node (less the disks still being made there) is refused with 507 insufficient_storage, with free_bytes and needed_bytes in the error’s details.

Web UI: Stop overcommit / Allow overcommit on the row. gxctl: gxctl datastore set fast --no-overcommit (or --overcommit).

The check happens when a disk is created or moved; files that grow later can still fill the datastore. Project disk_gib quotas count disks on every datastore together.

Changing and deleting

gxctl datastore set fast --nodes node1,node2,node4
gxctl datastore set fast --all-nodes
gxctl datastore set fast --node-path node4=/srv/glidex/ssd
gxctl datastore set nfs1 --no-overcommit
gxctl datastore rm fast

You can change the nodes, the nodes’ own paths, the default and overcommit (PATCH /datastores/{id}). The name, the path and whether it is shared can’t be changed: register a new datastore and move the disks.

Refused, with 409 conflict and the reason:

  • changing a node’s path while a running VM there has a disk on the datastore open: stop it first;
  • taking a node out of nodes while a disk on the datastore is bound to it;
  • deleting a datastore while disks are on it: move or delete them first. On the Datastores page, Delete is disabled meanwhile;
  • deleting an LVM-thin datastore while a node keeps an image’s volume in it (gxctl datastore show lists them as image volumes): delete those images first, or remove their gx-i-… volumes with lvremove. It can go once each node has looked again, within a minute (see Deleting an LVM-thin datastore).

Deleting a datastore leaves its directory and files, or its volume group and pool, alone; clean them up yourself.

Moving VMs and disks

  • A stopped VM whose disks are all on shared datastores can be placed on another node: Place on another node on its page, or gxctl place <vm> --node node2.
  • When a node is gone for good, gxctl node forget <node> --fenced marks its VMs lost; those on shared datastores can then be placed on a live node the same way (Place on a live node).
  • A disk can be moved to another datastore while no running VM uses it: gxctl disk move <disk> --datastore nfs1. Moving a node-local disk to a shared datastore is how a VM on a node’s own disk becomes free to move. Moving it straight to another node’s own disk isn’t possible: move it to a shared datastore first, then from there.

See Images and disks for moving disks, and Clusters for nodes. Nothing moves by itself, and running VMs don’t move.

Placing a stopped or lost VM again

A VM stays on the node it was placed on. A stopped VM can be placed again on another node, and so can a lost one, whose node was forgotten (see A node is gone for good).

Web UI: the VM’s page, Place on another node (Place on a live node for a lost VM): pick a ready node, or Where there is room.

gxctl:

gxctl place web1 --node node2      # on node2
gxctl place web1                   # wherever the scheduler finds room

It prints where the VM went, or Not placed yet with the reason it waits. Over the API: POST /vms/{id}/place with an optional node.

What can go with the VM:

  • disks on shared datastores (their worker follows the VM);
  • a disk on a node-local datastore only if it is already on the target node, and never for a lost VM: move it to a shared datastore first;
  • no host-path root disk, no PCI devices, and no networks that exist on one node only (use a cluster network).

Anything else is refused with 400 invalid_config, naming the cause. A VM that isn’t stopped is refused with 400 invalid_state: stop it first. On a standalone host there is nowhere else to go (400 invalid_config).

Placing a VM with --node pins it to that node, as choosing a node when creating it does; without --node it loses its old pin. Start it again afterwards. Files the VM kept on its old node stay there: its runtime directory (console log) and, for QEMU, its UEFI variable store; on the new node it starts with fresh UEFI variables from its firmware.

Placing VMs needs the system-admin role.

Moving a disk between datastores

A disk moves while no running VM uses it: from local to a shared datastore and back, or onto another node-local datastore, LVM-thin included. Users with the editor role in its project move it, on the Disks page or with gxctl disk move; see Moving a disk for the commands and what is refused.

  • One node, the one that has the disk’s file and reaches the destination, copies it into the destination, checks the copy, and only then switches the disk over and removes the old file. If the copy fails, the disk stays where it was (event MoveFailed).
  • Onto or off an LVM-thin datastore, the copy is always full, and raw on it (see Moving disks on and off).
  • A linked disk that isn’t flattened is rebased onto the image’s copy at the destination; on a shared datastore Glidex makes that copy first (see Images on a shared datastore).
  • A destination without overcommit that lacks the space refuses the move (507 insufficient_storage).
  • A disk can’t go straight from one node’s datastore to another node’s (for example from local on node1 to local on node2): move it to a shared datastore, then from there.

LVM-thin

An LVM-thin datastore (driver lvm) keeps each disk as a raw thin logical volume in a volume group and thin pool on each node. It is node-local: a disk on it lives on one node, and its VM runs there.

Glidex runs as an unprivileged user, so a small root helper, glidex-stord, makes, activates, grows and removes the volumes for it. stord acts only on the volume groups you allow, and only on Glidex’s own volumes: gx-d-<disk-id> for disks and gx-i-<image-id> for images. It never touches physical volumes, other logical volumes, or a volume group you didn’t list. The installer sets it up on every host (see Installation); it keeps no state of its own.

Prepare the volume group

You make the volume group and its thin pool, on each node that should have the datastore. Give Glidex a volume group of its own:

sudo apt-get install lvm2 thin-provisioning-tools   # dnf: lvm2 device-mapper-persistent-data
sudo vgcreate vg-glidex /dev/nvme1n1
sudo lvcreate --type thin-pool -l 95%FREE -n pool vg-glidex

Leaving some of the volume group free lets you grow the pool, or its metadata, later.

Allow it in glidex-stord

stord allows no volume group by default. List yours in /etc/glidex/stord.json, on each node:

cargo run -p glidex-install -- --stord-allow-vg vg-glidex

The installer adds the group to the file (repeat the flag for more than one; it is not saved for later runs, but the file keeps the list) and restarts glidex-stord. Or edit the file and restart stord yourself:

{ "allowed_vgs": ["vg-glidex"] }

sudo systemctl restart glidex-stord

A missing file means no volume group. A file stord can’t read or parse stops it from starting (journalctl -u glidex-stord); every node then shows the datastore as StordUnavailable. Restarting stord doesn’t disturb running VMs: they keep their devices open.

Register an LVM-thin datastore

Web UI: Datastores, Add Datastore, LVM-thin on each node: the Name, the Volume group and the Thin pool. In a cluster, Volume groups of their own takes one node=volume-group per line for nodes whose group is named otherwise.

gxctl:

gxctl datastore create thin1 --lvm vg-glidex/pool
gxctl datastore create thin2 --lvm vg-glidex/pool --nodes node1,node2 --node-path node3=vg-nvme
  • --lvm VG/POOL: the volume group and its thin pool, instead of --path.
  • --node-path NODE=VG: this node’s own volume group (same pool name).
  • --nodes, --default and --no-overcommit work as for a directory.

Over the API: POST /datastores with driver DATASTORE_DRIVER_LVM, volume_group and thin_pool, and no path (400 invalid_datastore otherwise); node_paths then maps nodes to their volume groups. Volume group and pool names are plain LVM names: letters, digits, ., _, - and +, not starting with -.

The volume group and the pool can’t be changed afterwards; a node’s own volume group can (gxctl datastore set thin1 --node-path node3=vg-nvme), but Glidex doesn’t move volumes from the old group.

Node status

Each node asks its glidex-stord about the pool, as it checks a directory (see What “reachable” means). A node that reaches it reports the pool’s size and free space; gxctl datastore show prints its path as vg-glidex/pool.

ReasonMeaningWhat to do
StordUnavailableglidex-stord isn’t running on this node, or doesn’t answersystemctl status glidex-stord; it isn’t installed with --no-services
NotAllowedThe volume group isn’t in /etc/glidex/stord.jsonAllow it
NoVolumeGroupNo volume group of that name on this node, or the LVM tools failed (the message says which)Create it, fix the node’s own volume group, or install lvm2
NoThinPoolThe volume group has no thin pool of that nameCreate the pool, or fix the name

It also warns, while the datastore stays usable, when the pool’s data or its metadata is 80% full (see Thin pool space).

What is different from a directory

  • Raw only. Every disk is a raw volume; asking for qcow2 is refused (400 invalid_disk).
  • Linked disks are thin snapshots. The first linked disk from an image on a node makes that node’s image volume, gx-i-<image-id>, from the verified image, and seals it read-only. Each linked disk is a thin snapshot of it: quick to make, and it takes pool space only for what the guest changes. A full disk is a converted copy.
  • Image volumes stay with their image. A node keeps an image’s volume until the image is deleted, even when no linked disk uses it any more. Deleting the image removes its volumes on every node.
  • Disks grow but never shrink (400 invalid_disk). Growing a disk made from an image extends its root partition as usual.
  • Device access per VM. Before a VM starts, stord lets that VM’s unit open exactly its own volumes; deleting the VM takes that away.
  • No volume lock of Glidex’s own. The volumes are on one node, and the hypervisors’ own locks refuse a second instance of a disk.

Moving disks on and off

A disk moves onto or off an LVM-thin datastore like any other (see Moving a disk between datastores), always as a full, standalone copy: a raw volume has no backing file. A disk moved onto it becomes raw. A disk moved off it to a directory stays raw, as a raw file.

Volumes are on one node, so the usual rules hold: a disk can’t go straight from one node’s volume group to another node’s; move it through a shared datastore. A VM with a disk on an LVM-thin datastore can be placed again only on the node that has the volume.

Metering

disk.stored for a volume is the pool space it holds, not its size. For a file it is still the file’s allocated size. For a linked volume it is what LVM reports as mapped, which includes the blocks it still shares with its image volume, so the linked disks of one image together can count more than the pool holds.

Thin pool space

Volumes are thin, so the pool, like a directory with overcommit on, can promise more than it has. With overcommit off, a new or moved disk that doesn’t fit in the pool’s free space is refused (507 insufficient_storage). Either way, keep an eye on it:

  • when the pool’s data or metadata is 80% full, the node shows a warning (reachable, with warnings on the Datastores page, warning: under the node in gxctl datastore show);

  • a full thin pool stops every guest on it at its next write. Grow the pool before that, from free space in the volume group:

    sudo lvextend -L +100G vg-glidex/pool                  # data
sudo lvextend --poolmetadatasize +1G vg-glidex/pool    # metadata

    LVM can also grow it by itself (thin_pool_autoextend_threshold in lvm.conf), as long as the volume group has room.

Deleting an LVM-thin datastore

Besides the disks, its image volumes keep an LVM-thin datastore: the delete is refused (409 conflict, naming the images and nodes) while any node keeps one. gxctl datastore show lists them under each node as image volumes (image ids). Delete those images, or remove the volumes on the node:

sudo lvremove vg-glidex/gx-i-<image-id>

The delete goes through once each node has looked again, within a minute. The volume group, the pool and anything else in them stay.

Hyperstor

A hyperstor datastore (driver hyperstor) keeps each disk as a volume of a hyperstor cluster’s pool, replicated across that cluster’s nodes. It is shared: a disk on it isn’t tied to a node, and its VM can run on any node that runs hyperstor-vhost, hyperstor’s vhost-user-blk service. The VM’s hypervisor opens the volume through that service’s socket, as a disk with 512-byte sectors.

Glidex manages the volumes (create, clone, grow, delete) through the cluster’s API, as a management identity of its own. A hyperstor volume is held by one node at a time: the node whose VM uses it holds its lease, and another node can’t attach it meanwhile.

A hold can outlive its VM there: the VM’s node crashed, or a detach failed. Each node lets go, within a minute, of the volumes it holds for VMs placed elsewhere. And a VM starting on a node takes its disks from another node’s hyperstor-vhost that still holds them, which cuts off only those volumes there; the node’s other VMs carry on. A disk that a Glidex disk operation holds (hyperstorctl, on a server) is waited for: the VM shows DiskBusy until it ends. This needs hyperstor with per-volume fencing on every node; with an older hyperstor-vhost, a held disk is waited for as before.

Prepare the nodes

On each node that should run VMs from hyperstor disks:

  • run hyperstor’s hyperstor-vhost for the cluster’s map service, with its default directory (/run/hyperstor/vhost), letting the glidex user use its control socket and giving its disks’ sockets the glidex group, so that the hypervisors may open them. hyperstor’s installer does this: hyperstor-install install --vhost --vhost-user glidex on a host that already runs a hyperstor role, or hyperstor-install install --role vhost --map ADDR[,ADDR...] --vhost-user glidex on a host that only runs VMs;
  • install hyperstorctl: Glidex writes images into volumes and edits their partitions with it.

Servers also need to reach the cluster’s API (port 8850 by default): they do the volume operations, because only they hold Glidex’s identity.

Register a hyperstor datastore

Make a single-use management token on the hyperstor cluster, and give it to Glidex in a file:

hyperstorctl token create --role mgmt --name glidex > glidex.token
gxctl datastore create hs1 --hyperstor 192.0.2.21:8850,192.0.2.22:8850 --pool 1 --token-file glidex.token
  • --hyperstor API,...: the cluster API’s addresses, tried in turn.
  • --pool N: the hyperstor pool for the disks (hyperstorctl pools).
  • --token-file F: the token. Glidex enrolls with it once, from the server that takes the request: it makes a key, gets a certificate for the identity the token names, and keeps the key sealed with the cluster’s secrets key. The token is used up and isn’t kept.
  • --nodes, --default and --no-overcommit work as for a directory. With --no-overcommit, a disk larger than the pool’s free space is refused (507 insufficient_storage).

While the pool is full (past hyperstor’s full ratio), new disks on the datastore are refused with 507 insufficient_storage, overcommit or not, and gxctl datastore show says so on each server’s line. A disk whose creation hyperstor refuses for it waits (DatastoreFull) and is tried again each minute, so freeing space (purging hyperstor’s trash, adding a device) lets it finish. Disks already there keep working. A nearly full pool is a warning only.

Web UI: Datastores, Add Datastore, hyperstor cluster: the Name, the Cluster API addresses, the Pool and the Token.

Over the API: POST /datastores with driver DATASTORE_DRIVER_HYPERSTOR, hyperstor_api, hyperstor_pool and hyperstor_token, and no path. gxctl datastore show prints the identity and when its certificate expires; the leader renews it when a third of its life is left.

Node status

Each node reports whether its hyperstor-vhost answers (VhostUnavailable otherwise), and each server whether the cluster’s API answers with Glidex’s identity (ApiUnavailable).

Free and total space are the pool’s, as hyperstor reports them: usable space, after its copies or erasure coding. Servers read them from the cluster’s API; other nodes report none (0 in gxctl datastore show, — on the Datastores page), and so does a server whose hyperstor doesn’t report space yet (a hyperstor too old to report it, or while one of the pool’s devices is yet to report). gxctl datastore list and the Datastores page show the most any node reports. Pools of one hyperstor cluster that share devices each count the same free space.

What is different from a directory

  • Disks are raw. A request for qcow2 is refused; a linked disk is a hyperstor clone of the image’s volume, made at once.
  • Images are written into one volume per image and datastore, the first time a linked disk needs it, and kept as its snapshot golden.
  • Disks grow, and never shrink. Growing and the root partition’s extension work as for a file; the partition is edited through hyperstorctl, not a block device.
  • Moves onto or off a hyperstor datastore aren’t supported yet.
  • Placing a lost VM again (--fenced) takes its disks’ leases from the forgotten node at its next start. Otherwise a VM takes only holds that another node’s hyperstor-vhost left behind (see above); a hold of a disk operation is waited for.
  • Metering reports the disks’ size, not the space they use.

Deleting

A deleted disk’s volume goes to hyperstor’s trash, where hyperstor’s operators can bring it back until its grace period ends. A volume left by a disk or image that failed to be made holds no one’s data: Glidex deletes it for good (purging it from the trash), so that a retry can make it again. A clone there still needs its image’s volume, so when the image is deleted that volume stays until the clone is purged; the leader then removes it, within a minute. Deleting the datastore removes Glidex’s sealed key; it needs no disks on it, and leaves the identity’s certificate to expire (revoke it with hyperstorctl cert revoke).

Images on a shared datastore

A linked disk (a thin overlay on an image) on a shared datastore needs the image on that datastore too. Glidex copies it there by itself, as images/<image-id>.qcow2 next to disks/, the first time a linked disk needs it, and checks it against the image’s checksum; the disk waits meanwhile (image … has not been copied into datastore … yet). Full copies, and disks on node-local datastores, use the node’s own copy of the image.

The Images page lists these copies apart from the node copies (in 1 shared datastore). They have no Remove button: they go when the image is deleted, which isn’t possible while a linked disk uses it.

Who may use a datastore

Every user who can create disks in a project can put them on any datastore. To keep one for some tenants, add a site policy that forbids useDatastore on it:

@id("site.fast-for-research")
forbid (principal, action == Glidex::Action::"useDatastore", resource == Glidex::Datastore::"<datastore-id>")
unless { principal in Glidex::Tenant::"<tenant-id>" };

gxctl datastore show <name> prints the datastore’s id. The check applies when a disk is created on the datastore (including a VM’s root disk on the default datastore) and when a disk is moved to it.

Limits

  • No live migration: a VM moves only while stopped, and only when you ask.
  • A node that leaves the cluster with its VMs (detach) can’t take its disks on node-local datastores other than local along: move them to local first.
  • A node that leaves the cluster drops out of each datastore’s status within a minute; a node that is only down keeps its last status.
  • Existing data can’t be registered as a datastore: Glidex doesn’t take over a directory that already has files in it.
  • Block storage is node-local LVM-thin only: no shared LVM, no Ceph RBD, no CSI plugins, no disk snapshots, and no per-datastore quotas yet.
  • A VM’s root disk made along with the VM always goes to the default datastore. To put it elsewhere, create the disk first (gxctl disk create … --datastore) and boot the VM from it.

PCI passthrough

A VM can take a host PCI device (a GPU, a NIC, an NVMe drive) through VFIO. Both hypervisors support it: Cloud Hypervisor with --device, QEMU with -device vfio-pci. Glidex lists the host’s devices, records which VM claims which device, checks who may use it, and hot-plugs it into a running guest.

Enabling the IOMMU is up to you. Glidex can bind a device to vfio-pci and give the glidex user access to it, or you do that by hand. Device pools, NUMA placement, device health and cordoning are in Host resources.

Host prerequisites

IOMMU

Turn on VT-d (Intel) or AMD-Vi (AMD) in the firmware, then on the kernel command line:

intel_iommu=on iommu=pt     # Intel
amd_iommu=on iommu=pt       # AMD (often on by default)

After a reboot, the IOMMU groups exist:

ls /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/

A device can only be passed through with every other device in its IOMMU group (except PCI bridges). gxctl pci shows each device’s group.

Bind the device to vfio-pci

Glidex can do this and the next step for you, per device, on any node:

gxctl node prepare-device <node> 0000:41:00.0   # its whole IOMMU group to vfio-pci; /dev/vfio/<group> to glidex
gxctl node release-device <node> 0000:41:00.0   # back on the drivers it had

Preparing loads vfio-pci if needed, binds every function of the device’s IOMMU group (bridges aside) to it, and writes a udev rule giving /dev/vfio/<group> to glidex, so the next step is done too. For a GPU with a resizable BAR it also shrinks the memory window when the host’s GPU windows would add up to its memory or more (see Prepare devices); the boot binding and pools with prepare: true do the same. It refuses a group with a NIC the host uses or an OVS-DPDK uplink, and needs net-admin or system-admin on that host. The host’s page in the web UI has Prepare and Release buttons. Like the manual way below, it doesn’t survive a reboot; a pool with prepare: true prepares its devices each time glidex starts, and the installer can bind them at boot (see Keep it across reboots). See Prepare devices.

To do it by hand, load the module, and bind the device to it instead of its usual driver. For a device at 0000:41:00.0:

sudo modprobe vfio-pci
echo vfio-pci | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0/driver_override
echo 0000:41:00.0 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0/driver/unbind
echo 0000:41:00.0 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/drivers_probe

This doesn’t survive a reboot; see the next section.

Keep it across reboots

The installer can bind devices to vfio-pci, and set SR-IOV VF counts, at every boot, before glidex, glidex-netd or any other hypervisor starts:

cargo run -p glidex-install -- --vfio-devices a100     # a pool from control-plane.json
cargo run -p glidex-install -- --vfio-devices 0000:41:00.0,0000:42:00.0
cargo run -p glidex-install -- --sriov 0000:61:00.0=8 --vfio-devices cx7-vfs
cargo run -p glidex-install -- --no-vfio-devices       # stop doing it
FlagWhat it does
--vfio-devices LISTPools of control-plane.json or PCI addresses, comma-separated. Each device and the rest of its IOMMU group go to vfio-pci. A new list replaces the old one.
--sriov PF=NN VFs on physical function PF, set before the binding so its VFs can be bound (by a pool with match.vf_of). Repeatable, or comma-separated; the last count for a PF wins.
--no-vfio-devicesForget both. What is bound now stays so until the next boot.
--nowApply them now as well. Not saved.

The settings are saved with the installer’s other choices, so a later run without these flags keeps them.

At boot, glidex-vfio-boot.service (a one-shot unit, there only while settings exist) runs after the kernel modules load and before glidex-netd, the control plane and libvirt:

  1. It sets the VF counts.
  2. It binds each selected device not yet on vfio-pci, with the same udev rule and refusals as Prepare, so Release works on it later.
  3. It prints what it bound, skipped and couldn’t do (journalctl -u glidex-vfio-boot). A device that fails stays on its driver; the boot goes on.
  • A device already on vfio-pci is never touched, at boot or with --now, so a running VM keeps its device.
  • With --now, a VF count is left as it is when a VF of that PF is on vfio-pci, since changing the count would remove that VF from its VM. Asking for the count it already has is fine.
  • Pools are copied as their match. Re-run the installer after changing a pool’s match. A pool needs /etc/glidex/control-plane.json on that host; addresses don’t.
  • Files: the settings are in /etc/glidex/vfio-devices.json, and vfio-pci is loaded from /etc/modules-load.d/glidex-vfio.conf. Uninstall and --no-vfio-devices remove both and the unit; devices stay where they are until the next boot.
  • Host drivers: for a GPU whose host driver loads first (nvidia, nouveau), binding at boot takes it from that driver. Make sure nothing on the host uses it.
  • The boot devices are set up with the host networking: an install with --no-networking doesn’t apply them.

Let the glidex user open it

VMs run in glidex-vm@<id>.service units as the glidex user. The unit allows the VFIO devices (/dev/vfio/vfio and the per-group /dev/vfio/<group>), but the group device must also be readable and writable by glidex through its owner, group or mode. Glidex reads those to decide whether a device is ready, as the VM’s unit would open it; ACLs aren’t considered. By default the group device belongs to root. Prepare and the boot binding write a rule per group; a udev rule of your own covers every group:

# /etc/udev/rules.d/90-glidex-vfio.rules
SUBSYSTEM=="vfio", GROUP="glidex", MODE="0660"

sudo udevadm control --reload && sudo udevadm trigger --subsystem-match=vfio
ls -l /dev/vfio/

The VM’s unit also lets the hypervisor lock all of the VM’s memory (LimitMEMLOCK=infinity): VFIO pins the guest’s RAM so the device can reach it. Without it, Cloud Hypervisor stops at Failed to DMA map VFIO device … Out of memory. A unit installed by an older Glidex lacks the line: run glidex-install again. The VM’s memory is still bounded by its size.

Find devices

gxctl pci                    # every host PCI device: address, ids, class, driver, IOMMU group, NUMA node, ready
gxctl pci 0000:41:00.0       # one device, with its sysfs path and why it isn't ready
gxctl node topology <node>   # a node's NUMA nodes with their CPUs, memory, hugepages and devices
gxctl node topology <node> --devices   # its devices with their root port, switch, link and VFs

A device is ready for passthrough when the host has an IOMMU, the device is bound to vfio-pci, every other device in its IOMMU group (bridges aside) is too, the glidex user can open /dev/vfio/<group>, it isn’t an OVS-DPDK uplink, and no other hypervisor on the host is using it. A device that isn’t says why; the reasons are listed in Ready devices. Over the API it is GET /pci-devices for this host, and GET /nodes/{id}/topology for any node. Both need a host role (auditor, net-admin or system-admin) on that host. In the web UI, a host’s page (Hosts, or Cluster → a node) has a Topology card. The topology’s fields and warnings are explained in Host topology.

Glidex names a device by its sysfs path, /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0. The API also accepts the bare address 0000:41:00.0, but use the full path: it is what Glidex stores and hands to the hypervisor. Claims and placement compare PCI addresses, so the path and the bare address are the same device.

Devices another hypervisor holds

On a host that also runs libvirt, OpenNebula or another hypervisor, a device can be on vfio-pci and still be in a running VM that isn’t Glidex’s. Such a VM may not show up with fuser /dev/vfio/<group>: libvirt gives each QEMU its own /dev. Glidex looks at every process’s open files instead (through glidex-netd), and:

  • marks the device not ready: in use by qemu-kvm-one (pid 37226). Pools and the scheduler skip it;
  • refuses Release of its group, and a VF count change on its PF: IOMMU group 30 is in use by qemu-kvm-one (pid 37226);
  • leaves it alone in the boot binding and --now, since it is on vfio-pci already;
  • shows it greyed out, with that reason, in the web UI’s VM form, where a node’s GPUs are picked, so nobody picks it.

Glidex’s own VMs (run as the glidex user) don’t count against readiness. Without glidex-netd, nothing is known about other holders. While another hypervisor keeps a device, cordon it in Glidex too (gxctl node cordon-device), so it stays out of pools once that VM stops until you hand it over.

Who may use a device

Passing a device through needs the usePciDevice permission on it. By default:

  • net-admin and system-admin may use any device. Given on one host (a per-host role), they cover that host’s devices only.
  • A project may use the devices granted to it in /etc/glidex/control-plane.json, by project or by tenant:
{
  "pci": {
    "allow": [
      { "bdf": "0000:41:00.0", "projects": ["ml-team"] },
      { "bdf": "0000:42:00.0", "tenants": ["research"] },
      { "bdf": "0000:87:00.0", "projects": ["vision"], "node": "gpu-02" }
    ]
  }
}

projects takes project ids or names, tenants tenant ids or slugs. In a cluster, the same address on two hosts is two devices: node (a node id or name) grants the one on that node; without it, the grant covers the device at that address on every node. A VM is then placed only on a node where the project may use all its devices (otherwise: its PCI devices are not granted to the project on this node); which nodes those are is worked out when its devices are set, so a later change to pci.allow applies to a waiting VM once its devices are set again. In Cedar a device is PciDevice::"<node>/<address>", in that node’s Host. Restart the control plane after changing the file. Site policies can widen or narrow this; see Access control.

Adding a device to an existing VM also needs attachDevice on the VM, and removing one detachDevice (both part of the editor role).

Attach a device

At creation, in the web UI’s VM form, VFIO PCI Devices (optional) takes comma-separated sysfs paths. Over the API, vfio_devices:

api -X POST https://localhost:8841/vms -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "name": "gpu-vm", "vcpu_count": 8, "mem_size_mib": 16384,
  "image": "ubuntu-26.04", "root_disk_size_gib": 40, "credential": "alice",
  "vfio_devices": ["/sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0"]
}'

On an existing VM, stopped or running:

gxctl attach-device gpu-vm /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0
gxctl detach-device gpu-vm /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0

Over the API these are POST and DELETE /vms/{id}/devices, or a PATCH whose change sets vfio_devices (with update_mask vfio_devices). The VM’s page lists its VFIO PCI Devices.

What happens:

  • A stopped VM gets the device at its next start.
  • A running VM gets it hot-plugged (Cloud Hypervisor’s API, QEMU’s device_add), and hot-unplugged on detach. While the guest is paused, the change waits (the VM shows DevicesPending with reason GuestPaused) and is applied once it runs. If the hypervisor refuses, the VM shows DevicesPending with reason HotplugFailed and the error; stop and start the VM to apply the change at boot.
  • One device belongs to one VM on its host. A second VM on the same host asking for it is refused (PCI device … is used by VM …), and the claim lasts until the instance that holds it is gone, not just until the spec drops it.
  • A device takes its IOMMU group with it: another VM can’t have a device of the same group (PCI device … shares IOMMU group … with …, used by VM …). The VM that holds the group may add the group’s other devices. PCI bridges in the group don’t count.
  • Both refusals are 409 conflict, at creation and when a device is added (attach-device, or a PATCH of vfio_devices).
  • A NIC that is a DPDK uplink of a glidex bridge can’t be passed through.

The guest sees the device on its PCI bus; install the guest driver there as on bare metal.

GPUs have large memory windows (BARs), up to the size of their memory. QEMU’s guest has room for 32 GiB of them by default; when a QEMU VM’s devices need more, Glidex gives the guest a 64-bit PCI window that holds them (-global q35-pcihost.pci-hole64-size=), sized from the devices it has when it starts. A device added to a running QEMU VM must fit what is left: if it doesn’t, stop and start the VM.

In a cluster

Devices are per host. The scheduler places a VM with vfio_devices only on a node that reports every one of those devices (otherwise: no PCI device …) and where no other VM holds them. Identical hosts with a GPU at the same address each take a VM with it. When every such node’s device is taken, a new VM waits as Unschedulable (its page says Waiting for a node) with the VM holding each one in its reason, and is placed once one is free. To choose the host, pin the VM: Placement in the VM form, or node (a node name or id) in the API request. A pinned VM asking for a device already taken on that node is refused. A node is also skipped where the device is cordoned, or where the project has no grant for it (its PCI devices are not granted to the project on this node). Prepare each host (IOMMU, vfio-pci, the udev rule) the same way.

Claims are per node: a VM on one node doesn’t hold the device at the same address on another. Adding a device to a placed VM is checked against its node’s VMs; a VM still waiting for a node is checked when the scheduler places it. A node running an older Glidex version reports no IOMMU groups, so until it is updated its claims are by address only.

gxctl pci lists the devices of the host it is connected to. For an agent’s, use gxctl node topology <agent>: the server asks the agent.

NUMA

A device is attached to one NUMA node of the host (cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0/numa_node, or the NUMA column of gxctl pci). A VM with numa_policy (and, for pinned vCPUs, cpu_policy: CPU_POLICY_DEDICATED) gets its memory and vCPUs on its devices’ NUMA node. With NUMA_POLICY_STRICT, devices on two NUMA nodes, or a device whose firmware reports -1, are refused. With NUMA_POLICY_ALIGNED (what a GPU request sets), a VM whose devices are on several NUMA nodes is split over exactly those, and its guest gets one NUMA node and PCI root per host node. See NUMA nodes and, for users, NUMA and dedicated CPUs.

Device pools

Instead of naming devices by address, a VM can ask for a number of devices from a pool (devices: [{"pool": "a100", "count": 2}]), and Glidex picks ready, uncordoned devices no other VM holds, near each other and the VM’s memory. Pools are defined in pci.pools and granted with pci.allow entries that name a pool:

{ "pool": "a100", "tenants": ["research"] }

The picked devices are claimed and passed through like devices named by address. For GPUs, "gpus": {"count": 4} also places and sizes the VM from the pool’s per_device. Pools, their grants, quotas, tenant pools, GPU requests and metering are in Device pools.

NVLink fabric (NVSwitch)

On an NVSwitch board (HGX A100, say), the host page’s Topology card lists the NVSwitches under NVLink fabric: their driver, IOMMU group and NUMA node. gxctl node topology <node> prints them too. They are never offered to VMs: NVIDIA Fabric Manager owns them, on the host or in a service VM (spec/27-gpu-vms.md). Today glidex VMs on such a board get their GPUs without NVLink between them.

SR-IOV virtual functions

A NIC (or GPU) with SR-IOV can be split into virtual functions (VFs), each passed through to its own VM. gxctl node topology <node> --devices shows a physical function’s vfs enabled/total and how many are ready.

gxctl node sriov gpu-01 0000:61:00.0 8     # 8 VFs on the PF
gxctl node sriov gpu-01 0000:61:00.0 0     # none

(POST /nodes/{id}/devices/{pf}/sriov with {"vfs": 8}, net-admin or system-admin; also the VFs… button on the host’s page.) A change removes every VF the PF had, so it is refused while a VM holds the PF or one of its VFs, and for a PF that is an OVS-DPDK uplink. To keep a VF count across reboots, give it to the installer: --sriov 0000:61:00.0=8 (see Keep it across reboots).

A PF with VFs enabled is no longer offered itself (passing it through would take its VFs with it). A pool takes VFs with match.vf_of, which matches their PF:

{ "name": "cx7-vfs", "class": "nic", "prepare": true,
  "match": { "vf_of": { "vendor_id": "0x15b3", "device_id": "0x1021" } } }

New VFs come up on the NIC’s own driver; prepare: true binds a pool’s VFs to vfio-pci at start and right after node sriov. Only VFs on vfio-pci are listed as pool devices. A VF inherits its PF’s NUMA node. Its MAC, VLAN and spoof checking are the PF’s defaults for now.

Device health and cordoning

Glidex watches the devices of running VMs: if one falls off the bus or has uncorrectable PCIe errors after the VM started, the VM’s DeviceHealthy condition turns False and a DeviceError event is recorded. It doesn’t stop the VM or take the device away.

A device you no longer trust can be cordoned: no new VM gets it, and the VM that has it keeps it.

gxctl node cordon-device <node> 0000:41:00.0     # new VMs asking for it: PCI device 0000:41:00.0 is cordoned
gxctl node uncordon-device <node> 0000:41:00.0

See Device health and cordoning.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCheck
invalid_config: … is not a PCI deviceUse /sys/bus/pci/devices/DDDD:BB:DD.F.
The VM fails to start: VFIO group not viableAnother device in the IOMMU group is still on a host driver. Bind all of them to vfio-pci, or move the card to another slot.
The VM fails to start: permission denied on /dev/vfio/<n>The udev rule above; ls -l /dev/vfio/.
No IOMMU group in gxctl pciThe IOMMU is off: firmware setting and kernel command line.
forbiddenThe project has no grant for the device in pci.allow, and you are not net-admin.
PCI device … is cordonedAn administrator cordoned it: gxctl node uncordon-device.
The VM shows DeviceHealthy=FalseThe device fell off the bus or had PCIe errors: gxctl node topology <node> --devices, the host’s dmesg.
conflict: PCI device … is used by VM …Another VM on that host holds the device, or its instance still does. Detach it from that VM. If the hot-unplug failed (DevicesPending), the device stays held until that VM stops. In a cluster, leave the VM unpinned so the scheduler can pick a node where the device is free.
conflict: PCI device … shares IOMMU group … with …Another VM holds a device in the same IOMMU group. Give the whole group to one VM, or move the card to a slot with its own group.
in use by qemu-kvm-one (pid …) on a device, or IOMMU group … is in use by … from Release or a VF countA VM has the group open: another hypervisor’s (libvirt, OpenNebula), or for Release and VF counts also Glidex’s. Being on vfio-pci doesn’t mean it’s free: check virsh list and virsh dumpxml <vm> (<hostdev>), and cordon the device in Glidex while the other VM keeps it. See Devices another hypervisor holds.
/dev/vfio/<n> can't be opened by this userThe group device’s owner, group and mode don’t give glidex read and write. Prepare the device, or add the udev rule above; ls -l /dev/vfio/.
After a reboot, devices are back on their host drivers, or VFs are goneKeep them with the installer’s --vfio-devices and --sriov. journalctl -u glidex-vfio-boot shows what the boot unit did.
pool …: 1 of 2 free, no device pool …See Host resources.
A VM stays Waiting for a node with PCI device … in a node’s reasonno PCI device …: the node doesn’t report it. … is used by VM … or … shares IOMMU group …: every node with it has it taken. The VM is placed once a device is free.

The hypervisor’s own error is in the VM’s events (gxctl events <vm>) and in journalctl -u glidex-vm@<id>. See also Troubleshooting.

Host resources

Besides vCPUs and memory, Glidex knows how each host is built: its NUMA nodes and cores, its hugepages, and its PCIe tree with the devices a VM could be given. It uses that to:

  • keep a VM’s memory, vCPUs and devices on one NUMA node, or split a GPU VM over exactly its GPUs’ NUMA nodes, and give it dedicated host CPUs;
  • count hugepages per node and page size, so VMs that need them get them;
  • hand out devices from pools by count, near each other, and size a VM that asks for GPUs from what each GPU brings;
  • prepare devices for passthrough, watch their health, and cordon the ones you don’t trust.

All of this works on a single host and in a cluster. On a single host the node is called local. Passing a device through by its address, and what the host needs for VFIO, is in PCI passthrough.

Host topology

Each node reads its topology from sysfs. A summary (NUMA nodes, cores, memory, hugepages, reserved CPUs, assignable devices) goes in the node’s record and is refreshed every two minutes, and right after a device is prepared or released. The full tree is read fresh on the node each time you ask for it.

gxctl node topology <node>             # NUMA nodes with CPUs, memory, hugepages and devices; reserved CPUs; warnings
gxctl node topology <node> --devices   # devices with NUMA node, root port, switch, link, VFs, PCIe errors
gxctl pci                              # this host's PCI devices, with NUMA node and readiness
gxctl pci 0000:41:00.0                 # one device, and why it isn't ready

<node> is a node name or id. In the web UI, a host’s page (Hosts, or Cluster → a node) has a Topology card: one column per NUMA node with its CPUs, memory, hugepages and devices, then devices with no NUMA node, the reserved CPUs, and the warnings.

ShownMeaning
CPUs, coresThe NUMA node’s CPUs, grouped by core (hyperthreads of one core together).
MemoryThe node’s memory, without its hugepage pool.
HugepagesPages per size on that NUMA node, less what OVS-DPDK takes there.
DevicesThe devices a VM could be given: GPUs, NICs, NVMe drives, accelerators, and anything bound to vfio-pci. Each with its class, ids, driver, IOMMU group, readiness, whether it is taken (a VM on the node holds it or its IOMMU group, or it is cordoned: in use on the card) and, with --devices, its root port, the PCIe switch above it, its link speed and width, SR-IOV VFs and PCIe error counts.
Reserved CPUsCPUs no VM gets: OVS-DPDK’s PMD and lcore CPUs, the two cores pylond uses on a Pylon host, and cluster.node_reserved.cpu_list.

Reading a node’s topology needs a host role (auditor, net-admin or system-admin) on that host. Over the API it is GET /nodes/{id}/topology (read on that node) or GET /host/topology (the host that answers).

Ready devices

A device is ready for passthrough when:

  • the host has an IOMMU and the device has an IOMMU group;
  • it is bound to vfio-pci;
  • the other functions of its IOMMU group are on vfio-pci or unbound (bridges stay with the host);
  • the glidex user can open /dev/vfio/<group>, judged by the file’s owner, group and mode, as a VM’s unit would open it;
  • it isn’t an OVS-DPDK uplink;
  • no process other than Glidex’s own VMs has its IOMMU group open, such as a VM of libvirt or OpenNebula on the same host.

A device that isn’t says why:

ReasonFix
not bound to vfio-pci (driver: nvidia)Prepare it.
IOMMU group 30 also holds 0000:07:00.1 on snd_hda_intelPrepare it: the whole group goes to vfio-pci.
/dev/vfio/30 can't be opened by this userPrepare it (its udev rule gives the group device to glidex), or see PCI passthrough.
in use by qemu-kvm-one (pid 37226)Another hypervisor’s VM holds it. Being on vfio-pci doesn’t make it free. See Devices another hypervisor holds.
it is an OVS-DPDK uplinkNot for passthrough.

Pools hand out ready devices only. Who holds a group is asked of glidex-netd, which can see every process; without it, that check is skipped.

Warnings

The topology reports what it notices. Glidex never acts on these.

WarningMeaningWhat to do
iommu_offNo IOMMU groups.Turn on VT-d or AMD-Vi and the kernel option; see PCI passthrough.
numa_unknownA device has no NUMA node (firmware reports -1) on a host with several.A firmware setting or update. NUMA_POLICY_STRICT VMs can’t have it.
group_sharedA device shares its IOMMU group with a device of another class.Passing one through takes the other; move the card to another slot.
link_degradedA device’s PCIe link runs slower or narrower than it can. GPUs aren’t flagged: they slow their link when idle.Reseat the card, or check the slot.
hugepages_unbalancedA device sits on a NUMA node with no hugepages while other NUMA nodes have some.Reserve hugepages on that NUMA node too (see Hugepages).

NUMA nodes

On a host with several NUMA nodes, a VM is faster when its memory, its vCPUs and its devices are on one of them. A VM asks for that with numa_policy (see NUMA and dedicated CPUs):

  • NUMA_POLICY_PREFERRED: on one NUMA node if one fits, else anywhere on the host. Then the VM’s NumaAligned condition is False.
  • NUMA_POLICY_STRICT: on one NUMA node, or not on that host. It refuses devices on two NUMA nodes and devices with no NUMA node.
  • NUMA_POLICY_ALIGNED: on exactly the NUMA nodes of its devices, its vCPUs and memory split between them by device count, and the same layout shown to the guest. A GPU request sets it. Every device needs a NUMA node, and each node’s share must fit there (NUMA node 7: not enough memory (… of … MiB taken)).

Glidex picks the NUMA node with most of the VM’s devices, then the least allocated, then the lowest number. Each NUMA node’s room is its memory times cluster.scheduler.memory_overcommit, and its hugepages of each size. VMs bound to a NUMA node count there; VMs without a policy count on every NUMA node in proportion to its size.

The guest’s memory is bound to the NUMA node (to each node’s share, when aligned). Shared vCPUs still float over the whole host, so no node’s CPUs sit idle. The VM shows where it went: numa_node, or numa (one share per node) when aligned over several, and for dedicated vCPUs cpus. Before an aligned VM starts, each node is checked for its share of free hugepages.

In a cluster, a strict VM that fits no node waits as Unschedulable with each node’s reason (NUMA node 1: not enough memory (… of … MiB taken), its PCI devices are on NUMA nodes 0 and 1). On a single host the create is refused with 409. A change to a placed VM’s vCPUs, memory, policies, devices or networks is fitted again on its node; what no longer fits is refused with 409.

Dedicated CPUs

A VM with cpu_policy: CPU_POLICY_DEDICATED gets a host CPU of its own for each vCPU, on one NUMA node if it can (it implies NUMA_POLICY_PREFERRED). Its vCPU threads are pinned there; other VMs don’t run on them.

  • Whole cores. By default a dedicated VM takes both hyperthreads of each core, so no other VM shares a core with it. Turn this off with cluster.scheduler.dedicated_whole_cores: false to hand out single threads.
  • Isolated CPUs first. CPUs the kernel keeps tasks off (isolcpus, nohz_full) are used first.
  • Reserved CPUs are never given out: OVS-DPDK’s PMD and lcore CPUs, the first two cores on a host running pylond, and by default the first core of each NUMA node, for the host. cluster.node_reserved.cpu_list replaces that default with your own list; an empty list reserves none.
  • Shared VMs give way. Once a node holds dedicated CPUs, VMs with shared vCPUs run only on the CPUs left, and running ones are moved when that set changes.
{
  "cluster": {
    "scheduler": { "dedicated_whole_cores": true },
    "node_reserved": { "cpu_list": "0-1,64-65" }
  }
}

cluster.node_reserved.cpu_list is per host: set it in each host’s /etc/glidex/control-plane.json. The reserved CPUs show in gxctl node topology. Restart the control plane after changing either key.

When no NUMA node has enough free CPUs, the reason says so (NUMA node 0: not enough free CPUs (8 dedicated vCPUs, 6 CPUs free)).

Hugepages

Hugepages are their own resource, counted per node and page size. Glidex doesn’t reserve them; the kernel does, at boot or later:

# kernel command line: reserve 1G pages at boot, before memory fragments
default_hugepagesz=1G hugepagesz=1G hugepages=64

# 2M pages, at run time, on NUMA node 1
echo 4096 | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/node/node1/hugepages/hugepages-2048kB/nr_hugepages

The node reads its pools per size and NUMA node (again within two minutes of a change). How they are counted:

  • What VMs may take is the pool less what OVS-DPDK takes for dpdk-socket-mem. Hugepages aren’t ordinary memory: a node’s allocatable memory leaves the pool out.
  • A VM with hugepages takes its whole memory in pages of its hugepage_size (2M or 1G; default: the host’s default size, usually 2M). They are never overcommitted, and a placed VM holds them whether it runs or not. Refusals: not enough 2M hugepages (2048 of 2048 MiB taken), no 1G hugepages, 1536 MiB is not a whole number of 1G pages.
  • A VM with a vhost-user NIC needs shared memory. It gets 2M pages without asking when the node has its memory plus a quarter (at least 256 MiB) to spare, and ordinary memory otherwise.
  • The VM’s page_kib says what it got: 4 for ordinary memory, else the page size in KiB.
  • Before a VM starts, its node checks that enough pages of the size are free (on its NUMA node, if it has one). If not, the start fails with the counts. Hugepages used outside Glidex show up this way.

On a single host, Glidex records the size of asked-for hugepages but doesn’t count them ahead; the check at start is what stops a VM. The size of vhost-user hugepages is decided at start too.

Device pools

A pool is a named set of devices, matched by ids or addresses. Instead of naming devices by address, a VM asks for a number of devices from a pool, and Glidex picks them. Pools are defined in /etc/glidex/control-plane.json (on each server, the same):

{
  "pci": {
    "pools": [
      { "name": "a100", "class": "gpu",
        "match": { "vendor_id": "0x10de", "device_id": "0x20b0" },
        "prepare": true,
        "per_device": { "vcpus": 14, "memory_mib": 57344,
                        "hugepages": true, "cpu_policy": "dedicated" } },
      { "name": "cx7", "class": "nic",
        "match": { "vendor_id": "0x15b3", "device_id": "0x1021" },
        "nodes": ["gpu-01", "gpu-02"] }
    ],
    "allow": [
      { "pool": "a100", "tenants": ["research"] },
      { "pool": "cx7", "projects": ["ml-team"] }
    ]
  }
}
KeyMeaning
nameThe pool’s name. Unique.
classA label for people and usage reports: gpu, nic, nvme, dpu, accelerator. gpu also marks the pools a GPU request can use without naming one, and that the web UI’s create form sizes VMs from.
matchvendor_id, device_id, class_code (or its start, 0x0302) and addresses. Every key given must match. A pool must have a match. With vf_of (itself a match of physical functions), the pool takes those functions’ SR-IOV virtual functions; see SR-IOV virtual functions.
nodesNode names or ids the pool is on. Default: every node.
prepareEach node binds its devices of the pool to vfio-pci when glidex starts (see Prepare devices).
per_deviceWhat a VM asking for gpus from the pool gets per device, unless it sizes itself: vcpus and memory_mib (both required), and optionally hugepages (true/false) and cpu_policy (shared or dedicated). See GPU requests.

The control plane refuses to start with two pools of the same name, a pool without a match, two pools with the same match on the same nodes, or a grant naming an unknown pool. Restart the control plane after changing pools or grants.

Who may use a pool

A pci.allow entry with pool grants the pool to projects (ids or names) or tenants (ids or slugs), like device grants (see Who may use a device). net-admin and system-admin may use any pool. In policies the permission is usePciPool.

How VMs get devices

A VM asks with devices, for example [{"pool": "a100", "count": 2, "same_switch": true}] (in gxctl create, a100:2:switch; in the web UI’s VM form, Device Pools). Glidex picks devices of the pool that are ready, not cordoned and not held by another VM (whole IOMMU groups counted), on the NUMA node of the VM’s other devices first, then by address. With same_switch, all of them sit under one PCIe switch, the one the VM already uses if it can.

The picks are shown on the VM as pool_devices and are passed through at its next start. They are claims like devices named by address: the VM keeps them while it exists. When a pool is short, the reason says why: pool a100: 1 of 2 free, pool a100: no 2 free devices under one PCIe switch, pool a100 is not on this node. In a cluster the VM waits for a node; on a single host the request is refused with 409.

GPU requests

A user can ask for GPUs by count instead of sizing the VM: "gpus": {"count": 4, "pool": "a100"} (in gxctl create, 4:a100; in the web UI, a GPU pool’s count). Glidex turns it into:

  • a pool request for 4 devices of a100;
  • NUMA_POLICY_ALIGNED, so the VM spans exactly its GPUs’ NUMA nodes (see NUMA nodes);
  • 4 × the pool’s per_device vCPUs and memory, its hugepages and its cpu_policy.

What the VM’s request gives itself wins. Without pool, the project’s only usable pool of class gpu is taken (cluster or tenant pool). A tenant pool sizes like its cluster pool. Quotas, grants and metering are those of the pool. Users see the sizing in the create form and as per_device_vcpus and per_device_memory_mib in the project’s pool listing. The refusals are in the user guide’s GPUs.

Size per_device so the GPUs of one NUMA node fit that node: its cores less the reserved ones, and its memory less the host’s share, divided by its GPUs. For a node with 16 cores (32 threads), one core reserved and 2 GPUs: 15 cores leave 7 each, so 14 vCPUs with whole cores, and about 56 GiB each out of 126 GiB. A VM that asks for more than a node can give is refused there, naming the node.

"nvlink": true is refused for now: NVLink between passed-through GPUs on NVSwitch boards needs a fabric Glidex doesn’t run yet. Without it, a request’s nvlink is false, and the VM shows it so. The same holds for GPUs that have no such fabric, such as AMD Radeon cards.

See what pools hold

gxctl pci pools                 # each pool's devices per node: free, held by a VM, cordoned or not ready
gxctl pci pools --project lab   # the pools project lab may use, with free counts

The full listing (GET /pci-pools) needs a host role. With --project (GET /pci-pools?project=<p>), anyone who can read the project sees the pools it may use and how many devices are free, without addresses or holders; it lists the project’s tenant pools too.

Quotas

A project quota devices.<pool> limits how many devices of a pool the project’s VMs ask for, counted like vcpus over all its VMs:

gxctl project quota lab devices.a100=2

Over the limit, a request is refused with quota_exceeded (resource devices.a100). A tenant’s cap limits the same over all its projects (tenant_quota_exceeded). A pool without a quota is unlimited. In the web UI, the project’s Quotas and usage card shows Devices: <pool> for each pool with a limit or in use, and Edit quotas offers a field for each pool the project may use. See Projects.

Tenant pools

A tenant granted a pool can split its share among its projects. Its tenant-admin creates tenant pools, each drawing from a cluster pool, with a maximum and the projects that may use it:

gxctl tenant device-pool set acme team-a-gpus --from a100 --max 4 --projects team-a,team-a-ci
gxctl tenant device-pools acme                 # pool, cluster pool, held/max, free, projects
gxctl tenant device-pool remove acme team-a-gpus

In the web UI it is the tenant page’s Device pools card. Over the API, PUT /tenants/{id}/device-pools replaces the tenant’s whole set.

  • The name is 1-63 lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and can’t be a cluster pool’s name. --from must be a cluster pool granted to the tenant, --max at least 1, and the projects the tenant’s.
  • A VM of one of those projects asks for {"pool": "team-a-gpus"}. It gets devices of a100, and the VM shows "pool": "a100", "tenant_pool": "team-a-gpus". Other projects are refused (403).
  • The tenant pool’s projects together ask for at most max devices (tenant_quota_exceeded, resource tenant_pool.team-a-gpus). The tenant’s cap and the project quota on a100 still apply.
  • If the tenant loses its grant on a100, the tenant pool shows ungranted and gives nothing new. VMs that hold devices keep them, as do VMs of a tenant pool you remove.

Usage

Metering counts device.alloc.<pool>: the devices of a pool a VM holds, in device-hours, from its start to its exit (paused too). Devices of a tenant pool count under the cluster pool’s name. Devices named by address aren’t metered. See Usage.

Prepare devices

Glidex can bind a device to vfio-pci for you, on any node:

gxctl node prepare-device <node> 0000:41:00.0   # its whole IOMMU group to vfio-pci
gxctl node release-device <node> 0000:41:00.0   # back on the drivers it had

In the web UI, the node’s Topology card has Prepare and Release next to each device. Over the API: POST /nodes/{id}/devices/{address}/prepare and .../release.

Preparing:

  • loads the vfio-pci module if it isn’t loaded, and fails if it can’t be;
  • binds every function of the device’s IOMMU group to vfio-pci. Bridges stay with the host;
  • makes a GPU’s memory window (a resizable BAR, such as a Radeon’s with resizable BAR on) smaller when needed, so that the windows of all the host’s GPUs on vfio-pci add up to less than the host’s memory. Each gets the largest size that fits, given the GPUs prepared before it: on a host with 32 GiB, a 32 GiB window becomes 16 GiB, and a second GPU’s 8 GiB. A window as large as the host’s memory froze a test host when its VM started. The guest still reaches all of the GPU’s memory through the smaller window. A GPU already on vfio-pci keeps its size, and a window that can’t be made small enough is refused;
  • remembers the drivers they had, and the window sizes, for release;
  • writes /etc/udev/rules.d/90-glidex-vfio-<group>.rules, which gives /dev/vfio/<group> to the glidex group with mode 0660, and applies it at once;
  • refuses a group holding a NIC the host uses (one with addresses or routes), an OVS-DPDK uplink, or a device without an IOMMU group.

The host’s driver lets go of the devices: a GPU on nvidia stops being the host’s. Release works with any function of the group, puts a resized window back to its size, and refuses a device Glidex didn’t prepare.

Release refuses a group that a process has open, a VM’s included (IOMMU group 30 is in use by qemu-kvm-one (pid 37226)), and so does a change to a PF’s VF count while its group or a VF’s is open.

Preparing and releasing need net-admin or system-admin on that host. A prepared device goes back to its usual driver at reboot. For devices that should always be ready:

  • give their pool prepare: true: each node then prepares its devices of the pool that aren’t ready when glidex starts, skipping devices without an IOMMU group and OVS-DPDK uplinks. A device that can’t be prepared stays not ready, and the control plane’s log says why;
  • or bind them at boot, before glidex and any other hypervisor starts, with the installer’s --vfio-devices (and keep VF counts with --sriov); see Keep it across reboots.

Device health and cordoning

Each node reads its devices’ PCIe error counters (AER: correctable, non-fatal, fatal). gxctl node topology <node> --devices shows them as aer correctable/nonfatal/fatal, and the Topology card marks a device with uncorrectable errors (PCIe errors).

Glidex watches the devices of running VMs. If one falls off the bus, or has new uncorrectable errors since the VM started, the VM’s DeviceHealthy condition turns False with the reason, and a DeviceError event is recorded once (gxctl events <vm>). Glidex doesn’t stop the VM or take the device away. Errors inside the guest (an NVIDIA Xid, say) only the guest sees.

To keep a device you don’t trust from new VMs, cordon it:

gxctl node cordon-device <node> 0000:41:00.0
gxctl node uncordon-device <node> 0000:41:00.0

Or Cordon and Uncordon on the Topology card, where a cordoned device is marked cordoned. Over the API: POST /nodes/{id}/devices/{address}/cordon and .../uncordon.

A cordoned device is refused to new VMs by address (PCI device 0000:41:00.0 is cordoned), and pools skip it. The VM that holds it keeps it. Cordoning needs net-admin or system-admin on that host. The node records its cordoned devices, so they stay cordoned across restarts.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCheck
not enough 2M hugepages (… of … MiB taken)The node’s pool of that size is used up. Reserve more, or use another size. gxctl node topology <node> shows the pool per NUMA node.
no 1G hugepagesThat node has none of that size. 1G pages are reserved on the kernel command line.
The start fails with hugepage countsPages the scheduler counted as free are in use outside Glidex (another process, or DPDK beyond dpdk-socket-mem).
NumaAligned is FalseA PREFERRED VM didn’t fit on one NUMA node and spans the host. Free room on one NUMA node, then stop and start the VM.
its PCI devices are on NUMA nodes 0 and 1, PCI device … has no NUMA nodeA STRICT VM can’t have these devices together. Use PREFERRED, or devices on one NUMA node.
not enough free CPUs (… dedicated vCPUs, … CPUs free)Dedicated VMs hold the rest, or the CPUs are reserved. See reserved cpus in gxctl node topology.
pool …: 1 of 2 freeOther VMs hold the pool’s devices, or some aren’t ready or are cordoned: gxctl pci pools.
no device pool … (400)No such pool, or a tenant pool of another tenant.
forbidden asking for a poolThe project has no grant for it in pci.allow, or isn’t one of the tenant pool’s projects.
PCI device … is cordonedAn administrator cordoned it: gxctl node uncordon-device.
A device on vfio-pci is not ready: in use by … (pid …)Another hypervisor’s VM on the host has it. Pools skip it. See Devices another hypervisor holds.
A device is not ready: /dev/vfio/<n> can't be opened by this userThe group device’s owner, group and mode don’t let glidex open it. Prepare the device, or add the udev rule.
PCI device … has no NUMA node for a GPU requestNUMA_POLICY_ALIGNED needs a NUMA node on each device, even on a one-node host. The user can set NUMA_POLICY_PREFERRED with gpus.
NUMA node …: not enough … for a GPU requestOne node’s share of the VM doesn’t fit there. Lower per_device, or free that node.
gpus: give vcpu_count and mem_size_mib, or set per_device on pool …The pool has no per_device.
A VM shows DeviceHealthy=FalseThe device fell off the bus or had PCIe errors: gxctl node topology <node> --devices, and the host’s dmesg.
Preparing is refusedThe group holds a NIC the host uses or an OVS-DPDK uplink, or the IOMMU is off.
Release or a VF count is refused: IOMMU group … is in use by …A VM (Glidex’s or another hypervisor’s) has the group open. Stop that VM first.

Clusters

Several Glidex hosts can run as one cluster: one API, one set of projects, users and images, and a scheduler that places VMs on the nodes. This page covers forming a cluster, adding and removing nodes, recovery, upgrades, and turning on cluster networks (OVN).

Cluster operations need the system-admin role. On the local socket, members of glidex-admin have it. Most of them (init, join tokens, removals, snapshots, CA rotation, OVN settings) also need a recent login: over TCP or in the web UI, you may be asked to log in again.

Roles and quorum

Every node runs the same software and runs VMs. A node is one of:

  • Server: keeps a copy of the cluster’s database, replicated with Raft, and serves the API. Servers sign node certificates and run OVN’s databases when OVN is on.
  • Agent: only runs VMs. It has no API of its own: gxctl on an agent says so and points you to a server. Opening an agent’s web UI takes you to a server’s web UI, at that agent’s Host page; you log in there, with SSO, passkeys or the servers’ users. Each host’s page (Hosts in the menu) manages its Open vSwitch, bridges and uplinks from any server.

The servers that vote in Raft are voters. A cluster keeps working while a majority of voters is up, so run 1, 3 or 5 servers: 3 survive one lost server, 5 survive two. Glidex refuses changes that leave an even number of voters or no majority, unless you --force the even case.

Nodes talk to each other on TCP 8842 (the node API), with mutual TLS under the cluster’s own certificate authority. The installer doesn’t open firewall ports; see the port list.

Before you start

Install Glidex on every host as in Installation. OVN is installed too unless you pass --no-ovn; its services stay off until the host is in a cluster. Give each host a stable address that the others can reach.

Create a cluster

On the first host, which becomes the first server:

gxctl cluster init --force

--force is required: init re-keys every record for clustering and can’t be undone from Glidex. It keeps a copy of the database first (glidex.db.pre-cluster-<time> in the data directory) and prints the cluster id and the CA’s SHA-256 fingerprint. VMs keep running.

The node advertises its first non-loopback address on port 8842. To choose, pass --advertise 192.0.2.11:8842; --tunnel-ip sets the address for Geneve tunnels (default: the advertised address).

In the web UI: Cluster → Make this host a cluster → Initialize cluster…, with the same two fields.

Check it:

gxctl cluster status
gxctl nodes

Join tokens

A host joins with a one-time token issued by a server. The token is a secret: it is shown once, works once, and expires (1 hour by default, up to 7 days). Write it straight to a private file:

umask 077
gxctl cluster join-token --role agent > join.token           # an agent
gxctl cluster join-token --role server --ttl 24h > join.token
gxctl cluster join-token --role agent --allow-import > join.token

--role is agent (default) or server, and the joining host must ask for the same role. --allow-import lets the host bring its existing VMs along (see Import). The command prints the servers to join through on standard error.

In the web UI: Cluster → + Add node, pick the Role, how long the Token valid for, and whether the host has VMs to bring along. The dialog shows the token once with the commands to run.

Copy the token to the new host over a secure channel (for example scp), keep it mode 0600, and delete it after use. The token also pins the cluster’s CA: the joining host refuses a server whose CA doesn’t match it.

Join a host

On the new host, from your Glidex checkout, with the token file:

cargo run -p glidex-install -- --join 192.0.2.11:8842 --role agent --token-file join.token

The installer installs or updates Glidex as usual, then joins. The token is read from the file (which must not be readable by others) or from standard input, never from the command line. Options:

  • --role server for a server (the token must be a server token).
  • --advertise IP:PORT: the address other nodes use for this one.
  • --node-name NAME: default is the host name.

A host that already runs Glidex can join with gxctl instead:

gxctl cluster join --server 192.0.2.11:8842 --role agent --token-file join.token

gxctl cluster join defaults to --role server, so pass the role the token was made for.

A host that has VMs, disks, networks or credentials can’t do a plain join: that would abandon them. Remove them, or join with --import.

Add servers

A new server joins as a Raft learner, then becomes a voter. To keep the voter count odd, learners are promoted in pairs: join two servers to go from 1 to 3 voters, two more to reach 5. A single extra server stays a learner until the next one joins, or until you promote it:

gxctl cluster promote node2 node3        # learners to voters; --force for an even count

gxctl cluster status lists voters and learners; the Raft card on the Cluster page shows the same.

An agent can’t become a server in place. To turn an agent into a server, take it out of the cluster and join it again with a server token.

Import an existing host’s VMs

A standalone host can join with its VMs, disks, networks and credentials:

  1. On a server: gxctl cluster join-token --role agent --allow-import > join.token (or tick The host already has VMs to bring along in + Add node).
  2. On the host: cargo run -p glidex-install -- --join 192.0.2.11:8842 --import --token-file join.token. Nothing changes yet: the host sends a plan and waits.
  3. An administrator reviews and approves the plan. On the Cluster page, Pending imports lists it; its page shows what the host brings, lets you map its projects, node networks and credentials to names in the cluster, and reports problems. Check, then Approve (or Reject). From the CLI:
gxctl node import list
gxctl node import show <plan>
gxctl node import approve <plan> --project lab=new:lab-imported --dry-run
gxctl node import approve <plan> --project lab=new:lab-imported --network default=lab-net
gxctl node import reject <plan>

--project src=existing puts a project’s resources into an existing project, src=new:name into a new one. --network a=b and --credential project/user=new rename networks and credentials whose name is taken. --over-quota accepts an import that takes a project over its quota. A plan expires after a day.

On approval the host joins and its resources become the cluster’s in one step. Its VMs keep running.

Placement

The scheduler picks a node when a VM is created. A node is a candidate only if it is Active, ready, not draining, has room, and has what the VM needs: the hypervisor, the image’s architecture, hugepages if asked, its PCI devices (granted to the project on that node, and not cordoned), free devices of the pools it asks for, a NUMA node with room under its NUMA or CPU policy, the physical networks of its provider networks, a userspace br-int for vhost-user NICs on cluster networks, an OVN version as new as the cluster’s, the node of any node-local disk or node network it uses, and every datastore its disks are on (Datastores). Among candidates it picks the least allocated (the largest of the CPU, memory and, for a VM in hugepages, hugepage shares after placing), then the one with fewest VMs.

A node’s hugepages are its own resource, per page size: the pool the kernel reserved, less what OVS-DPDK takes for dpdk-socket-mem. They don’t count as ordinary memory, and VMs placed on the node hold theirs whether running or not. NUMA nodes, dedicated CPUs, hugepages and device pools are described in Host resources; each node reports its topology (gxctl node topology <node>), which the scheduler uses.

PCI devices and their grants are per node: the same address on two nodes is two devices, and a pci.allow grant with node covers only that node’s. See PCI passthrough.

Room is each node’s CPUs and memory minus a reserve, times an overcommit ratio. The defaults, in /etc/glidex/control-plane.json:

{
  "cluster": {
    "scheduler": { "cpu_overcommit": 4.0, "memory_overcommit": 1.0 },
    "node_reserved": { "cpus": 1, "memory_mib": 2048 }
  }
}

The VM form’s Placement shows the scheduler’s choice (Automatic (now: …)) and each node’s free vCPUs and memory, or why it can’t take the VM. Pick a node to pin the VM there (node in the API). A VM no node can take is still created and waits, with each node’s reason in its status.

A VM stays on its node once placed. Glidex doesn’t move running VMs. A stopped VM whose disks are on shared datastores can be placed on another node: gxctl place <vm> [--node N], or Place on another node on its page. A disk on a node’s own datastore (local or another node-local one) keeps its VM on that node; move it to a shared datastore first. See Placing a stopped or lost VM again.

Node lifecycle

Each node has a phase: Active, Draining, Departing (a detach in progress), or one of the end states Departed, Removed, Forgotten. The Cluster page’s Nodes card shows phase and readiness; a node’s page has an Operations… menu for everything below. The gxctl node commands take a node’s name or its id.

A node is down for a while

Nothing to do. Every node, servers included, reports to the leader every 5 seconds. A node that stops reporting for 40 seconds (cluster.node_grace_secs) becomes not ready, and so do its VMs (NodeUnreachable). Nothing is restarted elsewhere. The node comes back by itself with its identity.

Drain

gxctl node drain node3
gxctl node undrain node3

A draining node gets no new VMs. VMs already there keep running; the command prints what is still on the node. Stop, delete or move them before removing it: a stopped VM whose disks are on shared datastores can be placed on another node.

Remove an empty node

  1. gxctl node drain node3, then delete its VMs, disks and node networks (or detach it with them).
  2. gxctl node remove node3. Refused while the node holds a VM, disk or node network, if it is the only gateway of the shared edge or of a project router, or if the Raft voters left would have no majority or an even count (--force for the even case only).
  3. On that host, from your checkout: cargo run -p glidex-install -- --leave. It refuses until the removal has committed, then makes the host standalone again. (On a removed server whose control plane still runs, gxctl cluster leave does the same; an agent has no local API for it.)

Removing a server rotates the CA afterwards: it held the CA key.

Detach a node with its VMs

gxctl node detach node3 --map-network lab=lab-standalone
gxctl node detach node3 --abort         # before the node acknowledged

The node leaves with its VMs, disks and node networks and becomes a standalone host that owns them. --with-access also carries the projects’ users, teams and role bindings (never sessions or tokens). The node is frozen while the handover runs. Its disks on node-local datastores other than local can’t leave with the node: the detach is refused (409) until they are moved to local. The Cluster page shows it under Detaches, with the networks it maps or drops by the names they had when it started, even if they are gone since.

If no server can be reached at all, a node can leave on its own:

cargo run -p glidex-install -- --leave --keep-resources --offline

It asks for confirmation: changes made in the cluster since the node last synced are lost. Then, on a server, run gxctl node detach node3 --departed so the cluster lets go of it.

A node is gone for good

  1. Make sure it is powered off or fenced. Then: gxctl node forget node3 --fenced (add --force if that leaves an even number of voters). Its VMs stay recorded, marked lost; its certificate is refused from now on; a forgotten server is rotated out of the CA. Lost VMs whose disks are on shared datastores can be placed on a live node: gxctl place <vm> (or Place on a live node on the VM’s page), then started. A lost VM with a disk on the node’s own datastores (local or another node-local one) can’t be placed: that disk is on the lost host. See Placing a stopped or lost VM again.
  2. When you no longer want its records: gxctl node purge node3. This deletes the records of the VMs still on it (place the ones you keep first), and of its disks and networks, not any files. Disks on shared datastores are not affected.

A repaired host comes back as itself

A forgotten node, or one whose certificate expired, can rejoin with the same identity, disks and VMs:

umask 077
gxctl node rejoin-token node3 > rejoin.token
gxctl node rejoin-token node3 --raft-lost > rejoin.token   # a server whose Raft state is gone

Use --raft-lost for a server whose cluster/raft directory is gone or older than its last vote: it then returns as a learner with fresh Raft state. On the host:

cargo run -p glidex-install -- --rejoin 192.0.2.11:8842 --token-file rejoin.token

Add --node-id <id> if the host lost its cluster files. A removed or departed node’s id is retired; it joins as a new node instead.

End the cluster

On the last node, after every other node has left:

gxctl cluster dissolve --force

The host becomes standalone with every VM, disk, network and user, and keeps a final snapshot. Restart the control plane afterwards. The Cluster page’s Danger zone has Leave (for a removed node) and Dissolve.

Certificates and the CA

The cluster CA is valid for 10 years, node certificates for one. Nodes renew their certificates by themselves 30 days before they expire. The CA rotates by itself after a server leaves and a year before it expires. To rotate on demand:
