gxctl cluster rotate-ca                  # old CA retires after 7 days, or once every node renewed
gxctl cluster rotate-ca --grace 0        # retire at once

--grace is in seconds (default 604800, cluster.ca_rotation_grace_secs). Every node trusts both CAs, renews its certificate under the new one, and the old one retires. A node that was unreachable the whole time needs a rejoin token. The Certificate authority card on the Cluster page shows the signing CA, its expiry, a rotation in progress, and nodes not yet renewed; Rotate starts one (grace in days there).

Join tokens pin the CA. A token issued before a rotation fails with “the server’s CA … is not the one the token names”: issue a new one.

The secrets key

Connector secrets are sealed with a key every server holds. Rotate it with:

gxctl cluster rotate-secrets-key

If a server can’t be reached, it stops before re-wrapping anything; run it again.

Admitting another organization’s tenant

A tenant whose directory is elsewhere (another organization’s glidex, or a host that serves its directory) uses this cluster after a handshake: you offer, its administrator accepts at their directory.

# On this cluster, as its operator: who, and which directory (its issuer)
gxctl admission offer acme --directory https://id.acme.example/d/acme

It prints an offer token (gxo_…) once. Send it to the tenant’s administrator; they run, at their directory:

gxctl tenant opt-in acme --offer gxo_…

In the web UI the same is on the Admissions page (Offers to other organizations’ tenants: the tenant’s slug, its directory’s issuer and how many days, then Make offer) and, at the directory, on the tenant’s page (Clusters of other organizations: paste the token and Accept offer; Opt out leaves). An offer needs this cluster’s API to serve TLS: the directory pins its certificate.

Their directory calls this cluster’s API (the address in the token: cluster.api_url, else the web UI’s host on port 8841), pinning its certificate; both sides keep the other’s keys and certificate from then on. gxctl admission directories lists the directories this cluster trusts; gxctl admission remove <tenant> ends a tenant’s admission and tells its directory; the tenant can opt out from its side too (gxctl tenant opt-out acme --cluster <id>). An offer works once and lasts 7 days (--days, at most 30); gxctl admission offers and revoke-offer manage open ones.

Once trust is set up:

  • People and roles. Every 30 seconds this cluster’s leader (or a standalone host) pulls a feed from each trusted directory. It holds the admitted tenants, their projects, members and tenant and project roles, and those people’s names and whether they are disabled; never emails, sign-ins or secrets. The cluster keeps them as that directory’s records, so policies and quotas work for them as for local users, and no one edits them here. Someone removed from the tenant, or disabled at their directory, loses access here with the next feed. A feed never replaces this cluster’s own records.

  • Signing in. The tenant’s people sign in at their own directory. The web UI’s sign-in page offers Sign in with <tenant>, which goes to the directory and back. On the API, an access token their directory issued for this cluster works too; it is for this cluster only. For that, the directory must know this cluster’s web UI address: it learns it when the tenant opts in (the published address, or the first of auth.allowed_origins). If the address changes, the cluster sends the new one with its next report, within a minute. Signing out at the directory ends the cluster’s sessions made from it with the next feed; logging out on this cluster ends, at the directory, the sign-in it was made from (and not the person’s session there, or on other clusters).

  • Reports. After each feed, this cluster tells the directory what it holds of each of its tenants: the admission (admitted or suspended, and the cap), and counts of projects, VMs (and running ones), disks (and their GiB) and networks. The tenant’s administrators see it on the tenant’s page under Clusters of other organizations, and in gxctl tenant clusters acme, with the time the directory received it.

  • When the directory is out of reach. VMs keep running, and the tenant’s people keep working with the sessions and tokens they have. New sign-ins need the directory. If no feed has come for longer than the directory’s limit (60 minutes unless you change it), this cluster stops accepting that directory’s sessions and tokens, since it can’t know who was removed meanwhile; your own users are not affected. The next feed that gets through lifts it. Responses to a directory’s people carry X-Glidex-Directory-Lag (seconds) once its feed is more than 90 seconds behind. gxctl admission directories (or the Admissions page’s Directories of other organizations) shows each directory’s last feed and limit; gxctl admission staleness <directory> <minutes> changes it (default goes back to trust.default_max_staleness_minutes in control-plane.json).

Feed, sign-in and report requests are signed by the sending side’s key and go to the other side’s API with its certificate pinned, on port 8841 both ways: open it between the two organizations’ hosts.

The web UI’s address

Agents send browsers to a server’s web UI, at the address that server publishes. By default it is what its glidex-ui answers on: its Tailscale name when the Tailscale certificate is on, else the first name in GLIDEX_UI_HOSTS, else the host’s full name, with port 5173.

On an agent, https://<agent>:5173/… answers with a redirect to the same path on a server’s web UI, and its home page goes to that agent’s Host page. Until a server has published its address (just after a join, say), the agent shows a page listing the cluster’s servers instead. API calls to an agent’s web UI are refused with 421 use_a_server, naming the server’s address; nothing is relayed through the agent.

Behind a load balancer, set the same address on every server, in /etc/glidex/control-plane.json:

{ "cluster": { "ui_url": "https://glidex.example.com" } }

It must be https://host[:port], with no path; restart the control plane after setting it.

That address is then also an accepted origin, the default SSO callback (register it once with your IdP), and a name each server’s web UI answers to. Agents of an older version still relay their web UI to the servers until they are upgraded. If users sign in with passkeys under more than one of these names, set their domain as well (see Passkeys).

Behind a load balancer or tunnel

Besides cluster.ui_url, a load balancer in front of several servers needs these:

  • The same build on every server. The UI’s page names its script files by a hash of their contents, so a page from one server can’t load its scripts from a server with another build (404 on /assets/index-….js). Two hosts building the same commit can still produce different files. Build once and install that build everywhere (./target/release/glidex-install --prebuilt in a workspace holding it), and turn on session affinity by cookie in the load balancer, which also covers a rolling upgrade.

  • Sign-ins per server. A password (PAM) sign-in belongs to the server that checked it: the same Unix account on two servers is two sign-in methods, and a sign-in on a server where the account isn’t linked yet makes a new user without roles. Link the account on every server to its user once (gxctl user link alice pam alice --all-nodes; see Linking a sign-in), or give the roles to each user. If the servers share one account database (LDAP, say), set cluster.shared_local_accounts instead: an account name is then the same person on every node.

  • The browser’s address. A tunnel daemon on the server (Cloudflare’s cloudflared) connects to the UI from 127.0.0.1. Set GLIDEX_UI_CLIENT_IP_HEADER to the header it puts the browser’s address in, so the audit log and per-client rate limits see users, not the tunnel:

    # sudo systemctl edit glidex-ui
[Service]
Environment=GLIDEX_UI_CLIENT_IP_HEADER=CF-Connecting-IP

    The header counts only on connections from the host itself, so a browser can’t choose its own address with it.

  • Scripts the load balancer adds. The UI’s Content-Security-Policy allows its own scripts only. A script a proxy injects into the page, such as Cloudflare’s Web Analytics beacon, is blocked and logged in the browser’s console; turn the injection off in the proxy instead.

  • The proxy’s caching. The UI marks its /assets/ files immutable (their names change with their contents) and everything else, errors included, no-cache. A proxy that sets its own browser cache time instead (Cloudflare’s Browser Cache TTL) can keep a 404 in browsers for hours, such as one served while a server was being upgraded. Set it to respect the origin’s headers.

  • Requests need no affinity. Apart from the script files above, any server can take any request: a server forwards writes to the leader with the page’s Origin and, for account changes, passkeys and sign-ins through an identity provider, its cookies. The leader runs both ends of a sign-in through an identity provider (its start and the provider’s callback), so the callback may reach another server than the start did. It also issues and redeems console tickets, so the ticket and the console’s WebSocket may reach different servers. A ticket lasts 30 seconds; if the leader changes in that time, open the console again.

Rolling upgrades

Upgrade one node at a time: agents first, then servers. On each host, update the checkout and re-run the installer (see Maintenance). VMs keep running while the control plane restarts. An agent stopped in the middle of reporting a status sends that report once it is back.

gxctl cluster status shows each node’s version and feature level. The cluster runs at the lowest feature level any server reports, and uses new formats only once every server has them. Keep servers within one release of each other while you upgrade, and finish the round before starting the next.

The installer also brings a node’s OVN up to the version the cluster’s ovn-northd runs. A node whose OVN is older gets no VMs on cluster networks; the Cluster page names it.

Backups and lost quorum

On a server, take a snapshot of the replicated database regularly:

gxctl cluster snapshot glidex-$(date +%F).gxsnap

The file is written 0600: it holds credential and token hashes. Store it like the database itself. The Cluster page’s Certificate authority card also offers Download a cluster snapshot.

If a majority of servers is destroyed, the cluster can’t elect a leader. Recover from one surviving server:

  1. On that server, stop the control plane (VMs keep running): sudo systemctl stop glidex-control-plane.

  2. Start a single-voter cluster from its own database, or from a snapshot. Copy the snapshot where the glidex user can read it (sudo install -o glidex -g glidex -m 0600 glidex-….gxsnap /var/lib/glidex-control-plane/latest.gxsnap), then:

    sudo -u glidex env HOME=/var/lib/glidex-control-plane \
  /usr/local/bin/glidex-control-plane --force-new-cluster --from /var/lib/glidex-control-plane/latest.gxsnap

    Leave out --from to use its local database. Then sudo systemctl start glidex-control-plane.

  3. Re-join the other servers with --rejoin and tokens made with gxctl node rejoin-token <node> --raft-lost.

  4. With OVN on, OVN’s own databases need the same: on a surviving server, convert its northbound and southbound database files to standalone (ovsdb-tool cluster-to-standalone), then re-cluster the servers.

Cluster networks on OVN

With OVN off, every network lives on one node. With OVN on, cluster networks span every node: VMs on different nodes share them over Geneve tunnels, and NAT cluster networks leave through a shared edge. Node networks and their VMs are not affected either way.

Turn OVN on

Every node needs OVN installed (the default). If the Cluster page’s OVN card lists a node as missing it, re-run the installer there with --ovn. Then Enable OVN… on that card. Every node follows within a minute, without a restart: servers start OVN’s databases, every node becomes a chassis.

You can instead set it in a server’s /etc/glidex/control-plane.json ("cluster": {"ovn": {"enabled": true}}) and restart the control plane; saving in the UI makes the setting the cluster’s.

With OVN on, the OVN card shows tunnels between nodes, and nodes whose OVN is out of date. OVN settings… holds the rest. Disable OVN… is there too, once no cluster network is left.

OVN settings

FieldMeaning
DNS servers for guestsResolvers handed to guests on cluster networks; default: the hosts’.
NAT supernetWhere NAT cluster networks get their subnets; default 10.89.0.0/16.
Underlay MTUThe MTU of the network between nodes; default 1500. Cluster networks get 58 bytes less, for the Geneve header.

The shared edge

NAT cluster networks reach the outside through a logical router on gateway nodes, with one outside address. Tick Shared edge for NAT cluster networks in OVN settings… and fill in:

FieldExampleMeaning
Physical networkuplinkThe LAN the edge sits on; each gateway node maps it to a bridge.
External network192.0.2.0/24That LAN’s subnet.
Gateway192.0.2.1The LAN’s router.
Edge address192.0.2.50The edge’s own address on the LAN; NAT traffic leaves with it.
Pool for VPC routers (optional)192.0.2.64/26Outside addresses for project routers that get their own.
Gateway nodes, by prioritynode1, node2Where the edge runs; the next takes over if one fails.

The fields are prefilled from what the nodes report (their uplinks, addresses and routes); Suggest values fills them again, with notes on anything uncertain. Each gateway node must map the physical network and have br-int on the kernel datapath; see Host networking. Use addresses on the LAN that nothing else uses.

The same settings can be given in a server’s control-plane.json under cluster.ovn (edge with physnet, external_cidr, gateway, external_ip, external_pool, gateway_nodes); the OVN settings dialog says when it is showing the file’s values.

Projects can have their own routers, each with its own outside address from the pool, and attach their NAT or isolated networks to them; see Networks.

The Cluster page

The web UI’s Cluster page (in the side menu) shows, on a cluster:

  • the cluster id and feature level, and + Add node;
  • warnings for ports that don’t answer, a CA rotation under way, and detaches in progress;
  • Nodes: role, phase, readiness, address, version and VM count; click a node for its Host page (below);
  • Pending imports and Detaches;
  • Raft: state, term, leader, voters and learners;
  • OVN: on/off, tunnels, settings;
  • Certificate authority, and the Danger zone.

On a standalone host it shows This host (name, phase, readiness, CPUs, memory and VM count, with a link to the host’s own page) and offers Make this host a cluster.

Host pages

Each host has a page at /hosts/<node>; Hosts in the side menu opens the Cluster page’s node list (on a standalone host, its one page), and every link to a node leads there. A host’s page shows:

  • capacity, versions, KVM / IOMMU / DPDK, the br-int datapath and physical networks;
  • Topology: its NUMA nodes and PCI devices (see PCI passthrough);
  • Networking: that host’s Open vSwitch, bridges and uplinks (see Host networking), shown once the host is ready;
  • its VMs and disks, the Roles on this host card (see On one host of a cluster), and the Operations… menu.

The server whose web UI you use runs a host’s requests on that host, so every host, agents included, is managed from any server’s web UI. What you may do there follows your roles on that host. The old /cluster/nodes/<node> addresses lead to the same pages.

Maintenance

Day-to-day care of a Glidex host: updates, what keeps running when the services restart, backups, logs, and removing Glidex.

Updating

Pull the new source and re-run the installer, from your checkout:

git pull
cargo run -p glidex-install

It reuses the choices saved in /etc/glidex/install.conf, updates what is outdated, and restarts only the services whose binary or unit changed. Running VMs keep running. Details are in Installation.

With the kernel OVS profile saved (the default), a re-run turns off DPDK it finds on in Open vSwitch, which restarts ovs-vswitchd; with bridges it waits for --allow-ovs-restart. If you turned DPDK on with gxctl or the web UI and want to keep it, pass --ovs-profile dpdk once. See Back to the kernel profile.

On a cluster member, a re-run also upgrades OVN when the cluster’s ovn-northd is newer than the node’s ovn-controller; see OVN on cluster members. After you upgrade OVN on the servers, re-run the installer on the other nodes.

Browsers check for a new web UI every time they load a page, so a reload is enough to get it. A tab left open from before the update keeps the old UI, and may fail to open pages it hadn’t loaded yet: reload it.

In a cluster, update one node at a time, agents first, then servers; see Rolling upgrades.

What survives a restart

Each running VM lives in its own systemd unit, glidex-vm@<vm-id>.service, in the glidex-vms.slice. The unit runs glidex-vm-shim, which supervises the hypervisor. These units are not part of the control plane’s service, so:

EventVMs
glidex-control-plane stops, restarts or is upgradedKeep running. At start the control plane finds each running instance and adopts it; nothing is relaunched.
glidex-ui restartsNot affected.
glidex-stord restartsKeep running: they hold their volumes open. stord keeps no state.
glidex-netd restartsKeep running. netd restores bridges, NAT and uplinks at start; vhost-user sockets survive in /run/glidex/vhost.
Host shutdownEach VM gets its power button and host_shutdown_grace_secs (default 60, at most 300) to shut down, then is stopped. VMs stop before netd and Open vSwitch.
Host bootThe control plane relaunches the VMs that were meant to be running (reconcile.on_host_boot: resume, the default) or leaves them stopped (stop). A VM on LVM-thin volumes has them activated and allowed again as it starts.

To see the VM units:

systemctl list-units 'glidex-vm@*'
systemctl status glidex-vm@<vm-id>

Don’t start or stop these units yourself: the control plane does, through polkit, and restarting a VM is its decision, never systemd’s. Use gxctl start / stop or the web UI.

gxctl events <vm> shows what happened to a VM: starts, exits, restarts and adoptions.

Where things are

PathWhat
/var/lib/glidex-control-plane/.glidex/glidex.dbThe control plane’s database: VMs, networks, projects, users, credentials, tokens.
/var/lib/glidex-control-plane/.glidex/secrets.kekThe key that seals connector secrets. Without it, sealed secrets in the database can’t be opened.
/var/lib/glidex-control-plane/.glidex/images/, disks/Cloud images, firmware and VM disks: the built-in local datastore.
/srv/glidex/<name>/Registered datastores: disks/, and on a shared datastore also images/ (copies for linked disks), .locks/ and the .glidex-datastore marker.
/dev/<vg>/gx-d-<disk-id>, gx-i-<image-id>Disks and image volumes of LVM-thin datastores, in your volume groups. A volume no VM is using may be inactive, with no device node.
/var/lib/glidex-control-plane/.glidex/tls/The API’s self-signed certificate and key, if you didn’t configure one.
/var/lib/glidex-control-plane/.glidex/cluster/In a cluster: this node’s identity, certificates and Raft log.
/etc/glidex/Site configuration: control-plane.json, netd.json, stord.json, policies/, install.conf, and certificates you put there.
/var/lib/glidex/netd.dbglidex-netd’s state: bridges, uplinks (with the host addresses they moved), NAT networks.
/var/lib/glidex/dnsmasq/DHCP leases of NAT networks.
/var/lib/glidex-ui/The web UI’s self-signed certificate.
/run/glidex-cp/Runtime: api.sock, ui.sock, tls.crt, and per-VM directories vms/<id>/ (sockets, console log, cloud-init seed).
/run/glidex/glidex-netd’s sockets and vhost-user sockets.

Backups

What to keep, on every host:

  • /var/lib/glidex-control-plane/.glidex/glidex.db and secrets.kek, together;
  • tls/ (or your own certificates), and cluster/ on a cluster node;
  • /etc/glidex/;
  • /var/lib/glidex/netd.db;
  • images/ and disks/ if you can’t re-create them, the disks/ of each datastore under /srv/glidex, and the gx-d-… volumes of LVM-thin datastores.

These files hold password hashes, token hashes and private keys. Keep backups encrypted, readable only by administrators, and in your approved backup system.

A standalone host

The database is written while the control plane runs, so stop it for a consistent copy. VMs keep running:

sudo systemctl stop glidex-ui glidex-control-plane
sudo tar -C /var/lib/glidex-control-plane -czf /root/glidex-$(date +%F).tar.gz \
  --exclude=.glidex/images --exclude=.glidex/disks .glidex
sudo tar -czf /root/glidex-etc-$(date +%F).tar.gz /etc/glidex /var/lib/glidex/netd.db
sudo systemctl start glidex-control-plane glidex-ui

Disks of running VMs change while you copy them. Copy a VM’s disk while the VM is stopped, or back up from inside the guest. gxctl disk show gives a disk’s datastore and the path of its file.

A disk on an LVM-thin datastore is the raw volume /dev/<vg>/gx-d-<disk-id> on its node. Copy it while its VM is stopped, with your usual LVM or block-device tools (activate it first with sudo lvchange -ay -K <vg>/gx-d-<disk-id> if it has no device node). Image volumes (gx-i-…) need no backup: Glidex makes them again from the image.

A disk file on a datastore is named by the disk’s id. A linked disk names its image by a relative path (../images/<image-id>.qcow2 on a shared datastore), so copy a shared datastore’s images/ along with its disks/, or restore into the same layout.

To restore, install Glidex, stop the two services, put the files back (owned by glidex:glidex, mode 0600 for files, 0700 for directories), and start them again.

A cluster

The cluster’s database is replicated on every server. Take snapshots from a server:

gxctl cluster snapshot glidex-$(date +%F).gxsnap

The file is written 0600 and holds credential and token hashes. A snapshot is what you recover from if a majority of servers is lost; see Clusters. The snapshot holds records, not disk files. Disks on local and other node-local datastores, LVM-thin included, stay on their nodes: back them up per node as above. Disks on a shared datastore are on the shared filesystem: back that up with the storage system’s own tools, or per disk while its VM is stopped.

If a node is lost for good, VMs whose disks are all on shared datastores can run on another node once it is forgotten; see A node is gone for good. VMs with disks on the lost node’s own storage need those disks restored from a backup.

Logs

Each service logs to the journal:

journalctl -u glidex-control-plane -f
journalctl -u glidex-netd
journalctl -u glidex-ui
journalctl -u glidex-authd
journalctl -u glidex-stord               # LVM-thin volumes, device access
journalctl -u glidex-metad               # the guests' metadata endpoint
journalctl -u glidex-pylond              # Pylon hosts
journalctl -u glidex-vfio-boot -b        # what the boot binding did
journalctl -u glidex-vm@<vm-id>          # one VM's shim and hypervisor
journalctl -u 'glidex-vm@*' --since today

More detail: set RUST_LOG in a drop-in, for example for the control plane:

sudo systemctl edit glidex-control-plane
# [Service]
# Environment=RUST_LOG=debug
sudo systemctl restart glidex-control-plane

glidex-netd, glidex-stord and glidex-ui read RUST_LOG the same way. Remove it when you are done: debug logs are large.

Other records:

  • A VM’s serial console log: gxctl log <vm>, or the console page. It is kept in the VM’s runtime directory and rotated past 16 MiB (console.log_max_bytes); one older generation is kept.
  • The audit log: gxctl audit, or the Audit page. Kept 90 days (audit.retention_days).

Uninstall

From your checkout:

cargo run -p glidex-install -- uninstall --dry-run
cargo run -p glidex-install -- uninstall

It stops every VM (each gets its power button and grace period), the services and glidex-netd, tears down host networking (uplinks give the host’s address back to its NIC), and removes units, binaries and installer-written configuration. Your data in /var/lib/glidex-control-plane, your files in /etc/glidex, Open vSwitch, cloud-hypervisor, pylon and pylond stay unless you ask:

OptionAlso removes
--remove-ovsOpen vSwitch (packages or the source build in /opt/glidex).
--reset-dpdkDPDK settings Glidex put in OVS.
--remove-cloud-hypervisorThe cloud-hypervisor binary.
--remove-pylonThe pylon and pylond binaries.
--purge-user-data/var/lib/glidex-control-plane (VMs, credentials, images, disks), ~/.glidex, and control-plane.json, netd.json and policies/ in /etc/glidex.

-y / --yes skips the confirmation. Back up first if you might want the data back.

/srv/glidex and the datastores under it always stay, with their disks, and so do LVM-thin volume groups and their volumes (remove gx-d-… and gx-i-… with lvremove); unmount and remove them yourself. /etc/glidex/stord.json stays with your other files there, unless --purge-user-data.

On a cluster node, take the node out of the cluster first (Remove an empty node or Detach), then uninstall. The uninstaller doesn’t check: on a host that is still a member it stops the node’s VMs and services like on any host, and the cluster sees the node as unreachable. Its cluster identity stays in /var/lib/glidex-control-plane/.glidex/cluster/ unless --purge-user-data.

Troubleshooting

Start with the services and their logs, then look up the error code the API returned. Most problems are a stopped service, a missing group membership, a path the glidex user can’t read, or the host network.

Check the services

systemctl status glidex-control-plane glidex-netd glidex-ui glidex-authd.socket glidex-stord glidex-metad
journalctl -u glidex-control-plane -b

At start, the control plane logs one line per check. Each should end in OK:

  Checking disk tools... OK
  Loading configuration... OK
  Opening database... OK
  Checking KVM access... OK (VMs open it in their glidex-vm units)
  Loading VMs... OK (2 VMs, 1 running, VM runner: systemd)
  Checking UEFI firmware (Cloud-Hypervisor)... OK (image cloudhv-edk2)
  Checking UEFI firmware (QEMU)... OK (image ovmf)
  Checking networking... OK
  Loading authorization policies... OK
LineMeansDo
Checking disk tools... MISSING (...)qemu-img, sgdisk or another disk tool is missing; image and disk operations fail.Re-run the installer.
Loading configuration... FAILED/etc/glidex/control-plane.json has an error or an unknown key. The control plane doesn’t fall back to defaults.Fix the file; the message names the field.
Checking KVM access... MISSINGNo /dev/kvm.See KVM.
Checking KVM access... NO ACCESSThe VMs, which run as glidex, can’t open /dev/kvm: glidex isn’t in its group (usually kvm), or its mode doesn’t let that group read and write it.ls -l /dev/kvm; re-run the installer, which adds glidex to the group.
Checking networking... LIMITEDThe control plane can only read netd’s status: it isn’t running as the glidex group.Use the installed unit; don’t run the control plane by hand as yourself.
Checking networking... UNAVAILABLEglidex-netd isn’t running or not installed.systemctl status glidex-netd; re-run the installer without --no-networking.
Waiting for the cluster... NO SERVER (running from the cache)On a cluster agent: no server answered within 20 seconds. The agent runs its VMs from its cached records and catches up once a server answers.Check the servers and port 8842; see Clusters.
Loading authorization policies... FAILEDA policy file in /etc/glidex/policies is invalid or unreadable.Fix it; the directory must be root:glidex, mode 0750.

Logs of one VM: journalctl -u glidex-vm@<vm-id>, and gxctl events <vm> for what Glidex did with it. For log locations and more detail, see Maintenance.

The control plane stops answering

systemctl status glidex-control-plane says active (running), but gxctl waits forever, web UI pages don’t load, and the journal has gone quiet. Check whether it answers at all:

curl -sk --max-time 5 https://localhost:8841/health    # {"status":"ok"} when it answers

Builds of main before 2026-10-31 could hang this way, most often on a cluster server: a request waiting for the database, a Raft commit, or a call to glidex-netd, glidex-stord or hyperstor could hold up every request after it. Builds that have #221, #227 and #228 (merged on 2026-10-31) wait without holding up the others. There is no setting for it: update the host.

Until then, restart the control plane. Running VMs keep running, and it adopts them again when it starts:

sudo systemctl restart glidex-control-plane

In a cluster, check gxctl cluster status afterwards; if the server was the leader, another one takes over while it restarts. If a build with those fixes still hangs, report it with the journal from before the restart.

gxctl can’t connect

MessageCause and fix
Permission denied on /run/glidex-cp/api.sockYou aren’t in glidex-users (or glidex-admin), or you were added and haven’t logged out and back in since. Check with id.
Connection refused on https://localhost:8841, or unauthenticated without --urlWith no local socket, gxctl falls back to TCP on this host. The control plane isn’t running (systemctl status glidex-control-plane), or /run/glidex-cp/api.sock is missing.
this host is a cluster agent: it has no local APIExpected on an agent. Use a server: gxctl auth login --url https://<server>:8841 (this works on the agent itself).
no current profile; choose one with --profileThe current profile was removed (auth profiles remove) and others remain.
unauthenticated over TCPNo token, or an expired one. gxctl login --oidc or --token, or gxctl auth login.
A TLS or certificate error over TCPSee Certificate fingerprints.

The web UI

SymptomCause and fix
421 Misdirected RequestThe browser used a name the UI doesn’t serve. Add it to GLIDEX_UI_HOSTS (see Configuration).
403 origin_not_allowedA change came from a page on another site, or a page calls the API on port 8841 directly from an origin not in auth.allowed_origins. Pages served by the web UI don’t need that list.
A page doesn’t load after an updateThe tab still runs the old UI. Reload it.
Every user shows as 127.0.0.1 in the audit logA proxy or tunnel on the host connects to the UI. Set GLIDEX_UI_CLIENT_IP_HEADER (see Configuration).
This host is a cluster agent (503)An agent’s web UI sends browsers to a server, and no server has published its web UI address yet. Open a server’s web UI, or set cluster.ui_url; see The web UI’s address.
421 use_a_server from an agent’s https://<agent>:5173/api/…Expected: agents serve no API. Use a server.
No Sign in with a passkey buttonPasskeys are off (auth.passkeys.enabled), or the page is plain http, where browsers offer no passkeys. Use https. See Passkeys.
this page (…) isn’t under the passkeys’ domain …The web UI was opened under a name outside auth.passkeys.rp_id. Use a name under it; see The passkeys’ domain.
That passkey can’t sign in here. (passkey_refused)The passkey was made under another name or domain, or removed, the user is disabled, or the prompt expired. Sign in another way; the reason is in the audit log.
Every passkey stopped working after a configuration changeauth.passkeys.rp_id changed. Users sign in another way and add new passkeys.

Error codes

API errors come back as JSON with a code, a message and sometimes details:

{"error": "quota_exceeded", "message": "…", "details": {"quota": "…"}}

gxctl and the web UI show the code and message. The common ones:

CodeMeansDo
unauthenticatedNo valid login or token.Log in again; check the token’s expiry.
reauth_requiredThe action needs a recent login (cluster changes, installing OVS, uplink and bridge changes, policies).Log in again and retry.
forbiddenYour roles or the site policies don’t allow it.Check gxctl whoami; ask for a role. See Access control.
not_foundNo such VM, network, image… in the project you’re using.Check --project / your default project (gxctl project use).
conflictA name is taken, or the resource is in use or busy (a disk claimed by a VM or being moved, a PCI device used by another VM on the same host or sharing its IOMMU group, a DPDK NIC, a kernel image a VM boots, a datastore that still has disks or, for LVM-thin, image volumes).Read the message: it names what holds it.
ambiguousA name matches more than one thing.Use the id.
invalid_stateThe VM can’t do that now (start a running VM, attach what’s already attached).Check its state with gxctl get <vm>.
invalid_config, invalid, invalid_network, invalid_image, invalid_diskA bad request: wrong path, out-of-range value, unknown network.The message says which field.
invalid_datastoreA datastore name or path that isn’t allowed: the path must be a directory under /srv/glidex; an LVM-thin datastore takes a volume group and thin pool, not a path.See Datastores and LVM-thin.
insufficient_storage (507)A datastore without overcommit lacks the space for a new or moved disk; details has free_bytes and needed_bytes.Free space, pick another datastore, or allow overcommit; see Overcommit and capacity.
quota_exceeded, tenant_quota_exceededThe project or tenant would go over a quota.Raise it (gxctl project quota) or free resources.
device_flow_unsupportedgxctl auth login --oidc through a google connector that has no device client.Add a TVs and Limited Input devices client to the connector (--device-client-id, then connector secret set <id> device_client_secret); see Google.
cannot_delete_self, last_adminDeleting yourself, or the last holder of system-admin or directory-admin.Have another administrator do it; give the role to someone else first. See Removing people.
last_identityRemoving a user’s last sign-in method, or one that would leave a single passkey as the only one.Disable the user first, or add another sign-in method (or a second passkey).
too_many_passkeys, passkey_not_addedAdding an 11th passkey; or adding one failed (the prompt expired, or the passkey is already registered).Remove one first; try again. See Passkeys.
passkey_refused, passkeys_disabledA passkey sign-in was refused (the reason is in the audit log); passkeys are off.See The web UI.
bad_target_nodeA request named a node in X-Glidex-Target-Node on a path that isn’t about one host, an unknown or departed node, or went to a host that isn’t a server.Send host requests for another node to a server, with the node’s id.
node_departedGiving a role on one host whose node has left the cluster.Pick a current node (gxctl nodes).
managed_by_connectorThe user or team is managed by a SCIM connector or a directory sync: its name, whether it is enabled, or a membership the IdP gave, belongs to the IdP. Also deleting a managed user that is still enabled.Change it at the IdP, or disable the user first. See Users an IdP manages.
not_provisionedMaking a SCIM token for a connector that isn’t provisioned by SCIM.gxctl connector update <id> --no-jit --provisioning scim first.
not_pulled, no_sourceRunning a directory sync of a connector that isn’t --provisioning pull, or isn’t a Google Workspace connector.See Directory sync from Google Workspace.
sync_runningA run of that connector’s directory sync is already going.Wait, then gxctl connector show <id>.
invalid_federationA workload federation’s settings were refused: a rule that pins none of repository, project_path, sub, a * in a value, a service account that isn’t one of the tenant’s (or no longer exists), --ttl outside 60–3600, or over 20 federations or 50 rules.The message names the rule; see Workload federation.
issuer_unreachableGlidex couldn’t read the issuer’s discovery document or keys when the federation was added or its issuer changed.Check the issuer URL is exactly the tokens’ iss, served over https without redirects, and that the control plane can reach it; see The issuer.
login_not_allowedThe connector’s rules refused the login. Through a SCIM connector or a directory sync: the person wasn’t provisioned (pulled), or their account is disabled.Check the user is assigned to the application at the IdP and was pushed; see Provisioning with SCIM.
precondition_failedSomeone changed the resource since you read it.Read it again and retry.
hypervisor_unavailableThe VM’s hypervisor isn’t installed on this host.Re-run the installer (without --no-qemu for QEMU).
hypervisor_errorThe hypervisor refused or failed.journalctl -u glidex-vm@<vm-id>, gxctl events <vm>.
tool_unavailableA disk tool is missing.Re-run the installer.
image_errorDownload, checksum or disk operation failed.The message says which; check disk space under /var/lib/glidex-control-plane.
netd_unavailableglidex-netd isn’t reachable.systemctl status glidex-netd.
netd_permission_deniednetd refused the control plane’s request.Check /etc/glidex/netd.json’s policy, if you set one.
netd_error, unsupported_on_hostnetd failed, or the host can’t do it (missing DPDK, AF_XDP, IOMMU).gxctl ovs status lists what is missing.
host_interface_in_useThe NIC carries the host’s address.Add the uplink with --migrate-ip; see Host networking.
confirmation_requiredThe change restarts Open vSwitch or similar.Repeat with --force (or confirm in the UI) when traffic may be interrupted.
migration_rolled_backMoving the host’s address to a bridge failed the gateway check and was undone.Fix the network, then gxctl uplink-reapply.
not_a_server, use_a_server, cluster_unavailable, leader_changedIn a cluster: asked an agent, no server reachable, or no leader right now.Use a server; check gxctl cluster status; retry.
node_unreachableThe VM’s node can’t be reached.Check that node; see Clusters.
gateway_not_readyA gateway node doesn’t map the edge’s physical network or runs br-int in userspace.See Gateway nodes.
internal, persistence_errorA bug or a storage problem.journalctl -u glidex-control-plane; check disk space.

SCIM provisioning

When an IdP can’t provision a SCIM connector, its test or logs show the endpoint’s answer:

AnswerCause and fix
401A wrong, expired or revoked token, or another connector’s. Check gxctl connector scim-token list <id>, make a new token, and enter it in the IdP.
403The connector is disabled, or isn’t --provisioning scim.
400 invalidFilterThe IdP filters on an attribute Glidex doesn’t: users by userName, externalId, emails, displayName; groups by displayName, externalId.
409 uniquenessA user with that userName, or a group with that name, already exists for the connector.
413A request body over 1 MiB.
429Over 20 requests a second for the connector. IdPs retry after Retry-After.
The connection fails or times outThe endpoint isn’t reachable from the IdP, or the path isn’t published; see Making the endpoint reachable.

Every SCIM write is in the audit log as system:scim:<connector-id>: gxctl audit --limit 50.

Workload federation

When a CI job can’t get a token from POST /auth/exchange:

AnswerCause and fix
400 invalid_requestThe request is malformed: check grant_type, subject_token_type and federation (<tenant slug>/<federation id>); see The exchange.
400 invalid_grantThe same answer for every refusal. The reason is in the audit log: gxctl audit --limit 50, entries exchangeToken by system:federation:<tenant>/<id>. Common ones: the federation is disabled or misnamed; the job asked for another audience; no rule matches (the branch, environment or repository differs; claims match exactly); the token was already exchanged (get a new one per exchange); the rule’s service account was revoked or expired.
429 slow_downOver 30 exchanges a minute for the federation. Exchange once per job and reuse the token while it lives.
401 unauthenticated on later callsThe Glidex token expired (expires_in), or the federation was disabled or removed, its rule changed, or the service account revoked.

Certificate fingerprints

Both the API (port 8841) and the web UI (port 5173) use a self-signed certificate unless you configured one. Before trusting it from another machine, compare its SHA-256 fingerprint with the one on the host:

sudo openssl x509 -in /run/glidex-cp/tls.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256              # API
sudo openssl x509 -in /var/lib/glidex-ui/tls/ui.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256       # web UI

The installer also prints both at the end.

  • The browser’s fingerprint differs. Something between you and the host presents another certificate (a proxy, or the wrong host). Don’t accept it until you know why.

  • gxctl says the certificate is not among the profile’s pins. The host’s certificate changed. Glidex regenerates it only in narrow cases (a configured certificate replaced, which is served within a minute without a restart; cluster rotate-ca; a re-init). Confirm the new fingerprint on the host through another channel, then:

    gxctl auth login --profile <name> --pin sha256/<new fingerprint> --rebind

    gxctl auth trust list shows a profile’s pins; gxctl auth trust fetch shows what a server presents.

  • The ts.net name still gets a certificate warning with --tailscale-cert on. The UI serves its usual certificate until tailscaled hands it one: journalctl -u glidex-ui says why (HTTPS certificates not enabled for the tailnet, TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID not glidex-ui, the first certificate still being issued). See Tailscale certificates.

  • A join says the server’s CA is not the one the token names. The cluster CA rotated after the token was issued (for example a server left). Issue a new token.

See TLS certificates to use your own certificates.

Paths the glidex user can’t read

The control plane and every VM run as the glidex system user, in a sandbox. Paths you give the API (disk images, kernels, cloud-init files) are opened by that user, so:

  • They must be readable by glidex. Your home directory usually isn’t, and /home, /root and /run/user are hidden from the services entirely.
  • They must not be under /tmp or /var/tmp: VMs have a private /tmp. The API refuses such paths (… is under /tmp, which VMs cannot see).
  • Passing host paths at all needs the host.paths permission (system-admin).

Put such files in a directory of their own, such as /srv/vm-files: sudo chgrp -R glidex /srv/vm-files && sudo chmod -R g+rX /srv/vm-files. Not under /srv/glidex: that is where datastores are mounted and registered, and the installer offers what is mounted there as datastores. Better still, import them as images (a kernel as a kernel image), which Glidex stores itself.

KVM

ls -l /dev/kvm
lsmod | grep kvm
  • No /dev/kvm. Turn on virtualization (VT-x / AMD-V) in the firmware settings, then sudo modprobe kvm_intel or sudo modprobe kvm_amd. In a VM, nested virtualization must be on in the outer hypervisor.
  • /dev/kvm exists but VMs fail with permission denied. The glidex user must be in the kvm group: id glidex. The installer adds it when the group exists; re-run it, then restart the control plane.

PCI devices

  • PCI device … is used by VM … or … shares IOMMU group … with …. Another VM on that host holds the device or a device of its IOMMU group. Claims are per host: in a cluster, an unpinned VM goes to a node where the device is free.

  • A VM with PCI devices waits for a node. Its page lists each node’s reason: no PCI device … (the node doesn’t report it), or the VM holding it on every node that has it.

  • A VM’s DeviceHealthy condition is False. One of its devices fell off the bus or had new uncorrectable PCIe errors (event DeviceError). Glidex leaves the VM running; check gxctl node topology <node> --devices and the host’s dmesg, and cordon the device if you don’t trust it.

  • A VM’s NumaAligned condition is False. A NUMA_POLICY_PREFERRED VM didn’t fit on one NUMA node and spans the host.

  • A device on vfio-pci is not ready: in use by <process> (pid …), or release and VF counts are refused with IOMMU group … is in use by …. A VM, Glidex’s or another hypervisor’s, has the group open. Stop it; see Devices another hypervisor holds.

  • After a reboot, devices are back on their host drivers, or VFs are gone. Keep them with the installer’s --vfio-devices and --sriov; journalctl -u glidex-vfio-boot shows what was bound, skipped or failed. See Keep it across reboots.

  • A GPU request is refused: PCI device … has no NUMA node. The firmware reports no NUMA node for the device (-1), common on one-socket hosts; gpus aligns to NUMA nodes. Send numa_policy: NUMA_POLICY_PREFERRED with gpus. See GPU requests.

See PCI passthrough for host setup problems (IOMMU, vfio-pci, /dev/vfio permissions), and Host resources for hugepages, NUMA, dedicated CPUs, device pools and cordoned devices.

Datastores and disks

SymptomCause and fix
A node doesn’t reach a datastore (NODES OK below the node count)gxctl datastore show <ds> gives each node’s reason (OutsideRoot, Missing, NotADirectory, ReadOnly, NoMarker, ForeignMarker, NotEmpty; for LVM-thin StordUnavailable, NotAllowed, NoVolumeGroup, NoThinPool); see What “reachable” means and LVM-thin node status.
A node shows reachable, with warnings (warning: lines under it in gxctl datastore show)The shared datastore is mounted over NFS with risky options: soft/softerr (mounted soft: …: an NFS server outage fails the guests’ disk writes), or node-local locks, nolock or local_lock= other than none (NFS locks are local to this node …: volume locks no longer keep other nodes off a disk). The datastore stays usable. Remount it hard with NFS locking on; the warning goes at the node’s next check. See Mount warnings.
A VM waits for a node: datastore … is not reachable hereIts disks are on a datastore that node doesn’t reach. Fix the datastore on the nodes it should be on.
A VM doesn’t start: disk … is in use elsewhere (… is locked) (condition reason DiskBusy)Another node holds the disk’s volume lock, for example a node that seemed gone still runs the VM. Find and stop it there; the VM starts once the lock is free.
A disk shows · moving, or Ready False with reason MovePendingA move is going on (MovePending: it waits, for example for a VM to let go of the disk or for the image’s copy). The disk’s events say Moved when it is done, or MoveFailed with the reason; it then stays where it was. While it moves, resizing it is refused (409 conflict), adding it to a VM is refused (400 invalid_config), and its VM waits to start (reason DiskNotReady: disk … is moving to datastore …).
A linked disk waits: image … has not been copied into datastore … yetThe disk’s worker copies the image into the shared datastore first; it carries on by itself. See Images on a shared datastore.
place answers Not placed yetNo node can take the VM yet; the reason follows. The VM’s events record Replacing. See Placing a stopped or lost VM again.
An LVM-thin datastore shows StordUnavailable on a nodeglidex-stord isn’t running there: not installed (--no-services), or /etc/glidex/stord.json is invalid. systemctl status glidex-stord, journalctl -u glidex-stord; fix the file and restart it.
An LVM-thin datastore shows NotAllowedIts volume group isn’t in stord’s allowed_vgs. re-run the installer with --stord-allow-vg <vg>, or edit /etc/glidex/stord.json and restart glidex-stord. See Allow it in glidex-stord.
An LVM-thin datastore shows NoVolumeGroup, the message saying lvs isn’t foundThe LVM tools aren’t installed: install lvm2.
A warning the thin pool is N% full (or the thin pool’s metadata is N% full), or guests on an LVM-thin datastore hang on I/OThe thin pool is filling; guests stall when it is full. Extend it from free space in the volume group (lvextend, lvextend --poolmetadatasize). See Thin pool space.
Deleting an LVM-thin datastore is refused: it still holds volumes of images …Nodes keep image volumes in it. Delete those images, or remove their gx-i-* volumes from the volume group, then wait for the next check (about a minute). See Deleting an LVM-thin datastore.
A disk on an LVM-thin datastore is refused: raw volumes; leave format out, or can’t be made smallerDisks there are raw and only grow. Leave the format out (in the web UI pick raw).
A VM doesn’t start: disk … volume is missingIts LVM volume was removed by hand, or the node’s own volume group changed.
A datastore can’t be changed or deleted (409 conflict)The message gives the reason: it is local, disks are still on it, a running VM with a disk open on a node whose path changes, or a node a disk is bound to. See Changing and deleting.

Kernel boot

SymptomCause and fix
A kernel image stays failedThe extraction failed: its message says why. gxctl image retry <image> (or Retry) runs it again. The image’s events (GET /images/{id}/events) record Retrying and, once done, Extracted.
kernel_from refused with 400 invalid_image (kernels can’t be extracted here), or catalog pulls bring no kernelThe message says why: extraction is off on this host (GLIDEX_KERNEL_EXTRACTION=off), there is no extractor for the image’s architecture, or the host is of another architecture than the image (x86_64 images are extracted on x86_64 hosts, aarch64 on aarch64). The host also needs Cloud Hypervisor (or QEMU, on x86_64 only). See Configuration.
Extraction fails with the extractor did not start: systemd refused (is the glidex polkit rule installed?)The host’s polkit rule predates kernel extraction and lets the control plane start only VM units. Re-run the installer (cargo run -p glidex-install) to update it, then Retry the kernel image.
The first extraction fails to downloadIt fetches pinned Debian packages over HTTPS from snapshot.debian.org once; allow that, or add kernel images from a URL or host files.
An aarch64 kernel-boot VM’s console is silentIt was made with console=ttyS0. Set its kernel_args to console=ttyAMA0 …; new aarch64 VMs get that by default. See The console.
A VM’s KernelExtracted condition is False (reason ExtractFailed, event KernelExtractFailed)Following the guest’s kernel failed; the VM boots the kernel it has, and the next start tries again. See Following the guest’s kernel.
A VM doesn’t start: Ready False, reason KernelNotExtractedA VM that follows its guest’s kernel has no kernel to boot yet. Fix the cause in the message, or set kernel to a ready kernel image.
A VM waits: kernel … has not been copied to this node yet (DisksReady False, DiskNotReady)The node fetches its copy of the kernel image; the VM carries on by itself.
409 conflict deleting a kernel imageVMs boot it or keep it to go back to; the message names them. A VM-owned kernel image goes by itself once unused (event Unused).

Networking

Start with what the host can do:

gxctl ovs status            # netd access, OVS version and state, what is missing
gxctl networks              # networks and their status
gxctl bridges
sudo ovs-vsctl show
SymptomCheck
The Networking page says glidex-netd is not reachablesystemctl status glidex-netd, journalctl -u glidex-netd.
A network stays not readygxctl networks and the network’s status in the UI give the reason.
A VM on a NAT network gets no addressdnsmasq is installed (gxctl ovs status); a host firewall (ufw, firewalld) may drop DHCP or forwarded traffic: allow the NAT subnet.
A VM has an address but no internetIP forwarding (sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward is 1), the host’s own route out, and the firewall’s FORWARD policy.
A bridged VM gets no addressThe bridge has an uplink (gxctl uplinks <bridge>), the link is up, and the LAN has a DHCP server (Glidex doesn’t run one there).
An uplink is held off the bridge after a rebootThe gateway didn’t answer at boot. Fix it, then gxctl uplink-reapply <bridge> <uplink>.
vhost-user NICs failThe host needs the dpdk profile, DPDK initialized and hugepages: gxctl ovs status.
The installer says OVS still runs DPDK from an earlier dpdk profileThe kernel profile turns DPDK off by restarting ovs-vswitchd. Re-run with --allow-ovs-restart, or with --ovs-profile dpdk to keep DPDK. See Back to the kernel profile.
The installer says OVS-DPDK stays on: DPDK ports need DPDK: …A DPDK uplink or vhost-user VM NIC is still on OVS. Remove the uplink and stop or move those VMs, then re-run.
br-int stays userspace (netdev) after going back to the kernel profileIt switches only while no VM port is on br-int: stop or move the node’s VMs on cluster networks.
Cluster VMs on different nodes can’t reach each otherUDP 6081 (Geneve) between the nodes’ tunnel addresses; the OVN card on the Cluster page shows the tunnels.
The installer stops: the cluster's ovn-northd is OVN …, this host has … or upgrading OVN would remove …This member’s OVN is older than the cluster’s and the installer couldn’t upgrade it: not an apt-get host, or the upgrade would replace another package. Install that OVN version or newer by hand, then re-run. See OVN on cluster members.
gxctl cluster status lists ports that don’t answerOpen them; see Ports between nodes.

If the host lost its own connectivity after an uplink change, wait a minute: an uncommitted address move is rolled back by itself. If you need to act at the console, gxctl uplink-rm <bridge> <uplink> puts the address back on the NIC.

Getting help

When you report a problem, include the Glidex version (gxctl cluster status in a cluster, or the control plane’s startup banner), what you ran, the error code and message, and the relevant journal lines. Remove host names, addresses, user names and anything secret from them first, and never include tokens, passwords or private keys.

Developer guide

This guide is for people who want to change Glidex: fix a bug, add an API operation, port a feature to clusters, or just find their way around the code. It assumes you know Rust and have used Linux VMs; it doesn’t assume you know KVM, Open vSwitch or Raft.

To install and run Glidex, read the Operator guide instead; to use it, the User guide.

Glidex from a contributor’s angle

Glidex is a Rust workspace of 16 crates. At its centre is one binary, glidex-control-plane: an axum server that answers a REST API and an RPC API (gRPC, gRPC-Web and Connect) through one transport-neutral service layer, authorizes every call with Cedar, writes desired state to a ReDB database, and runs level-triggered controllers that move the host toward it. Each VM runs under its own small supervisor, glidex-vm-shim, in its own systemd unit, so the control plane can restart without touching guests. Privileged work (Open vSwitch and NAT, LVM, PAM) is done by small root helpers that take requests only from the control plane; guests reach a metadata endpoint, glidex-metad, for their identity tokens. Several control planes form a cluster by replicating their database with Raft; cluster networks run on OVN. The web UI (React, served by glidex-ui) and the gxctl CLI are clients of the same API, with types generated from the same protos.

Pages

PageWhat it covers
Repository and code organizationEvery crate, which binary runs where, the control plane’s modules, the protos and generated code, the web UI, and where to find things.
ArchitectureProcesses, layers and how a request and a VM flow through them.
Design decisions and trade-offsWhy Glidex is shaped the way it is, and what each choice costs.
AlgorithmsReconciliation, scheduling, replication and the other non-obvious parts.
Performance and benchmarksMeasured figures, with their source, date and hardware.
Glidex comparedHow Glidex relates to other VM managers.
ContributingBuilding from source, tests, CI, conventions, adding an API operation end to end, and the pull request flow.

Three sets of documentation

SetWhereRead it for
This bookdocs/public/src, published at https://cmkl-apex.github.io/glidex/docs/What Glidex does and how to use it; for contributors, this guide.
Design specsspec/Invariants, contracts between components, decisions with their reasons, milestones. The authority on why; code and protos cite them as spec/<file>.md §n.
API reference (rustdoc)Built locally with cargo docEvery crate’s types and functions, private items included. Module docs (//!) name the spec section each module implements.

When to read which:

  • Before you change behavior, read the spec that owns it. A comment such as // spec/24-storage.md §8.3 or a decision number (D6, G-D11) points at the reasoning you must keep or update.
  • To learn what a feature does from the outside, read this book’s user and operator guides. They describe shipped behavior only.
  • To find your way in a module, read its rustdoc: start at the //! header of the file.

Build the specs as a book with mdbook build docs/internal (output in target/docs/internal), and the API reference with:

RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings -A rustdoc::private_intra_doc_links" \
  cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items   # -> target/doc

First day

  1. Read Concepts and the Operator guide overview: the objects and the systemd units you will be changing.
  2. Install Glidex on a test host or VM with KVM (Quick start), create a NAT network, pull an image and boot a VM. You will want a working host for the functional tests.
  3. Read Repository and code organization, then Architecture.
  4. Read the specs’ README, then spec/00-architecture.md and spec/12-reconciliation.md: desired state, the controllers and the shim.
  5. Read spec/18-grpc.md §2–§5 for how an API operation is declared once and served twice.
  6. Build and test: cargo build, then cargo test (Contributing).
  7. Run a control plane and the UI from source and trace one request, for example POST /disks/{id}/move, from the UI’s api.ts through api/storage.rs and service/storage.rs to the disk controller (Adding an API operation walks the same path).

Repository and code organization

This page maps the repository: what each crate is, which process runs where, how the control plane is split into modules, and where the protos, the web UI, the packaging and the docs live. For how these pieces work together at run time, see Architecture.

Links to source files point at main on GitHub.

glidex/

glidex-api: protos and generated code

The proto files are the source of truth for every API type (spec/18-grpc.md G-D3).

crates/glidex-api/
├── build.rs        protox → checks → operations.rs, fields.rs → connectrpc-build
├── buf.yaml        buf lint (STANDARD) and breaking (FILE) rules
├── buf.gen.yaml    TypeScript for the UI → ../glidex-ui/ui/src/gen
├── proto/glidex/<area>/v1/<area>.proto
│                   access, auth, cluster, common, directory, host,
│                   network, storage, system, tenancy, usage, vm, watch
├── proto/glidex/api/v1/options.proto   (glidex.api.v1.op), (glidex.api.v1.secret)
├── proto/glidex/api/v1/errors.proto, types.proto
├── proto/google/rpc/error_details.proto   vendored ErrorInfo
└── src/lib.rs      generated modules, OPERATIONS, operation(), unknown_field()

What build.rs does on every cargo build, with no protoc or buf needed:

  1. Compiles every .proto under proto/ with protox.
  2. Fails the build if a rule is broken:
    • every RPC has a (glidex.api.v1.op) option with an action, a kind (KIND_READ or KIND_WRITE) and, if any, a REST twin in the form "<METHOD> /path";
    • every field’s JSON name equals its proto name (json_name, G-D11), so REST stays snake_case;
    • no response message reaches a field marked [(glidex.api.v1.secret) = true].
  3. Writes operations.rs (glidex_api::OPERATIONS: procedure, service, method, Cedar action, kind, REST twin, streaming) and fields.rs (every message’s JSON field names, which the server uses to refuse unknown fields).
  4. Writes a descriptor set (glidex_api::DESCRIPTOR_SET, for server reflection) and runs connectrpc-build for messages (buffa types), service traits and clients, included as glidex_api::proto.

The TypeScript for the UI is not generated by cargo: run buf generate in crates/glidex-api (after bun install in crates/glidex-ui/ui). Its output in crates/glidex-ui/ui/src/gen/ is committed, and CI fails when it is stale.

glidex-control-plane

The control plane is one library (src/lib.rs) with two binaries: src/main.rs (the server) and src/bin/gxctl/ (the CLI). Its tests are in tests/; the Cedar schema and shipped policies in policies/.

Request path

 HTTP request
   │  api/mod.rs      router: global layers (UI relay, authenticate, cluster gate)
   ├─▶ REST route     api/<area>.rs     decode JSON → call service → encode
   └─▶ RPC procedure  api/rpc/<area>.rs decode message → call service → encode
                         │
                         ▼
                      service/<area>.rs   Cedar checks, not-found vs forbidden,
                         │                quotas, names, the store write
                         ▼
                      state.rs (VmManager), store/, images/, datastore/, …
                         │  spec written; controllers woken
                         ▼
                      controller/*        observe the host, take the next step

Module map

AreaModulesWhat is there
API adaptersapi/mod.rs, api/<area>.rsThe router and the route table (routes: method, path, Cedar action, handler), the Caller, auth and audit layers, REST handlers. api/errors.rs maps internal errors to REST responses.
api/rpc/RPC adapters per proto package (vm.rs, storage.rs, …) and unary, which finds the operation, applies the listener rules, runs the service function and audits.
api/gate.rs, api/relay.rsIn a cluster: reads after a barrier, writes forwarded to the leader; host-only requests relayed to the node they name.
api/op.rs, api/issuer.rs, api/scim.rs, api/trust.rs, api/exchange.rs, api/trusted_login.rs, …HTTP-only endpoints: a directory’s OpenID provider, SCIM, trust between clusters and directories, token exchange, login at a trusted directory.
api/metad.rsThe router on metad.sock: finds the running VM on this node behind a VM port’s peer address and answers glidex-metad for it.
Service layerservice/One transport-neutral function per operation (service::storage::move_disk, …). Every decision is made here, so REST and RPC can’t drift apart. ServiceError carries the stable error code both transports send.
Admissionstate.rsVmManager: validates and writes desired state, then wakes the controllers.
Controllerscontroller/Level-triggered loops on one work queue (queue.rs): vm.rs, disk.rs, image.rs, network.rs, ovn.rs, placement.rs, extract.rs, image_cache.rs, store_copies.rs; startup.rs for adoption at start.
Storestore/db.rs: Glidex’s tables (tables!) on glidex-raftstore. mod.rs: the VM envelopes, events, SCHEMA_VERSION and migrate. Locks held across a store write are taken through glidex_raftstore::wait (see Contributing).
Clustercluster/Membership, join tokens, node PKI and CA rotation, server and agent runtimes, import and departure; cluster/raft/ wires glidex-raftstore to Glidex’s schema.
Schedulingscheduler.rs, node.rs, topology.rs, pci.rsWhere a VM runs (decided once, then sticky), nodes, NUMA topology, PCI devices and pools.
VM instancesinstance/, hypervisor/, paths.rs, devaccess.rsRunning the shim (instance/runner.rs: a systemd unit, or detached for dev runs and tests), liveness; drivers turning a VM config into a Cloud Hypervisor, QEMU or Pylon command line (cloud_hypervisor.rs, qemu.rs, pylon.rs); per-VM runtime directories.

gxctl

src/bin/gxctl/main.rs holds the interactive shell (rustyline) and the dispatch; each area has its own file (vm.rs, storage.rs, network.rs, access.rs, cluster.rs, host.rs, directory.rs, tenancy.rs, usage.rs, admin.rs; dirlogin.rs for logging in at a directory). client.rs has the REST client and the Connect transport that carries the generated RPC clients over gxctl’s own connection; config.rs the login profiles; console.rs the console attach loop. Only the global options are clap; commands are parsed by hand.

Tests

tests/ holds one integration test binary per area (vm_tests.rs, storage_tests.rs, datastore_tests.rs, cluster_tests.rs, rpc_tests.rs, tenancy_tests.rs, …) with shared helpers in tests/common/. functional_tests.rs boots real guests; most of it is #[ignore]d. See Contributing.

Web UI

crates/glidex-ui/
├── src/main.rs        serve ui/dist (or GLIDEX_UI_DIR), proxy /api, TLS, Host allowlist; --dev
├── ui/                Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind
│   ├── src/App.tsx    routes → pages
│   ├── src/pages/     one file per page: Dashboard, VmDetail, Disks, Datastores, Cluster, …
│   ├── src/components/  forms, dialogs, cards (CreateVmForm, VmActions, PlacementPicker, …)
│   ├── src/api.ts     every API call; rpc() for RPCs, REST for the rest
│   ├── src/session.tsx  the kit's session layer with Glidex's adapter; capability checks (useCan)
│   ├── src/live.tsx   WatchService stream: live updates
│   └── src/gen/       generated by buf generate (committed; don't edit)
├── kit/               @glidex/ui-kit: Modal, TokenReveal, password form, SSO buttons,
│                      step-up dialog, session provider; takes an AuthApi adapter
└── e2e/               Playwright suite, run with bun

api.ts sends RPCs over gRPC-Web (createGrpcWebTransport, base /api) with JSON messages, through rpc(Service.method.x, req), which returns the proto JSON the REST twin would answer. REST stays for what has no RPC (health, login and logout, OIDC redirects, CSV exports, the console WebSocket, GET /auth/whoami). The browser reaches the control plane through glidex-ui, which forwards /api to ui.sock; that is the only listener that takes gRPC-Web with a session cookie.

The UI is built with bun (bun install, bun run build), never npm. ui/ is the bun workspace root and lists ../kit as a workspace, so bun install in ui/ covers both. The kit holds the login and session pieces that aren’t Glidex-specific, for reuse by other management UIs: it never imports api.ts or types.ts; the app hands it an AuthApi adapter (methods, whoami, login, startSso, logout). Passkeys, accounts, roles and capability checks stay in ui/. See kit/README.md.

Architecture

This page is a map of Glidex for contributors: which processes run, how a request travels through them, where state lives and how it turns into running VMs. Each section names the crates and modules involved and links to the design spec with the details. For why things are built this way, see Design decisions and trade-offs; for the algorithms (scheduling, reconciliation, Raft write sets, metering), see Algorithms; for the repository layout, see Repository and code organization.

Source paths below are relative to the repository root and link to main. The design specs live in spec/.

The big picture

Glidex is a set of ordinary Linux processes. Nothing is containerized. The work is split by privilege: the control plane runs as an unprivileged user, and each thing that needs root is a small helper daemon with a narrow protocol on a Unix socket.

   Browser                         gxctl
      │ HTTPS :5173                  │ api.sock (peer uid)  or  HTTPS :8841 (token)
      ▼                              │
 ┌──────────────┐  ui.sock           │
 │  glidex-ui   │────────────┐       │
 │ (glidex-ui)  │            ▼       ▼
 └──────────────┘   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐   :8842 mTLS
                    │  glidex-control-plane      (user glidex)     │◀──────────▶ other nodes
                    │  REST + RPC API · auth · Cedar · store       │
                    │  controllers · scheduler · hypervisor drivers│
                    └──┬──────────┬───────────┬───────────┬────────┘

EndpointServed byUsed by

/run/glidex-cp/ui.sockcontrol planeglidex-ui only (checked by peer uid)

TCP :5173 (HTTPS)glidex-uibrowsers
/run/glidex/netd.sock, netd-ro.sock, netd-admin.socknetdcontrol plane (full); anyone (status only); the admin group
/run/glidex-stord/stord.sock, stord-admin.sockstordcontrol plane; the admin group
/run/glidex-authd/auth.sockauthdcontrol plane

169.254.169.254:8775glidex-metadguests: netd’s rules DNAT 169.254.169.254:80 from each VM port on node NAT networks here, with the port’s own peer address
