Design decisions and trade-offs

This page explains why Glidex is built the way it is. It covers the choices a contributor is most likely to question, says what each one costs, and says when it should be looked at again. For what the parts are and how they talk to each other, see Architecture. For how specific mechanisms work (the write lane, placement, the metering ledger), see Algorithms. For how Glidex compares with other products, see Glidex compared.

How decisions are recorded

Decisions live in the design specs in spec/, not in this book. Each spec has a decision table near the top, with a number, the decision and the reason:

SpecNumbering
12-reconciliation.mdD1–D20
14-clustering.mdD1–D22
11-security.mddecisions 1–19
19-tenancy.mdD1–D71
18-grpc.mdG-D1–G-D12
24-storage.mdS1–S19
09-networking.mddecisions 1–10
23-kernel-boot.mdK1–K13
22-host-topology.mdH1–H19
27-gpu-vms.mdG1–G10
13-metering.mdD1–D18
25-passkeys.mdP1–P6
21-tailscale-tls.mdT1–T11
17-gxctl-auth.mdA1–A9

The numbers are scoped to their spec, so “D8” alone is ambiguous. The specs write 12-reconciliation.md D8, and so does this page. Where the reason for a single rule doesn’t fit a table, the spec carries a Why: or Invariant: note next to it. Settled open questions are kept, marked Settled, with the answer. Specs also record what they rejected, in “Settled questions” or “Why not” sections (for example 24-storage.md §12.1).

To change a decision:

  1. Open a pull request that edits the spec first: change the decision’s row (keep its number) or add a new row with the next free number, and give the reason. If a decision is replaced, say so in the row rather than deleting it silently.
  2. List the other specs the change touches. Larger designs do this in a section of their own (for example 14-clustering.md §16).
  3. Land the code in the PR of the milestone that changes the behaviour, and update the spec’s status table there.

Many past changes were reviewed this way: a “Spec: …” pull request, then one PR per milestone. See Contributing for the rest of the workflow.

The “Why” and “Alternatives considered” below come from the specs and from pull request descriptions. Where the project has not written a reason down, this page says so.

Platform

Rust, and one control-plane binary

Decision. Glidex is written in Rust. One binary, glidex-control-plane, runs on every host. It always runs the node role (VM, disk and image controllers, metering sampler, netd sync). On server hosts it also runs the server role (API, Raft, scheduler, cluster controllers, ledger). A standalone host runs both roles in one process (14-clustering.md D4). Small companion binaries exist only where a separate process is needed: the per-VM shim, the root helpers, glidex-ui and gxctl.

Why. The maintainers chose Rust for two reasons. Safety: memory and thread safety without a garbage collector, for a long-running service that holds root-adjacent privileges and talks to hypervisors, OVS and the store. AI-friendly code generation: much of Glidex is written with AI assistance, and Rust’s strict types and compiler checks catch generated mistakes at build time instead of in production. The specs also show a steady preference for pure-Rust dependencies over C ones. ReDB was “chosen over SQLite to avoid a C dependency” (03-data-model.md). Protobuf code is generated by protox so that cargo alone builds the workspace (G-D9). WebAuthn is checked in “pure Rust, no OpenSSL” (25-passkeys.md §7). Cloud Hypervisor, the default hypervisor, is also Rust. For one binary, the reason is recorded: the node role is the host-facing code, unchanged in substance, so a cluster adds the server role around it rather than a second program. README goal 4 asks for minimal host dependencies, and 14-clustering.md D1 adds “no new service to install, secure or upgrade”.

Alternatives considered. Separate binaries per role (an API server plus a node agent, as many orchestrators do). The specs don’t argue against this directly. D4’s reason is that the node role is the same code a standalone host already runs.

Consequences. Upgrades are one binary per host, and a standalone host carries no cluster cost (14-clustering.md D5). The binary is large and every host builds or receives all of it, including server-only code. Mixed versions during rolling upgrades are handled by versioned API packages (G-D7) and by write sets that replicate bytes, not logic (see below).

Hypervisors

Cloud Hypervisor and QEMU, with one feature set, driven directly

Decision. Glidex supports two hypervisors, Cloud Hypervisor (the default) and QEMU, behind one stateless driver trait (HypervisorDriver, 04-hypervisors.md). Callers see the same features on both (README goal 1). Glidex builds the hypervisor command line itself and talks to the hypervisor’s own API socket (Cloud Hypervisor’s HTTP API, QEMU’s QMP). There is no libvirt.

Why. Goal 1 of spec/README.md is “uniform microVM control across hypervisors … including VFIO PCI passthrough and interactive console I/O”. The parity work was done explicitly: PR #2 (“Bring QEMU to parity with Cloud Hypervisor”) gave QEMU tap and vhost-user NICs, UEFI boot of cloud images, the generated cloud-init seed and graceful stop, and added the qemu_* end-to-end tests. The driver is stateless (everything it needs is a socket path), so a restarted control plane manages a VM exactly as the one that launched it did. “Launch = configured” (12-reconciliation.md D9): both hypervisors get their whole configuration on the command line, so there is no half-configured instance and no crash window between “launched” and “booted”.

Libvirt was set aside for two reasons, in the maintainers’ words: it is XML-based (a domain definition format from older designs, which every feature would have to be expressed through), and it brings many external dependencies onto every host, against README goal 4 (minimal host dependencies). What the design needs from a VM runtime is also recorded, and it is specific: a supervisor per VM that owns the console PTY and the exit record (12-reconciliation.md D1), restart policy in one place (D6), and everything needed to adopt an instance persisted in its runtime directory (D7). Glidex runs alongside libvirt on the same host, and treats devices a libvirt-managed QEMU holds as not ready (22-host-topology.md §5, PR #133).

Alternatives considered.

  • Firecracker was considered first and supported early on, then removed (commit “Drop Firecracker support”) because it has no PCI passthrough, so no GPUs for VMs. It also has no UEFI firmware boot, which booting stock distro cloud images through EDK2 needs. It may come back later as the VMM of a lightweight, container-compatible layer, where its small footprint and fast start matter more than devices. Old Firecracker records are skipped at load, not treated as fatal (03-data-model.md).
  • One hypervisor only (Cloud Hypervisor). QEMU is kept because it can also emulate: run a VM of another architecture on a host, or run VMs on a host without KVM, in software (TCG). Cloud Hypervisor needs KVM and the host’s own architecture. This is the maintainers’ reason for keeping QEMU; emulation isn’t wired up yet. Today the QEMU driver runs qemu-system-x86_64 with -enable-kvm, and the scheduler places a VM only on nodes of its architecture.

Consequences. Every feature is built and tested twice. The specs are full of per-backend details: Cloud Hypervisor needs CAP_NET_ADMIN for taps (09-networking.md decision 9), QEMU needs a per-VM UEFI variable store, vCPU pinning differs (22-host-topology.md H9), and Cloud Hypervisor reports no usable disk latency (13-metering.md D17). Features that only one backend can offer have to wait or be refused. Revisit if one backend falls behind on a feature users need, or if maintaining parity starts to block features. A third driver, Pylon (30-pylon.md), is a Cloud Hypervisor fork for fast CPU core elasticity; its driver reuses Cloud Hypervisor’s command line and API client and adds its own flags and the host daemon pylond.

VM lifecycle

A shim per VM, in its own systemd unit

Decision. Each running VM is supervised by its own glidex-vm-shim. The shim is the hypervisor’s parent, owns the PTY master, the console socket and log, and records the exit (12-reconciliation.md D1). Under systemd the shim runs as glidex-vm@<vm-id>.service, started by the control plane over systemd’s D-Bus API (zbus) and allowed by a polkit rule (D2). systemd never restarts a VM (Restart=no); restart policy belongs to the VM controller (D6).

Why.

  • Whatever holds the PTY master and reaps the hypervisor must not be the control plane, or the guest dies, or loses console output, with it (D1). This makes “VMs survive control-plane restarts” (README goal 2) true: stopping, crashing or upgrading the control plane leaves guests running, and it adopts them on startup.
  • Only a separate unit escapes the control plane’s cgroup. A unit per VM gives per-VM accounting, journal and shutdown ordering (D2). Metering reads CPU and memory from that cgroup (13-metering.md D3).
  • Two supervisors with restart policies fight, and only the controller knows why a VM exited (D6).
  • D-Bus rather than systemctl, for typed errors and unit signals. Polkit rather than netd, so netd stays networking-only (D2).

Alternatives considered.

  • Hypervisors as children of the control plane, which is what Glidex did before PR #4. A control-plane restart killed or deafened every VM.
  • KillMode=process on the control plane’s unit: it leaves VMs in a cgroup systemd believes is stopped, without accounting (D2).
  • The same split exists elsewhere: containerd-shim and conmon (D1).

Consequences. The control plane never holds a process handle. It reaches a VM only through files and sockets in the VM’s runtime directory, and everything needed to talk to an instance is persisted (D7). Adoption after a restart is therefore the normal code path, not a recovery path. Before any launch the controller must positively establish that no instance is live, and reports Unknown when it can’t (D8). The price is one more process and one systemd unit per VM, a polkit rule the installer must install, and a second runner (a double-forked shim in its own session) for development and tests.

Desired state and level-triggered controllers

Decision. Every persisted resource is {meta, spec, status}. The API writes spec; only controllers write status (D3). Controllers are level-triggered, fed by a deduplicating work queue and a periodic resync (D4). Admission (validation, authorization, quotas, exclusive claims) stays synchronous; host actions are asynchronous and report in status (D5).

Why. “The user wants it running” survives “it isn’t running right now” (D3). Missed events are harmless, and the global lock that used to be held across hypervisor I/O is gone (D4). Invariants that protect data (exclusive disk use, quotas) must hold at commit time, not eventually (D5).

Alternatives considered. The earlier synchronous design, where a request did the host action under a global write lock (PR #4 describes the change).

Consequences. API writes answer 202 unless the caller passes ?wait. ?wait returns the same errors the synchronous calls used to return, so clients kept their behaviour (D20). Clients have to wait on Ready, which means “converged to the spec”, including for a VM that should be stopped (D13).

Privilege separation

An unprivileged control plane with small root helpers

Decision. The control plane runs as the unprivileged user glidex, under a tight systemd sandbox, and runs no hypervisor itself. Work that needs root goes to small helpers, each over a Unix socket with peer-credential checks and a per-operation allow-list:

HelperDoesSpec
glidex-netdOVS, bridges, uplinks, NAT, DHCP, VM ports, vfio-pci binding09-networking.md decision 1, 11-security.md §8
glidex-authdPAM password checks11-security.md decision 6, §5.3
glidex-stordLVM volumes and device access for VM units24-storage.md S12, S17, S18
polkit rulelets glidex start and stop glidex-vm@ units12-reconciliation.md D2

The web UI’s server, glidex-ui, runs as its own user with no authority of its own: it serves files and proxies /api (11-security.md decision 4). The guests’ metadata endpoint, glidex-metad, is the same kind of process: its own user, no key, parsing guests’ HTTP outside the control plane, which takes requests on metad.sock from that user alone (29-workload-identity.md W11).

Why.

  • netd is root “from the first milestone” (09-networking.md decision 1). The control plane is the policy point for users; netd only decides which local processes may ask it for what (11-security.md decision 2, §8), so netd doesn’t need Cedar.
  • PAM: a non-root process can’t check other users’ passwords with pam_unix. authd is separate from netd “so netd stays network-only” (11-security.md decision 6).
  • stord: creating and activating logical volumes needs root, and “the control plane must stay unprivileged”. Its allow-list of volume groups and its volume-name rule mean the control plane can make and remove Glidex’s own volumes and nothing else (24-storage.md S17).
  • Local callers are identified by SO_PEERCRED, never by claims in the request (11-security.md decision 5).

Alternatives considered. Running the control plane as root (the simplest option, and common for VM managers); one root helper for everything. The specs reject the second explicitly, each time keeping a helper to one job.

Consequences. Each helper is a protocol to version and a unit to install. Some things the control plane can’t do for itself: it can’t widen its own sandbox, which is why datastores must be mounted under one root, /srv/glidex (24-storage.md S11), and why per-VM CPU binding is done by the shim rather than by systemd drop-ins (22-host-topology.md H9). Cloud Hypervisor still needs cap_net_admin on its binary to bring taps up (09-networking.md decision 9). See Access control and Installation for what the installer sets up.

State and clustering

ReDB as the store

Decision. All control-plane state is in one ReDB file. Values are serde JSON.

Why. ReDB is an embedded, copy-on-write, ACID key-value store, “chosen over SQLite to avoid a C dependency and over sled for its simpler transactional model” (03-data-model.md). See the redb project.

Alternatives considered. SQLite and sled, as above. An external database is discussed in the next section.

Consequences. No SQL: queries are code over tables, and migrations are code with a schema version. Every write goes through one store API (Db/Tx), which records the write set; a lint in CI (scripts/lint-store-writes.sh) keeps it that way.

Embedded Raft (openraft), not etcd or an external database

Decision. In a cluster, the ReDB database is replicated by Raft embedded in the control plane, using the openraft crate, pinned to an exact version. The state machine is the existing ReDB database (14-clustering.md D1). The store and its Raft integration are the glidex-raftstore crate.

Why. “No new service to install, secure or upgrade.” Every table, migration and test keeps working on ReDB (D1). Losing a minority of servers doesn’t stop management, and VMs keep running through any control-plane outage anyway (14-clustering.md §2).

Alternatives considered (from D1):

OptionWhy not
etcdA separate daemon, value-size and per-transaction operation limits, and a rewrite of every table access
dqlite (Incus’s choice)C, and a move to SQL
An external database such as PostgreSQLNot discussed directly; it falls under the “no new external database” goal (14-clustering.md §2)

Consequences. Glidex owns its consensus code paths: snapshots, membership changes, and a voter that lost its state must never rejoin as the same voter (D18). The replicated store holds metering history, about 12 MB per VM, on every server; that sets the ceiling of roughly 5,000 VMs (§4.1). Past it, the plan is to move metering history out of the replicated store first. openraft is pre-1.0 and is upgraded deliberately. A write holds the one write lane across its Raft round trip, and that round trip needs the async runtime’s I/O. So synchronous code must never block a Tokio worker on the lane, on another lock held across a store write, or on a slow helper call: two control planes hung that way (PRs #221, #227, #228). Such waits go through glidex_raftstore::wait, which waits in block_in_place.

Leader-computed write sets

Decision. A write runs once, on the leader, against its applied state. The result, an ordered list of put/delete operations on table keys, is the Raft log entry. Applying an entry is a pure byte operation (D2). Writes go through one lane on the leader: a write’s closure runs only after the previous write is applied locally (D3).

Why. Admission, quotas and claims need serialized read-then-write logic. Replicating commands would need identical logic, clocks and UUID generation on every replica and every version, which breaks under rolling upgrades. Byte write sets are deterministic by construction and version-independent (D2). With one lane, the closure reads exactly the state its write set will apply to, so no conflict detection is needed; control-plane write rates of tens per second fit in a LAN round trip (D3).

Alternatives considered. Command replication (above). Optimistic concurrency with conflict detection, which the single lane makes unnecessary.

Consequences. Throughput is bounded by one lane: about 150–300 writes per second (§4.1). Status is written only when it changes, or a resync round alone would flood the log. Pipelining the lane is listed as later work (§18). See Algorithms for how the lane works.

Standalone stays non-Raft

Decision. A single host keeps writing ReDB directly. The store has two modes behind one API, local and replicated, and both take the same write sets. gxctl cluster init switches a host to replicated with one voter (D5).

Why. Existing single-host users carry no Raft cost and no risk until they opt in, and the code paths stay common (D5).

Consequences. Both modes must stay tested. Joining a cluster is an explicit, backed-up step (14-clustering.md §5.1), not a default.

Servers and agents

Decision. A cluster has 1, 3 or 5 server hosts (Raft voters, API, cluster controllers) and any number of agent hosts (node role only) (14-clustering.md §2). Agents serve no API: an agent’s web UI redirects browsers to a server (28-host-page.md W5). Node liveness is held in the leader’s memory; only transitions go through Raft (D7). There is no automatic failover of VMs (D8), and placement is sticky (D6).

Why.

  • Raft needs an odd, small voter set; the rest of the hosts only run VMs.
  • Root on a server already holds the whole database; root on an agent holds only its own VMs and must not escalate to the cluster, so break-glass access is honoured on servers only (D14).
  • A heartbeat per node every 5 s through Raft would be pure log churn (D7).
  • A partitioned node may still be running its VMs. Starting copies elsewhere would put two writers on one disk (D8), and “at most one instance per VM, ever” (12-reconciliation.md D8) comes first.
  • One origin for the browser: SSO, passkeys and cookies work (28-host-page.md W5).

Alternatives considered. Automatic restart of a lost host’s VMs elsewhere, rejected without fencing (14-clustering.md §2, D8).

Consequences. When a host dies, its VMs are Unknown until an operator acts. A VM whose disks are all on shared datastores can then be placed again after node forget --fenced (24-storage.md S10). Fencing and automatic evacuation are later work (§18). See Clusters.

API

One service layer under REST and RPC

Decision. Every operation is a transport-neutral service function. REST and RPC adapters only decode, call it and encode (18-grpc.md G-D1). RPCs are served on the same listeners and port as REST (G-D2). REST/JSON stays permanently, for curl, scripts and HTTP-only protocols (OIDC callbacks, SCIM, the console WebSocket) (18-grpc.md §1).

Why. Authorization, quota and audit are written once. “Two copies of a Cedar check is exactly the kind of drift that becomes a cross-tenant bug” (G-D1). One port means no new firewall rule or certificate name, and the existing TLS, pinning and peer-uid identification are reused (G-D2). The RPC side gives typed contracts, generated clients, a compatibility check in CI, and server streaming for watch (18-grpc.md §1).

Alternatives considered. Hand-written REST types mirrored by hand in gxctl, which is what Glidex had before (18-grpc.md §1). gRPC as a replacement for REST, rejected: REST stays.

Consequences. Every operation declares whether it reads or writes, because every RPC is a POST and cluster forwarding must still tell reads from writes (G-D6). See API overview.

Proto as the source of truth

Decision. Every API type is defined in protobuf, in the glidex-api crate. REST JSON is the proto3 JSON form of the same messages (G-D3), with field names in snake_case (G-D11). Packages are versioned, glidex.<area>.v1 (G-D7). buf lints, checks breaking changes and generates TypeScript; Rust code is generated in build.rs from a descriptor set made by protox (G-D9).

Why. Two type systems for one API drift apart; one definition serves REST, gRPC, gxctl and the UI (G-D3). proto3 JSON defaults to lowerCamelCase, and the REST API is snake_case; declaring the name in the proto keeps every generator on the same names (G-D11). Contributors and packaging build with cargo alone, with no protoc or buf (G-D9). Rolling upgrades run mixed versions, so field numbers and names are the compatibility contract (G-D7).

Alternatives considered. Rewriting descriptors at build time to fix JSON names (rejected in G-D11). A transition release carrying both REST shapes, waived because no release had shipped the proto shapes yet (G-D12).

Consequences. Porting a family of endpoints changed its REST shape once (G5). build.rs refuses an RPC without its operation option, a JSON name that isn’t the field name, or a secret field that can reach a response.

connectrpc rather than tonic

Decision. The RPC runtime is connectrpc for Rust, with buffa messages, pinned to an exact pre-1.0 version (G-D10). One tower service answers Connect, gRPC and gRPC-Web.

Why. It replaces tonic, tonic-web, tonic-health, prost and pbjson with one stack from the Connect project, the same protocol family as the browser client. Its messages carry their own proto3 JSON, which REST needs. It passes the ConnectRPC conformance suite (G-D10).

Alternatives considered. tonic with its companions, above.

Consequences. A pre-1.0 API that may still move; it is upgraded deliberately, like openraft (G-D10).

Connect-ES and gRPC-Web in the browser

Decision. The web UI uses Connect-ES (@connectrpc/connect-web) with a gRPC-Web transport and TypeScript generated by protoc-gen-es (G-D8). Session cookies are accepted only for gRPC-Web from glidex-ui on its socket (G-D4).

Why. gRPC-Web works over HTTP/1.1 without HTTP/2 trailers, so glidex-ui keeps proxying /api unchanged. The UI gets typed clients from the same protos as gxctl, and server streaming for watch (G-D8). Keeping cookies on the one browser path keeps CSRF and Origin rules where browsers are (G-D4).

Consequences. A few calls stay REST in the UI: login and logout, whoami (which provides the CSRF value), OIDC redirects, CSV exports and the console WebSocket (PR #41).

Authorization

Cedar

Decision. Authorization is Cedar policy, evaluated in process with the cedar-policy crate (11-security.md decision 9, §7). Roles are template-linked policies; invariants are forbid policies; every policy is validated against a schema. Every route maps to one Cedar action, and a route without one fails a test (decision 7). Operators add site policies through the API (decision 10).

Why (11-security.md §7):

  • roles, project scoping, grants and host-wide rules are policies instead of if chains spread over handlers;
  • strict validation against a schema: a typo in a policy fails startup instead of quietly allowing or denying;
  • forbid always overrides permit, so invariants such as step-up and same-project-only can’t be overridden by any role or site policy;
  • sites add rules without code changes;
  • every decision names the policies that produced it, which goes into the audit log.

What stays in code: authentication, quotas (they need counts), path canonicalization and netd’s peer check.

Alternatives considered. Not compared in the spec. The two usual alternatives are role tables in the database (RBAC), which can’t express the forbid invariants or site rules without code, and an external policy service such as OPA, which would be another service to run; 11-security.md says “there is no separate policy service”.

Consequences. Contributors change the schema and policies (crates/glidex-control-plane/policies/) along with handlers. Tenants can’t author Cedar; site policies belong to operators and directory owners (19-tenancy.md D28), because tenant-authored policies would need per-tenant validation scopes and lock-out rules. See Access control.

A shared authentication crate and UI kit

Decision. The parts of authentication that aren’t Glidex-specific live in their own crate, glidex-auth: secrets, session and token rules, the Cedar engine (generic over a Model that supplies the schema, policies, entity types and break-glass rule) and OIDC login. The control plane specializes them in auth/, authz.rs and directory/oidc.rs. The web UI’s login and session pieces live in @glidex/ui-kit (crates/glidex-ui/kit), which talks to the app through an AuthApi adapter.

Why. Other management services reuse the same sign-in, session, token and policy rules instead of reimplementing them, so a fix lands once.

Consequences. The crate and the kit must not depend on Glidex’s own records or api.ts; Glidex-only pieces (stored users, directories, passkeys, capability checks) stay in the control plane and the UI.

Tenancy and directories

Decision. A tenant is an organization’s account. Every project, VM, disk, network and credential belongs to exactly one tenant (19-tenancy.md D1). Each tenant is in exactly one directory, which holds its users, teams and connectors to the organization’s own identity provider (D2). Operator tenants operate clusters; only their members pass host-scoped actions, enforced by a forbid (D4). A cluster trusts a directory only after a pairwise handshake (D8), keeps a read-only replica of what the directory sends it (D12), and accepts only tokens addressed to it (D11, §7.3).

Why (19-tenancy.md):

  • Organizations keep their own identity and records; nothing about one is stored in another’s directory (D2).
  • Single sign-on is something organizations choose by sharing a directory, not something Glidex arranges across them (D3).
  • Independent organizations each decide whom they trust; adding a cluster or a directory touches only the pairs involved (D8).
  • Organizations and datacenters fail and partition independently; a cluster, compromised or not, can’t write a directory on anyone’s behalf (D12).
  • A cluster can’t replay a credential it received to another cluster or directory (§7.3).

Alternatives considered.

  • A global registry or shared store across clusters: rejected in favour of pairwise trust and feeds (“no Raft across clusters or directories”, D12). Fleets broker trust at scale without becoming a shared store (D33).
  • SAML connectors: rejected. Every listed IdP offers OIDC, and XML signature verification is a long-running source of bypasses (D30).
  • A built-in identity provider is a non-goal at the host level (spec README); a directory is an OIDC provider for its own users, which log in through their organization’s IdP.

Consequences. A cluster cut off from a directory keeps running workloads and serving credentials it can verify, and stops accepting that directory’s credentials after max_staleness (D13): an operator-chosen balance between availability and revocation. The model is large (over seventy decisions); the implemented parts are tracked in 19-tenancy.md §23.

Workload federation

Decision. A tenant can trust an external JWT issuer (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, any OIDC workload issuer) and map matching tokens to a service account; POST /auth/exchange returns a short-lived token acting as that service account (D26, D48–D51). Rules match exact claim values only and must name a repository, project path or subject (D50).

Why. CI uses the identity it already has (D26). Rights stay in one place, the service account’s role links, and a leaked exchanged token is short-lived and tied to one job (D48).

Alternatives considered. Long-lived API tokens stored as CI secrets, which is what federation replaces.

Consequences. Exchanged tokens last at most an hour and can’t be renewed. Identity for Glidex’s own VMs (a metadata endpoint and SPIFFE IDs) is a separate spec, 29-workload-identity.md, built in part: identity tokens, VMs’ service accounts and the endpoint on node NAT networks (glidex-metad); the other network kinds, vsock and agents are not built yet. See Workload federation.

Networking

Open vSwitch, driven through netd

Decision. VM networking is Open vSwitch. The control plane asks glidex-netd (root) for bridges, uplinks, NAT and VM ports. Glidex can install OVS from distro packages by profile (09-networking.md decision 6), or from a pinned source build when the distro lacks features (decision 10). Addressing is DHCP plus NAT through the host’s existing route (decision 4).

Why. OVS covers every port type Glidex uses under one model: tap and vhost-user VM ports, and kernel, AF_XDP and DPDK uplinks (09-networking.md §2; 14-clustering.md D15). It is also the base OVN needs for clusters. Its bridge-port counters are the one metering source that covers every port type, since vhost-user ports have no kernel network device (13-metering.md D5).

Alternatives considered. Linux bridges on a single host. They are simpler and in every kernel, but the maintainers chose OVS everywhere for one configuration model for a single host and a cluster: the same bridges, ports and counters on a standalone host as on a cluster node, so a host joins a cluster (and OVN) without its networking being redone. Linux bridges also have no userspace datapath for vhost-user or DPDK and no path to OVN.

Consequences. OVS is a large host dependency, and an OVS upgrade restarts ovs-vswitchd and interrupts VM traffic, so the installer leaves OVS upgrades to the distro (05-installer.md). Static guest addressing and persistent host network changes are non-goals. See Host networking.

OVN for cluster networks

Decision. Networks that span hosts use OVN on the OVS each host already runs. The leader’s network controller writes the OVN northbound database; netd only joins the host to OVN and plugs VM ports (14-clustering.md D9). Node-scoped OVS networks remain (D10). IPAM belongs to the control plane, not to OVN (D12). NAT egress is centralized on high-availability gateway chassis (D11).

Why. OVN provides the overlay, logical switches and routers, DHCP, SNAT gateway HA, port security and, later, multi-chassis port binding for live migration. The northbound database is reached over TLS, so the unprivileged control plane can write it while netd keeps everything privileged (D9). Centralized SNAT needs one external IP per router instead of one per VM, and is OVN’s standard HA gateway pattern (D11). One IPAM source of truth survives restarts and serves port security (D12).

Alternatives considered.

  • An eBPF datapath: rejected (D15). It would cover tap only, so Glidex would maintain two datapaths, with no migration or performance gain for tap VMs.
  • Distributed SNAT: needs an external IP per VM (D11).
  • OVN’s dynamic addressing: not used (D12).
  • Converting node networks to cluster networks: out of scope, because it means renumbering running VMs (D10).

Consequences. Two Raft groups run on the servers, Glidex’s and OVSDB’s, kept separate on purpose (14-clustering.md §4). External traffic on OVN is metered from conntrack accounting in each router’s SNAT zone, because OVN exposes no counters on logical objects (D22). Routed networks, floating IPs and security groups are later work (§18).

Storage

Datastores behind a CSI-shaped driver trait

Decision. A datastore is a cluster-scoped record naming where disks and images live (24-storage.md S2). A driver creates, sizes, deletes and opens volumes in it, and a topology says which nodes reach it (S4). The drivers are dir (node-local; the built-in local datastore), shared-dir (a filesystem the operator mounts on every node: NFS, CephFS, GPFS…), lvm (node-local LVM-thin) and hyperstor (a pool of a hyperstor cluster, served to VMs over vhost-user-blk; §11.2). Glidex’s driver trait, StorageDriver, follows CSI’s split between controller and node operations and its topology and capability model, but Glidex does not host CSI plugins yet (S1).

Why.

  • Nearly every vendor and open-source system offers an NFS or POSIX mount. A mount keeps qcow2 and its features (linked clones, sparse files, resize and shrink) and needs no root, because the mount is done outside Glidex (S1).
  • The existing directories become local with no file moves; nobody sees a change until an operator adds a datastore (S3).
  • New disks stay on local by default: it is the fastest store, and choosing shared storage is the operator’s call (S13).
  • LVM-thin gives the same thin, overcommitted, fast-clone behaviour as qcow2 files, on the devices a site gives VMs (S19).

Alternatives considered.

  • CSI as the first interface, rejected for now (S1, §12.1). Many plugins assume Kubernetes sidecars and objects (Secrets, CRDs, node labels); node plugins run as root, usually in privileged containers; VMs need CSI’s Block mode, which gives up qcow2; each plugin is another per-node service with its own release cycle; and nobody has asked for a particular plugin. The trait keeps the door open: a CSI adapter is milestone S7, gated on a real need (§12.3).
  • Ceph built in. Not discussed as such. Ceph is reachable as CephFS through shared-dir, and an rbd driver is planned after lvm (S19). Running a storage cluster is outside what Glidex installs: “glidex never mounts” shared filesystems (S1), and README goal 4 asks for minimal host dependencies.

Consequences. Moving a VM is explicit and offline, and needs every disk on a shared datastore (S10). Exactly one node acts on a volume’s files at a time, its worker (S6), and Glidex takes its own lock file on shared volumes, because placement alone can’t stop a partitioned node that kept running (S16). Mount points must live under /srv/glidex (S11). Block volumes are raw, grow and never shrink (S19). Live migration, snapshots and per-datastore quotas are out of scope for now. See Datastores.

Images

A catalog of checksum-verified cloud images, and linked disks

Decision. POST /images {"catalog": …} downloads a distro cloud image and verifies it against the checksum file the vendor publishes next to it, fetched over HTTPS (10-images.md §4). Firmware is different: its digest is pinned. A VM’s root disk is usually linked, a qcow2 overlay whose backing file is the image. Files are named only by id.

Why.

  • Cloud images are rebuilt weekly with security fixes, so pinning their digests would ship stale, vulnerable guests; a “current” image plus the vendor’s published checksum avoids that (10-images.md §4). One tested firmware build is what guests should boot, so firmware is pinned (§4.1).
  • Debian’s OVMF build is used because upstream EDK2 publishes no prebuilt OVMF and nightly builds can’t be pinned (§4.1).
  • Files named by id: renaming a record never touches the file, and a name can’t escape the directory (§2).
  • Orphan files and missing files are reported, never deleted: Glidex never destroys data because it guessed wrong (§2).
  • Everything runs as the control-plane user; no step needs root (goal 4).
  • On datastores, an overlay names its backing file by a relative path, because nodes may mount a datastore at different paths (24-storage.md S8).

Alternatives considered. Pinned digests for cloud images (above). Full copies instead of overlays remain available (clone: full).

Consequences. An image can’t be deleted while a linked disk uses it (10-images.md §3). A linked disk needs its image copy in the same datastore (S8). Disk snapshots, image building and non-cloud images (installer ISOs) are non-goals. See Images and disks.

Kernel extraction inside a VM

Decision. To boot a cloud image’s own kernel directly, Glidex reads the image’s filesystems inside a short-lived VM, never on the host. It boots a pinned extractor kernel and initramfs with the image attached read-only and no network; the extractor writes the boot files to a raw disk in a simple stream format that the host parses with strict limits (23-kernel-boot.md K9).

Why. No new host packages, no root, no loop devices, and the host never parses an untrusted filesystem (K9). A disk image, especially from a URL or a VM’s own disk, may hold a filesystem crafted to attack its parser; inside the extractor, the worst outcome is a failed extraction (§8). Extracting from the image also guarantees that the kernel matches the image’s modules (K3).

Alternatives considered (23-kernel-boot.md §9):

OptionWhy not
Host tools per filesystem (debugfs, btrfs restore)Parse untrusted filesystems on the host; nothing for XFS
libguestfsAlso uses a VM, but adds a large host dependency whose appliance needs a readable host kernel
Downloading distro kernel packagesNo initrd

Consequences. Extraction costs a VM boot per image, on a node of the image’s architecture. Firmware boot stays the default; kernel boot as the default is to be revisited “once boot-time numbers exist” (K2). See Kernel boot.

A generated cloud-init seed

Decision. Before each launch, the VM controller builds a NoCloud seed, a FAT volume labelled CIDATA, with mkdosfs and mcopy (cloud_init.rs). A VM gets a login only if it names a stored credential; there are no host-wide default keys or passwords (08-credentials.md).

Why. Distro cloud images ship with no usable login and wait for cloud-init. mkdosfs/mcopy build the volume without root or loop mounts, the same approach as Cloud Hypervisor’s own script. One host-wide key or password would open VMs in every project (11-security.md §6.2).

Consequences. The seed holds a password hash and is created 0600. cloud-init provisions users once per instance id, so changing a credential later doesn’t change an already-provisioned guest. See Guest credentials.

Devices and topology

PCI passthrough, device pools and NUMA

Decision.

  • A device is identified per node, (node, address); VFIO claims are per node and by IOMMU group (22-host-topology.md H3).
  • Each node reads its topology from sysfs, with no new dependency (H1). A small summary goes in replicated node status for the scheduler; the full PCIe tree stays on the node (H2).
  • Users request devices by class from pools the operator defines, not by raw PCI class codes; pools are what tenants are granted (H10, H11, H17).
  • VMs choose a NUMA policy (none, preferred, strict, and aligned for multi-GPU VMs) and a CPU policy (shared or dedicated) (H5, H6, 27-gpu-vms.md G2).
  • The scheduler, not the node, picks exact CPUs (H8). Hugepages are a resource of their own, never overcommitted (H19).
  • Glidex can bind a device to vfio-pci through netd, but never changes the kernel command line or firmware (H12).

Why. The scheduler needs topology on the leader, but the full tree is only for display, so Raft state stays small (H2). Address-wide claims broke once there were several nodes (H3). Pools let operators name devices by vendor, model or label and grant them, instead of every user knowing addresses (H10). One writer for CPU sets means two VMs can’t take the same CPU (H8). aligned is the only layout that keeps every GPU local once a VM outgrows one NUMA node, and a guest topology that mirrors the host makes nvidia-smi topo and NCCL see the real layout (G2, G3).

Alternatives considered. hwloc or lspci for discovery (rejected for a dependency-free sysfs reader, H1). systemd drop-ins for CPU binding (dropped: the unprivileged control plane can’t write them, H9). Guessing a device’s NUMA node from its bus number (rejected, H4). Running NVIDIA Fabric Manager on the host for NVLink (an option, not the default; a service VM keeps the driver off the host kernel, G6).

Consequences. Kernel parameters (IOMMU, hugepages) remain the operator’s job. Device health is reported, not used to refuse devices (H18). See PCI passthrough and Host resources.

Console

Decision. Each VM has one console (a serial port or virtio console on a PTY). The shim owns the PTY master, writes console.log, and serves any number of clients on a console socket. A new client first gets the current log replayed, then live output (02-console.md). Logs are appended across restarts and rotated once at 16 MiB (12-reconciliation.md D14).

Why.

  • Output the hypervisor wrote stays readable on the master after the hypervisor exits. When Cloud Hypervisor owned the master, its hangup on exit threw away unread output, so a guest’s last line (“reboot: Power down”) was routinely lost. Owning the master also captures firmware output from before boot completes (02-console.md, “Why the shim owns the master”).
  • The shim, not the control plane, because whoever holds the master decides when the guest’s terminal hangs up; while the control plane held it, a restart killed or deafened every VM.
  • Replay gives late-joining browsers the boot output (README goal 3).
  • Appending keeps the output from before a crash after the crash-restart (D14).

Alternatives considered. The hypervisor’s own PTY mode (above). A console held by the control plane (the design before PR #4).

Consequences. The browser reaches the console through a WebSocket with a single-use ticket, gxctl through a bidirectional RPC. In a cluster the ticket is kept in the leader’s memory, not replicated, so a load balancer with no affinity works, and a leader change drops tickets not yet used (11-security.md decision 21). The browser terminal is ghostty-web by default, with xterm.js as a choice, because ghostty-web renders to a canvas that screen readers can’t read (PR #50). See Console.

Metering

Decision. The meter runs inside the control plane (13-metering.md D1). It samples cumulative counters and stores deltas (D2), into an hourly, UTC ledger that is immutable once closed, with a per-source cursor written in the same transaction as the deltas it produced (D8). Sources: the VM unit’s cgroup for CPU and memory (D3), the hypervisor for disk operations (D4), OVS port counters for traffic (D5). Bandwidth and disk I/O also get a 5-minute 95th percentile per billing month (D15, D16).

Why.

  • The control plane already knows every VM, disk and NIC and holds the database; a separate daemon would duplicate adoption logic. Counters are cumulative, so downtime loses no data (D1, D2).
  • Without the cursor in the same transaction, a crash between “record delta” and “advance cursor” would count a delta twice or never (D8).
  • The shim writes a final counter snapshot when the hypervisor exits, because the cgroup and counters vanish with the unit (D12).
  • 5-minute p95 on the larger direction is the industry convention for burstable billing, so customers can check figures with their own tools. Group figures are the p95 of the summed series, because summing p95s over-bills (D15). Disk I/O uses read+write combined, because reads and writes share one queue (D16).
  • No disk latency for Cloud Hypervisor VMs, because its latency fields can’t give a correct average for any period, and a wrong figure is worse than none (D17).

Alternatives considered. A separate metering daemon (D1). Rates computed upstream (D2). OVS flow statistics or eBPF for external traffic (rejected for conntrack accounting, 14-clustering.md D15, D22).

Consequences. Metering history lives in the replicated store and is its largest table, about 12 MB per VM (14-clustering.md §4.1); moving it out is the first step past the scale ceiling. Usage outlives the VM and keeps the project and name from when it was sampled (D13). See Usage and Algorithms.

TLS and sign-in

Self-signed by default, pinned by fingerprint

Decision. The control plane (port 8841) and the web UI (port 5173) serve HTTPS on every address by default, with a self-signed ECDSA P-256 certificate unless one is configured (PR #7). gxctl trusts a self-signed control plane by pinning the leaf certificate’s SHA-256, trusted on first use at gxctl auth login (11-security.md decision 18, 17-gxctl-auth.md A4). A verify-nothing mode exists only as an explicitly confirmed, per-profile, loudly marked escape hatch (A5).

Why. A fresh host has no name a public CA would sign, but its API still must not be plain HTTP on the network. Pinning keeps signature, date and name checks running against the pinned certificate, instead of skipping verification (A4). A profile records the cluster id, and a server reporting another id is a hard error (A6). The certificate is reused until near expiry so the fingerprint stays stable (PR #7).

Alternatives considered. Plain HTTP on loopback, the earlier default (replaced in PR #7). A “skip verification” flag as the normal way to reach a self-signed server (rejected, A4, A5). Running a private CA for every standalone host (not discussed; clusters do have their own CA, 14-clustering.md D20).

Consequences. Browsers show a warning for the self-signed certificate, and HSTS is sent only with a configured certificate, because it would make that warning impossible to bypass (PR #7). See TLS.

Tailscale certificates for the web UI

Decision. On a host on a tailnet, glidex-ui may serve the node’s Tailscale (Let’s Encrypt) certificate for its ts.net names, fetched from the host’s tailscaled and chosen by SNI; every other name keeps the usual certificate (21-tailscale-tls.md T1–T3). It is opt-in (T4). The control plane keeps its own certificate (T8).

Why. Browser-trusted HTTPS with no certificate management. Opt-in because the node’s name is published in Certificate Transparency logs (T4). A Tailscale failure never fails a handshake; ts.net names fall back to the default certificate (T5).

Alternatives considered. Embedding Tailscale’s Rust library, tailscale-rs: it doesn’t issue certificates yet and is a later phase (T1).

Consequences. The installer must grant glidex-ui access through tailscaled’s TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID, and refuses when another user already holds it (T6).

Passkeys

Decision. Users of a local directory can sign in with WebAuthn passkeys. Credentials are discoverable, user verification is required, and a passkey sign-in counts as multi-factor (25-passkeys.md P3). No attestation is trusted (P1). Only the user adds its own passkeys, and a user can’t be left with a single passkey as its only sign-in (P4). The checks are implemented in Glidex (auth/webauthn.rs, pure Rust).

Why. No account names to type or enumerate; with verification, a passkey is possession plus a factor (P3). Trusting attestation would need an allow-list of authenticator makers that nobody asked for (P1). Losing one device must not lock a person out, and nobody can plant a passkey on another person’s account (P4). Passkeys belong to a configurable relying-party id so that passkeys made on one name of the UI work on its others and on other servers (P2).

Alternatives considered. Trusting attestation (P1).

Consequences. The ceremonies are HTTP-only, like OIDC callbacks, because WebAuthn is a browser protocol (P6). gxctl keeps its own logins. See Authentication.

Web UI

Decision. The UI is a Vite + React + TypeScript single-page app, managed with Bun (bun.lock). A small Rust binary, glidex-ui, serves the built files over HTTPS and proxies /api to the control plane; glidex-ui --dev runs the Vite dev server instead (07-web-ui.md).

Why. glidex-ui is a proxy with no authority of its own; the control plane authenticates and authorizes every request (11-security.md decision 4). Running it as its own user means a UI compromise can’t reach what the control plane can (11-security.md §4). Proxying keeps the browser on one origin, which cookies, CSRF checks, SSO and passkeys rely on. React, Vite and Bun were chosen for speed and ecosystem: Vite and Bun for fast builds, dev-server reloads and dependency installs; React for its ecosystem of components and libraries, and its TypeScript support, which the generated Connect-ES types build on.

Alternatives considered. Serving the UI from the control plane itself; not discussed in the specs.

Consequences. Building the UI needs Bun and the JavaScript dependencies; the installer installs a pinned Bun and verifies it. Generated Connect-ES code is committed, and CI fails if it is stale.

Installer

Decision. Glidex is installed from a source checkout with cargo run -p glidex-install. The installer is one linear, non-interactive and convergent program: each run detects what is missing or outdated and fixes just that, so the same command installs Glidex and later keeps it up to date (05-installer.md). It installs system dependencies through the host’s package manager (apt, dnf/yum or pacman). --prebuilt uses binaries already built in the checkout.

Why. README goal 4: minimal host dependencies and one command that stands the system up. Keeping all “check and fix” logic in one place lets the other crates assume their dependencies are present (05-installer.md “Philosophy”). Downloads are pinned and verified: the firmware and Cloud Hypervisor by sha256, and Rust and Bun at pinned versions with their published checksums (11-security.md §9).

Alternatives considered. Distro packages (.deb, .rpm) and prebuilt binaries. Installing from source is a stage, not a final choice: Glidex is under active development, so hosts follow main. Prebuilt binaries and distro packages are planned once it stabilizes. Much of what the installer does is host configuration that a package would also have to script: users and groups, units and the polkit rule, file capabilities, the OVS profile, hugepages and boot-time VFIO bindings.

Consequences. Each host needs a Rust toolchain and a build, unless --prebuilt is used. OVS upgrades are left to the distro, because they interrupt VM traffic. The installer never touches the firewall. See Installation.

Algorithms

This page explains how the non-trivial parts of Glidex work, as the code implements them. Each section covers the problem, the inputs and outputs, the steps, the invariants, where the code lives, and the tests that pin it. Section numbers in links point into the design specs, which hold the reasoning. Where a spec and this page disagree, the code is what this page describes.

For how the pieces fit together, see Architecture. For why they were built this way, see Design decisions and trade-offs.

Paths are relative to crates/glidex-control-plane/src/ unless another crate is named.

  • Scheduler

Scheduler

Problem. Choose the node a VM runs on. The choice includes the node’s NUMA node, dedicated CPUs, hugepage size and pool devices. A VM is placed once and stays where it is placed (spec decision D6). Nothing moves it automatically afterwards.

Inputs.

  • A Request: vCPUs, memory, hypervisor, architecture, hugepages, NUMA and CPU policy, pin, disks and the nodes they are bound to, datastore reachability, networks, physnets, VFIO devices, pool requests, and the cluster’s ovn-northd version.
  • Every node, with the Load already placed on it. A placed VM counts whether it is running or not.

Output. A Choice (node, page_kib, NUMA node or NUMA shares, CPUs, pool devices), or a list of why each node refused.

Load. loads() folds every placed VM into a per-node Load:

  • vCPUs;
  • ordinary memory and hugepage memory, kept apart and keyed by page size;
  • memory bound to each NUMA node;
  • dedicated CPUs held;
  • claimed PCI devices (address → VM name).

Claims are not stored separately. They are recomputed from placements each time.

Filters. failing() checks one node, in this order. The first failure is the node’s reason.

pin matches (id or name)
phase Active, not draining (unschedulable), Ready=True
shared vCPUs + req.vcpus <= (allocatable cpus - held dedicated) * cpu_overcommit
page size: page_kib()            # explicit hugepages must fit; vhost-user may get 2M pages
ordinary memory <= allocatable * memory_overcommit   # hugepage RAM not counted here
hypervisor installed
architecture matches (empty on either side matches)
every physnet mapped on the node
ovn-controller major.minor >= cluster ovn-northd       # cluster networks only
br-int on the netdev datapath                          # vhost-user NIC on a cluster network
each VFIO device: present, not cordoned, not taken (address or IOMMU group)
devices granted to the project on this node
node-local disks unbound or bound here
every datastore of an unbound disk reachable from here
node-scoped networks are on this node
place_on(): pool devices, then NUMA fit
memory recheck if implicit hugepages fell back to ordinary memory
dedicated CPUs leave enough shared capacity

allocatable is the node’s capacity minus a reserve (1 CPU and 2048 MiB by default) minus the hugepage pool (node.rs). The overcommit defaults are cpu_overcommit = 4.0 and memory_overcommit = 1.0. Hugepages are never overcommitted (cluster/config.rs, SchedulerConfig).

Device claims. device_taken() refuses a device in two cases: it is claimed, or another device in its IOMMU group is claimed. Devices in one group cannot be split between VMs. A node that reports no groups is checked by address only.

Hugepages. page_kib() works as follows:

  • Asked-for hugepages: the node’s default size, or the requested size. The memory must be a whole number of pages, and taken + mem <= capacity.
  • A vhost-user NIC without hugepages asked for: 2 MiB pages, if spare pages cover the memory plus max(memory/4, 256 MiB). Otherwise ordinary memory.

NUMA fit. numa_fit() applies after the filters:

  • Dedicated CPUs without a NUMA policy imply preferred.
  • aligned without devices behaves as preferred.
  • No policy and shared CPUs: no NUMA work is done.
candidates = NUMA nodes (strict: only those holding the VM's devices)
order candidates by (devices held desc, usage after placing asc, id)
for k in candidates:
    fit_on_numa(k)    # memory or hugepages on k; dedicated CPUs from k
take the best fit
none fits: strict -> refuse; preferred -> whole host, NumaAligned=False
  • fit_on_numa() charges each NUMA node its bound load. Load not bound to a NUMA node is spread over the NUMA nodes by their share of memory (or of pages).
  • pick_cpus() takes isolated cores first, then cores by id. It takes whole SMT cores unless dedicated_whole_cores is off.
  • The first core of each NUMA node is kept for the host unless the operator lists reserved CPUs (reserved_cpus()).

Aligned (GPU) placement. aligned_fit() uses exactly the NUMA nodes that hold the VM’s devices. It splits vCPUs and memory between them in proportion to their device counts, using the largest-remainder method (split_by()). Each share must fit its NUMA node, and every share must use the same page size.

Pools. pick_pool_devices() chooses devices for pool requests:

  • Candidates are ready, not cordoned and not taken.
  • It prefers devices on the NUMA node of the VM’s other devices, then goes by address.
  • Under aligned, it uses as few NUMA nodes as it can.
  • With same_switch, all devices come from one PCIe switch, preferring a switch the VM already uses.

A gpus request is expanded before scheduling, in service/vm.rs expand_gpus() and apply_gpus():

  • It becomes a pool request.
  • The NUMA policy defaults to aligned.
  • vCPUs and memory default to the pool’s per_device sizing × count.

Score. evaluate() scores each node that fits:

score = max(cpu share, memory share, hugepage share)   # after placing the VM
order: fits first; then score asc; then fewest VMs; then node name

The result is deterministic. schedule() returns the first node in that order. explain() joins the refusals, capped at 8 nodes plus “and N more”. The preview endpoint (POST /scheduler/preview) returns the full evaluate() list.

Where it runs.

  • At VM create, under the write lock on the VM map (state.rs, pick_node()).
  • Again for VMs created without a placement: the leader runs place_pending() (controller/placement.rs) every 3 s.
  • The placement, the disk bindings and the IPAM reservations are recorded in one store commit.
  • A standalone host runs the same place_on() against itself.
  • A change to a placed VM re-fits it on its own node (refit_placement()). What no longer fits is refused with 409.

Code. scheduler.rs: schedule, evaluate, failing, place_on, numa_fit, aligned_fit, pick_pool_devices, page_kib, device_taken, loads.

Tests. In scheduler.rs:

  • the_least_allocated_node_wins_and_ties_break_by_count_then_name
  • capacity_counts_stopped_vms_and_the_overcommit_factors
  • devices_are_claimed_per_node_and_by_iommu_group
  • hugepages_are_counted_apart_from_memory_and_never_overcommitted
  • the_hugepage_share_counts_in_the_score
  • preferred_falls_back_to_the_whole_host_and_says_so
  • aligned_over_two_numa_nodes_splits_cpus_memory_and_devices
  • pools_give_devices_near_each_other

Integration tests in tests/cluster_tests.rs: vfio_devices_are_claimed_per_node_and_by_iommu_group and hugepages_are_counted_per_node_and_fill_up.

  • 22-host-topology.md §8

The code goes slightly beyond §9.1 in two ways: the score also includes the hugepage share, and placement also happens at VM create, not only on the leader’s pass.

VM reconciliation

Problem. Make each VM’s instance (the shim and its hypervisor) match the VM’s spec. This must survive crashes of the control plane, the shim and the host.

Desired state.

  • spec.power: Running, Paused or Stopped.
  • restart_policy: OnFailure (default) or Never.
  • on_host_boot: Resume (default) or Stop.

Observed state. status.phase is one of Stopped, Provisioning, Starting, Running, Paused, Stopping, Failed or Unknown, plus conditions such as Ready, CrashLoopBackOff and RestartRequired.

Liveness

Before acting, the controller establishes whether an instance exists. instance::liveness() runs these checks, and the first that shows life wins:

1. the systemd unit is active
2. shim or hypervisor (pid, start time) is alive, from status.instance and
   instance.json, but only if their boot id is the current boot id
3. api.sock or shim.sock accepts a connection
all checks made, none alive   -> Dead
any check could not be made   -> Unknown   # never acted on

The start time guards against pid reuse. The boot id makes a host reboot read as “no instance”.

One round

controller/vm.rs reconcile_vm() runs one round. Every step is idempotent. A round ends with “done” or “requeue after t”.

skip VMs placed on another node
observe liveness
Unknown                      -> phase Unknown, Ready=Unknown, requeue 10 s
Live, instance.json has an id we have no record of -> adopt it (AdoptedUnrecorded)
Live, shim reports Exited    -> release the shim, phase Stopping
not Live, instance recorded  -> finish_exit (exit cause, restart policy)
deleting and not Live        -> run finalizers in order
desired Stopped:  Live -> stop_round   else detach ports, phase Stopped, Ready=True
desired Running/Paused:  not Live -> launch_round   else running_round (drift)

  • stop_round: asks the shim to stop with the VM’s grace period. The deadline is grace + 15 s. Past the deadline it escalates to stopping the unit, and 15 s later to killing it.

  • launch_round:

    1. Waits for next_restart_at.
    2. Checks that disks, images and network records are there.
    3. Provisions: seed, NIC ports, launch.json.
    4. Writes the intent record (status.instance) before it starts the runner.

    A failure before the intent detaches the ports that this round added. A failure after it is found by the next round’s observation.

  • running_round: corrects drift: pause and resume, VFIO hot-plug, ports and CPU affinity. It sets RestartRequired when a launch-relevant field differs from what was launched.

Exit handling and restart policy

finish_exit() first classifies how the instance ended:

How it endedCause
Boot id changedHostReboot
The shim recorded an exitthat cause
No instance.jsonLost (an intent that never launched)
instance.json without an exit recordLost (the shim died)

Then it acts on the cause:

CauseAction
Requested; Lost that never launchednone
Terminated (unit stopped outside Glidex), CleanExit (guest powered off)set spec.power = Stopped
HostRebootResume: launch again; Stop: set spec.power = Stopped
LaunchFailedphase Failed; retry after backoff(launch_failures)
Crashed; Lost from a dead shimOnFailure: restart after crash_delay(n), CrashLoopBackOff; Never: set spec.power = Stopped
 
crash_delay(n) = min(10 s << (n-1), 300 s)        # 10, 20, 40, ... 300
restart_count resets after 600 s of running (STABLE_SECS)
backoff(n)     = clamp(1 s << (n-1), 1 s, 300 s)  # queue and launch failures

There is no limit on the number of restarts. They continue at most 300 s apart. When the controller sets the spec to stopped, it writes only if the generation has not changed since it observed the exit (stop_spec_after_exit()).

Work queue

controller/queue.rs holds one queue for every kind of object, keyed by (kind, id).

  • A key is queued at most once.
  • A key is processed by at most one worker at a time. A key added while it is being processed is marked dirty and processed again afterwards.
  • Failures back off per key with backoff(n). A success resets the count. An explicit “requeue after” is not a failure.

Triggers:

  • API writes.
  • A pidfd exit watch on each live shim and hypervisor (controller/mod.rs wait_for_exit()).
  • Cross-object events, such as a disk becoming ready.
  • A resync of every object every resync_secs (30 s by default), spread evenly over the period.

reconcile.workers (4 by default) run rounds in parallel.

Adoption after a restart

controller/startup.rs adopt_instances() runs before any controller starts. It launches, stops and changes nothing. For each local VM:

  • If the VM is live, it refreshes the recorded pids. If instance.json names an instance the record lacks, it rebuilds the record from instance.json and launch.json. It emits Adopted.
  • Runtime directories and units with no VM record are reported as orphans and never touched.
  • Only after this does it tell netd which VMs own ports.

There are no pid files. A running VM is found again from:

  • instance.json, which the shim writes;
  • the persisted status.instance;
  • the systemd unit glidex-vm@<id>.service.

Tests.

  • queue.rs: dedupes_and_never_runs_a_key_twice_at_once, delayed_keys_come_when_due, backoff_doubles_and_caps.
  • vm.rs: crash_backoff_is_10s_doubling_to_5min, an_unchanged_status_writes_nothing.
  • instance/mod.rs: each_check_alone_shows_life.
  • Restart and adoption end to end: restart_e2e in tests/functional_tests.rs, and systemd_runner_launches_adopts_and_stops.

Replicated store and Raft

Problem. Keep one database consistent across the cluster’s servers. Applying the replicated log must give the same bytes on every member and on every software version.

Library. openraft 0.9.25, pinned exactly. It implements Raft. The store is redb. Code: crate glidex-raftstore (store.rs, raft/) and cluster/.

Write sets

A write set is the ordered list of key changes one write made:

WriteSet { format, origin, ops: [ Put{table, key, value} | Delete{table, key} ] }

The leader computes write sets. Db::write(origin, f) works like this:

take the single write lane
new leader? first apply everything committed before it (ensure_linearizable)
open a real redb write transaction; run f against it
    every insert/remove is recorded as an Op; reads see the transaction's writes
empty write set   -> abort, nothing happens
local mode        -> commit
replicated mode   -> abort the local transaction, propose the write set,
                     return once it is committed and applied

Application logic runs only on the leader. The Raft log entry holds the outcome, not the request.

Followers, and the leader itself, apply each entry with Db::apply(). This is a pure byte operation: the puts and deletes are applied in one redb transaction, and last_applied is written in that same transaction. A crash therefore never applies an entry twice and never skips one. After the commit, the revision becomes the Raft index and subscribers are told.

Constraints:

  • A write set larger than the schema’s limit (4 MiB of JSON) is refused.
  • Table ids are append-only, because they are stored in the log.
  • The lane is held across the Raft round trip, which needs the runtime’s I/O. Db::begin tries the lane first and, when it is held, waits in block_in_place on a Tokio worker (glidex_raftstore::wait), so the worker’s other tasks and its I/O move to another thread.

Replay check. Setting GLIDEX_CHECK_WRITE_SETS enables the replay check. CI runs cargo test with it set. With the variable set:

  1. Every fresh database journals the write sets it publishes.
  2. When the database is dropped, the journal is replayed into an empty database.
  3. The two databases must dump identically, otherwise the test panics.

This pins the invariant that the write set alone reproduces the state (Drop for Db, Db::replay).

Snapshots.

  • A snapshot is a read-transaction view of the live database, so building one costs nothing.
  • It is streamed to a file only when it has to be sent to a member.
  • Installing it replaces the replicated tables and sets last_applied in one transaction.
  • The log is a separate redb file, raft/log.redb. Entries are durable before they are acknowledged.

Defaults. Heartbeat 250 ms, election timeout 1000–2000 ms, 10,000 log entries kept.

Writes on a follower

  • API writes. A follower forwards the whole HTTP or RPC request to the leader over the cluster port, with the authenticated principal attached (api/gate.rs, cluster_gate() and forward()).
    • The leader accepts forwarded requests only from server certificates. It authorizes the request itself.
    • With no leader known, the follower waits up to 3 s, then answers 503.
    • A 421 that names the leader is retried.
  • Node status writes (controller, images and network origins). These go to the leader as write sets. The leader replays them inside its own write, under a check of what that node may write (cluster/sync.rs, check_status_write()). The node then waits until its replica reaches the returned index (read-your-writes).
  • Agents (nodes that are not servers) keep a mirror of the store. Status writes they can’t deliver are queued on disk and resent.

Reads

Reads are linearizable by default:

leader:   read index = raft.get_read_log_id()
follower: ask the leader for its read index (POST /cluster/v1/read-index)
wait until the local replica has applied that index (<= 10 s)
read the local replica

Concurrent reads share one round trip. Without a quorum, a read fails with 503 cluster_unavailable, unless the client asks for a possibly stale local read with X-Glidex-Consistency: local. Read responses carry X-Glidex-Revision.

Liveness and readiness

  • Each node sends a heartbeat to the leader every 5 s.
  • Every 2 s, the leader compares each node’s silence with cluster.node_grace_secs (40 s by default).
  • A silent node becomes Ready=Unknown/NodeUnreachable. So do its VMs, in the same write. Nothing is stopped or moved.
  • A new leader resets every node’s grace to the time it took over, so a leader change never marks healthy nodes unreachable (cluster/lifecycle.rs liveness_round(), cluster/sync.rs Liveness).

A VM becomes Lost only when an operator forgets a fenced node.

Watch streams

The public watch (GET /watch as server-sent events, and the RPC WatchService.Watch) works as follows:

  1. It sends every visible object as added, then synced.
  2. When the store’s change bell rings, or every 10 s, it waits 250 ms for changes to settle, lists again with the list endpoints’ own authorization, and sends the differences.
  3. Keep-alives go out every 15 s.
  4. A stream ends after 300 s. The client reconnects and gets a fresh snapshot, so policy changes always apply.

Code: service/watch.rs, api/watch.rs, api/rpc/watch.rs.

Agents follow the store with a long poll by revision (/cluster/v1/watch). A revision older than the server’s in-memory log gets 410 Gone, and the agent lists again.

Tests.

  • glidex-raftstore: write_sets_replay_to_the_same_bytes.
  • glidex-raftstore/tests/raft.rs: a_lagging_learner_catches_up_from_a_snapshot, killing_the_leader_keeps_writes_going, a_partitioned_leaders_writes_are_rejected.
  • tests/cluster_tests.rs: reads_without_a_quorum_fail_unless_stale_is_asked_for, a_follower_server_writes_its_status_through_the_leader, a_silent_node_is_unreachable_not_gone.

Metering

Problem. Turn host counters and gauges into hourly usage rows that are counted exactly once. This must hold across crashes, counter resets and leader changes. Code: metering/.

Sampling

A round runs every sample_secs: 30 s by default, which must divide 300, and rounds align to the wall clock (metering/mod.rs, metering/sampler.rs). Each round reads:

SourceMeters
cgroup (or /proc)CPU time and memory
Hypervisordisk I/O
OVS port statisticsNIC and bridge bytes
nftables counters (NAT networks)external traffic
Conntrack (OVN gateways)external traffic
VM phaseallocation gauges

The ledger

metering/ledger.rs keeps:

  • a cursor per counter: last value, time and reset key;
  • open-hour accumulators;
  • closed hourly rows;
  • 5-minute slots for percentiles.
counter reading (value, at) with reset key r:
    same r, value >= cursor  -> delta = value - cursor
    same r, value <  cursor  -> delta = value (a reset), flagged
    new r (a new run)        -> counted from 0 (from launch time if known)
    first sight, before metering started -> baseline only, no backfill
gauge reading: integrate level x elapsed time; carry the sub-unit remainder
spread each delta over [from, to] into hours and 5-minute slots by overlap
commit: cursors + accumulators + slots in ONE transaction
close every open hour that ended more than close_grace_secs (120 s) ago
    first row for (hour, subject) has seq 0; a later one is an adjustment, seq n+1

Exactly once rests on the commit: a delta and the cursor that produced it commit together. A failed commit changes nothing, and the next round recomputes from the old cursor.

split_by() splits a delta with cumulative integer arithmetic, so the parts always sum exactly to the delta. A delta spread over a gap longer than two sampling intervals is flagged interpolated and gives no peak.

In a cluster

  1. Each node keeps its open state in a local meter.db.
  2. Every 60 s it ships its closed rows to the leader (POST /cluster/v1/ledger).
  3. The leader merges them in one replicated write (Ledger::import()). It records a key per node and row in ledger_inbox. A row already in the inbox is skipped.
  4. The node deletes its local copies only after the acknowledgement.

Shipping is at least once and merging is idempotent, so the cluster ledger is exactly once. The cluster’s completeness is the least that any live node has closed.

Billing month

  • A billing month is a calendar month in metering.billing_timezone.
  • Only zones whose offset is a whole number of hours all year are accepted. An hour row therefore never straddles a month boundary, and month totals are exact sums of hourly rows, adjustments included (metering/query.rs month_bounds()).
  • The open hour is reported as provisional.

95th percentile

Bandwidth, disk I/O and compute percentiles use the 5-minute slots (metering/rates.rs):

slots = 5-minute slots in range where any member of the group was present
series[slot] = sum of members' deltas in that slot      # p95 of the sum (D15)
sort series; rank = ceil(0.95 * N); p95 = series[rank - 1]   # nearest rank
Mbps = bytes * 8 / 300 / 1e6
billable = max(p95 rx, p95 tx)

Once a billing month is complete, its final percentiles are written once (metering/retention.rs). After retention, hourly rows roll up into daily rows at the billing zone’s midnight.

Derived meters

Derived meters are computed at read time (query.rs derive()):

  • net.bytes = rx + tx.
  • net.internal_bytes = total − external.
  • Average rates over the bucket.
  • Disk latency = time / operations.

Metering stops at usage. Glidex applies no prices.

Tests.

  • ledger.rs: exactly_once_across_rounds_and_failed_commits, counter_deltas_and_reset_cases, no_backfill_before_metering_started, split_parts_sum_to_amount, hours_close_with_grace_and_late_deltas_become_adjustments, shipped_hours_merge_exactly_once, gauges_lose_nothing_to_rounding.
  • rates.rs: nearest_rank, group_p95_is_of_the_summed_series.
  • query.rs: month_buckets_in_a_whole_hour_zone.

Images and disks

Verified download

images/download.rs run_download() and verify_and_install():

stream to <id>.qcow2.part, hashing as bytes arrive
    (sha256 always; also the vendor's algorithm, e.g. sha512)
retry up to 4 attempts, backing off 2, 4, 8 s
    resume with a Range request only if the server gave an ETag or Last-Modified;
    the part already on disk is rehashed first
compare digest with the expected one; mismatch -> Failed
qemu-img info: refuse a backing file, refuse over the size limit
qcow2: re-probe with the format forced; raw: convert to qcow2 and rehash
fsync, chmod 0444, rename into place

The rename is the commit. A file under its final name is complete and verified.

Linked disks

A linked disk shares its image’s data and stores only its own writes.

  • File datastores (datastore/file.rs): a linked disk is a qcow2 overlay whose backing file is the image. The backing path is relative to the datastore directory, so it doesn’t depend on where the directory is mounted. Every change is made on a dot-file and renamed into place.
  • LVM datastores (datastore/lvm.rs): each node builds the image’s thin volume gx-i-<image> once from the verified file, then seals it (makes it read-only). A linked disk is a thin snapshot of that volume.
    • A half-filled, unsealed image volume left by a crash is deleted and rebuilt.
    • Disk volumes are built as <name>.new and renamed, so a volume under its final name is complete.
    • Privileged LVM operations go through glidex-stord.

Extend root

images/partition.rs and images/disk.rs extend_root_at() grow the root partition into free space at the end of the disk.

read GPT or MBR from the disk's first MiB
root = partition with the Discoverable Partitions root type for the arch,
       else the physically last partition if it is a Linux filesystem
refuse unless root is the physically last partition
offline mode:
    raw: edit in place
    qcow2 or block: sparse "shadow" raw file the disk's size, holding copies of
        the first and last windows (<= 1 MiB each)
    sgdisk -e (GPT), then growpart <root>
    check the tools wrote nothing outside the windows; write changed windows back
on-boot mode, or partition tools missing: set pending_growpart; the guest grows it

Only the partition table changes. The guest grows the filesystem on its next boot (cloud-init). The shadow file avoids FUSE and NBD exports, so no root privileges are needed. Partition numbers don’t matter; position does.

Image copies across nodes

  • Each node holds its own copy of each image it needs (controller/image_cache.rs). A node fetches the file from a node that holds it, over the cluster port, checks its sha256 and renames it into place.
  • A shared datastore with linked disks gets its own copy of the image (controller/store_copies.rs). The copy is made under a lock file, checked by digest, made read-only and renamed.

Tests.

  • download.rs: hashing.
  • partition.rs: gpt_root_by_type_last, ubuntu_layout_root_is_partition_one_at_the_end, gpt_root_not_last_is_refused, edit_qcow2_through_shadow_keeps_data.
  • tests/datastore_tests.rs: a_linked_disk_on_a_shared_datastore_overlays_the_datastores_copy.

Kernel extraction

Problem. Boot a VM directly from a kernel, using the kernel, initramfs and command line found inside a disk image or the VM’s own disk. The guest’s filesystems must never be parsed on the host.

How. The extractor is a small appliance VM: a pinned Debian kernel with an initramfs that Glidex builds. It runs as a one-shot shim job with:

  • 1 vCPU and 1 GiB of memory;
  • no NIC and no seed;
  • the image attached read-only;
  • an output disk;
  • a 120 s timeout.

Code: images/extractor.rs, images/extract.rs and controller/extract.rs.

Inside the VM, the appliance mounts each partition read-only and writes one stream to the output disk. The stream holds the vmlinuz-* files, the initramfs files, grub.cfg and BLS entries:

GXFILE <partition>:<path> <size>\n<bytes> ... GXEND\n

The host parses the stream with every length checked. It refuses:

  • malformed headers;
  • unsafe names;
  • more than 64 files;
  • oversized files;
  • a total over 2 GiB.

Choosing. choose() picks the kernel and its command line:

candidates = vmlinuz-<v> that have initrd.img-<v> or initramfs-<v>.img
             (same partition preferred)
kernel = highest <v>, compared segment by segment, digit runs numerically
cmdline = "options" of the BLS entry whose "linux" names vmlinuz-<v>,
          else the first grub.cfg "linux"/"linuxefi" line naming it
drop $VARS, BOOT_IMAGE=, console=, earlyprintk=; append the arch's serial console
no root= -> fail

Boot loader defaults (GRUB set default, saved_entry) are not consulted. The newest kernel that has an initramfs wins.

Following the guest’s kernel. With kernel_from_disk, the VM controller checks the root disk before each launch:

  • It compares the disk file’s size and modification time (disk_stamp) with the values at the last extraction.
  • If they are unchanged and the kernel image is still usable, it boots that kernel without extracting.
  • Otherwise it extracts again. A result whose digests match a stored kernel image reuses that image.
  • On failure it boots the kernel it already has and sets KernelExtracted=False.

The kernel that boots is recorded in status.disk_kernel, not in the spec.

Tests. In extractor.rs: newest_kernel_with_an_initramfs, versions, choice_on_the_catalog_layouts, bad_streams_are_refused, choice_fails_cleanly.

  • 23-kernel-boot.md §10.4
