Disk move and volume locks

Volume locks

On a shared datastore, two nodes must never open one volume.

Glidex uses one lock file per volume, <datastore>/.locks/<disk-id>.lock, held with a non-blocking fcntl(F_OFD_SETLK) write lock. The lock is glidex_vm_shim::util::try_lock_file().

  • OFD locks belong to the open file, not to the process. The descriptor is close-on-exec, so a child process never inherits the lock.
  • Over NFSv4 the lock applies cluster-wide.
  • Node-local datastores take no lock file. Placement and claims already protect them.

Holders:

  • The shim takes the locks of the VM’s shared disks before it starts the hypervisor, and holds them until it exits (glidex-vm-shim/src/supervisor.rs). A held lock fails the launch.
  • Disk operations take the lock around the work (StorageDriver::lock()). A held lock returns Busy, and the operation waits.

The lock is on a separate file, not on the disk itself, because the hypervisor takes its own lock on the disk file.

Moving a disk

POST /disks/{id}/move is checked in datastore/manage.rs move_disk() and carried out by the disk controller’s move_round() (controller/disk.rs) using images/disk.rs move_volume().

preconditions: Ready, not deleting, not already moving, no running VM using it,
               destination reachable from the mover and the VM's node, space
choose one mover node: the disk's node (node-local), else its worker if that
    reaches the destination, else a node reaching both datastores
record disk.moving = {datastore, node, mover, flatten}; the disk stays Ready
mover:
    take source and destination volume locks
    destination already there? done (resume after a crash)
    copy to a temp: qemu-img convert when flattening, else a sparse copy
    linked, not flattened: rebase (-u) onto the destination's image copy
        (not there yet -> MovePending, retry every 5 s)
    qemu-img check (qcow2), rename into place
one write: datastore, node, worker, origin mode; clear moving; event Moved
delete the source file
any other error: clear moving, event MoveFailed; the source is untouched

In a cluster, the mover’s final write is accepted only if it ends exactly the move that was asked for (cluster/sync.rs check_move_write()). Moving a node-local disk to another node goes through a shared datastore.

Tests.

  • datastore/file.rs: a_shared_volume_is_locked_once.
  • glidex-vm-shim: a_file_lock_is_held_once, a_locked_disk_stops_the_launch.
  • tests/datastore_tests.rs: disks_move_between_datastores.
  • tests/cluster_tests.rs: a_node_local_disk_moves_to_a_shared_datastore_and_its_vm_can_go_anywhere.

  • 24-storage.md §8.3
  • 24-storage.md §10

Directory pull sync

Problem. Mirror an identity provider’s groups into users and teams, without letting a bad read disable everyone. Code: directory/sync.rs.

Steps.

  1. Read a snapshot of the connector’s groups and their members (nested members included).
  2. Compute a plan with plan(), a pure function.
  3. Apply the plan in writes of at most 500 changes.
wanted = members of the snapshot's groups that the snapshot has users for
for each wanted source user s (matched by the IdP's user id, never by email):
    a managed user with external_id = s.id  -> Update if fields differ;
                                               Enable if active and disabled by sync;
                                               Disable if suspended or archived
    else a user who signed in with that subject -> Adopt (Disable if inactive)
    else if active -> Create
managed users not wanted and not disabled -> Disable
groups: the snapshot's groups, members mapped to glidex ids

An administrator’s disable is never undone by sync. Only users that sync disabled are re-enabled.

Safety stop.

limit = max(managed users * max_disable% / 100, 5)    # max_disable defaults to 10
if count(Disable ops) > limit and the run isn't confirmed:
    state Blocked, list who would be disabled, apply nothing

A failed read applies nothing.

Scheduling. The sync runs on the leader, or on a standalone host. It runs every interval_minutes (15 by default, at least 5) and at most one run per connector at a time. A blocked run is retried on the next interval.

Tests.

  • sync.rs: a_plan_follows_the_groups_and_states, the_disable_limit_has_a_floor.
  • tests/connector_tests.rs: a_pull_follows_the_directory_and_stops_before_removing_many.

Spec. 19-tenancy.md §8.2

Console log replay filter

Problem. A new console client is first sent the console log, then live output. The log holds the guest’s queries to its terminal; systemd, for example, probes a serial console’s size at each getty start. A terminal that receives a replayed query answers it again, and the guest reads the stale answer as typed input.

How. glidex-vm-shim/src/replay.rs strip_queries() removes queries from the replayed log only. Live output passes unchanged.

scan the log; at ESC:
    CSI ... final byte  -> drop if a query: DSR (n), DA (c), DECRQM ($p),
                           XTVERSION (>q), kitty flags (?u), XTWINOPS reports (t)
    DCS +q / $q ... ST  -> drop (XTGETTCAP, DECRQSS)
    OSC 4,5,10-19,52 with a "?" field ... ST or BEL -> drop (colour/clipboard queries)
    anything else       -> copy
unterminated string or a query cut off at the end -> copy (the rest arrives live)

It runs in one pass, in linear time. It is used in glidex-vm-shim/src/proxy.rs when a client connects.

Tests.

  • replay.rs: systemds_serial_probes_are_left_out, every_kind_of_query_is_left_out, output_that_only_looks_alike_is_kept, a_query_cut_off_at_the_end_is_passed_on, an_abandoned_string_does_not_swallow_what_follows.
  • proxy.rs: replay_leaves_out_the_guests_terminal_queries.

Spec. 02-console.md, log files

IPAM

Cluster (OVN) networks

ipam.rs. All allocations are store writes, so they replicate with everything else.

allocate_subnet(network):
    already has one -> return it (idempotent)
    requested       -> /16../29, must not overlap the node NAT range or any subnet
    else            -> first /24 in ovn.nat_supernet (default 10.89.0.0/16)
                       that overlaps nothing; none -> SupernetFull
    gateway = .1; pool = .2 .. last host
reserve(network, mac):
    already reserved -> same address (stable across stops and restarts)
    else lowest free address in the pool; none -> PoolFull
  • Reservations are made at placement, in the same commit as the placement.
  • They are freed when the VM or NIC is gone, by the leader’s OVN reconciler (controller/ovn.rs gc_reservations()).
  • Each reservation becomes the port’s addresses and port_security in OVN. Addresses reach guests through OVN’s native DHCP.
  • Router external addresses come from allocate_external(): the requested address, or the lowest free one.

Node-local NAT networks

Node-local NAT networks follow the same rules in glidex-ovs/src/nat.rs:

  • The first /24 of 10.88.0.0/16 that overlaps no host route and no other NAT network.
  • dnsmasq serves DHCP with a hosts file of reservations.

MAC addresses are 02: followed by 5 bytes of SHA-256(VM id, NIC index): locally administered, and stable per NIC (glidex-ovs/src/names.rs).

Tests.

  • ipam.rs: subnets_come_from_the_supernet_and_never_overlap, addresses_are_the_lowest_free_and_stable, external_addresses_come_from_the_pool_once_each.
  • nat.rs: picks_first_free_subnet.

Spec. 14-clustering.md §11.4

OVN northbound sync

Problem. Keep the OVN northbound database equal to the cluster’s networks, routers and placed VM ports. Glidex must not disturb rows it didn’t create.

How. It reconciles declaratively.

  1. The leader’s network controller builds a Desired value from networks, IPAM and placements every 5 s (controller/ovn.rs).
  2. glidex_ovn::sync() (crates/glidex-ovn/src/lib.rs) reads the rows, then creates, updates or deletes only rows tagged external_ids:glidex-owner=glidex.
  3. A foreign row where a Glidex object should go is reported, never changed.
  4. A row that already matches costs no write.
  5. Every call is an ovn-nbctl command line, so tests assert exact commands.

Supporting details:

  • derived_mac() gives router ports stable, locally administered MACs (FNV-1a of a seed).
  • DHCP options carry the gateway, MTU and DNS servers.
  • Each port is bound to the chassis of the node its VM is placed on.

Tests. In crates/glidex-ovn/src/tests.rs: a_port_that_is_already_right_costs_nothing, ports_and_networks_gone_from_the_plan_are_removed_and_foreign_rows_are_left, macs_are_stable_and_locally_administered.

Spec. 14-clustering.md §11

Rate limiting

Glidex uses two simple in-memory limiters.

Token bucket. This limiter is used for passkey sign-in (per client), workload federation token exchange (per federation) and the SCIM endpoints (per connector). Each key holds (last time, level):

level = min(capacity, level + elapsed * refill_rate)
if level >= 1: level -= 1; allow
else: refuse (429)

Code: auth/passkeys.rs Ceremonies::attempt(), directory/exchange.rs take(), api/scim.rs take(). See token bucket.

Sliding window of failures. glidex-authd/src/limiter.rs keeps the times of recent failed logins: one queue per user and one global queue. Old entries are pruned on each check. A login is refused while either queue is full. A success clears that user’s failures. Memory is bounded, because failures are not recorded while the global window is full.

Tests.

  • limiter.rs: per_user_window_slides, global_window_slides, success_resets_the_user.
  • tests/passkey_tests.rs: sign_in_attempts_are_limited_by_the_real_client.

Spec.

  • 11-security.md §5.3
  • 25-passkeys.md

CA rotation and certificate renewal

Problem. Replace the cluster CA with no downtime, and renew node certificates before they expire. Code: cluster/rotation.rs, cluster/pki.rs.

Keys are ECDSA P-256. A node certificate lasts 365 days and the CA 10 years. The signed subject is set by the CA from the node’s identity, never taken from the request.

Rotation state. One replicated row, CaState, holds:

  • the trust bundle every node installs;
  • the signing CA’s fingerprint;
  • the retiring CAs’ fingerprints;
  • the time the old CA is retired.
leader: generate a new CA; send it to every live server (any refusal aborts)
one write: trust = new + old, signing = new, retire_at = now + grace (7 days)
every node, every 3 s:
    trust_sync: install the replicated bundle if it differs, reload TLS
    renew if the cert's issuer isn't the signing CA, or < 30 days remain:
        new key, CSR to the leader, save cert + key + bundle
leader: once every member's latest cert is from the new CA (and its own),
        or retire_at has passed:
        one compare-and-swap write: trust = new only, clear retiring
servers then delete the old CA key

During the window, every node trusts both CAs. A node with an old certificate and a node with a new one can therefore still talk to each other.

Rotation starts:

  • on demand (gxctl cluster rotate-ca);
  • after a server leaves;
  • when less than a year of CA validity remains.

Tests.

  • cluster/pki.rs: a_node_cert_is_signed_for_its_id_and_role, fingerprints_pin_the_ca.
  • cluster/identity.rs: identity_round_trips_and_the_signing_ca_is_found_in_a_bundle.
  • tests/cluster_tests.rs: the_ca_rotates_and_every_node_renews_before_the_old_one_is_retired.

Spec. 14-clustering.md §12.5

For measured costs of these paths, see Performance and benchmarks.

Performance and benchmarks

This page collects the figures a contributor should know: what has been measured, where, when and how, and how to measure it again. Glidex has no benchmark suite yet (see Gaps), so most figures come from host acceptance runs recorded in the specs and in pull requests, from CI timings, and from a few read-only measurements on a development host.

How to read the numbers

  • Every figure was taken once, on one date, on one machine. It is a data point, not a guarantee or a service level.
  • The hardware is stated where it was recorded. Many host runs in the specs say only “this host” (the project’s development host); for those the hardware is given as not recorded.
  • Some figures are design estimates, not measurements. They are marked as such. The cluster scale envelope is the main one.
  • Test durations (for example “the kernel-boot test passed in 68 s”) are the wall time of a whole test: pulling or building artifacts, booting, logging in, checks and teardown. They are not boot times.
  • Fixed rates in the metering runs (iperf -b 100M, fio at 500 IOPS) check that metering counts correctly. They say nothing about the maximum throughput of the data path.
  • Defaults and limits (timeouts, retry intervals, size caps) are configuration, not measurements. Where they help read a figure they are listed separately and labelled as defaults.

Measurement host

The figures marked measured on 2026-10-22 were taken on this machine:
CPUAMD EPYC 9124, 16 cores, 32 threads, 1 socket, 1 NUMA node
Memory31,293 MiB
Diskone consumer NVMe SSD (1 TB)
KernelUbuntu, 7.0.0-34-generic
Glidexinstalled release build of 2026-10-22, the server and Raft leader of a three-node cluster (one server, two agents) holding 1 VM, 8 images, 2 networks and 1 disk

The host was running its normal workload (load average about 2.8 on 32 threads) during the measurements.

Measured on 2026-10-22 on the measurement host. That includes curl’s connect and the full response, not process start-up. Reads on this host are served by the Raft leader.

Measured in tests rather than at scale:

  • The slowest single cluster test took about 16.5 s on CI (#43, 2026-10-17).
  • cluster_tests (42 tests) took 265 s in the CI run of 2026-10-22, the longest test binary in the workspace.
  • Write-set replay checking (GLIDEX_CHECK_WRITE_SETS=1) costs little: the control plane’s tests took 461.9 s plain and 469.2 s with it, on CI (#43).

Metering

From 13-metering.md §15.6–§15.7 and #13 (2026-10-07). The load test is metering/bench.rs: 200 VMs in 10 projects, 2 NICs and 2 disks each, 10 networks, a month of history with every 5-minute slot filled. Hardware not recorded.

First buildCurrent (per-project key ranges)
One sampling round41 ms39 ms (budget 15 s)
Usage query, one project, one month, by VM972 ms146 ms (target 200 ms)
Bandwidth p95, one project, one month, by VM1.65 s254 ms

With 2 days of history and CPU and memory slots (M4): a round takes 49 ms and the CPU and memory p95 query 20 ms; VM slot rows add about 20 % to the slot table.

Size: one day for this fleet is 23k hourly rows (387 B each) and 19k slot rows (669 B each). The database file grows to about 3× the live data (copy-on-write pages). At the default retention that is about 2.5 GB for 200 VMs, roughly 12 MB per VM.

Accuracy on a host (2026-10-05, two Debian 13 guests): metered CPU was within +0.03 % (Cloud Hypervisor) and +0.13 % (QEMU) of the cgroup’s own counter over 300 s of load, and within +0.21 % across a control-plane restart.

Measure it yourself

All of these read only, except where a test says it creates VMs; run those on a host you can use for testing.

API latency

On a host running Glidex, as a user who can use the API socket:

for p in /health /vms /images; do
  for i in $(seq 100); do
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}\n' \
      --unix-socket /run/glidex-cp/api.sock "http://x$p"
  done | sort -n | awk -v p=$p '{a[NR]=$1*1000}
    END {printf "%s p50 %.1f ms p95 %.1f ms\n", p, a[int(NR*0.5)], a[int(NR*0.95)]}'
done

Note the number of objects each list returns, the node’s Raft role and the host’s load with the figures.

Gaps

Not benchmarked yet, stated plainly:

  • No cargo bench or Criterion suites. The only load test is the ignored metering/bench.rs.
  • No cluster scale run. The §4.1 envelope is an estimate; Raft write latency, leader CPU, database growth and snapshot install time have not been measured.
  • No API write latency or throughput figures, and no figures for the RPC API, TLS, or requests forwarded from followers.
  • No VM boot, stop or start-to-network times separate from test wall time.
  • No storage throughput (IOPS or MB/s ceilings) for dir, shared-dir or lvm datastores, and no timings for disk moves or image copies.
  • No network throughput for tap, AF_XDP or vhost-user with OVS-DPDK, and none across a Geneve tunnel.
  • Hardware is missing from most recorded host runs.
  • No regression tracking: nothing is measured on every change.

Suggested next benchmarks:

  1. The §4.1 scale run: 2,000 VMs on 50 simulated nodes with a fake netd and real Raft on three hosts; record write rate, write latency per entry, leader CPU, database size and snapshot install time.
  2. An API latency script in the repository (reads and writes, Unix socket and TLS, on the leader and on a follower), with object counts.
  3. Time from POST /vms/{id}/start to Running and to the first console line, per backend and boot mode, from the ignored tests’ own timestamps.
  4. fio and iperf3 at full rate per datastore driver and per port type, with the hardware recorded.
  5. A Criterion suite for hot paths: scheduler filtering and scoring at 50 nodes, OVN NB diff per round, metering queries.
  6. Record the hardware with every host run in the specs and pull requests.

Glidex compared

This page places Glidex next to other platforms that run virtual machines on your own hardware. It is for contributors: what Glidex does differently on purpose, and what it does not try to do.

Facts about other products are as of October 2026, checked against their official documentation and project pages (see References). Products change quickly; check the linked pages before you rely on a detail. Facts about Glidex are from this repository at the same date. A dash (—) marks a cell this page does not claim.

Positioning

Glidex is a KVM control plane written in Rust. It runs VMs on Cloud Hypervisor (the default) or QEMU, on one host or on a cluster of hosts that replicate their state with Raft embedded in the control-plane binary. One proto-defined service layer serves both a REST API and gRPC/gRPC-Web/Connect; a React web UI and the gxctl CLI use it. Networking is Open vSwitch on a host and OVN across a cluster. Authorization is Cedar policy over projects and tenants, with identities from local accounts, passkeys, OIDC providers, SCIM and directory sync.

It sits between a single-host tool and a full private cloud (OpenStack, CloudStack). It aims at labs, teams and small clouds of up to about 50 hosts, especially ones that hand out GPUs and other PCI devices. It is young (v0.0.x tags, first commit December 2025) and has fewer features than any mature product below.

Products

Proxmox VE

A Debian-based server virtualization platform for QEMU/KVM and LXC, with a web UI, a REST API, HA, SDN and broad storage support.

  • Differs: every Proxmox node is equal and ships as a distribution; Glidex installs onto an existing distro and separates server and agent roles. Proxmox has live migration, HA restart with fencing, mediated devices and many storage types; Glidex has none of these today. Glidex has tenants, Cedar policy and SCIM and directory sync built in.
  • Pick Proxmox when you want a mature, all-in-one virtualization host for a small or medium site, with VMs and containers.

OpenStack

A family of services (Nova compute, Neutron networking, Cinder block storage, Keystone identity…) that make a full IaaS cloud, run by the OpenInfra Foundation.

  • Differs: Glidex is one binary with an embedded store, not a set of services over a message queue and SQL database. It uses similar ideas at a smaller scale: OVN networks with routers, projects and quotas, federated identity. OpenStack covers far more: many hypervisor and storage drivers, vGPU, bare metal, very large deployments.
  • Pick OpenStack when you need a full cloud API, many back ends, or a large deployment with a team to run it.

oVirt and Red Hat Virtualization

oVirt manages KVM hosts from a central Engine (web UI and REST API) on PostgreSQL, with the VDSM agent on each host. Its current release is 4.5.7, and it describes itself as community-driven. Red Hat Virtualization 4.4, the product built on it, left its Maintenance Phase on 31 August 2024 and its Extended Life Phase on 31 August 2026. Red Hat points RHV users to OpenShift Virtualization.

  • Differs: oVirt keeps state in a central PostgreSQL database behind the Engine; Glidex replicates its own store with Raft and needs no external database.
  • Pick oVirt when you already run it and the community release meets your needs; former RHV customers are directed to OpenShift Virtualization.

VMware vSphere and vCenter

ESX hosts managed by the vCenter appliance, with vMotion, vSphere HA, Fault Tolerance and vSAN. Broadcom ended perpetual licensing; vSphere is sold as subscriptions, chiefly in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) and VMware vSphere Foundation (VVF), licensed per core.

  • Differs: Glidex runs on stock Linux and KVM, is open source and has no license cost. vSphere is far ahead on live migration, HA, storage, ecosystem and vendor support.
  • Pick vSphere when you need those operational features and vendor support, and the subscription fits.

Harvester and KubeVirt

KubeVirt adds VMs to Kubernetes as custom resources, run in pods with libvirt and QEMU. Harvester (SUSE) is a bare-metal HCI distribution built on Kubernetes, KubeVirt and Longhorn, managed alongside Rancher.

  • Differs: Glidex does not need Kubernetes; its state is in its own Raft store, and VMs are not pods. Glidex’s draft app layer (26-apps.md) would run Kubernetes on Glidex VMs, not Glidex on Kubernetes.
  • Pick Harvester or KubeVirt when your team already runs Kubernetes and wants VMs and containers under one API and toolchain.

Incus and LXD

Incus is a community-driven alternative to Canonical’s LXD, maintained by many of LXD’s original developers. Both manage system containers and VMs through a REST API, on one host or a cluster with a replicated database (Cowsql for Incus, Dqlite for LXD). Incus is Apache-2.0; LXD is AGPL-3.0 and maintained by Canonical.

  • Differs: the closest in shape: one daemon, a REST API, embedded replicated state, OVN networks. Glidex chose Raft over ReDB instead of a replicated SQL database (14-clustering.md D1), manages VMs only, offers Cloud Hypervisor as well as QEMU, and puts more into the control plane for tenants, identity and NUMA-aware device placement. Incus has containers, live migration and many storage drivers, and years of use.
  • Pick Incus or LXD when you want containers and VMs together, or a mature, packaged tool.

OpenNebula

A cloud manager with a front-end (oned, HA through Raft across front-end servers) and KVM or LXC hosts, with VDCs for multi-tenancy, LDAP and SAML sign-in, GPU passthrough and vGPU.

  • Differs: both target private clouds. Both replicate front-end state with Raft; OpenNebula replicates SQL statements to its database, Glidex replicates write sets to ReDB. OpenNebula has live migration, broad GPU support and many integrations; Glidex has a smaller feature set, REST and gRPC from one schema, and Cedar authorization.
  • Pick OpenNebula when you need a proven private cloud today.

Apache CloudStack

An IaaS platform: Java management servers on MySQL drive KVM, vSphere, XenServer/Xen, Hyper-V and other hosts, organized as regions, zones, pods and clusters, with domains, accounts and projects.

  • Differs: CloudStack supports many hypervisors and is built for multi-zone clouds; Glidex is KVM-only and much smaller.
  • Pick CloudStack when you run a multi-zone cloud for many tenants and need broad hypervisor and storage support.

MicroVM stacks (Firecracker, Kata Containers)

Firecracker is a minimal KVM-based VMM built at AWS for serverless and container services (it runs AWS Lambda and Fargate). Kata Containers is a container runtime that runs workloads in lightweight VMs, through OCI and the Kubernetes CRI, with QEMU, Cloud Hypervisor or Firecracker. Cloud Hypervisor, Glidex’s default VMM, is built on the same rust-vmm crates.

  • Differs: these are VMMs or runtimes, not control planes. Glidex manages long-lived VMs with disks, networks and devices; it does not aim at per-request VM creation or container semantics. Glidex supported Firecracker early on and dropped it for its lack of GPU passthrough (Design decisions); it may return as the VMM of a lightweight, container-compatible layer.
  • Pick them when you need sandboxed, short-lived workloads in large numbers.

Key differentiators

Each follows from a design decision; see Design decisions and trade-offs for the reasoning.

DifferentiatorDesign decisionEvidence
No external database or message bus, even in a clusterRaft embedded in the control plane over ReDB; the leader computes write sets, others apply bytes14-clustering.md D1–D5, crates/glidex-raftstore
A single host stays a single hostStandalone uses the local store; Raft only after gxctl cluster init14-clustering.md D5
Guests survive control-plane restarts and upgradesEach VM runs under its own glidex-vm-shim in its own systemd unit; the control plane adopts them on start12-reconciliation.md
Two hypervisors behind one APIOne driver contract for Cloud Hypervisor and QEMU04-hypervisors.md
One API, two transportsProtos are the source of truth; one service layer under REST and gRPC/Connect18-grpc.md
Policy as codeCedar policies with shipped roles, decisions recorded in the audit log11-security.md §7, §10
Identity from the organizationConnectors (OIDC presets), SCIM, Google Workspace pull sync, invitations, passkeys, workload federation19-tenancy.md T1–T5, 25-passkeys.md
Topology-aware device placementEach node reports NUMA, CPUs, hugepages and PCIe tree; scheduler aligns devices, memory and dedicated CPUs; pools and GPU requests22-host-topology.md, 27-gpu-vms.md
Unprivileged control planeRoot work goes through small helpers (glidex-netd, glidex-authd, glidex-stord); guests’ metadata requests are parsed by glidex-metad, under its own userarchitecture.md, 24-storage.md S12, S17
Storage by mounts, not plugins firstshared-dir uses mounts the operator makes; driver trait shaped like CSI for later24-storage.md S1
Verified images and kernel bootChecksum-verified catalog, linked qcow2 disks, kernels extracted from cloud images10-images.md, 23-kernel-boot.md
Metering built inHourly exactly-once usage ledger, per-VM and per-network traffic13-metering.md

Non-goals and current gaps

Non-goals (by design):

  • Automatic VM failover. A node that stops heartbeating leaves its VMs unknown; nothing restarts them elsewhere, because a partitioned node may still run them (14-clustering.md D8). Moving a stopped or lost VM is an explicit operator action.
  • Containers. Glidex runs VMs only.
  • Running on Kubernetes, or an etcd/SQL dependency.
  • An eBPF datapath (14-clustering.md D15).
  • vGPU and mediated devices (22-host-topology.md §1).

Gaps (not built yet, some planned):

  • Live migration (planned after shared datastores; 14-clustering.md §18).
  • Disk snapshots, backups, encryption at rest (24-storage.md §1).
  • Shared block storage beyond hyperstor: lvm is node-local LVM-thin; shared LVM, Ceph RBD and a CSI adapter are later milestones. Ceph is usable only as a mounted CephFS through shared-dir.
  • Serial console only: no VNC/SPICE or graphical display. Cloud Hypervisor itself runs Windows guests, but Glidex’s catalog holds Linux cloud images provisioned by cloud-init, and Windows guests are not a target today. They may come later, once the tooling supports them (a graphical console and Windows provisioning).
  • Security groups, floating IPs, BGP and load balancers (14-clustering.md §2).
  • Scale: designed for about 50 hosts and 2,000 VMs (14-clustering.md §4.1).
  • LDAP, Entra ID and GitHub connectors (19-tenancy.md T2b, T4b); directories apart from clusters and fleets (T6, T7).
  • Distribution packages: install is from source with Rust while Glidex is under active development; prebuilt binaries and distro packages are planned later.

Contributing

This page covers building and running Glidex from source, the test layers, what CI checks, the conventions the code and docs follow, a walk-through of adding an API operation, and the pull request flow.

What you need

ForYou need
Building and cargo testLinux, a current stable Rust (the workspace is edition 2024), a C linker. The tests also use dosfstools, mtools, qemu-utils, gdisk and cloud-guest-utils (what CI installs).
The web UIbun. The project uses bun, not npm, for the UI, its e2e suite and the generated TypeScript.
ProtosNothing for the Rust side (build.rs compiles them). buf for lint, breaking checks and the UI’s TypeScript.
Real VMsKVM, Cloud Hypervisor and/or QEMU, the UEFI firmware, a cloud image; glidex-netd and Open vSwitch for networked VMs. A host set up by glidex-install has all of these.
The docsmdBook (cargo install mdbook --locked; CI uses 0.5.4).

Building and running from source

cargo build                      # every crate
cargo build -p glidex-control-plane --bin gxctl

On a host where the installer runs Glidex as services, stop them first: they use the same ports.

sudo systemctl stop glidex-control-plane glidex-ui

A control plane

A control plane you start yourself keeps its data in ~/.glidex and its sockets in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/glidex (api.sock, ui.sock). It runs VMs detached, with the glidex-vm-shim binary found next to its own, so build both:

cargo build --bin glidex-control-plane --bin glidex-vm-shim
cargo run --bin glidex-control-plane     # API on https://localhost:8841

It reads /etc/glidex/control-plane.json, or the file in GLIDEX_CONFIG; a missing file means the defaults. On an installed host, give your run its own file, so you are its administrator and its UI user:

mkdir -p ~/glidex-dev
cat > ~/glidex-dev/control-plane.json <<EOF
{
  "listen": ["127.0.0.1:8841"],
  "admin_group": "$(id -gn)",
  "users_group": "$(id -gn)",
  "ui_user": "$(id -un)"
}
EOF
GLIDEX_CONFIG=~/glidex-dev/control-plane.json cargo run --bin glidex-control-plane

admin_group makes members of that group break-glass administrators on api.sock; ui_user is the only user ui.sock accepts. Every setting and its default is in packaging/control-plane.json.example and Configuration. The UI e2e suite’s start-control-plane.sh is a complete example of a scratch instance with its own home, run directory and datastore root.

The web UI

(cd crates/glidex-ui/ui && bun install)
GLIDEX_API_SOCKET=$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/glidex/ui.sock \
  cargo run -p glidex-ui -- --dev        # Vite with hot reload on https://localhost:5173

--dev runs bun run dev in crates/glidex-ui/ui with the UI’s certificate, and points the Vite proxy at the control plane. The UI’s RPCs are gRPC-Web, which the control plane takes only on ui.sock, so the dev server should reach it there: without GLIDEX_API_SOCKET it uses /run/glidex-cp/ui.sock if it exists, else TCP, where RPCs need a bearer token.

To serve a production build instead: bun run build in crates/glidex-ui/ui (it type-checks with tsc -b, then writes ui/dist), then cargo run -p glidex-ui.

gxctl

cargo run --bin gxctl                    # interactive shell; `help` lists commands
cargo run --bin gxctl -- list            # one command

On the host, gxctl finds a hand-started control plane’s api.sock in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/glidex and identifies you by your Unix account. See the gxctl reference.

Tests

LayerWhereNeedsRuns in CI
Unit tests#[cfg(test)] modules in each crateNothingYes
Integration testscrates/*/tests/*.rsThe disk tools aboveYes
Functional tests#[ignore]d tests, mostly crates/glidex-control-plane/tests/functional_tests.rsKVM, hypervisors, an image; some need glidex-netd, OVS, OVN, LVMNo
UI e2ecrates/glidex-ui/e2e (Playwright)bun, Chromium; KVM and an image for the boot testsNo
Nested cluster e2ecrates/glidex-e2e/tests/nested_cluster.rsA Glidex host with nested KVM, about 9 GiB of memoryNo
Metadata endpoint e2ecrates/glidex-e2e/tests/metadata.rsA Glidex host installed from your workspace (glidex-metad, netd’s rules) with a NAT networkNo

Unit and integration tests

cargo test                                        # the whole workspace, no VMs
cargo test -p glidex-control-plane --test datastore_tests   # one test binary
cargo test -p glidex-raftstore                    # one crate
GLIDEX_CHECK_WRITE_SETS=1 cargo test              # as CI runs it

GLIDEX_CHECK_WRITE_SETS=1 replays every database a test opens from its write sets and compares the result, which catches a write that a replicated store couldn’t reproduce.

The control plane’s integration tests start the whole router in process and call it as clients do; a test file’s harness has rest(…) and grpc(…) helpers so one test can check both transports. Networking tests run against an in-process glidex-netd with a recording executor (no root, no OVS). cluster_tests.rs runs three control planes on one machine over real mutual TLS.

Functional tests

These boot real guests. Run them one at a time:

GLIDEX_TEST_IMAGE=~/images/ubuntu-cloudimg.img \
  cargo test -p glidex-control-plane --test functional_tests -- --ignored --test-threads=1
Variable or stepFor
GLIDEX_TEST_IMAGEA UEFI-bootable cloud image; most boot tests.
GLIDEX_TEST_KERNEL, GLIDEX_TEST_INITRDDirect kernel boot tests.
The glidex groupTests that use the host’s glidex-netd. The installer keeps you out of that group; run them with sudo -u $USER -g glidex env PATH=$PATH HOME=$HOME cargo test ….
GLIDEX_TEST_DPDK=1vhost-user tests, with OVS-DPDK.
sudo scripts/dev/fake-lan-setup.sh, GLIDEX_TEST_LAN=1Uplink tests, on a fake LAN in a network namespace. Undo with fake-lan-teardown.sh.

Other ignored tests, each documented in its file’s header:

cargo test -p glidex-control-plane --test real_ovn -- --ignored           # ovsdb-server, ovn-nbctl
GLIDEX_TEST_NB=unix:/var/run/ovn/ovnnb_db.sock \
  cargo test -p glidex-ovn -- --ignored                                    # a throwaway OVN
GLIDEX_STORD_SOCKET=/run/glidex-stord/stord.sock GLIDEX_STORD_VG=<vg> GLIDEX_STORD_POOL=<pool> \
  cargo test -p glidex-stord --test real_lvm -- --ignored                  # a throwaway volume group
cargo test -p glidex-control-plane --test systemd_runner_tests -- --ignored  # user systemd, KVM, GLIDEX_TEST_IMAGE

glidex-vm-shim’s tests run against an idle Cloud Hypervisor and skip themselves when it isn’t installed.

UI end-to-end tests

scripts/dev/ui-e2e.sh -i ~/images/ubuntu-cloudimg.img       # both hypervisors
scripts/dev/ui-e2e.sh -H ch                                 # the ui project plus one hypervisor
scripts/dev/ui-e2e.sh -- --headed -g "create form"          # extra Playwright arguments
scripts/dev/ui-e2e-full.sh -i ~/images/ubuntu-cloudimg.img  # fails if any test skips

The script installs the suite’s dependencies and Playwright’s Chromium with bun, starts a throwaway control plane on :8851, the Vite dev server on :5174 and a production glidex-ui on :5175, and runs the suite. Tests that need KVM, an image or glidex-netd skip when those are missing. Only one run goes at a time on a machine: the script refuses a second. Set E2E_API_PORT (and E2E_UI_PORT, E2E_UI_SERVER_PORT) when something else holds those ports. Build first (cargo build -p glidex-control-plane -p glidex-ui): the harness times out while cargo builds. On a host with an install, run it in the glidex group so the boot tests reach glidex-netd:

sudo -n -g glidex -u $USER env HOME=$HOME PATH=$PATH GLIDEX_E2E_GROUP=glidex-admin \
  scripts/dev/ui-e2e.sh -H ch -- tests/<spec>.spec.ts

Without the script, from crates/glidex-ui/e2e:

(cd ../ui && bun install) && bun install && bunx playwright install chromium
GLIDEX_TEST_IMAGE=~/images/ubuntu-cloudimg.img bun run test   # or test:ch / test:qemu
bun run typecheck

See the suite’s README for how it signs in and what each server is for.

Nested cluster test

cargo test -p glidex-e2e --test nested_cluster -- --ignored --nocapture

It makes two VMs with this host’s Glidex, installs Glidex from your workspace into both (glidex-install --prebuilt), forms a cluster with OVN, runs a guest on each and checks they reach each other over the Geneve tunnel. It takes 10 to 20 minutes.

The metadata endpoint test runs against this host’s own Glidex, which must be installed from your workspace and serve a NAT network. From inside a guest it reads /v1/instance, fetches an identity token and a Glidex token, and checks that a request without Metadata-Flavor: Glidex is refused:

cargo test -p glidex-e2e --test metadata -- --ignored --nocapture

CI

Two workflows run on every pull request to main and every push to main.

rust.yml:

JobChecks
buildscripts/lint-store-writes.sh; cargo build; GLIDEX_CHECK_WRITE_SETS=1 cargo test. Times out after 45 minutes.
fmtcargo fmt --all --check
protoIn crates/glidex-api: buf lint, buf format --exit-code; buf generate leaves crates/glidex-ui/ui/src/gen unchanged; buf breaking against origin/main.

docs.yml:

JobChecks
publicmdbook build docs/public, assembled with docs/site into the site artifact.
deployOn pushes to main only: publishes the site to the gh-pages branch.
internalmdbook build docs/internal (the specs); cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items with rustdoc warnings as errors.

CI does not run clippy, the ignored tests or the UI e2e suite: run the ones your change touches before you push.

Checks before pushing

Run these on every commit of a stack, not only its top, since each stacked pull request is merged on its own (the same list as AGENTS.md):

cargo fmt --all --check
cargo check --workspace --tests
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings -A rustdoc::private_intra_doc_links" \
  cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items
GLIDEX_CHECK_WRITE_SETS=1 cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast
scripts/lint-store-writes.sh

And when they apply:

ChangedAlso run
A .protoIn crates/glidex-api: buf lint, buf format --exit-code, buf generate (commit the regenerated crates/glidex-ui/ui/src/gen), buf breaking --against '../../.git#branch=main,subdir=crates/glidex-api'.
The web UIbun install (after a package change) and bun x tsc -b --noEmit in crates/glidex-ui/ui; the UI e2e for the pages touched.
Docsmdbook build docs/public (and docs/internal for spec/).
VM, disk, network or host pathsThe #[ignore]d functional tests that cover them, on a host.

The cluster tests are timing-sensitive: a failed build job may be rerun once; a second failure is real.

Conventions

Specs first

A change to behavior, an invariant or a contract between components starts in spec/. Update the spec that owns it in the same pull request, or land a spec pull request first. In specs:

  • File paths are relative to the repository root; code references use path:line.
  • A claim about runtime behavior that the source doesn’t make obvious gets a Why: or Invariant: note.
  • Decisions are numbered within their spec (D6, G-D11) and milestones named (S5, T6), so code and commits can cite them.

Code cites the spec it implements: a module’s //! header names the spec section (//! The scheduler (spec/14-clustering.md §9.1)), and a comment that depends on a decision names it. Specs are never moved or renamed, because code cites them by path.

Rust

  • Formatting is rustfmt’s defaults: cargo fmt --all.
  • Keep clippy clean: cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings. When a lint must be allowed, allow it narrowly with the reason in a comment, as api/mod.rs does for clippy::result_large_err.
  • Keep rustdoc clean: CI builds it with -D warnings.
  • Every write to the control plane’s database goes through the store (Db::begin / Db::write in crates/glidex-control-plane/src/store/), so every write has a write set a replicated store can propose. scripts/lint-store-writes.sh fails the build if begin_write appears anywhere else in the crate.
  • Never block a Tokio worker on a lock held across a store write (the write lane, the network store’s mutex, the image cache, the directory key lock) or on a slow blocking call (netd, stord, hyperstor). In a cluster a write holds the lane until Raft commits, and Raft needs the runtime’s I/O. Wait through glidex_raftstore::wait (lock, read, write, blocking), which uses block_in_place on a worker.
  • Operations are decided in service/, never in an adapter: REST handlers and RPC adapters only decode, call one service function and encode.

Protos and JSON

  • Packages are versioned, glidex.<area>.v1. A breaking change needs a new package served next to the old one; buf breaking (FILE rules) enforces it against main.

  • buf lint with the STANDARD rules: services are <Noun>Service.

  • Every RPC carries option (glidex.api.v1.op); build.rs refuses a method without one.

  • Every field whose name has an underscore declares [json_name = "<name>"], so REST JSON stays snake_case; build.rs refuses it otherwise.

  • Secrets are request-only fields marked [(glidex.api.v1.secret) = true]; build.rs refuses a response that reaches one, and the audit never logs them.

  • REST bodies are the proto3 JSON form of the same messages: enum values take their full names (HYPERVISOR_QEMU), and an unknown field is refused with 422 and code invalid.

  • After changing a proto, regenerate the UI’s TypeScript and commit it:

    (cd crates/glidex-ui/ui && bun install)
(cd crates/glidex-api && buf generate)

The full rules are in spec/18-grpc.md §4.

Docs voice

The public book is plain, terse and concrete: short sentences in the present tense, sentence-case headings, tables for anything with more than two attributes, a command for every task. It describes what Glidex does, not how it might evolve. It doesn’t depend on the specs (only this developer guide links to them, always by full GitHub URL), and it contains no security-sensitive details: no internal host names, addresses, credentials or unreleased plans. Use placeholders such as host.example.org, <token> and documentation addresses (192.0.2.0/24). Benchmark figures name their source, date and hardware.

Adding an API operation end to end

This walk-through follows an existing operation, MoveDisk (POST /disks/{id}/move), through every layer. To add your own, change the same places.

1. Spec

Describe the operation in the spec that owns its area: what it does, who may call it, what state it writes and which controller acts on it. MoveDisk is in spec/24-storage.md §8.3.

2. Proto

Add the RPC and its messages to the area’s proto, here crates/glidex-api/proto/glidex/storage/v1/storage.proto:

// Move the disk to another datastore, offline (spec/24-storage.md §8.3):
// the node that has it copies it there, then removes the old file.
rpc MoveDisk(MoveDiskRequest) returns (MoveDiskResponse) {
  option (glidex.api.v1.op) = {
    action: "moveDisk"
    kind: KIND_WRITE
    rest: "POST /disks/{id}/move"
  };
}

message MoveDiskRequest {
  string id = 1;
  // Datastore id or name.
  string datastore = 2;
  optional string node = 3;
  optional bool flatten = 4;
  // Wait this long (at most 300 s) for the move to finish.
  optional uint32 wait_secs = 5 [json_name = "wait_secs"];
}

The option says three things:

  • action: the Cedar action checked for the call, or public / authenticated.
  • kind: KIND_READ operations are served by any server after a read barrier; KIND_WRITE operations run on the leader, and a follower forwards them.
  • rest: the REST twin, exactly as registered in the route table, or empty for an RPC-only operation.

3. Build: the operation table

cargo build -p glidex-api regenerates the messages, the DiskService trait and client, and glidex_api::OPERATIONS, which now has an entry for /glidex.storage.v1.DiskService/MoveDisk. The build fails here if the option is missing or malformed, or a json_name is wrong.

4. Service function

Write the operation once, in service/storage.rs. It takes the Call (principal, Cedar action, audit) and the request message, makes every decision, and returns a ServiceResult (comments added):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub async fn move_disk(call: &Call, req: pb::MoveDiskRequest) -> ServiceResult<DiskReply> {
    let d = visible_disk(call, &req.id).await?;               // not found vs forbidden
    let datastore = disk_datastore(call, Some(&req.datastore))?; // may the caller use it?
    call.manager()
        .move_disk(&d.id, &datastore, req.node.as_deref(), req.flatten.unwrap_or(false))
        .await
        .map_err(manager_err)?;
    disk_reply(call, &d.id, req.wait_secs).await
}
}

The manager checks the disk and records the move on it (moving); the disk controller (controller/disk.rs) copies the disk and removes the old file, and wait_secs lets the caller wait for it to settle.

5. REST adapter

Register the route with its Cedar action in routes in api/mod.rs:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
.add(
    "POST",
    "/disks/{id}/move",
    "moveDisk",
    post(storage::move_disk),
)
}

and write the handler in api/storage.rs. It decodes the proto JSON body (unknown fields refused), fills in path and query values, calls the service function and encodes the reply:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub async fn move_disk(
    c: Caller,
    Path(id): Path<String>,
    Query(w): Query<WaitQuery>,
    Json(v): Json<Value>,
) -> Result<Response, ApiErr> {
    let mut req: pb::MoveDiskRequest = body(v)?;
    req.id = id;
    req.wait_secs = req.wait_secs.or(w.secs());
    let r = svc::move_disk(&c, req).await?;
    Ok(disk_reply(r, StatusCode::OK, StatusCode::ACCEPTED))
}
}

6. RPC adapter

Implement the generated trait method in api/rpc/storage.rs. Adapters go through unary, which finds the operation in the table, applies the listener’s protocol and credential rules, builds the Call, runs the service function and audits the result:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
async fn move_disk(
    &self,
    ctx: RequestContext,
    req: ServiceRequest<'_, MoveDiskRequest>,
) -> ServiceResult<MoveDiskResponse> {
    disk_write!(self, ctx, req, svc::move_disk, MoveDiskResponse)
}
}

A new service (not just a new method) is also registered in the file’s register function.

7. Cedar

Declare the action in policies/glidex.cedarschema, with its permission groups and the resource type it applies to:

action deleteDisk, resizeDisk, extendRoot, moveDisk in ["disk.write", "tenant-scoped"]
  appliesTo { principal: [User, Token], resource: [Disk], context: Ctx };

The groups decide who gets it: disk.write is in role.editor, so editors and every role above them may move disks with no change to roles.cedar. Pick an existing group where one fits; a new group needs a place in the role hierarchy at the top of the schema. Add step-up for actions that need a recent login.

The test every_route_maps_to_a_schema_action in api/mod.rs checks that every route and every RPC names an action the schema declares, and that each RPC’s REST twin is registered with the same action.

8. gxctl

Add the command in the area’s file under src/bin/gxctl/, here storage.rs (disk move <disk> --datastore D [--node N] [--flatten]), calling the generated client:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let req = MoveDiskRequest {
    id: name.to_string(),
    datastore: ds.to_string(),
    node: flag_value(args, "--node").map(String::from),
    flatten: has_flag(args, "--flatten").then_some(true),
    wait_secs: Some(300),
    ..Default::default()
};
match svc.move_disk(req).await.map(|r| r.into_owned()) { … }
}

Update the usage string with it, and the subcommand list the shell’s Tab completion offers in main.rs.

9. Web UI

Regenerate the TypeScript (buf generate, above), then add a function to crates/glidex-ui/ui/src/api.ts that calls the RPC with its proto JSON request:

export const moveDisk = (id: string, datastore: string, flatten?: boolean) =>
  diskWrite(rpc(DiskService.method.moveDisk, { id, datastore, flatten: flatten || undefined, wait_secs: WAIT_SECS }));

Use it from the page (pages/Disks.tsx). Show or hide the control with useCan from session.tsx, asking for the action on the right resource type. A new host-wide capability also goes in HOST_ACTION_RESOURCE there; tests/ui_capabilities.rs checks each one against the schema’s appliesTo.

10. Tests

  • An integration test in the area’s file (datastore_tests.rs has disks_move_between_datastores): the REST call, and the RPC through the harness’s grpc(…) helper for anything the two transports could answer differently. Cover the forbidden and not-found cases.
  • Unit tests next to the controller logic.
  • A UI e2e test in crates/glidex-ui/e2e/tests/ if the UI gained a flow.
  • A functional test if it changes what happens to a real VM.

11. Docs

  • The user-facing behavior in the user or operator guide (for disk moves: Images and disks and Datastores).
  • The endpoint in REST API, the RPC in RPC API, and the command in the gxctl reference. These are written by hand from the route table and the protos.
  • The spec’s implementation status, if it tracks one.

Updating the docs

ChangeWhere
How to use or operate a featuredocs/public/src/ (this book)
Why the code is shaped this way, an invariant, a decisionspec/
The architecture or decisions, for contributorsdocs/public/src/developer-guide/
A type or functionIts rustdoc comment

When a design in spec/ ships, write its user-facing part in the book and link from the spec to the book, not the other way round. Pages in the book are listed in docs/public/src/SUMMARY.md; the build doesn’t create missing pages, so add a page there when you add the file.

mdbook serve docs/public          # live preview on http://localhost:3000
mdbook build docs/public          # -> target/docs/public
mdbook build docs/internal        # the specs -> target/docs/internal

Pull requests

  1. Branch from main. Branch names say what kind of change it is: feat/…, fix/…, spec/…, docs/…, refactor/….
  2. Keep each commit one change, with a short summary line and a body that says what changed and why. Reference spec sections and decisions (spec/24-storage.md §8.3, D71).
  3. A design change goes in a spec/… pull request, reviewed before or with the code that implements it. Say so when a pull request is stacked on another.
  4. Describe the pull request with a summary, the changes and how you tested them, including any ignored or e2e tests you ran by hand.
  5. CI must pass: build and tests, fmt, proto and the docs builds.
  6. Several people and coding agents work on Glidex at once. AGENTS.md has the working rules they share (a worktree each, the checks on every commit of a stack, how stacks are merged), and spec/progress.md what is built, claimed and next; a pull request that starts or finishes a milestone updates it.

Contributions are dual-licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0, as the README says.

gxctl

gxctl is the Glidex command-line client. It runs as an interactive shell, or runs one command and exits:

gxctl                                   # interactive shell: gxctl> …
gxctl list                              # one command, then exit
gxctl --project lab disk list
gxctl --url https://host.example.org:8841 auth login --oidc

In the shell, help (or ?) lists the commands, Tab completes command names, subcommands and file paths, and exit (quit, q) leaves. Words can be quoted: project create lab --description "Lab VMs". Noun commands also answer to their plural (images, projects, tenants, …), and many subcommands to short forms (ls, rm).

gxctl --help shows the global options. Commands have no --help of their own: run one without its arguments to see its usage line, or gxctl help for the full list. Both are authoritative over this page.

Global options

OptionEnvironmentEffect
--socket <path>GLIDEX_SOCKETTalk to this Unix socket. Default: the first that exists of /run/glidex-cp/api.sock, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/glidex/api.sock, /tmp/glidex-<uid>/api.sock; with none, https://localhost:8841
-s, --url <url> (alias --server)Talk to a control plane over HTTPS instead, e.g. https://host.example.org:8841. Wins over --socket. Plain http:// only to loopback
--profile <name>GLIDEX_PROFILEUse this login profile instead of the current one
-p, --project <id|name>GLIDEX_PROJECTProject for creates, lists and name lookups; default: your default project (project use)

Other environment variables:

VariableEffect
GLIDEX_TOKENAPI token to send over HTTPS; wins over the saved one
GLIDEX_CA_CERTA PEM file to trust, e.g. a copy of the host’s /run/glidex-cp/tls.crt
GLIDEX_CONFIGPath of the profile file (default ~/.config/glidex/config.json); empty means no profile file, which is what CI should use
GLIDEX_TLS_INSECURE=1With a profile that has no pinned fingerprint or CA: skip certificate checks for this run, with a warning. For throwaway test setups only: anyone on the network path can read your token
GLIDEX_UI_URLWhat ui prints (default https://localhost:5173)

Connecting and logging in

  • On the host, gxctl uses the Unix socket and you are your Unix user: no login. You need to be in glidex-users (or glidex-admin for administration).
  • From another machine, log in once with auth login, which saves a profile (target URLs, TLS trust and token) in ~/.config/glidex/config.json (mode 0600). Later runs use the current profile. The older login command saves just a token in ~/.config/glidex/token.
  • A self-signed server certificate is either trusted through GLIDEX_CA_CERT, or pinned by fingerprint at auth login (compare it with the one the server printed at start).
  • On a cluster agent, which has no API of its own, other commands fail with this host is a cluster agent: it has no local API; auth login, auth use, auth profiles and auth trust still run. Log in to a server: gxctl auth login --url https://<server>:8841.

See Logging in.

CommandEffect
auth login [--url U]… [--profile P] [--directory [ID] [--via PROFILE] | --oidc | --token | --pam-user U] [--connector ID]Log in and save a profile. --server U is the same as --url U. --directory: device flow at a glidex directory (default local); --via: the profile of another organization’s directory servers; --oidc: device flow in a browser; --token: paste a token (read without echo); --pam-user: a password login. Also --pin sha256/… (expected fingerprint), --insecure, --rebind, --use (make it current), --name N / --days N (the token’s name and lifetime), --save (record a new target as a profile named after its host: a host name’s first label, or a whole IP address with dashes: 192.0.2.10 gives 192-0-2-10, [fd00::1] gives fd00-1), --non-interactive
auth logout [--profile P] [--revoke] [--keep-token]Drop a profile’s credential; --revoke also revokes the token on the server
auth status [--profile P]Target, cluster, trust mode, token and expiry
auth use <profile|->Set the current profile (- clears it)
auth profiles [--all]List profiles
auth profiles remove <name> [--forget-token]Delete a profile from the config file. One that still holds a token is refused: revoke it first with auth logout --profile <name> --revoke, or --forget-token drops it unrevoked. Removing the current profile leaves none current: while other profiles remain, commands fail with no current profile; choose one with –profile; pick one with gxctl --profile <other> auth use <other>
auth trust list | fetch | remove <pin> | remove --all [--yes]A profile’s pinned certificate fingerprints; fetch shows what the server claims, sending nothing else
auth token …, auth whoamiSame as token …, whoami
login --oidc [--connector ID] | --tokenOlder form: log in over HTTPS and save the token file. Not needed on the socket
logout [--revoke]Delete the token file; --revoke revokes the token first
whoamiWho you are: login method, teams, roles, default project
uiPrint the web UI’s address
healthCheck that the API answers

VMs

<vm> is a VM name or id.

CommandEffect
list, lsList VMs; STATE shows state → desired while they differ
get <vm>VM details, and why it isn’t ready yet if it isn’t; a Pool: line per device pool request with the devices it got; for a GPU request, GPUs: <count> from <pool> (with (NVLink) when asked), and for a VM aligned over several NUMA nodes a NUMA <i>: line per guest NUMA node: its host node, vCPUs, memory and devices
createCreate a VM, asking for name, GPUs (count[:pool][:nvlink], such as 4:a100; optional: with GPUs, an empty vCPU or memory answer takes the pool’s per-device sizing), size, hypervisor, firmware, image or disk, credential, networks, PCI devices and device pools (a100:2, or a100:2:switch for one PCIe switch). none at the firmware prompt is kernel boot from host paths: it asks for the kernel image path, the root filesystem path and the kernel arguments (default console=ttyS0, ttyAMA0 on aarch64, root=/dev/vda reboot=k panic=1)
start <vm> [--no-wait]Start or resume; waits up to 60 s for the VM to run
stop <vm> [--graceful [secs]] [--no-wait]Stop. --graceful presses the power button and stops it hard after secs (default 60)
pause <vm> [--no-wait]Pause
service-account <vm> [--set <account> | --none]Show or change the VM’s service account, the identity its guest gets glidex tokens for (from its next token)

scale <vm> [--vcpus N] [--min N] [--max N] [--weight N]Show a VM’s vCPUs, elastic range and weight, or change them. On an elastic Pylon VM the vCPU count is the maximum. See Elastic CPU
delete <vm> [--keep-disk] [--no-wait], rmDelete after confirmation, with its own root disk unless --keep-disk
place <vm> [--node N]Place a stopped or lost VM on another node, or where there is room (its disks on shared datastores; system-admin). Prints the node, or Not placed yet with the reason it waits
events <vm>What happened to the VM: starts, exits, restarts
connect <vm>, console, attachSerial console; Ctrl+] detaches
log <vm>, logsThe console log (last 1 MiB)
attach-device <vm> <path>Attach a PCI device (/sys/bus/pci/devices/<address> or the bare address)
detach-device <vm> <path>Detach a PCI device
attach-disk <vm> <disk>Attach a data disk; on a running VM from its next start
detach-disk <vm> <disk>Detach a data disk, which is kept; on a running VM at its next start

start, stop, pause and delete wait for the controller and print where the VM ended up; --no-wait returns at once. See Virtual machines; for place, Placing a stopped or lost VM again.
